Cell 3 — Starburst Damage

  • DC 14 Arcana: identifies sei discharge as cause — magical energy released suddenly without control
  • DC 17 Arcana: reconstructs the attempt — a priest tried to weaponize their own sei reserves in a single concentrated release against something already in the corridor; discharge was too large and uncontrolled; killed the priest and damaged Cell 8 through the shared wall

Cell 5 — Swept Clean

Someone tidied this cell after the fall — older than the Nagaji's arrival. Platform moved deliberately, replaced; nothing beneath it now. Intentionally unresolved — possible connection to Tomohiro.

Cell 6 — Nagaji-Searched / Planetary Gear Assembly

DC 13 Investigation locates the planetary gear assembly — seven interlocking bronze rings of graduated size, partially disassembled, discarded in debris under overturned platform. The rings are nested concentrically, each engraved with tiny orbital notations in Old Imperial. The outermost ring is bent but not broken. A character proficient in Tinker's Tools, Smith's Tools, or Navigator's Tools recognizes this as a precision gear mechanism — a planetary drive designed to model multiple simultaneous orbital periods through a single input rotation. DC 14 History (DC 11 for Ko'jiri) connects the orbital notations to the seven known planets of the Miyosai system. (Observatory component: planetary gear assembly. The Nagaji found it, examined it, could not understand it, and discarded it.)

The Sealed Room — Senior Priests' Quarters

The priests who sealed themselves in were not hiding — they were staying. They had made their peace and chose not to participate in the violence. Four sleeping platforms, each occupied by skeletal remains — hands folded, bodies oriented toward the room's center. The sealed room has been untouched since their death.

Breaking the door: AC 15, 40 HP. Alternatively, the bar can be lifted through the gap at the base (DC 12 Thieves' Tools or Dexterity check).

On the writing desk: The scroll case (DC 12 Thieves' Tools or carefully broken open) contains a last account — a personal record of the final days, from Priest Tomohiro's perspective. This is a major handout (see Handout: The Last Record of Priest Tomohiro) detailing how the infiltrators were discovered too late, who gave the order to seal the inner sanctum, and the name of the head infiltrator — a detail that, with a DC 17 History check, connects to a lineage that still exists in present-day Kagekuni.

The bronze disc is a formal order seal, granting the bearer recognition as a member of the Golden Dragon order — useful as a key within the temple for certain sealed areas (specifically the Jushoku no Ma hidden door).

The Bronze Disc — Additional Detail: The reverse face of the disc bears fine engravings invisible without close examination (DC 13 Investigation or automatic if studying the disc under good light). Concentric rings scored into the bronze correspond to orbital tracks, with seven small notches along the outer edge and four along an inner ring. A character who has found the planetary gear assembly recognizes the match immediately — the disc is designed to seat into a mechanical device as a positional reference. (Observatory component: calibration disc. When seated in the orrery's control interface, it establishes the reference date from which the mechanism can advance or rewind. The order seal and calibration key were the same object — the person authorized to operate the observatory was, by definition, a member of the order.)

Evidence of the Nagaji

Two of the individual cells (including Cell 6) show recent disturbance — the dust displaced, a pallet dragged aside to reveal the floor. The Nagaji have been searching these rooms. What they were looking for is unclear, but the cells they searched belonged (per the scroll case record) to the two most senior non-priest scholars of the order. Whatever those scholars possessed or knew, something is looking for it.

Uragiri no Onryō — Trigger and Escalation

Corrupted priests who were the infiltrating force that destroyed the order from within. Named to reflect the specific sin that defines them — not just evil, but betrayers of the order they swore to serve. Each haunts a specific cell — emerge when the corridor is disturbed.

Trigger: Corridor disturbed (loud noise, running, light brought close to an occupied cell, combat vibration from elsewhere in the temple)

Initial state: Confused and territorial — emerge from cells, move erratically, cannot fully perceive the party. Window of non-hostility.

Escalation to hostility: Party attacks any of the four, OR the sealed room is interfered with disrespectfully (forcing door loudly, attempting to break it).

Respectful entry (picking the bar, asking permission aloud, moving quietly) does not trigger escalation.

Cell 3 spirit: Manifests first if party lingers near Cell 3 without triggering combat. Most volatile. Use Specter (MM p.279) with maximum HP and one additional action option.

De-escalation: A character who speaks to them calmly in any language (the intent reads through, even across the language barrier) and succeeds on a DC 14 Persuasion check can quiet one Onryō; it dissipates with a sound like a long exhale.

DM Architecture Notes — First Floor

The Temple's Two States The central dramatic tension of the first floor is the contrast between what has decayed and what has not. The statue and pools are perfect. Everything else is dying. This should never be explained — just felt. Players will draw their own conclusions. The correct conclusion (that Kinryu's lingering presence, however attenuated, maintains what is closest to their effigy) is available to a DC 16 Arcana or Religion check, but it should not be handed out.

The Nagaji as Former People The party does not yet know the Nagaji are transformed Gekko clan members. Everything in this floor should add weight to that eventual revelation without revealing it. The intact bowl placed in the kitchen. The Nagaji drawn to the meditation space. The chief seimaster who has made a nest in the sanctum and sorted the debris with scholarly instinct. When the truth lands — they will look back at all of this differently.

The Nagaji Zasu — Playing the Encounter The chief seimaster is not a simple monster. If the party manages to communicate — through magic, through gesture, through patience — fragments of the original person respond. They remember the ritual. They remember it going wrong. They cannot fully articulate what they know, but a character who succeeds on a DC 15 Insight check during any interaction realizes: this thing is trying to tell them something. A DC 18 Persuasion check (with appropriate magical translation) can open a halting exchange. The abomination knows the temple's layout, including the scriptorium above. They cannot reverse what happened to themselves. But they might help someone else try.

Connecting to the Floors Above The scriptorium — where the Gekko reversal documentation lives — is on an upper floor. The first floor exists to prepare the party for that discovery: the sei-lacquer pointer from the surviving scroll, the celestial-timing insight from the star shrine, the bronze disc as a key, the Kinryu no Chikara mandate as a credential. Everything here is a tool for what comes next.

The Observatory Thread: Five observatory components are distributed across the first floor (Susanoo lens in the Grand Hall, planetary gear assembly in the dormitories, calibration disc on the bronze order seal, Tsukuyomi lens in the Star Shrine relic collection, sei conduit filament in the sanctum scroll). Additional components exist on the second floor. A party that explores thoroughly will accumulate components without necessarily understanding what they're for — the observatory itself, when they reach it, provides the context. The first component a player identifies (likely the planetary gear assembly, lowest Investigation DC) should prompt a "what is this part of?" question. Do not answer it directly. Let them carry the mystery upward. The orrery, when they find it, is the answer.

The Pools — Spending Wisely With approximately 48 charges of healing, condition removal, curse cleansing, and blessings available, the pools are a meaningful mid-dungeon resource. The party should understand they are finite. A character who examines the pools carefully (DC 13 Arcana) senses that the supply is not replenishing — each use is a permanent expenditure of something the temple has been holding in reserve for a very long time. Note: Kegare no Yamai (from Yaminezumi bites) auto-cleanses on pool entry at 1 charge per stack — the party may spend charges without realizing it.

Read-aloud text: ../supplements/read-aloud-floor-1.md § Grand Hall

[KNOWN]

Physical Description:

Oval chamber, 125 ft east-to-west × 100 ft north-to-south. Ceiling not visible (statue is 250 ft — ceiling is at least that high). Accessed via double set of double doors on south wall (from N-S hallway, ~10 ft vestibule between door sets); second double set of double doors on north wall leads directly into the Inner Sanctum. Scale is disorienting; the statue at center is the only fixed reference point.

Kinryu Statue (center): 250 feet of gold, coiled around a central plinth. Resting posture, head slightly lowered. Inlaid amber eyes oriented forward. Surface untarnished — no degradation whatsoever. Radiates perceptible warmth within 30 feet (afternoon-sun quality, not body heat).

Pools: Four shallow pools at the statue's base (south and east faces). Water perfectly clear with faint blue-white self-luminescence. Not dried, not stagnant — preserved by the same magic sustaining the statue.

Surrounding space: In sharp contrast to the statue and pools, everything else has decayed. Banners on wall brackets reduced to ribbons. Offering tables collapsed. Debris of food, incense vessels, and ceramics scattered. Floor beyond the pools buried under dust and debris.

[DISCOVERABLE]

Discoveries

  • The Statue's Magic — Passive (within 30 ft)
  • The Pools — Mechanics (DC 13 Arcana for finite nature; DC 14 Religion for ritual existence; DC 18 Religion for full ritual details)
  • The Fallen Offerings (DC 15 Investigation)
  • The Blue-White Crystal / Susanoo Projection Lens (DC 14 Investigation; DC 13 Arcana to identify) (Observatory component #1)

The Statue's Magic — Passive: The statue radiates warmth perceptible within 30 feet — not body heat, but the warmth of afternoon sun on stone, present even in the cold of the mountain interior. This warmth is real; cold-based effects within 30 feet of the statue have their damage reduced by 1d4. This property has no daily limit.

The Pools — Mechanics: The four pools are a single magical resource — approximately 48 total charges across all four pools (~12 per pool). Charge state is visually communicated: water dims and gold inlay loses glow as charges deplete. The Nagaji instinctively avoid the pools — a clue that the Golden Dragon's lingering presence repels their corruption. The pools do not regenerate. Once exhausted, the water becomes ordinary — clean, cold, but inert.

Skill Checks:

Check DC Result
Arcana 13 Identifies magical nature; reveals finite charge mechanic; charge state estimable on success
Religion 14 Identifies that holy pools of this tradition have multiple associated rituals; generic knowledge that blessings and rites exist — not their specifics
Religion 18 Reveals full ritual details — healing ritual, condition ritual, blessing ritual

The DC 18 Religion result can also be obtained from the hidden archive on the second floor.

Automatic Effects (Entry — no action required):

Effect Cost
Kegare no Yamai cleansed 1 charge per stack
Disease cleansed 1 charge per disease

Ritual 1 — Healing:

  • Trigger: Simple prayer (discoverable via DC 18 Religion check or second floor hidden archive)
  • Effect: 2d8+5 hit points restored
  • Cost: 1 charge per use

Ritual 2 — Condition Removal:

  • Trigger: Ritual activation (discoverable via DC 18 Religion check or second floor hidden archive)
  • Conditions removed: Poisoned, Blinded, Deafened, Paralyzed
  • Cost: 1 charge per condition removed

Ritual 3 — Blessing of Kinryū:

  • Trigger: Prayer to Kinryū (discoverable via DC 18 Religion check)
  • Cost: 2 charges per blessing
  • Effect: Random blessing from the Kinryū no Megumi table (see floor-1/kinryu-no-megumi.md)
  • Duration: 8 hours

The Fallen Offerings: Among the debris of collapsed offering tables, a DC 15 Investigation check finds: three bronze coins minted during the First Golden Age (worth 50gp each as antiques), a ceramic incense vessel cracked but intact with a faded clan sigil, and a fragment of silk embroidered with Old Imperial text. This fragment is a handout opportunity.

The Blue-White Crystal: Near the southernmost pool — close enough that the Nagaji would not approach — a faceted crystal the size of a fist lies half-buried in offering debris. DC 14 Investigation to notice (automatic if actively searching near the pools). The crystal is blue-white, cold to the touch, and faintly translucent with what appears to be a frozen light source at its center. DC 13 Arcana identifies it as a projection lens designed to channel sei into structured illusory output — a component of a larger device, not a standalone object. The craftsmanship matches the temple's foundational enchantment style. (Observatory component: Susanoo projection lens. Rolled near the pools during the final conflict; avoided by the Nagaji due to the pools' proximity.)

[SEALED]

Encounters

  • 2 Kageban (影番 — "Shadow Watch"; upper darkness — descend when disturbed; avoid pools)
  • Nagaji Bushi ×1 (squad leader, rotation from Naijin)
  • Nagaji Hohei ×2 (rotation from Naijin)
  • Nagaji Ashigaru ×6 (rotation from Naijin)

DM Notes

The Statue's Magic — Active (Ko'jiri): If Ko'jiri approaches within 15 feet, the amber eyes shift. Not dramatically — no glowing, no sound, no proclamation. They simply orient. Anyone watching (DC 14 Perception to notice) sees the carved irises move in their settings to face him directly. If Ko'jiri speaks aloud in the statue's presence, he hears a single sound in response — not words, not language, but a low resonant hum from the stone itself, felt more in the chest than heard with the ears. It is acknowledgment. The con artist who built a career performing Golden Dragon authority is being recognized by the thing itself. What that means is for Ko'jiri to reckon with.

Scale of the Space: Emphasize the disorientation of the scale. The ceiling is not visible. The far walls require a light source or darkvision to confirm. The statue at the center is the only fixed reference point — everything orients toward it.

Undead Presence: Two Kageban (影番 — "Shadow Watch"; Shadows, MM p.269) inhabit the upper darkness of the Grand Hall — former temple guards of the loyal order, still at their post after millennia. They are not hostile by default — they are the loyalists, still watching their post. They do not descend into the light near the statue. They watch from above. If the party makes noise, desecrates offerings, or moves toward the dormitories, they descend. They do not pursue into the pools' radius of warmth.

Read-aloud text: ../supplements/read-aloud-floor-1.md § Inner Sanctum

[KNOWN]

Physical Description:

North end of the temple — most sacred space on the first floor. Octagonal chamber, 90 ft wide × 35 ft deep. Accessed via double set of double doors from the Grand Hall's north wall.

Doors: Black-lacquered wood banded with bronze. Frame carved with a frieze of the seven dragon clans in a ring. Standing open. Inlaid silver locking mechanism lines visible inside the frame — dark and dead. Wards broken from the outside (shadow-aspected magic, Kokuryu tradition).

Walls: Eight scroll positions. Six empty (mountings remain, scrolls gone). One holds only floor-level fragments with faded ink. One (far wall) holds an intact scroll — Kinryu in flight, gold and deep blue on black silk, colors perfectly preserved by active sei-lacquer. Contains hidden sei conduit filament in the decorative border.

Center: Floor cleared deliberately. Original furnishings (shattered pedestals, broken braziers) pushed to walls. Circular depression in swept floor — nest shape, formed by repeated use by something large. Edges built from broken furniture and torn fabric. Currently empty. Radiates warmth and a sense of presence.

Hidden door (east wall): Stone-framed, flush with surface, seam filled with centuries of grit. Accessed via a 5 ft wide, 20 ft long secret hallway. Opened by pressing the bronze disc against a specific carved scale in the dragon-frieze border. Leads to the head priest's private chamber (15 ft wide × 20 ft deep — never entered since the order fell).

[DISCOVERABLE]

Discoveries

  • The Surviving Scroll — sei-lacquer identification (DC 13 Arcana)
  • The Scroll's Hidden Thread / Sei Conduit Filament (DC 16 Arcana, or DC 14 if lens already found; DC 14 Sleight of Hand to extract) (Observatory component #5)
  • Breaking the Wards — analysis (DC 15 Arcana — shadow-aspected, Kokuryu)
  • The Hidden Door to Jushoku no Ma (DC 15 Perception, or automatic if searching walls; bronze disc opens)
  • Jushoku no Ma — Kinjiro's Journal (in bronze box, DC 16 Thieves' Tools or disc as key)
  • Jushoku no Ma — Kinryu no Chikara Mandate (in bronze box)
  • Jushoku no Ma — Operational Ledger (in bronze box)
  • Jushoku no Ma — Kinjiro's Remains
  • The Zasu's Ritual Scrolls — Hebi no Hensen (found on Zasu's body after encounter; see zasu-ritual-scrolls.md)
  • Hoko (secret door S wall behind dresser — contents TBD)

The Surviving Scroll: The preserved scroll of Kinryu in flight is worth 800gp as an antique, more to the right buyer. More importantly, the sei-lacquer preserving it is still active — a character who examines it closely (DC 13 Arcana) identifies the preservation technique as Golden Dragon order craft, and notes that the same technique was almost certainly used on the most important records kept in this temple. Records preserved this way would survive in far better condition than anything else here. This is a subtle pointer toward the scriptorium on the floor above.

The Scroll's Hidden Thread: DC 16 Arcana (or DC 14 for a character who has already identified a projection lens elsewhere in the temple) reveals something additional: woven into the scroll's decorative border is an impossibly fine golden filament — not thread, not wire, something between the two. It carries a faint, steady sei charge, distinct from the preservation enchantment. This filament is a sei conduit — a transmission line designed to carry magical resonance between connected systems. Removing it without destroying the scroll requires DC 14 Sleight of Hand or Tinker's Tools; on failure, the scroll's preservation enchantment collapses and the image fades to nothing within minutes (the scroll is destroyed, but the filament is recovered). On success, both the scroll and filament are preserved intact. (Observatory component: sei conduit filament. Connects the orrery's mechanical output to the arcane projection system. The scroll was stored in the sanctum — closest room to the observatory's position on the floor above — because the conduit needed to remain within the temple's foundational magic field to retain its charge.)

Breaking the Wards: The magical seals on the door were broken from outside. The magic used to break them — DC 15 Arcana — is shadow-aspected. Kokuryu tradition. The infiltrators unsealed this room during the order's fall, gaining access to the sanctum's contents. Whatever was in here, they took it or destroyed it.

The Jushoku no Ma (Abbot's Chamber): Behind the rubble on the east side of the room, almost invisible unless the party is actively looking (DC 15 Perception, or automatic if they are searching the walls), is a section of wall that is actually a door — stone-framed, flush with the surface, its seam filled with centuries of grit. The locking mechanism is a pressure sequence on specific carved scales in the dragon-frieze border; the bronze disc from the sealed dormitory room, when pressed against a specific scale, triggers the release. The room beyond — the head priest's private chamber — has never been entered since the order fell.

What Is In The Jushoku no Ma: A small, very austere room (15 ft wide × 20 ft deep). A sleeping platform against the west wall with a dresser beside it. A writing desk with a locked bronze box (DC 16 Thieves' Tools or the disc again as a key). Inside the box: three documents, each sealed separately.

  1. The personal journal of Head Priest Kinjiro — final entries. The journal is personal, written in a direct hand that does not match the formality of the other documents. The final entries describe the order's disintegration — not the external pressures (those are in the ledger) but the internal experience of watching a community fracture. Kinjiro names no traitors. The journal's emotional weight is in what it does not accuse.

  2. The Kinryu no Chikara mandate — a sealed tube containing a formal document conferring specific authority within the temple to named individuals. The mandate is blank on the recipient line, left that way deliberately — Kinjiro did not know who would find it and chose to leave it open. A character who performs the short ritual described in the journal (10 minutes, spoken in any language, a genuine statement of intent to protect rather than exploit what lies within) can inscribe their name. The mandate grants its bearer advantage on all Charisma checks within the temple and allows passage through one magically sealed door elsewhere in the structure.

  3. The operational ledger of the hub — a formal record of network activity kept by the head priest. Each significant entry logs the full operational cycle: distress signal received, acknowledgement authorized and sent, dispatch ordered, field report on findings. The ledger records both inbound signals and outbound responses — a complete cycle document, not a record of actions alone.

Ledger physical condition: Sei-lacquered selectively in the same technique as the surviving sanctum scroll. Routine entries written in ordinary ink have faded to illegibility. Entries the head priest considered significant were lacquered and remain fully readable. Which entries were treated is itself information about what the head priest considered to matter.

Standard entry format: Prior entries from the order's functional period are complete. Signal received, response sent, investigator dispatched, findings returned and summarized. These entries establish the template clearly. The party understands what a finished cycle looks like before they reach the entries that are not finished.

The fall-period entries — what is absent: The distress signals sent by Kaze and Sora at the fall of 13088 are not recorded in the ledger. No entry exists for either signal — not the incoming alert, not an acknowledgement, not a dispatch, not a field report. The ledger's last entries are whatever completed operational cycles preceded the fall. Then the record ends. The absence is not by design — distress signals appear in prior entries. Kaze and Sora are simply not there because the collapse overtook the record-keeping.

Sora acknowledgement gap: The acknowledged state exists in the network (visible on Tapestry III). It does not exist in the ledger. Possible explanations: a monitor acting independently during the chaos; the head priest sent it but was interrupted before recording; someone who didn't survive sent it; or the entry was among those that faded. The document cannot close the gap.

Kaze in the ledger: Whether Kaze was ever acknowledged cannot be determined from the ledger. The signal is absent from the record entirely.

Placement note: The journal is personal. The mandate confers authority. The ledger is institutional memory. Together they represent what the order chose to preserve when everything else was falling.

The Remains: On the sleeping platform, partially covered by a threadbare blanket that has largely disintegrated, lie the skeletal remains of Head Priest Kinjiro. The posture is deliberate — hands folded across the chest, body aligned with the room's cardinal orientation, head turned slightly toward the writing desk. He went to his bed and did not rise. The bones are undisturbed. Nothing in this room has been touched since the door sealed.

[SEALED]

Encounters

  • Nagaji Zasu (Inner Sanctum lair — currently patrolling; returns periodically)
  • Head Priest Kinjiro's Bōrei (Jushoku no Ma — manifests when bronze box or remains touched)

DM Notes

Kinjiro's Spirit: The head priest did not move on after death. His spirit persists in this chamber as a protector — bound not by curse or unfinished personal business, but by the weight of institutional obligation. He was the last keeper. No one relieved him of the duty. The spirit is dormant until the chamber is entered; it manifests when someone touches the bronze box or the remains.

Manifestation: Not aggressive by default. The spirit appears as a translucent figure seated at the writing desk — the posture of someone still working, still keeping records. Cold fills the room. The torchlight dims but does not go out. Kinjiro does not speak first. He watches. His expression carries exhaustion rather than menace.

Peaceful Resolution: A party that approaches with respect — speaks to the spirit, identifies themselves, or demonstrates they are not here to loot — can engage Kinjiro in limited communication. He cannot speak freely (the binding is too old, his connection too frayed), but he can answer direct questions with gestures, single words, or by directing attention to specific objects in the room. He knows the temple's layout, the purpose of the documents in the box, and the broad shape of what went wrong. He does not know the current state of the Nagaji — he died before the transformation. If the party undertakes to cleanse the temple (removing the corruption, restoring order to the sacred spaces), and succeeds, Kinjiro can finally release. His departure is quiet — the cold lifts, the translucence fades, the bones settle slightly as whatever held them together withdraws.

Combat Resolution: If the party acts aggressively — drawing weapons in the chamber, attempting to force the box open without care, or showing clear intent to desecrate — the spirit defends. Use Revenant (MM p.259) as a base, adjusted: Kinjiro is not pursuing vengeance but defending a post. He fights to drive intruders from the chamber, not to kill. If reduced to 0 HP, he reforms in 24 hours (as Revenant) unless the party has cleansed the temple, in which case he passes on regardless.

Reward: TBD — see dm/plot-threads.md for open decision. Consider: direct knowledge that shortcuts a discovery elsewhere in the temple, a blessing granting advantage on a specific check type within the temple, or a narrative reward connected to the Kinryu no Chikara mandate (the priest confirming the ritual, or adding weight to the inscription).

The Hoko (Storehouse): A secret door on the south wall of the Jushoku no Ma, west side — behind the dresser, west of the bed. Completely concealed. Contains the priest's and the temple's most sacred items. This room has been left entirely untouched since the order fell — sealed within a sealed room within a hidden chamber. The deepest-hidden space on the first floor. (Contents: TBD — see dm/plot-threads.md)

The Zasu's Scrolls: When the Zasu is defeated, the party finds a cracked leather scroll case lashed to its midsection with strips of torn formal silk bearing the Gekkō mon. Contains seven documents in varying states of preservation — the transformation ritual research the chief seimaster gathered before performing the ritual on himself. Full details: zasu-ritual-scrolls.md

The Occupant: A Nagaji Zasu (MM p.308) has made this space its lair — a Nagaji of particular power, one of the original senior members of Clan Gekko, transformed more completely than the others. This individual was once Gekko's chief seimaster — the architect of the failed ritual. The transformation has cost them nearly everything, but not quite. Deep within the abomination, fragments of the original person remain: a scholar, a leader, someone who made a catastrophic decision trying to protect their clan. They are not in the sanctum when the party first arrives (they patrol the temple), but they will return.

Atmosphere: The nest radiates residual warmth and something harder to name — a sense of presence, of being watched, even in an empty room. The cleared center of the room feels deliberately territorial. Players with high Passive Perception (14+) notice that the debris pushed to the walls has been sorted — materials of value (intact objects, sealed containers) are in one pile; pure refuse in another. Whatever lives here is not mindless.

Type: Curse (not disease)

Reflects kegare as spiritual pollution — a Shinto concept of ritual impurity — not physical illness. Removal requires Remove Curse (3rd level spell), not Lesser Restoration.

Transmission

Vector: Yaminezumi (闇鼠 — Darkness Rats) bite

On a successful hit, the target makes a DC 12 Constitution saving throw. Failure: gains one stack of Kegare no Yamai.

Effect

Each stack reduces Wisdom by 1.

  • Stacks accumulate — multiple failed saves = multiple stacks = increasing Wisdom reduction
  • Affects Insight, Perception, Wisdom saving throws, and spellcasting for Wisdom-based casters

Removal

  • Remove Curse spell removes all stacks
  • The restorative pools in the Grand Hall auto-cleanse on entry — 1 charge per stack removed

19 Kokoro no Mamori 心の守り — Ward of Heart Advantage on Wisdom saving throws
20 — — Reroll twice (see rules below)

Blessing Rules

Maximum: 2 active blessings at a time per creature.

Natural 20 — Reroll Twice:

  • Roll twice on the table; receive both blessings (if under the 2-blessing maximum)
  • If already at 2 blessings when rolling 20: roll twice, keep one (DM chooses if the two results are different; if one result matches a blessing already held, the other automatically applies)
  • If the two rerolls produce identical results: the blessing is applied once — no bonus, no enhancement
  • A subsequent 20 on a reroll follows the same rules — reroll twice again for that slot

The only way to receive 2 blessings is with a natural 20 on the initial prayer roll.

Type
location
Status
design

"Chamber of the Star Mirror"

The Golden Dragon Clan built the most complete model of the Miyosai system ever constructed — mechanical and arcane, capable of projecting celestial positions across millennia. It has not been operational since the temple fell in 13088. The Great Aphelion — the nadir of the sei drought — occurred approximately 1,256 years later (~14344), long after the last operator walked away.

What It Is

A circular domed chamber on the second floor of Oryuzan Tenku-ji. At its center, a mechanical-arcane orrery — a system of bronze armatures, gear tracks, and arcane projection lenses that together model the full Miyosai system:

Type Bodies Armatures
Stars Amaterasu, Susanoo, Tsukuyomi 3
Moons Aokiba, Kagetsu, Nagikumo, Ryugetsu 4
Planets Akahoshi, Akasa, Asahikawa, Seizan, Shizukanami, Korigami, Yamiyo 7
Total 14 tracked bodies

The mechanical layer uses precision bronze gearwork to model orbital periods. The arcane layer projects illusory light around each armature — color, scale, atmospheric effects — transforming the bare mechanism into a functioning planetarium. A control interface at the base allows an operator to set a date, and the mechanism advances or rewinds to show the celestial configuration at that moment.

Miyosai System — Orbital Structure

The Miyosai system is a gravitationally bound trinary stellar system. All three stars orbit a common barycenter. Amaterasu is the most massive and carries its planetary family as it orbits. Seizan, as one of those planets, travels with Amaterasu.

The three stars travel on different orbital inclinations, producing a three-dimensional dance rather than a flat disc. The named astrological events — Nagorikaze, Long Shadow — are routine expressions of this dance.

Critical for the orrery: The seven planets orbit Amaterasu and do not participate in the Great Aphelion. The four moons orbit Seizan and are similarly unaffected. In the orrery, the sei drought is visible as exclusively a two-star withdrawal — Susanoo and Tsukuyomi receding while everything else continues its ordinary motion. The machine keeps working, the planets keep moving, and two of the three stars are simply not where they should be.

How It Connects to the Tapestries

The orrery is integrated with the temple's foundational magic. When the orrery reaches full operational status (all 9 components restored), its sei resonance propagates through the construction-level enchantment that permeates the entire structure. On the first floor, the ori-kioku tapestries — fabric woven with the Golden Dragon order's memory-recording technique — respond to the restored sei field by activating simultaneously.

In play: Full orrery restoration triggers all four surviving tapestries at once. The scenes do not loop or replay — they run continuously as sustained living images, the way a fire is sustained rather than the way a torch is lit and guttered. The woven figures move, the stitched landscapes shift, color deepens and flows. The tapestries remain active for as long as the orrery is operational.

The physical separation between the orrery and the tapestries still matters — the party must descend from the second floor to the South Entrance to witness the result. The first descent after restoring the orrery is a dramatic beat: they have been in this room before, they know these walls. Now the tapestries are alive.

The orrery's date-display function — its ability to model celestial configurations across millennia — is a separate capability, independent of tapestry activation. The party can use the orrery to explore the Miyosai system's history (including the dramatic approach of the Great Aphelion) without affecting the tapestries, which respond to the orrery's operational state, not its displayed date.

The 11 tapestry positions in the South Entrance correspond to 11 moments in the temple's history. Four survive intact. Seven are destroyed or removed. The observatory can only activate what physically remains — no tapestry, no scene.

Component System

The observatory requires 9 components to reach full operation. Five are found on the first floor; four are on the second floor (in the observatory itself or in adjacent second-floor rooms). Components fall into four repair categories.

First Floor Components (5)

# Component Category Location Found Via Notes
1 Susanoo projection lens Arcane Grand Hall — pool debris DC 14 Investigation Blue-white crystal; rolled near pools during the fall; Nagaji avoided it
2 Planetary gear assembly Mechanical Dormitories — Nagaji-searched cell DC 13 Investigation 7 interlocking bronze rings; found and discarded by Nagaji
3 Calibration disc Calibration Dormitories — sealed room (bronze order seal) Already found if party has the disc Reverse face has orbital engravings; seats into control interface
4 Tsukuyomi projection lens Arcane Mess Hall — sealed ceramic jar DC 14 Investigation (automatic if jar opened) Deep red crystal; hidden deliberately by a priest during the fall
5 Sei conduit filament Arcane Inner Sanctum — surviving Kinryu scroll border DC 16 Arcana (DC 14 if lens already found) Golden filament; extraction risks destroying the scroll (DC 14 Sleight of Hand / Tinker's Tools)

Second Floor Components (4)

# Component Category Location Found Via Notes
6 Amaterasu projection lens Arcane Observatory — still mounted, cracked Visible on inspection Golden-yellow crystal; largest of the three; cracked but repairable in place (DC 15 Arcana + Tinker's Tools)
7 Stellar drive mechanism Mechanical Observatory — seized in place Visible on inspection The main drive that connects to planetary gears; bronze gearwork frozen by corrosion and debris; requires cleaning and lubrication (DC 13 Tinker's Tools or Smith's Tools; Athletics DC 12 to free the main shaft)
8 Lunar armature set Mechanical Scriptorium / adjacent room — removed and stored DC 14 Investigation in the scriptorium area Four delicate arms removed by the order for maintenance or safekeeping before the fall; stored in a sealed cabinet with other precision instruments
9 Operator's manual Calibration Scriptorium — among preserved texts DC 13 Investigation (DC 10 for Ko'jiri) A sei-lacquered instructional scroll detailing calibration and operation procedures; written in Old Imperial with technical diagrams

Repair Sequence

Repairs happen in stages as the party acquires components and makes checks. The observatory does not need all 9 components for partial function — it can be brought online incrementally.

Stage 1 — Assessment (No components required)

When: The party first enters the observatory. What happens: The room is visually impressive even damaged — the armature framework is visible, the dome's inner surface is etched with constellation guides, the central mechanism is clearly a device of extraordinary complexity. A character can assess the damage without tools:

  • DC 12 Investigation or Arcana: Identifies this as an astronomical device; recognizes missing/broken components
  • DC 14 History (DC 11 for Ko'jiri): Connects it to Golden Dragon Clan records of a celestial observatory; understands its purpose
  • DC 14 Tinker's Tools or Smith's Tools: Identifies what specific repairs are needed and in what order

DM note: If the party has already found components on the first floor, this is the "aha" moment — the mysterious crystals and bronze rings suddenly have context.

Stage 2 — Mechanical Restoration

Requirements: Planetary gear assembly (#2), stellar drive mechanism (#7, freed in place) Checks:

  • Free the seized stellar drive: DC 12 Athletics to break the main shaft loose, then DC 13 Tinker's Tools or Smith's Tools to clean and realign
  • Install planetary gear assembly: DC 13 Tinker's Tools (the bent outer ring must be straightened first — DC 12 Smith's Tools or improvised)

Result: The mechanical layer begins to move. Armatures track, but without lenses the movement is bare bronze — functional but producing no light or projection. The party can see the shape of celestial motion without the detail. This is still impressive and demonstrates the mechanism works.

Stage 3 — Arcane Restoration

Requirements: At least one projection lens (#1, #4, or #6 repaired), sei conduit filament (#5) Checks:

  • Install sei conduit filament: DC 14 Arcana — thread the filament through the conduit channel running from the mechanism's base to the projection mounts. A character attuned to sei (Ko'jiri, Relc) has advantage.
  • Mount projection lens(es): DC 12 Tinker's Tools per lens. Each lens seats into a specific mount — Susanoo (blue-white) in the inner ring, Tsukuyomi (deep red) in the outer ring, Amaterasu (golden) in the central position.
  • Repair cracked Amaterasu lens: DC 15 Arcana combined with Tinker's Tools (two characters can work together). Failure does not destroy the lens but leaves its projection dim and incomplete.

Result per lens:

  • Amaterasu only: The primary star projects — golden light fills the dome, warm and steady. The mechanical armatures are now illuminated. Beautiful but incomplete.
  • Susanoo added: Blue-white companion star appears; ghost-light effects play across the dome walls when its orbit draws close. Water magic ambient effects become faintly perceptible.
  • Tsukuyomi added: Deep red dwarf star appears on its elongated orbit. Shadows in the room shift subtly as it moves. The full stellar system is now operational.

Partial function note: With even one lens installed and the sei conduit connected, the orrery begins producing sei resonance — the room comes alive with partial projection. However, tapestry activation requires full orrery restoration (all 9 components). Partial restoration produces no tapestry response. The orrery's sei output at partial stages is sufficient for the observatory's own projection effects but not for propagating resonance through the temple's foundational magic to the South Entrance.

Stage 4 — Lunar Arms

Requirements: Lunar armature set (#8) Checks:

  • Install four lunar arms: DC 13 Tinker's Tools (single check for all four — they mount as a set into pre-built receivers)

Result: The four moons appear in the projection — each with its canonical character (Aokiba crystalline, Kagetsu shadow-absorbing, Nagikumo softly glowing, Ryugetsu color-shifting). Tidal calculations become visible. The compound stellar + lunar alignments that produce the named astrological events (Nagorikaze, Tatsunami, Hikarisho, etc.) are now trackable.

Stage 5 — Calibration

Requirements: Calibration disc (#3), operator's manual (#9) Checks:

  • Seat the calibration disc: DC 12 (automatic if a character understands its purpose)
  • Read the operator's manual: DC 14 History to read Old Imperial technical text (DC 11 for Ko'jiri; advantage if Comprehend Languages is active)
  • Set the reference date: DC 14 Navigator's Tools or Arcana — using the Star Shrine's fixed etching of the Great Aphelion as a known reference point (if the party studied it). Without the Star Shrine reference, DC 17.
  • Alternative calibration method: A character who meditates in the Star Shrine under moonlight and then returns to the observatory has advantage on the calibration check — the shrine's projected sky provides the "current" reference, and the orrery can be wound backward from there.

Result: The control interface is operational. The operator can set any date and the orrery advances or rewinds to display the celestial configuration at that moment. The tapestry activation reaches full clarity — but the party must descend to the South Entrance to witness the result.

Using the Observatory

Setting a Date

The operator turns the calibration disc to advance or rewind time. The mechanism moves smoothly — the room fills with light and shadow as centuries pass in minutes. Watching the Great Aphelion approach is dramatic: Susanoo's blue-white dims and vanishes from its armature; Tsukuyomi's deep red bleeds away even earlier. The planetary and lunar armatures continue their ordinary motion — the machine keeps working while two of its three stars go dark. The light dims to Amaterasu alone. The room grows cold. Then it passes, and the slow return begins — Susanoo first, then Tsukuyomi, centuries apart.

Orrery Projection Sequence

What the party observes when scrolling through the dial. Mechanical armature motion continues normally throughout — only the arcane projection layer responds to sei availability. See core/great-aphelion.md for the full detailed sequence with individual star profiles.

Pre-Decline (pre-~12605): All three stars at full intensity. The dome warm and fully lit — the room functioning as designed. When the party scrolls to a Golden Age date, they understand for the first time what they have been looking at in its damaged state.

Early Decline (~12605–12700): Tsukuyomi's deep red begins to bleed at the edges. Subtle. Susanoo holds full brightness. The dome is visibly but not dramatically wrong.

Deepening Decline (~12700–12806): Tsukuyomi's red is clearly diminished. Susanoo still holds. The first star crosses below visibility threshold at approximately 12806. Dark ages begin.

Late Decline (~12806–14264): Tsukuyomi's arm is dark. Susanoo still holds but dimming. The dome is Amaterasu's gold, Susanoo's fading blue-white, and one silent arm.

Susanoo's Failure (~14264–14344): Susanoo's projection dims and goes dark. The dome is Amaterasu alone. All planetary and lunar armatures continue their ordinary motion. The room does not feel like an observatory.

Great Aphelion (~14344): All three stars at maximum mutual distance. Three separate arms on three separate planes, all pointing away from each other. The geometry is legible before the party processes the darkness. Amaterasu alone in the dome. The nadir.

Post-Nadir (~14344–15883): Scrolling forward changes nothing visible. Amaterasu holds. The two secondary arms remain dark. Advancing centuries in seconds and seeing no change has its own effect at the table. The absence is not passive.

Dawn (~15883): Susanoo's armature shows the first ghost of blue-white. A character with sei sensitivity may feel warmth in their sternum before the light is visible to anyone. The dark ages end.

First Talents (~15883–15962): Susanoo's blue-white strengthens slowly. Tsukuyomi's arm remains dark. The match between star position and magical accessibility is legible if they think to look for it.

Return Arc (~15962–16693): Susanoo continues strengthening. Tsukuyomi's deep red begins its slower return. The return does not feel like restoration — it feels like recovery from a very long illness.

Great Awakening (~16693): Tsukuyomi's red crosses into clear visibility. All three stars present.

Current Date (16744): The orrery shows the present sky. All three stars lit. A comparison against a Golden Age date reveals Tsukuyomi's projection carries slightly less intensity than its pre-decline readings. The return is real. It is not yet complete.

This is the only moment in the orrery sequence where the party is looking at their own world in real time.

Tapestry Activation

When the orrery reaches full operational status (all 9 components restored), sei resonance propagates through the temple's foundational magic down to the South Entrance. All four surviving tapestries activate simultaneously.

  • Intact tapestry: The woven scene comes to life on the fabric itself. Stitched figures move within the weave, colors deepen and flow, the static image becomes a sustained living state. Faint sound — not words but the ambient texture of the recorded moment (wind, fire, distant voices) — emanates from the fabric. The scene does not loop or replay. It runs continuously, the ori-kioku sustaining the recorded moment as a living state rather than a playback.
  • Damaged tapestry: The surviving portions animate; damaged sections remain static or flicker with partial, distorted motion. Where the fabric is torn, the scene cuts off at the tear edge. Information is partial, shaped by what physically remains.
  • Destroyed tapestry: The position is dark. If the frame is still mounted but the fabric burned or decayed beyond recognition, a faint pulse of warmth and the ghost of color ripples across the ruined surface — the ori-kioku is trying to activate in material that can no longer carry it. Nothing readable comes through.
  • Missing tapestry (cut down and removed): Nothing at all. The empty wall shows no response. But a character standing at the empty position during activation (DC 12 Perception) feels a brief pulse of warmth in the stone behind the mounting brackets — confirming the system expected something here. The missing tapestries exist somewhere, if they can be found.

Tapestry III — Architectural Distinction

Tapestry III is architecturally distinct from the other three. Where Tapestries I, II, and IV hold fixed historical moments in their ori-kioku, Tapestry III was built as a monitoring surface — its ori-kioku records ongoing network state rather than a single event. When the orrery activates it, it does not play back the past. It shows the current state of the sanctuary network as of the moment of activation.

This distinction is discoverable: the motion quality of Tapestry III is subtly different from the others. Historical ori-kioku playback has a smoothness — complete, consistent, rendered the way memory renders the past. Tapestry III has the slight irregular quality of a live feed. The tidal motion does not loop. It follows an actual current. DC 14 Arcana to identify the distinction formally; observant players may notice it without a check.

This property means that Tapestry III's value is not fixed at the moment of orrery restoration — it continues to reflect the network's actual state. If a site changes status after the party restores the orrery, Tapestry III will show the change.

Ruling: The Tapestry Is the Medium

The ori-kioku technique records into the fabric. The fabric is not a screen — it is the recording. What was physically destroyed is gone. Cut sections, gouged faces, missing panels — the activation animates what remains, nothing more. Destroying a tapestry destroys the record. Removing a tapestry removes the record from this location.

This means:

  • The destroyed tapestries' content is permanently lost unless the physical fabric is recovered from wherever it was taken
  • The deliberate damage matters — the infiltrators who gouged the first head priest's face and cut sections from multiple tapestries successfully erased that information. Their act of destruction holds weight across millennia.
  • Finding missing tapestries becomes a potential quest thread — several were cut down and removed, not destroyed. They exist somewhere. Returning them to their positions and activating the orrery would reveal their scenes.
  • The activation rewards thorough exploration without cheapening the physical damage — the party sees four living moments of Golden Dragon history, each one powerful but incomplete. The incompleteness is the point.

Character Moments During Repair

Ko'jiri

The observatory is the genuine article of everything he has performed knowledge of. Working on the real mechanism — reading the operator's manual, recognizing the planetary notations from his research — is a moment where the con artist's scholarly knowledge proves to be real expertise. His Golden Dragon Clan advantage applies throughout. The orrery doesn't judge him the way the statue does; it just needs someone who knows what it is. He does.

Relc

The calibration process benefits from druidic celestial attunement. Relc can feel when the mechanism is correctly aligned — not through calculation but through the same instinct that connects him to natural cycles. The Star Shrine meditation path (advantage on calibration) is his contribution. The sky is a text he already reads.

Sun Wukong

The mechanical precision required for armature installation and lens mounting rewards steady hands and disciplined focus. Ki-guided fine motor work — the monk's equivalent of Tinker's Tools. The monastery's emphasis on patience and precision maps directly onto the repair work.

Dian Wei

The seized stellar drive requires physical strength (Athletics DC 12) before the fine work can begin. The structural assessment — identifying load-bearing cracks, ensuring the mechanism's frame is stable — is practical, martial knowledge applied in a new context. Dian holds the room together while the others do the delicate work.

Pacing Across Sessions

The observatory repair is designed to span the second floor exploration, not dominate it. The party returns to the observatory between other second-floor activities.

Suggested flow:

  1. Discovery: Party reaches second floor, finds the observatory. Assessment checks. "Aha" moment if they have first-floor components.
  2. First repair session: Mechanical restoration (Stage 2). The mechanism moves. Brief, satisfying.
  3. Exploration break: Party explores scriptorium and other second-floor rooms. Finds lunar armatures, operator's manual, other second-floor content.
  4. Second repair session: Arcane restoration (Stage 3). First lens installed. Light fills the dome. Major atmospheric moment.
  5. More exploration: Continue second-floor content. Maybe encounter. Return with remaining components.
  6. Final repair session: Lunar arms (Stage 4), calibration (Stage 5). Full activation.
  7. The descent: After full restoration, the party goes back downstairs to the South Entrance — the very first room they entered. They have been here before. They know these walls. Describe the South Entrance differently now. The moment they see the first tapestry moving, the room they thought they understood becomes something else entirely. Let that beat land.
  8. The living tapestries: All four surviving tapestries are now active simultaneously. The party can move between them freely. Budget 45-60 minutes for the full experience. This is a sustained state, not a timed event — they can return to the tapestries whenever they want as long as the orrery is running.

Each repair session should take 15-30 minutes of table time. The tapestry activation scene is the big set piece. Budget 45-60 minutes.

locations.name: The Mess Hall and Kitchen — Shokudo

text.content:
Type
location
Status
active

Southwest wing, accessible via L-shaped hallway from the south side of the west E-W hallway.

Read-aloud text: ../supplements/read-aloud-floor-1.md § Mess Hall

[KNOWN]

Physical Description:

Accessed via an L-shaped hallway (10 ft wide) from the south side of the west wing — south 35 ft, then east 45 ft into the mess hall. No direct line of sight from the main corridor. Pervasive old char smell baked permanently into the stone. Draft of clean mountain air from a gap in the kitchen's west wall.

Mess Hall (50 ft × 50 ft): Long low tables running the length of the space. Tables nearest kitchen charred to legs; farther tables rotted, surfaces caved in. Cracked and blackened ceramic bowls scattered on the floor. Dark stains on stone. Scattered bone fragments. One ceramic bowl upright, intact, placed (not fallen) near the far wall — recently wiped clean of grime.

Kitchen (35 ft × 35 ft, west side of mess hall): Ceiling scorched black to significant depth. Great central hearth partially collapsed inward. Iron crane above hearth bent by extreme heat (far beyond normal cooking fire — this was a deliberate blaze). Gap in west wall mortar admits outside air and thin natural light.

Larder: Far corner of kitchen, door half-open. Shelved goods collapsed into uniform grey dust. Contains a sealed double-fired ceramic jar with intact wax seal (magical preservation).

[DISCOVERABLE]

Discoveries

  • The Intact Bowl (DC 13 Investigation)
  • The Sealed Jar — inscription (DC 14 Investigation) (Handout: "They are already inside. Hiroki knows.")

The Intact Bowl: The single upright, unbroken bowl is a small mystery with a simple answer — it was placed there by a Nagaji. They found it intact in the larder rubble and set it on the floor for reasons even they could not articulate. An instinct toward ritual. A faint echo of the person they used to be. DC 13 Investigation to notice the bowl has been wiped clean of grime, recently.

What Can Be Found: DC 14 Investigation in the larder reveals, beneath the uniform dust and decay: a sealed ceramic jar, double-fired with a wax seal that has held. Inside — preserved vegetables, technically still edible though profoundly unpleasant (the preservation is magical in nature, a minor kitchen enchantment common to the order). More importantly, scratched into the inside of the jar's lid in hasty characters: "They are already inside. Hiroki knows. The gate will not save us." This is a message from a priest who died in this room, writing in the moment of understanding. It is a handout. It confirms that the order's destruction came from within, not from outside assault.

Note: The Tsukuyomi projection lens was originally hidden in this jar by a priest during the fall. It has since been found and moved by the Nagaji Kannushi to the Star Shrine (Okuden), where it now resides among the Kannushi's collected relics. The jar contains only the inscription and preserved vegetables.

[SEALED]

Encounters

  • 4 Yaminezumi (闇鼠 — "Darkness Rats"; nest in collapsed west wall section of kitchen; not aggressive unless cornered; carry Kegare no Yamai)

DM Notes

Yaminezumi (闇鼠 — Darkness Rats): Four Swarms of Rats (MM p.339) that have lived in the dark corruption of the temple long enough to have changed. They have nested in the collapsed section of the west wall. Not aggressive unless cornered. Their presence means something edible was here recently — they have been feeding on the Nagaji's food stores, which are stashed in the larder area. Carry Kegare no Yamai: On a successful hit, target makes a DC 12 Constitution saving throw or gains one stack of Kegare no Yamai (see floor-1/kegare-no-yamai.md).

The Fire: The kitchen fire was deliberate — set by the Akaryu/Kokuryu infiltrators as part of the final assault on the order. It was intended to drive the priests out of this wing and into the Grand Hall, cutting off retreat to the southern entrance and funneling the defenders. It worked. The conflict that killed most of the order happened in the dormitory corridor and the Grand Hall, not here.

Atmosphere: The room smells of old char and cold stone. The draft from the gap in the west wall carries mountain air — clean, sharp, a relief from the closed smell of the rest of the temple. Sound behaves normally here, unlike the shrine.

frontmatter.name: The Mess Hall and Kitchen — Shokudo

text.content:
Type
location
Status
active

"Great Dragon Mountain — Temple of the Celestial Sky"

The temple has slept for thousands of years. Something in it has not.

Overview

Oryuzan Tenku-ji was the paramount sacred site of the Golden Dragon Clan — a monastery, archive, and living temple raised in honor of Kinryu at the height of the First Golden Age. It sat at the heart of the Kinkozan Mountain Range, now called Tenchusan Ren, and served as both a place of worship and a center of learning for the clan's order of dragon-priests.

The temple's destruction came not from outside invasion but from within. Infiltrators aligned with the Crimson Clan (Akaryu) and Onyx Clan (Kokuryu) embedded themselves within the order over decades, working to fracture the Golden Dragon Clan's influence during the War of Fractured Banners. The internal violence was swift and devastating — but what finally sealed the temple's fate was the sei drought. By 13088, the secondary stars — Susanoo and Tsukuyomi — had retreated far enough along their barycentric orbits that sei was no longer accessible. The foundational magic held — the torches still burned, the statue still radiated warmth — but the living connection to Kinryu went silent. The Great Aphelion itself would not arrive for another 1,256 years (~14344), but the temple's inhabitants had no way to know that. They only knew the magic was gone. The surviving worshipers, already fractured by infiltration and war, found themselves in a temple that still worked while they no longer could. They walked away. None returned.

What remains is a place in two states simultaneously: ruin and preservation. Most of the temple has suffered as stone suffers — slowly, under the weight of time, water, and neglect. But the great statue at its heart has not aged a single day. The pools surrounding it still hold water of unearthly clarity. The star shrine still casts its pinprick constellations across the floor when moonlight falls. The temple remembers what it was, even if no one alive does.

Campaign Role

The temple's primary structural role in the campaign is as a progress point leading into an expansive cavern system, most likely accessed through the basement level. The caverns are how the Nagaji have been moving rapidly from their mountain retreat toward Hokori without detection — the party discovering this network is a significant intelligence find.

Multiple entry paths to the caverns exist in case the party bypasses or skips the basement. At least one alternate route is findable on the first floor for groups who don't go down.

The cavern system is canonically the Nagaji's operational highway — it explains the mystery of how serpentine creatures have been appearing in lowland areas far from their known mountain territory.

Spatial Layout

First Floor

Full spatial layout (ASCII map, nodes, connections, chokepoints, sight lines, vertical connections) is in floor-1.md § Spatial Layout.

Quick adjacency:

South Entrance (1) → [tapers 70ft→20ft] → N-S Hallway → Grand Hall (2) [double double-doors]
                                            │
                              Center Intersection (20×20)
                                    │
                    ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
                    ▼               ▼               ▼
              W wing (120ft)   stairs up/dn    E wing (120ft)
              N: Star Shrine (3)  (45ft out)   N: Dormitories (5)
              S: Mess Hall (4)                 S: Dormitories (entrance collapsed)

Grand Hall (2) → [double double-doors] → Inner Sanctum (6) [90W × 35D]
Naijin (6) → [secret hall, 5W × 20L] → Jushoku no Ma (6a) [15W × 20D]
Jushoku no Ma (6a) → [secret door, S wall] → Hoko (6b)

Current Inhabitants — First Floor

Location Inhabitants Notes
Grand Hall (upper dark) 2 Shadows Descend when disturbed; avoid pools
Hiroba (general) Nagaji Bushi ×1, Hohei ×2, Ashigaru ×6 On rotation from Naijin
Dormitory Wing 4 Specters Confused, not immediately hostile
Shokudo 4 Swarms of Rats Not aggressive unless cornered
Inner Sanctum Nagaji Zasu Currently patrolling; returns periodically
Okuden Nagaji Kannushi Returns to meditate; drawn to the space

Loot Framework

Common/open areas: Essentially devoid of valuables after millennia of decay and Nagaji habitation. Don't reward casual searching — set that expectation early.

Creature hoards (spiders and other dwellers): Small collections of incidental treasure accumulated from prey over generations — coins, small jewelry, a snapped-off belt buckle, occasionally something more interesting. Keep individual finds small and flavorful.

Relics (good rolls required): Genuine Golden Clan artifacts still exist in the temple — in places protected by preservation magic, in sealed or collapsed areas, in spots the Nagaji wouldn't have accessed or recognized as valuable. These require active searching and meaningful rolls to locate.

Design principle: The temple rewards curiosity and thoroughness, not just combat. A party that rushes through finds very little. A party that investigates carefully finds things that matter.

Connected Entries

  • Floor 1 Overview & Spatial Layout: floor-1.md
  • Floor 1 Room Files: floor-1/ (south-entrance, grand-hall, star-shrine, mess-hall, dormitories, inner-sanctum, central-hallway)
  • Floor 1 — Read-Aloud Text: supplements/read-aloud-floor-1.md
  • Floor 1 — Tapestries: supplements/tapestry.md
  • Floor 2 — Observatory & Scriptorium: supplements/mechanical-arcane-orrery.md (repair design), room descriptions pending
  • The Buried City of Kinkokyou: pending
  • Cavern System: pending

Type
location-supplement

In-game narration for each room. Reference individual room files in floor-1/ for mechanical details, DCs, and DM notes. Reference floor-1.md for spatial layout and floor-level overview.

1. The South Entrance — Kinko no Mon (Gate of Golden Light)

The doors open and the cold comes first — dry and still, carrying the faint mineral scent of old bronze and something beneath it with no name, the absence of smoke from flames that do not burn the way fire burns.

There is light where there should not be. Gold sconces line both walls at intervals, and the torches set into them are burning — pale blue-white, absolutely still, each flame identical to the last. The draft from the open doors moves past them without effect. The shadows they throw are long and fixed, pooling between the sconces in bands of blue-black the light never quite reaches.

Eight pale stone pillars stand in two rows down the hall's length, freestanding, set well in from the walls — four to a side, reaching toward a ceiling sixty feet above. Their surfaces were carved once; the evidence of that is visible in the grooves and spirals that remain. The evidence of something else is visible too: chisel marks at a height someone could reach from the ground, working across every surface with patience. Faces removed. Wing-edges broken away. The hollows where features used to be catch the cold torchlight and cast shadows that shift faintly as you move through the space — following you, though the flames do not.

In the northeast corner, two of the pillars are down. They have fallen toward the center of the hall, the nearer one lying across the tile path in three large pieces, the farther one broken at the base and leaning against the first, the two together forming a low obstacle of pale stone and settled debris. The ceiling above shows raw mountain rock at both gaps. The gold sconces at those positions are still mounted on the wall — but the torches in them are gone, and that section of the hall, where Tapestry I hangs behind the rubble, is the darkest part of the room.

Between the standing pillars and the tapestried walls, the sconce-light does not reach. The space there runs the length of the hall on both sides, deeper shadow than the rest.

The walls between the sconces are hung floor to ceiling with fabric — overlapping in places, three layers deep in at least one section. What time and something more immediate have done to most of them is thorough: blackened frames, collapsed structures, images reduced past any reading. But not all. Here and there, where the light catches at the right angle, a shape holds. A color that should not have survived. A figure that resolves differently depending on where you are standing.

Down the center of the hall, where something has scraped through the accumulated grit, the floor tile is visible: gold and deep blue, geometric, precise.

Above the inner door, two iron brackets protrude from the stone. Between them, nothing.

2. The Grand Hall — Hiroba (Wide Hall)

The passage opens and the walls fall away.

The space is large enough that your light doesn't reach the far sides — the walls at the edges are blue-grey shapes, barely suggestions. The ceiling is not visible at all. You are not in a room so much as you are at the base of something.

And at the center: gold.

Two hundred and fifty feet of it, coiled around a central plinth in a posture that takes a moment to read. Not rearing. Not threatening. The great head is lowered slightly, the body settled as if resting, but the inlaid amber eyes are open and they are aimed at the space directly in front of them — at you, if you are standing in front of them. The surface of the statue has not tarnished. Not a single scale has lost its sheen. Your light arrives at it and comes back warmer than it left.

Around the base, on the south and east faces, four shallow pools. The water in them is so clear you can see the tile below it as though the water is not there. It carries its own faint light — blue-white, steady, the color of something that has been holding its breath for a very long time.

Away from the statue, the room has aged. Banners hang from wall brackets in ribbons, their colors long since gone. Offering tables have collapsed. Whatever was brought here — food, incense, vessels — has fallen, broken, or been reclaimed by gravity and time. The floor beyond the pools is hidden under decades of dust and debris.

The statue has not aged. The water has not dried.

3. The Star Shrine — Okuden (Inner Hall)

The hallway that leads here is unmarked — no carvings, no script, no alcoves. Just stone, ten feet wide, stretching sixty feet ahead of you with the narrowing sense that you are going somewhere set apart.

The room at the end is broad and still — forty-five feet across, thirty-five deep, the ceiling rising into shadow above you. The floor is polished obsidian, black and seamless, still reflective despite the centuries — you see your own feet in it, blurred, moving just behind you. At the center, a low stone dais sized for a single seated figure, unadorned.

Then you notice the ceiling.

Thousands of small holes, each one no wider than a finger, pierce it in an arrangement that is clearly deliberate — too consistent for accident, too complex for simple decoration. Through a narrow shaft in the outer northwest wall, moonlight enters the chamber and passes through the holes, each one casting a single pinprick of shadow down onto the obsidian below.

The shadows together form the sky.

Not an approximation of it. Not a simplified rendering. The actual night sky above this latitude, mapped in negative across the reflective floor: the constellations of Seizan, the positions of the four moons, the dim stellar clusters between the named stars. The room is holding the sky in place.

Sound arrives at the threshold and stops. Whatever you carried in from the hallway — footsteps, breath, the creak of armor — becomes, within a step, nothing.

The dais has been used recently. The dust on it is disturbed: a circular impression, the shape of something large and coiled, pressed into the surface more than once.

4. The Mess Hall and Kitchen — Shokudo (Dining Hall)

The hallway turns — south, then east — and the smell finds you before the room does. The fire was a long time ago. The smell of it is still here.

Not a fresh smell — old char, baked into stone so thoroughly it has become part of the stone.

The passage opens into a broad space — fifty feet across, fifty deep. Long low tables run the length of it. The ones nearest the kitchen archway to the west are charred down to their legs. The ones farther away have simply rotted, their surfaces caved in over years of neglect. Ceramic bowls are scattered across the floor, cracked and blackened, lying where they fell.

One bowl is upright. Intact. Set on the floor near the far wall as if someone placed it there.

Dark stains mark the stone in places. The occasional fragment of bone, scattered, has been here long enough to look like part of the room.

Through the kitchen archway to the west, the damage is worse. The ceiling there is black, scorched to a depth that centuries of stillness have not touched. The great central hearth has partially collapsed inward; the iron crane that hung above it is bent at an angle that suggests heat far beyond anything a cooking fire would produce. In the far wall, a section of mortar gave out — from the heat, from the cold, from something — leaving a ragged gap that lets in a thin blade of mountain air, clean and sharp against everything else in the room.

In the far corner of the kitchen, a larder door stands half-open. Inside, shapes on shelves that might have been preserved goods — jars, sacks, something — have collapsed into uniform grey dust.

5. The Dormitories — Bo (Monks' Quarters)

A long corridor, wide enough for two people to walk side by side, with doors branching left and right. Most of the doors are open. At the far ends of the corridor, larger chambers.

The doors that are open were not left that way. The frames are splintered — forced inward, or outward, depending on the door. Several bear scoring at shoulder height, the kind left by edged weapons. Inside the cells: sleeping pallets collapsed into their own decay. Personal effects on hooks or shelves, long since fallen — a sandal, a cloth, a small painted tile lying face-down in the dust.

In the southern shared chamber, the evidence is heavier. Furniture was moved — pushed against walls, pushed away again, the drag marks visible in the grit. Impact marks at various heights. On the floor near the far wall, the stone itself is damaged: a starburst pattern, cracked outward from a central point.

The northern shared chamber is different. Its door has a bar, and the bar is in its brackets. This door was never forced. You lift the bar yourself and push the door open.

The air inside is old in the way only sealed places can be — still, and slightly too dry, as if the room has been holding its breath. The pallet inside holds a complete skeleton. They are facing the wall. They lay down on their own.

On the floor beside the pallet: a small bronze disc on a cord. An ink-block, dried to nothing. A sealed scroll case.

6. The Inner Sanctum — Naijin (Inner Sanctuary)

The doors to the inner sanctum are black-lacquered wood banded with bronze, a frieze of the seven dragon clans carved into the frame in a ring. They are standing open.

Inside the frame, where some kind of locking mechanism was once anchored, lines of inlaid silver run dark and dead. Whatever held these doors closed was undone. The damage is on the outside of the frame.

The chamber within is octagonal, high-ceilinged, each wall originally bearing a hanging scroll. Six of the eight positions are empty — the mountings remain, but the scrolls are gone. One position holds fragments on the floor, the ink faded to invisibility. One, against the far wall, still holds its scroll intact: a dragon in flight, rendered in gold and deep blue on black silk, the colors as vivid as if it was made this year. Looking at it, you understand what the artists in your own era are attempting.

The center of the floor has been cleared. Not cleaned — cleared. Whatever stood here originally has been pushed to the walls: shattered pedestals, broken braziers, debris. In the cleared center, a depression in the swept floor, low and circular, shaped by something large that has lain there many times. The edges of it are made from broken furniture, torn fabric, shredded material that was once something else.

The depression is empty. It is warm.

locations.name: The South Entrance — Kinko no Mon

text.content:
Type
location
Status
active

Read-aloud text: ../supplements/read-aloud-floor-1.md § South Entrance

[KNOWN]

Physical Description:

70 ft wide × 75 ft long, 60-foot ceiling. Tapers to 20 ft wide at approximately 50 ft in, connecting to the N-S hallway. Cold, dry, still air with faint bronze mineral scent and an absence of smoke-smell. Eight pale stone pillars in two rows of four, freestanding, set inward from the walls — creating shadowed side-aisles between pillars and walls. Pillar carvings deliberately defaced with chisel marks at reachable height (faces removed, wing-edges broken). Hollow carved surfaces catch torchlight and appear to shift with movement.

Lighting: Gold sconces at seven-foot intervals along both walls holding torches that burn pale blue-white — cold, still, unaffected by drafts. Roughly half still hold torches; of those, about two-thirds still burning. Light pools along walls but does not reach the side-aisles.

Northeast corner (dead zone): Two pillars collapsed toward center — one across the tile path in three pieces, the other broken at base and leaning against the first. Sconces intact but torches missing. Darkest area of the hall. Tapestry I hangs behind the rubble. Ceiling above shows raw mountain rock.

Walls: Tapestries hung floor to ceiling between sconces. Eleven positions total. Seven destroyed (blackened, collapsed, unreadable). Four retain imagery. Several frames are empty — tapestries cut down, not deteriorated.

Floor: Gold and deep blue geometric tile, visible along a scraped center path. Rest buried under accumulated grit.

Inner door: Two iron brackets mounted above the door frame. Whatever hung between them has been removed — no bracket damage, no debris.

[DISCOVERABLE]

Discoveries

  • The Magical Torches (DC 13 Arcana; 18+ critical)
  • The Dead Corner torches (DC 14 Investigation)
  • The Pillar Carvings (DC 13 History / DC 10 Ko'jiri)
  • The Two Fallen Pillars (DC 14 Arcana)
  • The Tapestries — cut-down frames (DC 12 Perception)
  • The Missing Brackets

The Magical Torches: Gold sconces are mounted at seven-foot intervals along both walls — fixed, permanent, part of the temple's original construction. The magical effect requires both the sconce and the torch together; neither alone produces light. Roughly half the sconces still hold their torches; of those, approximately two-thirds are still burning. The flames burn cold — no heat, no fire damage, no smoke — and do not respond to drafts or movement. A DC 13 Arcana check identifies the enchantment as Golden Dragon order craft, a practical sustained effect designed to light the hall indefinitely. On a critical success (18+), the character reads further into the enchantment's structure and finds something unexpected: this is not a maintenance effect, not a slow-burning spell consuming stored energy over time. The magic embedded in these sconces is foundational — woven into the stone at the level of the temple's original construction, not cast on top of it. The sophistication required to work enchantment this deeply into physical material is far beyond what even skilled practitioners can achieve today. A torch removed from its sconce goes dark immediately and completely — not guttering, just out. Replaced into any sconce, it resumes burning at once.

The Dead Corner: The two fallen northeast pillars have left their sconces intact on the wall but their torches are missing — pulled free or knocked loose during the final conflict, the exact circumstances unclear. The result is a pronounced dark zone in the northeast corner, deepened by the rubble of the two pillars. Tapestry I hangs behind that rubble in near-darkness. A character who wants to examine it closely will need to either bring light into the corner or find and replace the missing torches. The torches themselves are somewhere in the pillar rubble — DC 14 Investigation to locate them. Replaced into their sconces, they resume burning immediately.

The Pillar Carvings: Damage is deliberate — multiple tools, over time, not a single event. DC 13 History (DC 10 for Ko'jiri, who has advantage on Golden Dragon Clan checks) to read the pattern as methodical erasure rather than battle damage. The hollow faces track movement subtly in the torchlight. Worth remarking on for attentive players; do not explain it.

The Two Fallen Pillars: Both collapsed during the final conflict from localized magical detonations — not from age, not from each other. DC 14 Arcana detects trace sei residue at the base of each, consistent with explosive force applied at close range, centuries old. Two separate detonations, the same method. Someone destroyed these pillars deliberately, and the dark corner they created — directly adjacent to Tapestry I — was the point. The rubble has never been disturbed since they fell.

The Tapestries: Eleven positions total. Seven destroyed beyond reading; four retain usable imagery. Among the destroyed: DC 12 Perception reveals several frames are empty — tapestries cut down and removed, not deteriorated. Full content in ../supplements/tapestry.md.

The Missing Brackets: Whatever hung above the inner door was unmounted cleanly — no bracket damage, no debris on the floor. Taken deliberately. If ever recovered, it grants advantage on Insight checks within the temple for the duration of that visit.

[SEALED]

Encounters

(No combat encounters in this room under normal circumstances.)

DM Notes

The Shadow Corridors: The space between the freestanding pillars and the tapestried walls was architecturally intentional — a processional center path with lateral side-aisles. With the sconces throwing light outward toward the walls, those aisles are in deep shadow. Any creature in the side-aisles has three-quarters cover from anyone standing in the center path. DC 12 Perception to notice the depth before committing to the center. The Nagaji know this space and use the aisles. The scraped path runs down the center — whatever came through most recently was not moving with caution.

Atmosphere: Cold, dry, still air. The bronze smell is the sconce metalwork. The flames produce no smoke and no char — a strange olfactory absence where fire-smell should be.
