Sound echoes with a slight delay from the vault, footsteps returning a half-beat late. Near the tapestried walls that echo dies entirely. The silence there is notable.

frontmatter.name: The South Entrance — Kinko no Mon

text.content:
Type
location
Status
active

Northwest wing, accessible via the west end of the E-W hallway.

Read-aloud text: ../supplements/read-aloud-floor-1.md § Star Shrine

[KNOWN]

Physical Description:

Accessed via a 10 ft wide, 60 ft long unmarked hallway extending north from the west wing of the E-W hallway. Room is 50 ft wide × 40 ft deep, high ceiling. Complete sound suppression at the threshold — all external noise ceases on entry.

Magical Darkness: The rear two-thirds of the room is consumed by magical darkness — a clean circular boundary approximately 20 ft radius centered on the dais. The entrance third remains lit. Light sources stop precisely at the boundary and do not spill inward. Darkvision does not function within the darkness. The boundary is visible and investigable from the entrance before committing.

Floor: Polished obsidian, black and seamless, still reflective. Functions as the projection surface for the star map (currently inactive — obscured by darkness).

Ceiling: Thousands of finger-width holes piercing the dome in a precise arrangement. A narrow shaft in the outer northwest wall admits moonlight, which passes through the holes and casts pinprick shadows onto the obsidian floor — reproducing the actual night sky at this latitude (constellations of Seizan, four moons, stellar clusters). Full map renders under Kagetsu (largest moon). Currently inert while darkness persists.

Dais: Low stone platform at center (within the darkness), sized for a single seated figure. Shows recent use — dust disturbed, circular coiled impression pressed into the surface repeatedly. A cursed urn sits on the dais, radiating the darkness.

Permanent etching: A fixed star configuration carved into the obsidian floor (not projected) depicting the Great Aphelion — all three stars and four moons at maximum distance from Seizan. Partially visible in the lit entrance third; full configuration only visible once darkness lifts.

[DISCOVERABLE]

Discoveries

  • The Darkness — source identification (DC 12 Arcana or Perception; DC 13 Arcana curse aura; DC 16 Arcana protective ward)
  • The Purification Rite (DC 18 Religion or second floor hidden archive)
  • How It Works — star map mechanism (DC 10 Arcana for navigator check) (requires darkness to be lifted)
  • The Dais Impression — Nagaji Kannushi attunement
  • Relic Collection (DC 14 Investigation — once darkness lifts)
  • Meditation Benefit (short rest on dais during moonlight) (requires darkness to be lifted)

The Darkness

Source Identification:

Check DC Result
Arcana or Perception 12 Identifies the urn on the central dais as the epicenter of the darkness
Arcana 13 Confirms curse aura on the urn
Arcana 16 Identifies curse as a deliberate protective ward, not corruption — can be unwound
Religion 18 Reveals the purification rite to lift the darkness

Purification Rite: One action, both hands on the urn's surface, spoken invocation to Kinryū. Lifting the darkness does not damage the urn. The rite can also be learned from the hidden archive on the second floor.

If the party lifts the darkness mid-combat: The darkness collapses instantly. The Kannushi loses concealment.

How It Works (Star Map)

The shaft in the outer northwest wall is angled precisely to admit moonlight at specific lunar positions. Under Kagetsu (the largest moon), the full star map renders on the floor. Under Ryugetsu, certain star positions shift slightly — reflecting that moon's complex orbit — creating what the order called the "Dragon's Compass," a subtle pattern within the map pointing toward celestial events of significance. A seimaster or character with proficiency in Arcana or Navigator's Tools who studies the map for 10 minutes can extract one piece of information about current celestial alignment (DM's discretion based on current campaign date — Aki season, Kugatsu 1).

The Dais Impression

The circular coiled impression in the dust was left by the Nagaji Kannushi who inhabits this space. It was not meditating in the conventional sense — it was drawn here, instinctively, by something in the stone that resonates with its transformed nature. The Nagaji connection to Kokuryu's shadow rituals creates a faint attunement to certain sei-charged spaces. The Kannushi has been tidying the space — making it a meditation chamber.

Relic Collection (DC 14 Investigation — once darkness lifts)

The Kannushi gathered and preserved these objects from elsewhere in the temple:

  • Three intact ceremonial incense burners (gold-inlaid bronze; functional; 120gp each as antiques)
  • A silk-wrapped bundle of seven prayer slips in Old Imperial script — celestial observation function
  • A cracked but sealed lacquer box containing brass astronomical instruments — grant advantage on celestial Navigation checks
  • A carved jade medallion bearing Kinryū's clan sigil — devotional; radiates faint warmth; worth 200gp
  • Tsukuyomi projection lens — deep red crystal, warm to the touch; moved here by the Kannushi from elsewhere in the temple (Observatory component #4 — originally hidden in the mess hall sealed jar by a priest during the fall; the Kannushi found and relocated it)

Star Map — Activates When Darkness Lifts

The full ceiling becomes visible and active once darkness ends. Silver and gemstone inlay responds to current celestial date. DC 14 Arcana or Nature (10 minutes study) reveals current celestial alignment and sei implications.

Mechanical Benefit — Meditation

A character who spends a short rest seated on the dais (during a moonlit period, darkness lifted) receives the benefits of the Calm Emotions spell upon completing the rest, and has advantage on their first Wisdom saving throw before their next long rest. This is a one-time benefit per creature per visit.

[SEALED]

Encounters

  • Nagaji Kannushi (present and meditating on the dais when party arrives; fully hostile once triggered; has Devil Sight)

The Kannushi — Tactical Notes

  • Present when the party arrives — meditating on the dais within the darkness; may have heard the party and chosen stillness
  • Devil Sight — sees in the darkness as bright light to 120 ft; is not imposed on by the darkness she created
  • Trigger: Loud noise, light spells directed toward her, or anyone crossing the darkness boundary
  • No non-combat resolution — she is fully hostile once triggered
  • Fights to protect the dais and urn — does not abandon them aggressively
  • If the party reaches the urn mid-combat and succeeds on DC 18 Religion: darkness collapses instantly

The Cursed Urn

The Kannushi cursed the urn deliberately as a guardian measure — her intent is protective. She created the darkness to shield the space she has claimed. This is a ward, not corruption.

DM Notes

Relc's Vision: When the darkness lifts and the star map activates, green luminescence briefly appears in one constellation matching Solas's letter sigil — visible to Relc only, for a moment only. Pass note to player directly.

Relc's Moment (Dais): This is a meaningful space for Relc specifically. The Sacred Grove and the Golden Dragon Clan had a historical relationship — both traditions understood the sky as a living text. When Relc stands on the dais, Solas's next vision arrives: not words, not instruction — just the image of Solas in the grove above Koriwara, one hand on a standing stone, dawn light striking it from the east. The vision lasts three seconds. It is quiet. It is pointing him home, after this is done.

The Last Observation — The Great Aphelion: The star map contains a fixed reference configuration etched into the obsidian floor — not projected by moonlight but carved permanently. It depicts all three stars (Amaterasu, Susanoo, Tsukuyomi) and all four moons at their maximum distance from Seizan: the Great Aphelion (formal in-world name TBD). This configuration appears to be the last documented celestial observation made by the temple's order. No subsequent observations were recorded, suggesting the temple fell at approximately the same time as this event. A character proficient in Arcana, History, or Navigator's Tools who studies this etching (DC 16) recognizes it as an extreme astronomical configuration — one that would occur only on cycles measured in millennia. A seimaster or Ancient Guard member would understand its potential connection to the sei drought. The party is unlikely to grasp the full significance without outside expertise, but the etching stands as physical evidence linking the temple's abandonment to a cosmic event.

What Was Taught Here: This room was the order's primary space for sei study linked to celestial alignment. Dragon-priests would sit for days on the dais, mapping the movements of the star shadows as the moon tracked across the shaft, correlating them with sei fluctuations they could feel in the mountain stone. The knowledge developed here fed into the Golden Dragon Clan's deep understanding of Kinryu's transformation-reversal work — the idea that sei corruption can be unmade through precise celestial timing. That insight is relevant to the Gekko situation, and a character who meditates here and succeeds on a DC 14 Arcana or History check intuits it: the stars matter. Whatever is broken, the sky must be right when it is mended.

Moral Weight: When the darkness lifts, the party sees what the Kannushi was guarding — the tidied floor, the arranged relics, the straightened shelf. She was not protecting a threat. She was tending a sanctuary. This lands without narration.

Type
location
Status
active

Static examination and orrery-activated behavior for the four surviving tapestries in the South Entrance.

Static content describes what the party can learn from examining the tapestries as still fabric. Activation content describes what happens when the orrery is fully restored and the tapestries come alive.

How This Works

Each tapestry supports two independent skill tracks. A player may attempt either or both, in any order — the two tracks produce genuinely different information, not the same content reframed from a different angle.

Track One — Reading the Image Use Investigation (analytical, connective, inferential) or Perception (sensory, visual, observational) interchangeably. Both engage with what is physically present in the tapestry. A player who attempts both rolls does not stack content — the second check may add a small sensory or contextual detail at DM discretion, but core information does not compound.

Track Two — The Secondary Skill Each tapestry has a distinct secondary skill that unlocks a different layer of information entirely.

Tapestry Secondary Skill Lens
I — Kinryu Descends History Iconographic meaning, clan conventions, lineage
II — The Rite of the Golden Flame Arcana Sei resonance, enchantment traces, magical residue
III — Hokori Before the Reckoning Insight Intent — what was chosen, hidden, or deliberately omitted
IV — The First Head Priest Religion Sacred symbolism, devotional context, divine significance

Ko'jiri's Advantage: On Tapestry I, Ko'jiri may apply his Golden Dragon Clan History advantage to the History (Track Two) check. On Tapestry IV, he may apply it to his Track One check — the founding priest's identity falls within his documented research.

The Four Tiers

Result DC What It Means
Failure Below 10 Misreads, wrong conclusion, or finds nothing
Partial 10-13 Surface impression only; limited or ambiguous
Success 14-17 Observations first, then one interpretive possibility
Critical Success 18-21 Full picture plus a tangible or mechanical reward
Exceptional 22+ Critical success plus one detail not otherwise visible

Tapestry I — Kinryu Descends to the Mountain

West wall, north end. Best preserved of the four. Approximately two-thirds intact.

At a glance: Gold thread on deep indigo — a massive figure descending from a night sky filled with precisely rendered stars. The lower portion is gone, a diagonal tear removing most of the bottom quarter.

Track One — Investigation or Perception

FAILURE: Something large descending. Gold, or close to it. The damage at the bottom takes most of the scene with it. Whatever the figure was descending toward, you cannot see it.

PARTIAL: A dragon, or a depiction of one — coming down through a starlit sky toward something in the missing lower section. The posture is deliberate: unhurried, the movement chosen. At the torn edge, just at the damage line, the faintest hint of figures below.

SUCCESS: The stitchwork is extraordinary — individual scales in thread of at least three different weights, each catching the cold torchlight at its own angle. The stars in the indigo field are rendered with the same precision: not decorative, not approximate. The posture — wings folded back, head inclined — has the quality of a choice rather than a movement. Just above the tear, the tops of ground figures are barely present: one robed, arms raised, the forearms bearing a textured pattern stitched in thread that might read as scales. In the raised hands, something small and circular, stitched in thread that has tarnished nearly black.

The deliberateness of the descent — wings folded, head lowered — suggests this moment was considered important enough to record with unusual care.

CRITICAL SUCCESS: The figure at the torn edge is positioned as a recipient, not a witness — arms raised in a specific formal gesture, weight forward, attention directed upward. The circular object at their belt is a disc, and its proportions match something you have encountered or will encounter elsewhere in this temple. The star arrangement above is not generic — it is a specific configuration, a particular night, rendered as precisely as everything else here.

Tangible Reward: Recognizing the disc shape connects this figure to the bronze disc found in the sealed dormitory. The character gains advantage on the next Investigation check made while searching for hidden mechanisms or sealed doors anywhere in the temple.

EXCEPTIONAL: The tear line is too uniform. The threads along the diagonal show the tension pattern of a cut, not a break — the surrounding fabric confirms it. The bottom quarter was removed deliberately, not lost to time. Whatever stood below the descending figure at the moment this image depicts, someone decided it should not be visible here.

Track Two — History

FAILURE: A dragon arriving. The posture reads as territorial — a claim being made, a place taken. This reading is wrong, and conclusions built on it will be wrong.

PARTIAL: A standard subject in Golden Dragon clan commemorative imagery — a formal depiction of Kinryu in descent. Nothing here immediately distinguishes this from common examples of the genre.

SUCCESS: The posture — wings folded, head inclined — is a specific iconographic convention used by the Golden Dragon clan exclusively for one kind of moment: not conquest or arrival, but voluntary binding. This pose appears when Kinryu is depicted choosing to commit — to a place, a purpose, a relationship. This image is not commemorative. It records a promise.

The star arrangement is rendered with the same specificity as everything else in the image. It appears to be a real configuration, not a decorative one.

CRITICAL SUCCESS: The star arrangement is datable. Ko'jiri — if present and engaged — recognizes it from his research notes: a celestial alignment recorded in a secondary source as "the night Kinryu first spoke to a mortal in the age before the clans were named." This event was cosmologically timed. The founding of this temple was not incidental to larger events — it was coordinated with them.

Ko'jiri Tangible Reward: Advantage on his next History check made inside the temple.

EXCEPTIONAL: The voluntary-binding pose appears in three surviving examples of Golden Dragon clan iconography: once here, once in a fragment held at the Great Library of Seirei Mizuumi, and once in a carving reported — before the Dark Ages, unverified since — somewhere in the highlands of Kaze province. Three separate moments. Three separate bindings. This, by available record, is the first.

Activation Behavior

The activation is not passive. The descending figure's gaze tracks Ko'jiri specifically throughout the scene. It does not track other party members. The quality of attention in the image reads as recognition, or the desire for it — the ori-kioku recorded a moment of directed intent, and Ko'jiri carries whatever quality that intent was directed toward. The wanting in it is not subtle once noticed.

Other party members observing will notice the eyes are not following them.

Cross-reference hum: If Ko'jiri is present during activation, he hears the resonant hum from the Grand Hall statue — faint, directional, traveling through the temple's stone. Not an echo of the tapestry. The building is cross-referencing him through its foundational magic. Do not explain this to the players.

Tapestry II — The Rite of the Golden Flame

East wall, center. Approximately half intact; significant damage on the left, right side largely preserved.

At a glance: Robed figures in a circle around a fire that rests on nothing. Hands raised. The left half of the image is mostly gone.

Track One — Investigation or Perception

FAILURE: A ceremony of some kind around a fire. The left side is too damaged to add anything. Common enough subject matter.

PARTIAL: The robes carry a distinctive collar treatment — high and structured, not seen in other contexts. The fire at the center has no source: no brazier, no platform, no floor contact. The hand gestures are specific rather than open.

SUCCESS: Each figure's gesture is precise and directional — hands angled as though managing something, not appealing to it. The fire responds to whatever they are doing; its shape bends in ways consistent with being guided. On the surviving right side, one figure's face is visible beneath a lowered hood: Dragonborn, gold-scaled, expression watchful rather than absorbed. This figure's hands carry the same basic posture as the others but angled differently — oriented away from the fire, toward something outside the frame.

The divergence is subtle. It may have been missed by whoever made this image. Or noticed and preserved deliberately.

CRITICAL SUCCESS: The figure with the differently-angled hands is doing something separate from everyone else in the circle. The energy the others are directing into the fire — this figure's hands are oriented away from it, toward whatever lies beyond the image's edge. The fire is not diminished for it; whatever is being redirected draws from a different source. The image captured a moment in which two things were happening in the same ceremony, and only one of them was visible to most participants.

Tangible Reward: This understanding — that the order's end was patient, embedded, and invisible to most of those inside it — grants the party advantage on Insight checks when interacting with the creature in the Inner Sanctum.

EXCEPTIONAL: The damage on the left side follows the frame edge in a way consistent with cutting rather than deterioration. The thread tension along the left margin suggests the fabric was under stress before it failed — as though pulled before it was cut. Whatever stood on the left side of this circle was removed along with that section of the tapestry. The circle is incomplete.

Track Two — Arcana

FAILURE: Old sei in the thread — a preservation enchantment of some kind. Common enough in high-value objects from this period.

PARTIAL: The thread treatment is more involved than standard preservation — the sei was woven in during construction, not applied afterward. Significant craft went into this. The age is consistent with the temple's overall timeline.

SUCCESS: The technique is ori-kioku — woven memory, a Golden Dragon order practice allowing fabric to hold sei resonance as a form of record. This tapestry is not merely depicting the rite — a faint echo of the actual sei present at the moment of weaving is still held in the thread. Two distinct signatures are layered in the fabric: one warm and gold-aspected, one cold and shadow-edged. They do not come from the same source. One belongs to this tradition. The other does not.

What the shadow-edged signature fits is a different question entirely.

CRITICAL SUCCESS: The shadow-edged signature is Kokuryu-aspected — Onyx Clan tradition, identifiable to anyone trained in historical sei lineages. It was present and active during this rite, masked by the surrounding warmth of golden sei, preserved by the ori-kioku process because that process records indiscriminately. The tapestry held what the participants may not have seen: a second hand at work inside the circle.

Tangible Reward: The Kokuryu-aspected sei signature is now recognizable as a fingerprint. The same signature appears on the broken ward anchors in the Inner Sanctum door frame — and on a fresh trace in this room, weeks old rather than centuries. Something with this sei character has been near this tapestry recently.

EXCEPTIONAL: The fresh trace is localized — concentrated near the tapestry's surface as though whatever left it stood here for a period of time, attentive, before moving on. Dry. Faintly mineral. Nothing like the cold bronze of the sconce metalwork. Not all of the temple's current inhabitants moved through this entrance without stopping.

Activation Behavior

The activation allows a character to read the ceremony being performed — not possible from the static image.

DC 14 Arcana: Identifies the working as a consecration ceremony — sei made visible and held in collective form by multiple trained practitioners. The suspended flame is the working itself, made manifest. The circle is sealing something into the building's structural magic: a ward, a record, an authorization layer. This is how the temple's foundational enchantments were laid. The party is watching the building's own creation ritual.

DC 18 Arcana: Recognizes the specific technique as identical to the method woven into the torches, the pools, and the ori-kioku itself. Every preservation enchantment in the building traces back to ceremonies like this one.

The divergence: Once the working is understood, the gold-scaled Dragonborn's redirected hands carry specific meaning. They are not withholding their contribution from the flame. They are tapping the working as it runs — drawing a thread of the collective sei output and routing it outward toward whatever lies in the missing left half of the tapestry. The ceremony succeeded from the inside. The binding was completed. But a portion of whatever was sealed into the foundations was simultaneously copied and transmitted elsewhere. The order sealed something into this building. Someone else received a key.

This does not replace the existing Arcana Track Two content (the Kokuryu-aspected sei signature) — it adds a layer accessible specifically during activation that was not accessible from the static image. The dissonant harmonic heard during activation is that same signature rendered audible.

Tapestry III — Hokori Before the Reckoning

West wall, south end. Least preserved of the four — approximately forty percent remains across three disconnected sections.

At a glance: Fragments of something cartographic. Coastlines in places, shapes suggesting mountain ranges, small symbols whose purpose is not immediately clear. The sections do not connect. Large areas are simply absent.

Track One — Investigation or Perception

FAILURE: Geographic imagery — possibly. The sections don't orient to anything recognizable, and there isn't enough intact to extract information with confidence.

PARTIAL: A map, probably Hokori based on the coastline shapes, though the conventions differ from anything in current use. Old, significantly older than any administrative archive. Too fragmented to read for specific information.

SUCCESS: This is Hokori — the distinctive shape reads across the gaps for someone who knows what to look for. The rendering predates current cartographic conventions entirely; the visual language suggests not just age but a different understanding of what a map is for. Mountain ranges appear here with no equivalent on modern maps. Settlements cluster in places corresponding to no current town — some now wilderness, some now open water. In the most intact section, a symbol appears three times in a loose triangle: a small circle with a line through it, distinct from the settlement markers, rendered with the same care as everything else in the image. Near one instance, partial script: "—ryu—."

The symbol does not appear in any cartographic convention you have encountered. It was placed here deliberately, meaning something specific to whoever made this.

CRITICAL SUCCESS: The three instances of the symbol form a rough triangle across the surviving sections. One falls at a location corresponding to this mountain range. The other two triangulate — approximately, accounting for the damage — to areas that would now be Kaze province interior and Sora province. Whatever the symbol marks, this temple is one of three on Hokori, and the other two are elsewhere.

Tangible Reward: Geographic leads recorded — Kaze province interior and Sora province. Both connect to threads active in the current investigation.

EXCEPTIONAL: A fourth instance of the symbol exists on the map, partially obscured by damage but recoverable with careful examination. It carries an additional mark above it — a small vertical stroke — that the other three instances lack. A distinction of some kind. Its location, accounting for the fragment's position, places it in what is now Hi province or the Hi/Tsuchi border region. Whatever stands there was considered differently from the other three. The additional mark suggests category rather than just presence.

Track Two — Insight

FAILURE: A map made to be used. Practical, careful. The damage makes it difficult to read anything deeper into the intent.

PARTIAL: The maker knew this geography — the care in the rendering, even in fragments, suggests someone who spent time in this landscape rather than working from secondary sources. The omissions feel more like damage than choice, but there is not enough intact to be certain.

SUCCESS: The settlement symbols are styled in a way that reads as decorative on casual inspection — integrated with surrounding imagery, easy to overlook as aesthetic rather than functional. The three circle-and-line symbols are embedded even more deliberately, placed where the surrounding palette and detail naturally draw the eye toward more prominent features. This information is present, but it is not announced. Whoever made this expected the map might be seen by people who should not understand it.

The intent behind this is not scholarly caution.

CRITICAL SUCCESS: The map was made during a period in which the maker could not protect what they were recording through concealment, so they protected it through obscurity instead. The mundane layer — coastlines, settlements, mountain ranges — is the camouflage. The symbol-marked locations are what the map actually exists to preserve. The damage, whatever caused it, removed the camouflage while leaving the symbols partly intact. The information survived in the layer that was most deliberately hidden.

Tangible Reward: Understanding how this order concealed information grants advantage on Investigation checks made to find hidden things elsewhere in the temple. The party now knows how these people hid what mattered.

EXCEPTIONAL: There is a fifth element on this map — not a symbol but an absence. The area corresponding to the mountains above a settlement in Kaze province has been left entirely blank. No topography. No symbols. No notation of any kind. On a map that renders even open water with some notation, this blank is not an oversight. Whatever stands in that location was known to the people who made this. They did not record it, and the absence of a record is itself a kind of record.

Activation Behavior

What Tapestry III shows on activation

The tapestry shows the sanctuary network's current state as of 16744. The terrain animates — coastlines, mountain shadows, settlement lights. The three circle-and-line markers do not behave identically.

Site states at time of activation:

Site State Visual
This temple (hub) Operational Steady single pulse, warm gold
Sora Acknowledged Slow double-beat, warmer tone than distress
Kaze Distress — unacknowledged Rapid pulse, sharp and bright
Hi/Tsuchi Offline No signal; fabric cold around marker

Why Kaze and Sora are frozen in these states

The Kaze distress signal and the Sora acknowledged state are not current communications. They are the last states set by practitioners at those sites during the fall of 13088, locked in when those practitioners were lost before they could stand them down. Both have been running into silence for thousands of years. The party, on restoring the orrery, is the first entity capable of receiving these signals since they were sent.

The emotional weight of this should be allowed to land without explanation. These signals may have been running for the entire duration of the temple's abandonment. The people who sent them did not know if anyone would ever receive them.

Kaze — re-escalation ambiguity

It cannot be determined from the tapestry alone whether Kaze's current distress state is the original unacknowledged transmission from 13088, or whether Kaze was acknowledged at some point and a surviving practitioner re-escalated before the site went silent. Re-escalation requires a deliberate act by a practitioner physically present at the site. Without a written record of hub operations, both possibilities remain open. Resolution requires the operational ledger from the chief priest's chamber.

Sora — acknowledged state

Someone sent the acknowledgement that shifted Sora into its current state. That acknowledgement exists in the network record. Whether it was the head priest, a junior priest acting independently, someone at the hub during the chaos of the fall — the tapestry cannot say. The acknowledgement was sent. Help never followed. Sora has been sitting in the held state of a promise that was made and not kept for thousands of years.

Hi/Tsuchi — offline distinction

A dormant site looks like an unlit lamp — infrastructure present, nothing feeding it. An offline site is distinguishable: the fabric around the Hi/Tsuchi marker is cold in a way dormant sites are not. The network registers the difference between a site that has gone quiet and a site that has been severed. Hi/Tsuchi is severed. The additional mark above its symbol, which distinguished it categorically from the other three sites in the historical rendering, takes on retrospective weight: whatever made it different may be connected to how it ended. Two sites died still transmitting. One died without making a sound.

The signal vocabulary — full system

State Visual Meaning How set
Operational Steady single pulse Site functional, no action needed Active practitioner at site
Distress Rapid pulse Urgent — unacknowledged crisis Active practitioner; locks if practitioner lost before standing down
Acknowledged Slow double-beat, warmer tone Distress received by hub; situation not resolved Hub sends double-pulse toward that site
Deliberate dark Two-beat then full stop Going quiet by choice; do not send Active practitioner at site
Offline No signal; cold fabric Connection severed or site destroyed Happens to the site, not set by it

The acknowledged state is processed by the network's foundational logic — it does not require a living practitioner at the receiving site to register. A frozen distress signal can receive and hold an acknowledgement millennia after the practitioner who sent it is gone.

The acknowledgement action

The party can send a double-pulse acknowledgement to Kaze and Sora from the hub. Doing so requires either the operator's manual or a DC 15 Arcana check to reason out the protocol from the mechanism. Sending the acknowledgement to Kaze shifts its display from rapid distress to the slow double-beat acknowledged state. The distress signal that has been running since the fall finally receives a response.

There is no one at either site to receive it. The acknowledgement is a record, not a rescue. A character who understands this and sends it anyway is doing something that is not tactically useful. Whether any of the party members are that kind of person is worth finding out at the table.

Hub pulse and party presence

The temple's operational marker does not require party presence to remain lit — the restored orrery feeds the node. Active sei presence brightens the signal. The pulse strengthens noticeably when the full party stands before the tapestry, dims when the hall is empty. Observable at DC 12 Perception.

The Kaze blank

The area in the Kaze highlands that was never recorded remains blank during activation — the ori-kioku cannot render what was never embedded in the fabric. The surrounding topography brightens slightly each time the hub pulses. Whatever occupies that location is responsive to the network signal without being part of the network. It receives without returning.

Hi/Tsuchi — Exceptional result only

If the party found the fourth symbol (the one with the additional vertical mark in Hi province or the Hi/Tsuchi border), look for it when the tapestry activates. It is offline. The fabric around it holds residual warmth distinct from the cold stillness of the other unlit markers — recent enough that the tapestry is still reading it. Something with sufficient sei presence to register as a network node was active at that site and is no longer. Days or weeks, not centuries.

Tapestry IV — The First Head Priest

East wall, north end. Well-preserved upper two-thirds; lower third missing entirely.

At a glance: A single figure, large in scale, occupying the full width of the tapestry. Robed. Dragonborn. One hand extended, palm up, holding something small. The face has been worked at — the eyes gouged out with the same kind of tool that left marks on the pillars, but applied with more force.

Track One — Investigation or Perception

FAILURE: An important figure whose face has been removed. The object in the extended hand is too small to make out from this distance.

PARTIAL: A formal portrait — the defacement matches the pillar work in technique. Gold-scaled Dragonborn. The hand is extended in a specific gesture, something small resting on the palm.

SUCCESS: The object in the extended hand is a disc — circular, palm-sized. The gesture is specific: weight shifted, arm extended, the body's orientation suggesting receipt rather than offering. The free hand rests on something in the missing lower third, angled as though what lay beneath it mattered enough to present. Around the gouged sockets where the eyes were, the thread beneath the damage is still faintly visible at the right angle of light — a ghost of color. Something amber, or close to it.

The defacement here was not applied with the same evenhandedness as the pillar work. This face was addressed with more force than the others.

CRITICAL SUCCESS: The amber thread at the eye sockets is not the warm brown-amber of the clan's general palette — it is a specific, vivid shade that reads almost luminous in the cold torchlight. The disc in the extended hand matches in proportion the bronze disc carried by the figure in the sealed dormitory room. The posture is an investiture gesture — not the assumption of authority but the moment of its bestowal from somewhere above. This figure is being given something.

Ko'jiri Tangible Reward: The amber eyes. The statue in the Grand Hall. The eyes that oriented toward Ko'jiri when he crossed the threshold. Ko'jiri gains advantage on all Charisma checks within the temple for the remainder of this visit. Do not explain the connection. Let him make it.

EXCEPTIONAL: Along the lower border of the surviving fabric, running the full width just above where the missing third begins, a line of very small, very dense Old Imperial text is stitched into the decorative border. Most is lost with the missing section. At the right edge, perhaps eight characters survive: "...wa shinanai." The rest of the sentence is gone.

Track Two — Religion

FAILURE: A devotional portrait — standard format for a religious institution commemorating its leadership. The defacement is desecration of a familiar kind.

PARTIAL: The vestments are high-order ceremonial, indicating significant religious authority. The posture marks a moment of formal consecration rather than administrative appointment.

SUCCESS: The robe's border is not decorative — it is a liturgical record in the Golden Dragon order's visual theology. Reading left to right across the surviving fabric: four symbols in sequence, each rendered distinctly. Creation. Covenant. Stewardship. Silence. These are obligations, rendered in the order's formal symbolic language — not descriptions of rank but declarations of commitment. The fourth symbol, Silence, is stitched at a larger scale than the other three. In this tradition, the final duty of the founding priesthood was not to speak but to keep — to hold something without disclosing it.

This portrait does not record what this person did. It declares what they promised not to say.

CRITICAL SUCCESS: The extended hand — the specific gesture, not the general posture — appears in Golden Dragon religious imagery in only one context: the receipt of a direct commission from a divine source rather than a human or institutional authority. This person was not appointed by a council or a clan. They were commissioned directly. In the tradition's theology, this gesture is reserved for moments when a dragon has personally conferred an obligation on a mortal.

Tangible Reward: Understanding the order's founding as a direct commission — not devotion but a task assigned at the source — reframes the purpose of every room in this temple. The party gains advantage on Religion and History checks for the remainder of the first floor.

EXCEPTIONAL: The four symbols — creation, covenant, stewardship, silence — appear on this tapestry's border. They also appear elsewhere: fragments in the stonework of the dormitory corridor, in the carved frieze around the Inner Sanctum door, at the base of the great statue in the Grand Hall. The order embedded its founding charge into the architecture of the entire building. The message is consistent across every surface. Silence is always rendered largest.

Activation Behavior

The mandate connection: The Kinryu no Chikara mandate requires a short ritual — a spoken statement of genuine intent — for inscription. This works regardless of whether the party has witnessed the activation. However, a character who has watched the border sequence perform its obligations in order, who has seen the investiture gesture as it was originally made, who has felt the weight of Silence holding longest — is performing the inscription ritual with knowledge that changes what the ritual is. Not a bureaucratic formality but a deliberate repetition of a specific act witnessed across millennia.

The practical distinction of this additional layer is left to the DM. It could manifest as an extended benefit, a deeper attunement to the temple's foundational magic, or simply the understanding that the Silence obligation is the most significant one and has been accepted knowingly rather than incidentally.

The glance and the paper: At one point in the activation cycle — after the border sequence has run at least once, not at the opening — the figure's formal posture breaks slightly. The head turns briefly toward the position of Tapestry III on the opposite wall. Then the hand not holding the disc lifts a loose sheet of paper into the lower frame of the surviving image, held preparatory to writing. The gesture lasts a beat. The posture returns. The border sequence continues.

The paper is not ceremonial. The glance is not part of the ritual. This is the head priest doing their job between the moments the record was made to commemorate. No check required to see it — it occurs in the surviving upper two-thirds and is visible to anyone watching the full cycle. A character who notices the direction of the glance and looks where the figure looked will find themselves facing Tapestry III.

The head priest's monitoring practice: The head priest did not personally monitor Tapestry III — that was the assigned duty of a designated monitor, a junior priest or specialist whose role was to watch the network and escalate state changes up the chain. What the activation shows is the head priest receiving a report and moving to log it. The glance toward the map tapestry is verification — checking the displayed state against what they have just been told — not direct observation.

This means the ledger in the bronze box is the head priest's record of significant events that rose to their level, not a complete operational record. The monitor's working log, which would contain routine activity, almost certainly existed and is not preserved.

[SEALED]

DM NOTES — Tapestry Supplement

Running Two Tracks Naturally: Do not present this as a skill-check menu. Let players declare their approach — "I try to read the thread texture closely" is Arcana on Tapestry II; "I try to understand what this ceremony depicts" is Track One. Name the secondary skill option only if a player seems stuck or asks what else they might try. The system should feel like natural investigation, not a mechanical selection.

The Most Strategically Significant Content: Tapestry III carries the most consequential information across both tracks. The sanctuary markers (Track One, Critical Success and above) point toward locations relevant to the Order of the Ancient Guard's deepest purpose. The Insight track's Exceptional result — the deliberate blank over a Kaze province location — connects the Gekko investigation to the temple's founders in ways the party cannot yet fully map. If this information reaches the wrong hands, it has tactical value. Consider whether any faction learns the party was in this temple and might reason backward to what they found.

The Fresh Sei Trace in Tapestry II: The Arcana track's Exceptional result is the supplement's most immediately actionable piece of information. The Kokuryu-aspected sei fingerprint readable in the tapestry appears again on the broken ward anchors in the Inner Sanctum door frame. A party that makes both connections has identified — before ever meeting the temple's primary occupant — which of the current inhabitants broke the sanctum's seals. That is meaningful foreknowledge for what follows.

The Border Theology of Tapestry IV: Creation, covenant, stewardship, silence. A player who engages with this on the Religion track and then later notices the same symbols on the sanctum frieze or at the statue's base will understand the order's purpose before they find any written record of it. That is the preferred sequence — let the architecture teach first, let Kinjiro's journal confirm. Not the reverse.

"...wa shinanai": Do not translate unless a player asks and makes DC 12 History or a relevant language check. When they ask: give them exactly "does not die" and nothing more. The subject of the sentence is gone with the missing lower third. What does not die is a question the text cannot answer. Let it remain one.

Ko'jiri Across All Four: Tapestry I (History track advantage, celestial alignment recognition), Tapestry II (Arcana — his sorcerous nature may sensitize him to the sei residue), Tapestry IV (Track One advantage, Charisma reward, the amber eyes). A player who engages seriously with all four tapestries as Ko'jiri should leave this hall with a meaningfully different sense of what this place is and what his character's relationship to it might mean. Do not rush this accumulation.

Pacing: Not every player will examine every tapestry. Not every tapestry needs both tracks explored. The Exceptional tier rewards genuine investment — it is not obligatory. Everything here remains available on return visits if the party moves through quickly on first pass.

locations.name: The Zasu's Ritual Scrolls — Hebi no Hensen

text.content:
Type
location-item
Status
active

Found on or near the Nagaji Zasu's body after the encounter in the Inner Sanctum (Room 6). A bundle of documents carried by the creature — some rolled tightly inside a cracked leather scroll case lashed to the body with strips of torn silk, others loose and partially crushed beneath its coils.

[KNOWN]

Physical Description:

The scroll case is lacquered hardwood, once fine, now split along one seam and discoloured by sustained contact with scaled flesh. It is lashed to the Zasu's midsection with strips of silk torn from what was once a formal obi — deep indigo fabric with a barely visible mon: a crescent moon above still water.

Inside: seven documents in varying states of preservation. Not a single unified text — a collection, assembled from multiple sources over time. Some are written in the same hand. Others are not.

The Bundle:

  1. Three intact sheets — Heavy mulberry paper, brushwork in formal seimaster notation. Dense. Technical. Written in a dialect of Classical Kagekunian that predates the current era by centuries. Not a language any living scholar would read fluently, but structural elements are recognizable to anyone trained in arcane or historical study.

  2. One large diagram — Folded repeatedly and worn soft at the creases. Ink faded at the edges but the central image is clear: a human figure enclosed in concentric rings of notation, with lines radiating outward to seven points. The figure's outline blurs at the extremities — the arms taper, the legs merge, the head elongates. Whether this depicts a process or a result is not immediately clear.

  3. Two damaged pages — Charred along one edge, as though pulled from a fire before the damage was complete. The surviving text is fragmentary. Diagrams of something anatomical — bones? Muscles? The proportions are wrong for a human body. Marginal annotations in a second, more hurried hand.

  4. One loose leaf — Thinner paper, different ink, different hand entirely. A list or index of some kind — short entries, each followed by a location reference and a symbol. Several entries have been circled. One has been crossed out with a single deliberate stroke.

[DISCOVERABLE]

Investigation & Identification

  • Identify the scroll case's origin (DC 12 Investigation)
  • Identify the obi fabric and mon (DC 13 Investigation or DC 11 History with Gekkō knowledge)
  • Read the intact sheets — surface meaning (DC 14 Arcana)
  • Read the intact sheets — deeper understanding (DC 17 Arcana)
  • Interpret the large diagram (DC 13 Arcana or DC 14 Medicine)
  • Read the damaged pages (DC 15 Arcana; DC 13 if diagram already interpreted)
  • Interpret the loose leaf index (DC 14 Investigation)
  • Identify the crossed-out entry (DC 16 History or DC 14 with Ko'jiri's Golden Dragon advantage)
  • Recognize the reversal reference (DC 18 Arcana; DC 15 if intact sheets already read at deeper understanding)

Check Results

The Scroll Case — DC 12 Investigation: The case itself is seimaster's equipment — purpose-built for transporting documents that carry active sei residue. The interior is lined with a thin copper-leaf layer designed to insulate the contents from ambient magical interference. This is not a general-purpose scroll case. It was made for carrying something dangerous, or at least something that interacted with sei in ways that required containment.

The Obi and Mon — DC 13 Investigation (or DC 11 History with prior Gekkō knowledge): The silk is from a formal obi — the width, weave, and indigo dye are consistent with dress worn by clan leadership or senior retainers during official functions. The mon embroidered into the fabric is a crescent moon reflected in still water. Any character who has encountered Clan Gekkō's heraldry — or studied the independent clans — recognizes this as the Gekkō clan crest. The Zasu was carrying documents bound to its body with a strip of its own formal clothing.

The Intact Sheets — DC 14 Arcana (Surface Reading): The notation system is recognizable as seimaster technical writing — the equivalent of a magical research language. The three sheets describe a process. Something is being channelled through a living subject. The terminology is archaic but the structural grammar matches transformation magic — not illusion, not transmutation in the temporary sense, but permanent alteration of a living form. References to "the vessel" and "the shape beyond" appear repeatedly. The tone is clinical. There is no ethical framing anywhere in the text — no discussion of consent, consequence, or reversal. It reads like instructions, not philosophy.

The Intact Sheets — DC 17 Arcana (Deeper Understanding): At this level of comprehension, specific details emerge. The transformation described is not a single event but a cascading process — once initiated in one subject, it propagates through sei-bonded individuals in proximity. The ritual was designed for a group, not an individual. The source tradition is not Golden Dragon — the foundational theory, the sei-alignment patterns, the structural logic all point to Kokuryu. Onyx Dragon magical tradition. A character who knows anything about the dragon clans understands immediately: this was never Kinryū's work. Someone found Kokuryu research and tried to use it.

The text also references a prerequisite — a "site of origin" where the sei conditions are correct for the initial casting. The site is not named. But the geographic and environmental markers described (acoustic distortion, thermal anomalies, hollow stone formations) do not match any location the party has visited. They match somewhere else. Somewhere in Kaze Province.

The Large Diagram — DC 13 Arcana or DC 14 Medicine: The figure at the center is human. The process depicted moves outward through the concentric rings — each ring representing a stage. The outermost ring shows a form that is no longer human. Limbs have fused. The spine has elongated. The skull has narrowed and stretched. A medical eye (DC 14 Medicine) recognizes that this is not artistic abstraction — the anatomical transitions are rendered with the precision of someone who understood exactly how a human body would need to change to arrive at the depicted result. The seven radiating points correspond to sei meridian nodes in the body — the same points targeted in advanced healing magic, but inverted. Whatever this process does, it rewrites the subject at the level of their sei architecture. There is no "off" described anywhere on the diagram.

The Damaged Pages — DC 15 Arcana (DC 13 if diagram already interpreted): Fragmentary, but enough survives to understand: these pages describe what happens after the transformation. Behavioral changes. Cognitive deterioration over time — described not as a flaw but as a known parameter. The phrase that survives most completely translates roughly as: "the mind narrows to the form." A character who has already interpreted the diagram understands: the transformation was known to degrade rational thought. Whoever designed this ritual documented the cognitive cost and included it anyway. The annotations in the second hand — more hurried, less formal — appear to be someone's attempt to calculate timelines. How long before the subject loses coherent speech. How long before decision-making capacity degrades below functional thresholds. The numbers are partially burned away, but the progression described is measured in months, not years.

The Loose Leaf Index — DC 14 Investigation: A reference list. Each entry consists of a short descriptor (a place or a thing, not a person), a location reference using a coordinate system the party does not recognize, and a symbol from a set of about a dozen recurring glyphs. The format is consistent with a research index — a scholar's shorthand for tracking source materials across multiple sites. Several entries have been circled in the same ink as the intact sheets. One entry — near the bottom of the list — has been crossed out with a single, deliberate horizontal stroke. The ink used for the strike-through is different from everything else on the page. Newer.

The Crossed-Out Entry — DC 16 History (DC 14 with Ko'jiri's Golden Dragon Clan advantage): The struck entry's descriptor translates loosely as "the golden restoration" or "the golden counter-work." Its location reference, while in the same unrecognized coordinate system as the rest, includes a secondary notation that uses directional language consistent with mountain-interior positioning. A character with knowledge of the Golden Dragon Clan's history (Ko'jiri) recognizes the phrasing: "counter-work" is a term used in Golden Dragon magical tradition for a specifically developed countermeasure to another clan's magic. The crossed-out entry refers to a Golden Dragon response to whatever this ritual represents. It exists — or existed — somewhere. And whoever crossed it out knew it was there and chose to mark it as eliminated, completed, or irrelevant.

The Reversal Reference — DC 18 Arcana (DC 15 if intact sheets already read at deeper understanding): Buried in the technical language of the intact sheets, between two passages describing sei-channel alignment during the transformation's second phase, is a parenthetical notation — almost an aside. It translates approximately as: "Restoration of original form requires inversion at the site of origin, using the counter-work of the golden tradition, during a convergence of the three lights." Three components. A location (site of origin — wherever the ritual was first performed). A method (the Golden Dragon countermeasure — the crossed-out entry on the index). A timing condition (convergence of the three lights — a celestial alignment involving Kagekuni's three stars). The notation is not a guide. It is a footnote — an acknowledgement that reversal is theoretically possible, recorded with the clinical detachment of someone cataloguing edge cases, not someone who expected it to matter.

[SEALED]

DM Notes

Why the Zasu carries these: The chief seimaster gathered these documents before performing the ritual on himself — the last to undergo it, trying to maintain enough awareness to lead his transformed people. He kept them because some fragment of the scholar he was still compels him to. The scrolls are lashed to his body the way a drowning person holds a rope. He cannot read them anymore. He cannot remember why they matter. But he will not let them go.

The obi: The strip of formal clothing binding the case to the Zasu's body is a detail that should land quietly. This creature dressed itself. Or — more precisely — something that was becoming this creature took the time to secure these documents to its body using a piece of its own ceremonial clothing before the transformation completed. The crescent moon mon is facing outward. Whether that was intentional is unknowable.

Narrative function: These scrolls serve three purposes simultaneously:

  1. Dot-connection for the Gekkō investigation. The Gekkō mon on the obi, the transformation ritual in the sheets, and the Nagaji the party has been fighting begin to form a single picture. The party doesn't need to reach the full conclusion here — but they should leave this encounter with a growing unease that the Nagaji are not what they assumed.

  2. Breadcrumb toward the Order of the Black Lily. The "site of origin" referenced in the reversal notation — with its acoustic distortion, thermal anomalies, and hollow stone — describes a location in Kaze Province. The party doesn't know that yet. When they reach Kaze and encounter those geographic features, the scrolls become a key that unlocks a door they didn't know they were carrying.

  3. Breadcrumb toward the Golden Dragon countermeasure. The crossed-out entry on the index tells the party two things: a reversal exists (or existed), and someone — the Zasu, before the transformation — knew about it and struck it from the list. Whether he crossed it out because he believed it was destroyed, because he had already looked for it and failed, or because he wanted to ensure no one pursued it, is deliberately ambiguous. The party may interpret this differently depending on their read of the Zasu — as a warning, a surrender, or a sabotage.

What the scrolls do NOT reveal:

  • They do not name Clan Gekkō, Masota Gekkō, or any individual
  • They do not explain why the ritual was performed
  • They do not describe where the "site of origin" is (geographic markers only — no place names)
  • They do not confirm that the Nagaji the party has fought are transformed people (the connection is inferential, not explicit)
  • They do not provide enough information to perform the reversal — only to know that one theoretically exists and requires three components the party does not yet have

Ko'jiri's unique position: Ko'jiri's advantage on Golden Dragon History checks makes him the most likely party member to identify the crossed-out entry's significance. This is by design — the con artist who faked Golden Dragon expertise is now the person whose genuine research matters most. If Ko'jiri is the one who identifies the "golden counter-work" reference, the narrative irony completes: the knowledge he built to deceive is the knowledge that may save an entire clan.

Timing and pacing: The scrolls are meant to be studied, not instantly decoded. Encourage the party to examine them over a short rest or between encounters. The check DCs are set so that a single character is unlikely to extract everything in one pass — this is a puzzle that rewards collaboration. The fighter won't read the Arcana. The sorcerer won't catch the History. The druid might notice the Medicine angle on the diagram. Everyone has something to contribute, and the full picture only emerges when they share what they've found.

frontmatter.name: The Zasu's Ritual Scrolls — Hebi no Hensen

text.content:
Type
core

The archipelago's recorded history stretches back more than eight thousand years — and its unrecorded history stretches back further still. What follows is the account as it is understood by scholars, priests, and the educated classes of Kagekuni. Some of it is reliable. Some of it is myth layered over truth. Some of it is truth layered over something deeper that no one alive fully remembers.

The Ages of Kagekuni

Period Years Name
Pre-Imperial Before ~8000 Age of Dragons
Imperial Founding ~8000–8611 Era of the First Emperors
First Golden Age 8611–13050 The Golden Age
Age of Strife 13050–13088 War of Fractured Banners
Dark Ages 13088–15642 The Long Dark
Recovery 15642–15691 Jinshō Reformation
Second Golden Age 15691–15757 Era of New Discovery
Subtle Awakening 15757–16620 Return of Talents
Great Awakening 16620–present Magic Restored
Current 16744 Post-Imperial Crisis

Age of Dragons — Before ~8000

Before there were emperors, before there were clans, before there were borders drawn on maps or roads cut through mountains — there were dragons.

Seven dragon clans ruled the archipelago of Kagekuni, each sovereign over its own island or territory. Their domains were not kingdoms in the human sense but spheres of influence, shaped by the nature of each dragon and the land they inhabited. The Crimson Clan held the volcanic island of Fushichō. The Azure Clan commanded the waters around Kawa. The Emerald Clan tended the forests and plains of Hokori. The Onyx Clan ruled from Tatara in shadow and cunning. The Golden Clan mediated from the highlands of central Hokori. The Silver Clan kept the cold northern waters and the island of Fuukajima. The Amethyst Clan studied the arcane from Shizukajima.

The earliest mortal settlers arrived in this world and found it already governed. They did not conquer — they integrated. The first communities paid tribute to their local dragon clan, adopted their customs, and in time became part of the social fabric the dragons had built. Intermingling between dragonborn, humans, and the founding clans produced the near-immortal Arcadian leaders who became the first daimyō — mortal rulers who carried draconic blood in their veins and governed with the implicit blessing of the dragons above them.

Over centuries, the dragons gradually withdrew from direct rule. Whether this was a deliberate abdication, a slow retreat into contemplation, or something else entirely depends on which account you trust. By the time the first emperor rose, the dragons had become figures of reverence rather than governance — still present in memory and tradition, but no longer sitting at the head of the table.

Era of the First Emperors — ~8000–8611

The age of dragons ended and the age of emperors began with a single figure: Tenryū no Mikado.

Tenryū ascended to power around the year 8000. He was already 852 years old — an Arcadian of mixed Crimson and Golden dragon lineage, carrying the blood of fire and justice in a single line. His unification of the archipelago was not achieved through war alone. Tenryū was a diplomat as much as a conqueror, binding clans through marriage alliances, trade agreements, and appeals to shared identity as often as through force of arms.

Not all clans submitted willingly. The Crimson Clan fractured over the question of imperial loyalty. The eastern faction accepted Tenryū's authority and joined the empire. The western faction, loyal to the dragon Akaryū, refused submission and withdrew into the volcanic ranges of the Akaho Sanmyaku on Fushichō. Their descendants live there still — loose tribal confederacies preserving traditions the rest of the empire forgot.

The Battle of Seirei Mizuumi secured the island of Kawa and broke the naval power of the Azure Clan, bringing the eastern waters under imperial control.

The gravest threat to the young empire came from Tatara. Kokuryū — the Onyx Dragon — refused to accept Tenryū's authority and launched the Onyx Rebellion in 8238. What followed was not a war in the conventional sense but a four-hundred-year guerrilla campaign fought across the shadowed mountains and tunnels of Tatara. The rebellion ended only with the destruction of Kuroi Yama — the Onyx Clan's fortress mountain — though Kokuryū himself escaped. The dragon was never captured, never killed, and never seen again.

Tenryū no Mikado died in the year 8694. His son, Ryūhiko no Mikado, was already 794 years old when he ascended the throne. The imperial dynasty was established, and the long peace began.

The Golden Age — 8611–13050

For nearly four and a half thousand years, Kagekuni flourished.

Eight emperors reigned across the Golden Age: Tenryū, Ryūhiko, Seiryū, Byakuryū, Kinryū, Shoryū, Inaryū, and Kōryū. Under their rule, the archipelago achieved a level of civilisation, artistic refinement, and magical sophistication that has never been equalled.

The great constructions of the Golden Age defined the physical landscape of the empire. The Imperial Palace in Heian became the architectural heart of the nation. The Great Library at Seirei Mizuumi on Kawa gathered the accumulated knowledge of civilisation under one roof. The Grand Canal of Mizushima connected inland waterways into a navigable system spanning provinces. The Hoshino Tō — a grand observatory — rose on the slopes of Shirogane Yama, and the Kokuyō Ryūkyūjō fortress on Tatara brought order to the Onyx Clan's former territory. The Emperor's Highway, completed in 11248, extended from Heian in three directions, and to this day everything important in Hokori is measured by its distance from that road.

Sei — the magic energy flowing through all living things — was fully accessible and deeply understood. Seimasters studied with the rigour of astronomers, supported by institutions whose traditions stretched back to the dragon clans themselves. Architecture incorporated magical principles. Agriculture was enhanced by sei-attuned cultivation. The boundary between the natural and the supernatural was not a line but a gradient, and the educated classes moved through both with fluency.

It could not last. Nothing built on that scale ever does.

The War of Fractured Banners — 13050–13088

The Golden Age ended in blood.

The spark was Tatara. The eternal feud between the Zirak and Glimfyr — dwarves and gnomes sharing an island neither was willing to surrender — had been managed for millennia through imperial intervention. When that intervention weakened, the feud spread. What began as a regional conflict metastasised into empire-wide war as clans chose sides, old grievances resurfaced, and the bonds that had held civilisation together for four thousand years snapped one by one.

Emperor Kōryū no Mikado was slain on the battlefield in 13053 — the first emperor to die in combat in the empire's history. His son, Ryūjin no Mikado II, ascended the throne and made the decision that would shape the next era: he established the Shogunate, appointing Kazutaka no Kazuhiko as the first Shōgun — supreme military commander with the authority to compel obedience from the daimyō.

The war raged across the archipelago. The Defence of Midoriko, the Pursuit to Kumoji, the Campaign in Tatara, the Burning of Shirotsuru, the Siege of Fushichō, the Ambush at Tatsumaki Gorge, and the Battle of the Thunder Plains — each left its mark on the land and the people who survived it. Two clans — the Seiryū and the Hagane — were destroyed entirely, their names erased from the rolls of the living.

The war ended in 13062. But something else ended with it — something no one understood at the time.

Magic vanished.

The Long Dark — 13088–15642

The disappearance of sei was not a sudden event but a slow bleeding that scholars only recognised in retrospect. By the time the war ended and the empire looked up from its wounds, the bleeding was catastrophic.

The secondary stars in the sky — Susanoo and Tsukuyomi — had been fading. Within decades of the war's end, both had crossed below naked-eye visibility. The night sky, which had burned with three stars for all of recorded history, now held only the golden light of Amaterasu. The other two were simply gone.

With them went the complex magical expressions that had sustained civilisation. Healing failed. Transformation magic fell silent. What remained was Amaterasu's baseline: enough sei to sustain life, agriculture, and the physical world, but not enough to power the institutions, the architecture, or the knowledge systems that the Golden Age had built.

The collapse was total. Famine swept the archipelago as sei-enhanced agriculture reverted to conventional farming on land that could not support the populations the Golden Age had sustained. Disease followed famine. The population of the archipelago fell by nearly half. The Temple of Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji — one of the great institutions of the Golden Age — fell in 13088, its surviving worshippers departing into an empire that no longer had use for their knowledge.

The Dark Ages lasted approximately three thousand years. Little documentation survives. Entire cities were abandoned to silence and weather. The knowledge of sei, the scholarly traditions, the institutional memory of how magic worked and what it meant — all of it was lost. The world that emerged on the other side was not the same world that had entered the darkness.

DM Note — The Great Aphelion

The sei drought was not caused by the war or by any mortal action. It was a cosmological event.

The three stars of the Miyosai trinary system orbit a common gravitational centre on independent orbital inclinations. Once in recorded history, all three reached maximum mutual distance simultaneously — the Great Aphelion, approximately 14344. Amaterasu, carrying Seizan with it, swung to one extreme of its barycentric arc while Susanoo and Tsukuyomi retreated to opposing extremes on their own inclined planes. The distances compounded geometrically.

Amaterasu never went dark — its baseline sei sustained life throughout. But the complex magical expressions that depended on the full trinary system became inaccessible. The dark ages were cultural and intellectual collapse, not extinction.

The Progenitor dragons entered their slumber during this same period. Whether the aphelion caused the slumber, the slumber caused the sei drought, or both share a common cause remains unknown — even to the Order of the Ancient Guard.

No living scholar has assembled the complete picture. The data exists in fragmentary astronomical records across multiple institutions, but no one has connected the dots. The Golden Dragon Clan's observatory at Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji contained the most complete model of the Miyosai system ever constructed — a mechanical and arcane orrery capable of projecting celestial positions across millennia. It has not been operational since the temple fell.

The Jinshō Reformation — 15642–15691

Recovery, when it came, was not magic returning. It was a single emperor deciding that the empire would not die quietly.

Jinshin no Mikado ascended the throne in 15642 and enacted sweeping reforms that dragged Kagekuni back from the edge. Agricultural revival came first — new cultivation techniques, land redistribution, irrigation projects that did not rely on sei. Infrastructure followed — roads rebuilt, bridges repaired, harbours dredged. Trade stimulation reopened routes that had been abandoned for centuries. An educational revival rebuilt the scholarly institutions, and the Great Library — destroyed by an earthquake during the dark ages — was partially restored.

Jinshin also established the Kokushi Kyōkai in its recognisable modern form, creating the positions of Seimu Daijin (Minister of Administration) and Zaiumu Daijin (Minister of Finance) to manage the empire's civilian machinery. The framework he built — imperfect, incomplete, but functional — is the same framework that governs Kagekuni today, eight hundred years later.

The Era of New Discovery — 15691–15757

The Jinshō Reformation stabilised the empire. What followed was the discovery that the empire was not alone.

In 15691, an expedition led by Admiral Taira no Akinori and General Tokugawa no Ryūji, with diplomat Hōjō no Kaoru as its political voice, sailed beyond the known waters of the Raijin no Fukai sea and discovered lands beyond Kagekuni. They returned with slaves, precious metals, new knowledge, and the unsettling revelation that the world was larger than anyone had imagined.

Over the next sixty years, more than 150 expeditions followed. The discoveries were transformative — and destabilising. New wealth poured into the archipelago, but it flowed unevenly. Clans with naval reach grew rich. Clans without it watched their neighbours outpace them. Rivalries that had simmered for centuries found new fuel.

The Emperor responded by appointing Minamoto no Katsuro of the Tenshiko Clan as Shōgun around 16012. Katsuro enacted a series of regulatory acts — the Expedition Regulation Act, the Resource Distribution Act, the Peace and Mediation Act, and the Defence Enhancement Act — that imposed order on the chaos. When the crisis passed, the Shogunate retired voluntarily. Hōjō no Kaoru was appointed the first Gaikō Daijin (Minister of Foreign Affairs), extending the Kokushi Kyōkai to five ministers.

The Return of Talents — 15757–16620

The stars were coming back. No one knew it yet.

Around 15757, a child was born in Kagekuni with the ability to call lightning from clear air. His name was Hikari no Kenta, and he was the first known Talent — an individual born with innate magical ability in a world that had not seen magic in over three thousand years.

The reaction was not welcoming. Kenta was feared, studied, and eventually persecuted. He was not alone for long — other Talents emerged across the archipelago, each manifesting different abilities without training, without teachers, and without a society that had any framework for understanding what they were. Many were hunted. Many formed underground communities for survival.

Notable Talents of this era included Mizuki no Hana of Clan Gekkō, who manifested shadow magic, and Fujimoto no Aiko of Clan Ryūkaze, who could manipulate wind. The Seishin Enclave was founded on the island of Unmeijima as a place of study and refuge for Talents — it eventually grew into the city of Seishin, the premier magical research institution in Kagekuni. Hikari no Shizuku, a healing and light magic tradition, established itself within the imperial capital of Heian.

The Epoch of Factional Flux — 16204–16434

The return of magic coincided with a period of intense political reorganisation. Over two centuries, the clan structure of Kagekuni was remade.

The Hōjō Clan tore itself apart in civil war, and the survivors merged with the Minamoto Clan to form Clan Kaminari — named in honour of Raijin, the spirit of thunder. Clan Ryūkaze absorbed smaller clans and became dominant in the northwest. The Yamamoto Clan splintered. The Ishikawa Clan dissolved entirely, and from its remnants the mercenary Clan Tetsujin emerged.

The political map that exists today — the alliances, the rivalries, the independent clans — was drawn during this period.

The Peasant Uprising — 16442–16461

Not all upheaval came from above. In 16442, a crackdown in Midoriko village sparked a peasant uprising that spread across multiple provinces. The emperor appointed Takeda no Hiroshi as Shōgun in 16443 to restore order. But this was not a rebellion that could be solved by swords alone. In 16453, the emperor created the position of Fukushi Daijin (Minister of Welfare) and appointed Hayashi no Haruto to address the underlying grievances — healthcare, education, and public assistance for the common people.

A combined military and diplomatic approach ended the uprising in 16461. The Shogunate again retired when its purpose was fulfilled.

The Plague Campaign of Kuroyami — 16609–16616

The defining trauma of the post-Awakening era.

Kuroyami no Akuma — born Takeda no Arata — discovered a necromantic tome in the cursed Kuroshi Temple on the haunted island of Yūrei. What he found there transformed him. He established the Eikyū Yami Clan — a cult of death — and raised armies of the undead. For seven years, his legions waged war across the archipelago, leaving devastation and plague in their wake.

The response united unlikely allies. Shōgun Minamoto no Katsuro was appointed in 16610 and made the unprecedented decision to recruit Talents — magical individuals the empire had spent centuries marginalising — into the war effort. The magical enclaves of Seishin, the Raimeiin, and the Forest of Spirits revealed themselves publicly for the first time, stepping out of the shadows to defend the world that had persecuted them.

Kuroyami was defeated. He was never captured or killed. His cult, the Eikyū Yami Clan, persists in some form. The question of where Kuroyami is — and what he has been doing for the last 128 years — is one that very few people ask aloud.

The Great Awakening — 16620–Present

Magic officially returned to the world around the year 16687, though the process had been building for decades. The Great Awakening was not a single moment but a threshold — the point at which sei became reliably accessible to trained practitioners rather than appearing only in rare Talents born with innate ability.

The daimyō moved quickly. Every clan began recruiting mages into their service. The magical institutions that had emerged during the era of Talents suddenly found themselves courted rather than feared. Seishin expanded from an enclave into a city. Magical study became a path to advancement rather than a mark of suspicion.

But the world that magic returned to was not the world it had left. The institutions, the knowledge, the scholarly traditions of the Golden Age were gone. The current generation of practitioners is rebuilding from fragments — studying sei with the tools of a civilisation that lost three thousand years of progress. They are learning fast, but they are learning without teachers, and the gaps in their understanding are significant.

DM Note — The True Cause of the Great Awakening

The Great Awakening was not a natural restoration of cosmic balance. It was the consequence of waking a single malevolent Progenitor.

Murasakiryū — the Amethyst Dragon — was awakened by dark mortals who believed they were performing a ritual to rouse Kokuryū (the Onyx Dragon). They were wrong about which dragon they found. Murasakiryū woke, and the dragon is now actively masquerading as Kokuryū — pretending to be the Onyx Dragon while pursuing its own agenda.

The moment of Murasakiryū's waking corresponds to the Great Awakening. Every sei user in Kagekuni draws power through the Amethyst Dragon's waking awareness. The implications of this are staggering and entirely unknown to the world at large.

Kinryū (the Golden Dragon) would serve as the natural counterbalance to Murasakiryū. The assassination of Solas Evergreen — a member of the Order of the Ancient Guard — was a deliberate act to prevent Kinryū's awakening. The cipher leading to methods for waking the Golden Dragon now rests with Relc, who may not fully understand what he carries.

The Post-Imperial Crisis — 16732–Present

The current crisis did not begin with war. It began with a reform.

In 16732, Emperor Ryūjin no Mikado — the eighteenth emperor, the last of the near-immortal Arcadian line — decreed that the Kokushi Kyōkai could no longer appoint a Shōgun without imperial approval. It was a safeguard. It may also have been a warning.

Seven years later, in 16739, Ryūjin died. The official cause was old age. He was the final link to an unbroken chain of rulers stretching back over eight thousand years. No confirmed successor has emerged. Multiple claimants have presented genealogical proof of varying credibility. None has secured recognition.

The Shogunate — the military authority that has historically held the empire together during periods of crisis — is legally frozen. There is no emperor to approve a Shōgun, and no Shōgun to impose order.

In 16742, war erupted between the Genso Alliance and the Arashi Alliance. Two years of escalating hostility have produced no decisive outcome. Three independent clans — Kaminari, Kurohana, and Gekkō — hold the balance of power, and every faction knows it.

The year is 16744. The throne sits empty. The war grinds on. Magic has returned to a world that does not fully understand it. And somewhere in the archipelago, things that slumbered during the long dark have begun to stir.

DM Note — The Emperor's Death

Ryūjin's death is not what it appears. The official story is old age, but foul play is suspected. Two independent daimyō — Raijin no Kazuhiko (Clan Kaminari) and Akihiko Kurohana (Clan Kurohana) — are both quietly investigating the circumstances. Neither has shared their suspicions publicly.

The 16732 reform that froze the Shogunate may have been motivated by Ryūjin's awareness of threats against the imperial line — a last attempt to prevent his enemies from consolidating power after his death.

Type
core

The archipelago of Kagekuni — the Shrouded Isles — rises from the Raijin no Fukai sea like the spine of something ancient and half-submerged. Five major islands and a scattering of lesser ones form a chain shaped by the collision of four tectonic plates, each island bearing the scars and gifts of the geology beneath it.
