Volcanic peaks trail smoke into skies where three stars wheel. Coastlines shift with the complex tides of four moons. Bamboo forests climb mountain flanks where the trees give way to pale crystal trunks that chime in the wind, and lowland rivers run faintly luminous at night through paddies of indigo grass.

This is a land that moves. Earthquakes shake its foundations. Typhoons rake its coasts. Monsoons swell its rivers and drown its roads. The people of Kagekuni have never known a still world, and their architecture, their agriculture, their faith, and their politics all reflect it. Castles are built to flex rather than resist. Villages relocate rather than rebuild. Shrines stand where the earth is quietest, and the earth is rarely quiet for long.

The pages that follow describe the islands, provinces, and settlements of Kagekuni — the places where power concentrates, where trade flows, where clans hold their seats, and where the spaces between destinations are as important as the destinations themselves. The roads of Kagekuni are not empty connective tissue. They are where travellers encounter the world as it actually is: the weather, the terrain, the people moving between places with purposes of their own. A three-day journey through the mountains is three days of the world revealing itself — not a gap to be skipped.

DM Note — Geography and Progenitor Domains

Each of the five major islands is connected to one or more of the seven Progenitor dragons. Their slumbering places are woven into the geography — hidden beneath mountains, within volcanic hearts, beneath lakes, or deep in forests that have grown undisturbed for millennia. The geography section entries do not reveal these connections, but the physical character of each island is shaped in part by the dragon that sleeps within it. When describing terrain, weather, and the feel of a place, the Progenitor's domain bleeds through: Fushichō's volcanic fury reflects Akaryū (Crimson); Kawa's waters reflect Aoryū (Azure). These are not coincidences — they are consequences.

Type
core

Kagekuni is a civilisation built on hierarchy. It is not a suggestion, not a tradition that has softened with time — it is the architecture of daily life, enforced by law, reinforced by custom, and internalised by nearly everyone who lives within it. From the moment a child is born, their place in the order is known. What they may do, where they may go, how they must speak to those above and below them — all of it is governed by structures older than most of the buildings they live in.

Understanding this society is essential to moving through it. The adventurer who ignores social rank will find doors closed, prices raised, and patience exhausted long before any blade is drawn.

The Imperial Order

At the apex of Kagekuni's political structure sits the Emperor — or, more precisely, the empty throne where an emperor should sit. For over eight thousand years, the imperial line traced its descent from Tenryū no Mikado, the first emperor, who united the warring dragon clans and forged the archipelago into a single civilisation. The emperor's authority was absolute in theory and considerable in practice, tempered by the realities of governing a vast island chain through intermediaries.

Beneath the emperor, the Shogun served as supreme military commander — a wartime appointment granted by imperial decree, carrying the authority to mobilise armies, impose martial law, and compel obedience from the daimyō. The position was never permanent by design. In practice, some shoguns held power for decades.

The Kokushi Kyōkai — the Council of Five Ministers — administers the empire's civilian machinery. Five departments cover the essential functions of governance:

Title Role
Anzen Hoshō Daijin Minister of Security — intelligence, imperial protectorate
Fukushi Daijin Minister of Welfare — healthcare, education, public assistance
Gaikō Daijin Minister of Foreign Affairs — diplomacy, trade, foreign nationals
Seimu Daijin Minister of Administration — provincial governance, infrastructure
Zaiumu Daijin Minister of Finance — treasury, taxation, revenue

Below the national level, provincial administration follows its own chain: Chiji (Governor) to Gunji (County Magistrate) to Shi (Municipal Assembly) to Shichō (Mayor) to Sonchō (Village Leader). In theory, each level answers to the one above. In practice, local power depends heavily on who controls the samurai in the region.

The Teikoku Keisatsu — the Imperial Police — maintain order at a local level. Once an empire-wide institution, the police have retreated to a regional footprint in the absence of central authority. They cooperate with local clan forces where relations allow it and operate independently where they do not.

The Three Castes

Kagekuni's population is divided into three castes. Movement between them is rare, difficult, and in most cases functionally impossible. A person's caste determines what occupations they may hold, who they may marry, where they may live, and how they are treated under law.

Kugai — The Elite

The ruling class. Kugai families claim descent from the imperial founders or the dragon clans that preceded them. In practice, the caste is dominated by humans and dragonborn, though other races with sufficient political connections have occasionally been elevated. The Kugai includes the daimyō, their courts, senior scholars, and the highest-ranking samurai — the hatamoto, or bannermen, who serve as personal retainers to clan lords.

Kugai families maintain genealogical records stretching back centuries. Some are genuine. Some are creative. All are taken seriously.

Zokumin — The Commonfolk

The broad middle of society, encompassing everyone from samurai to merchants. The Zokumin are not a single class but a gradient, and the distinctions within it matter enormously to those who live them.

At the top sit samurai in active service — warriors sworn to a lord, carrying the authority of their clan. Below them, rōnin — masterless samurai — occupy an uncomfortable middle ground: they retain the right to carry weapons but lack the social anchor of a lord's name. Below rōnin come peasants, who work the land and form the backbone of the food supply. Artisans follow — craftspeople whose skills are valued but whose social standing reflects the society's bias toward land and loyalty over craft. At the very bottom of the Zokumin sit merchants.

This last distinction is the source of chronic social tension. Merchants often possess considerable wealth — in some cases more than the samurai who look down on them. But wealth without rank buys comfort, not respect. A merchant who forgets this distinction will be reminded of it quickly and without sympathy.

Burakumin — The Outcasts

Those whose work involves death or pollution. Leather workers, butchers, executioners, undertakers, gravediggers — anyone whose livelihood touches the boundary between life and death. The Burakumin live in segregated communities called buraku, subject to limited civil rights and systemic harassment. They are not enslaved, but the freedoms available to them are narrow and the prejudice they face is open.

The caste system predates the current empire. It survived the Dark Ages, the return of magic, and every political upheaval in between. It will likely survive whatever comes next.

Honour

Honour in Kagekuni is not an abstraction. It is a currency, a weapon, and a sentence.

A samurai's honour determines their standing within their clan, their right to speak in councils, the marriages their children may make, and the manner of their death. Honour is earned through service, loyalty, and sacrifice. It is lost through cowardice, betrayal, or failure — and once lost, it is extraordinarily difficult to recover. A samurai who loses their honour may face exile, ritual punishment, or the expectation that they will take their own life to restore their family's name.

The codes of bushidō — the way of the warrior — govern samurai conduct. Duty to one's lord supersedes personal desire. Courage in battle is expected, not celebrated. Loyalty is absolute until the moment it isn't, at which point it becomes treason. The tension between these demands — when duty conflicts with conscience, when loyalty to a corrupt lord meets personal honour — is the engine that drives much of Kagekuni's political drama.

Honour applies differently across the castes. Peasants and merchants are not bound by bushidō, but they live within its shadow. A merchant who shames a samurai may find their shop burned. A peasant who fails to show proper deference may be struck without legal consequence. The social codes are enforced not by law alone but by a pervasive understanding that hierarchy is the natural order — and that those who disrupt it invite consequences not just for themselves but for their families.

The Peoples of Kagekuni

The archipelago is home to many races, though not all enjoy equal standing. Humans and dragonborn — particularly those claiming descent from the founding dragon clans — move through society with the fewest barriers. Other races face varying degrees of prejudice depending on the region, the local clan's attitudes, and the circumstances of their presence.

Race Cultural Name Notes
Elves Arcadians Near-immortal; the imperial line was Arcadian; last emperor Ryūjin died 16739
Dwarves Zirak Ancestral homeland in Mizuho, on the island of Tatara
Gnomes Glimfyr Ancestral homeland in Shugyoku, on the island of Tatara
Great Apes Guhuza Distinct race of Seizan; powerful build; fur from black to silvered; capable of great age
Dragonborn Dragonborn Prominent among the Kugai; claim descent from the founding dragons
Halflings Halflings Present across the archipelago; lower social standing

The Zirak and Glimfyr have maintained an eternal feud on their shared island of Tatara. They rarely stop fighting. Historically, only an emperor's direct command has imposed truces — and those truces have always ended sooner than intended. Their conflict once sparked the empire-wide War of Fractured Banners. With no emperor to restrain them, the feud has recently escalated again.

Characters who are not dragonborn, human, or the locally dominant non-human race will encounter prejudice in social situations. Doors close. Prices rise. Patience runs thin. This is not universal — individual NPCs may be more or less tolerant — but the systemic bias is real and pervasive.

The Military

War in Kagekuni is the domain of the samurai, but the dying is shared widely.

The military command hierarchy runs from the Shōgun (currently a vacant position) down through the daimyō, who command their clan's forces directly. Below the daimyō, the chain continues:

Sotaishō (Supreme Commander) → Karō (Chief Retainer) → Taishō (General) → Kumigashira (Squad Leader) → Kogashira (Corporal)

Samurai form the officer class, ranked from gokenin (housemen) through goshi (rustic warriors) to hatamoto (bannermen — the elite retainers of a daimyō). Below them, the ashigaru — peasant infantry — fill the ranks with sword, spear, and bow.

An extensive logistics corps of bugyō (commissioners) manages everything from weapons and armour to provisions, boats, and battlefield flags. War in Kagekuni is not simply a matter of warriors meeting on a field — it is an administrative enterprise requiring coordination across difficult terrain, unpredictable weather, and supply lines that stretch through mountains and across water.

The Ronin Crisis

The current political vacuum has produced a surge in rōnin — masterless samurai — at numbers not seen in living memory. Some lost their lords to the war. Others served clans that dissolved during the upheaval. Some walked away by choice, unable to reconcile their duty with their conscience.

Rōnin are a destabilising force. They retain the right to bear arms and the training to use them, but lack the social anchor of a lord's authority. Some seek new masters. Some sell their swords. Some turn to banditry. The roads of Kagekuni are significantly less safe than they were a decade ago, and rōnin are the primary reason.

Type
core

It has been fifty-one years since the Great Awakening. Within living memory, magic returned to a world that had forgotten it existed. The energy called sei — once woven through every living thing on Seizan — went silent for over three thousand years. When it returned, it returned to a world that had changed. Institutions built on magical foundations had long since crumbled. The knowledge, the traditions, the scholarly lineages that once sustained sei practice were gone. What emerged in their place was something rawer: individuals born with innate magical talent — Talents — appearing without warning, without teachers, and without a society that knew what to do with them.

The first Talents were persecuted. Later ones were tolerated, studied, and eventually recruited. Magical enclaves formed — Seishin on the island of Unmeijima became the premier research institution; Hikari no Shizuku established a healing tradition within the capital. By the time the Great Awakening made sei fully accessible again, the daimyo of Kagekuni were already competing to recruit mages into their service. Magic had returned. The question of who would control it had only just begun.

An Empire Without an Emperor

Emperor Ryūjin no Mikado — the eighteenth emperor, the last of the near-immortal elven line stretching back to the founding — died in 16739. The official cause was old age. He was the final link to an unbroken chain of rulers that began with Tenryū no Mikado over eight thousand years ago.

No confirmed successor has emerged. Multiple claimants have presented genealogical proof of varying credibility, but none has secured recognition from the Kokushi Kyōkai — the five government ministers who administer the empire. The ministers themselves are holdovers, functioning in constitutional limbo. They maintain taxation, law, infrastructure, and diplomacy, but they lack the authority to resolve the central crisis: who rules?

The problem is compounded by Ryūjin's final reform. In 16732, the emperor decreed that the Kokushi Kyōkai could no longer appoint a Shogun without imperial approval. The Shogunate — the military authority that has historically held the empire together during periods of crisis — is legally frozen. There is no emperor to approve a Shogun, and no Shogun to impose order.

DM Note — The Emperor's Death

Ryūjin's death is not what it appears. The official story is old age, but foul play is suspected. Two independent daimyo — Raijin no Kazuhiko (Clan Kaminari) and Akihiko Kurohana (Clan Kurohana) — are both quietly investigating the circumstances of the emperor's death. Neither has shared their suspicions publicly. The 16732 reform that froze the Shogunate may have been motivated by Ryūjin's awareness of threats against the imperial line — a last attempt to prevent his enemies from consolidating power after his death.

Hiroshi Nakamura, Shugo (military governor) of Heian in Kaminari territory, is a traitor working with the Genso Alliance. He is using his position to feed intelligence to Genso — likely connected to the larger political destabilisation.

War Between the Alliances

Into this vacuum, war has come. In 16742, tensions between two major clan alliances erupted into open conflict.

The Genso Alliance — Clans Fuyugiri, Homoruyama, Ryūkaze, and Tsuchiura — governs the provinces of Kusa and Tsuchi. The Arashi Alliance — Clans Arashiyama, Hoshizora, Shirotsuru, and Yūgure — governs Mizu and Nami. Two years of escalating hostility have produced no decisive outcome. Battles are fought, borders shift, villages burn, and the common people pay the price.

Three clans remain independent: Kaminari, Kurohana, and Gekkō. Their allegiance — or continued neutrality — could tip the war decisively. Every faction knows this. The independents are courted, threatened, and watched. They are the fulcrum on which the future of Kagekuni may turn.

The Clans

Clan Kaminari (Independent)

Governed by Raijin no Kazuhiko, the Storm-lord — a human warrior of 47 years who was born outside the clan and rose through martial prowess alone. Kaminari controls the Province of Hana and its capital, Heian — the imperial capital, now without an emperor. Known for mastery of storm magic and fierce warriors, Kaminari occupies the most politically sensitive position of any clan: they hold the seat of empire without the authority to claim it.

Clan Kurohana (Independent)

Led by Akihiko Kurohana — a black dragonborn of 54 years, tall and imposing, with scales like polished obsidian and eyes that glow faintly red. Kurohana maintains independence through strength and reputation. Their daimyo's intentions are difficult to read, which is precisely as he prefers it.

Clan Gekkō (Independent — Status Uncertain)

Daimyo Masota no Gekkō has not been seen publicly in some time. His clan's silence has drawn attention from both alliances and from the other independents. Rumours vary — illness, a power struggle within the clan, or something worse. The truth of Clan Gekkō's situation is one of the most pressing questions in Kagekuni's current politics.

DM Note — Clan Gekkō

Clan Gekkō attempted a dark ritual with catastrophic consequences. The entire clan — including Daimyo Masota no Gekkō — was transformed into Nagaji (serpent folk). Masota retains fragmented awareness, but his mental coherence is degrading over time. The longer the situation persists, the less of him remains to reach.

The Order of the Black Lily (Monastery of the Black Lily, above Akatsuki village in Kaze province) knows the truth and has been monitoring the situation. The party has already encountered and killed several Nagaji without knowing they were Gekkō clan members. The moral reckoning is pending.

A reversal may be possible but requires rare materials, specific conditions, or Progenitor involvement. The details are TBD.

Society in Flux

The Caste System

Kagekuni's social order is rigid, ancient, and under strain. Three castes define a person's place in the world:

The Kugai — the elite — are primarily humans and dragonborn who claim descent from the imperial founders. Daimyo, courtiers, scholars, and high-ranking samurai occupy this tier. Below them, the Zokumin — the commonfolk — encompass everyone from samurai and ronin to peasants, artisans, and merchants. Merchants sit at the bottom of the Zokumin despite their often considerable wealth, a source of constant social friction. At the lowest rung, the Burakumin — the outcasts — are those whose occupations involve death: leather workers, butchers, executioners, undertakers. They live in segregated communities with limited civil rights and face systemic harassment.

Race compounds caste. Dragonborn and humans — particularly those of the locally dominant lineage — move through society with relative ease. Others do not. Characters who are not of the dominant race in a given territory find doors closed, prices raised, and suspicion constant.

The Ronin Surge

With the political vacuum, the frozen Shogunate, and open war between the alliances, the number of masterless samurai — ronin — has reached an all-time high. Former retainers of dead lords, warriors whose clans dissolved during the Epoch of Factional Flux, and samurai who simply walked away from service they no longer believed in — all of them crowd the roads, the teahouses, and the employment boards of every town. Some seek honourable service. Others have abandoned honour entirely. The roads of Kagekuni have never been less safe.

Matters of the World

The Eruption of Akaho Sanmyaku

On Hachigatsu 29, 16744 — just days ago — the volcanic range of Akaho Sanmyaku on the northern island of Fushichō erupted. Ash is visible from as far as the Tenchūsan Ren mountains on Hokori. The eruption is ongoing. Fushichō has always been a land of fire and ancient secrets; what this eruption means for the settlements and peoples of that island remains to be seen.

Tatara — The Eternal Feud

On the southern island of Tatara, the ancient feud between the Zirak (dwarves) and the Glimfyr (gnomes) has escalated again. The conflict — which predates the War of Fractured Banners — has historically been held in check only by imperial decree. With no emperor to command restraint, old hatreds have resurfaced. Recent reports suggest the gnomes deliberately sabotaged a dwarven relic site, an act of provocation that the Zirak are unlikely to answer with diplomacy.

The Shadow of the Plague Campaign

The Plague Campaign of 16609–16616 remains the defining trauma of the post-Awakening era. Kuroyami no Akuma — once Takeda Arata, before he found a necromantic tome in the cursed Kuroshi Temple on the haunted island of Yurei — raised undead legions and waged a war that scarred the archipelago. The response united unlikely allies: the Shogun recruited Talents, and the magical enclaves of Seishin, the Raimeiin, and the Forest of Spirits revealed themselves publicly for the first time.

Kuroyami was defeated. He was never captured or killed. His cult, the Eikyū Yami Clan, persists in some form. The question of where Kuroyami is — and what he has been doing for the last 128 years — is one that very few people ask aloud.

The Magical Landscape

Magic is new. Not new to the world — new to the people living in it. Sei sustained civilisation for millennia before the dark ages, but the dark ages lasted long enough to erase nearly all institutional memory of how magic worked, who wielded it, and what it meant. The current generation of practitioners is rebuilding from fragments.

The major magical institutions known publicly are:

  • Seishin (Unmeijima) — The premier research institution, founded around the figure of Hikari no Kenta, the first known Talent. Now a city in its own right.
  • Hikari no Shizuku (Heian) — A healing and light magic tradition operating within the capital.
  • Raimeiin — Revealed during the Plague Campaign; methods and focus not widely known.
  • Forest of Spirits — Revealed during the Plague Campaign; associated with naturalistic sei traditions.
  • Order of the Tranquil Lotus (Unmeijima) — A nature-based monastic order near the town of Kazehama. Elder Benkei, a Guhuza of 198 years, leads the order.
  • Order of the Sacred Grove — A druidic tradition protective of specific sacred sites. Its former Guardian, Solas Evergreen, is deceased. A new Guardian has been appointed.

DM Note — The Order of the Ancient Guard

Behind the known orders lies the most secret organisation in Kagekuni: the Order of the Ancient Guard. Their purpose is the silent protection of the living founding dragons — the seven Progenitors who are believed dead but are in fact in deep slumber. The Ancient Guard maintains hidden sanctuaries, exerts subtle influence to prevent any single power from dominating, and guards the conditions under which the dragons remain safe and hidden.

Known members include Benkei (rank TBD) and the deceased Solas Evergreen (rank likely Protector or higher). Solas's murder means someone killed a member of the order protecting the dragons. The scope of the threat is unknown.

DM Note — The Progenitor Dragons

All seven founding dragons are alive, hidden in deep slumber across the archipelago. Their dormancy coincided with the Great Aphelion and the sei drought. Whether one caused the other, or both share a common cause, is unknown even to the Ancient Guard.

One exception: Murasakiryū (Amethyst Dragon, domain of arcane knowledge and divination) is awake — woken by dark mortals who believed they were awakening Kokuryū (Onyx). Murasakiryū is actively masquerading as Kokuryū. The Great Awakening (~16687) was not a natural restoration of magic — it was the consequence of waking a single malevolent Progenitor. Every sei user in Kagekuni draws power through Murasakiryū's waking awareness.

Solas Evergreen was killed to prevent the awakening of Kinryū (Golden Dragon, domain of honour and justice) — the natural counter-balance. Relc now holds Solas's mission: the Warden's Wisdom cipher that leads to methods for waking Kinryū.

The Season

It is Nagatsuki 1, 16744 — the first day of the Month of Long Nights, the opening of Aki. Autumn has arrived. The harvest is underway across the lowlands. Violet grasses are darkening toward black on the hillsides. Crystal-barked trees have begun to chime in the cooling mountain winds. The goldtail fish runs have started in the rivers.

Above, all three stars of the Miyosai system burn in the sky — Amaterasu's gold, Susanoo's blue-white, and Tsukuyomi's deep red. Fifty-one years ago, that was not the case. The eldest among you remember a sky with only one star. The world is brighter now. Whether it is safer remains to be seen.

Type
core

The Miyosai system is governed by three stars that orbit a common gravitational center. Their movements drive the great astrological events of Seizan, shaping weather, tides, and the flow of sei across the world. These are purely celestial phenomena — named after older divine concepts but not worshipped directly.

Amaterasu — The Golden Anchor

Type: Primary star, golden-yellow Character: Stable and foundational. Amaterasu is the most massive of the three stars and carries the entire planetary family — including Seizan — with it as it moves. Its warmth sustains life, agriculture, and the physical world. Magical Influence: Core life energy; baseline sei. The foundation upon which all other magical expression rests.

Susanoo — The Blue Storm

Type: Smaller blue-white dwarf Character: Complex and variable orbit. Susanoo produces both the closest stellar approaches and meaningful retreats. When it draws near to Seizan, the skies fill with blue-white atmospheric phenomena — ghost rainbows shimmer across the horizon and the air takes on a crystalline quality. This close approach is the celestial event known as Nagorikaze. Magical Influence: Water magic, healing, and purification. Susanoo's proximity intensifies all water-aspected sei. Coastal communities, healers, and maritime practitioners track its position closely.

Tsukuyomi — The Red Shadow

Type: Larger deep-red dwarf Character: Elongated orbit with the most dramatic near-far swing of the three stars. Tsukuyomi's routine orbital variation produces the astrological event known as Long Shadow — periods when transformation magic weakens and shadows behave strangely across the land. At perihelion (closest approach), its deep red light casts visible daytime shadows that move independently of Amaterasu's golden light. Magical Influence: Transformation magic and energy manipulation. When Tsukuyomi burns close, shapeshifting, transmutation, and raw sei channelling reach their peak. When it retreats, these disciplines falter.

Solar Astrological Events

Event Celestial Cause Effects
Nagorikaze Susanoo draws close to Seizan Blue-white atmospheric phenomena; ghost rainbows shimmer across the sky; water magic intensifies throughout Kagekuni
Long Shadow Tsukuyomi at furthest orbital point (aphelion) Transformation magic weakens; shadows behave strangely — stretching, splitting, or moving against the light
Shinmyōji Kōrigami at peak influence Luminescent mists settle over Kagekuni; winter severity increases; the cold carries an edge that cuts deeper than temperature alone

Additional solar events exist but are less commonly named or studied. Seimasters at Seishin maintain observational records of celestial alignments and their correlations to sei fluctuation.

DM Note — The Three Stars and the Great Aphelion

The three stars orbit a common barycenter on independent orbital inclinations, producing a three-dimensional dance rather than a flat orbital disc. The named astrological events (Nagorikaze, Long Shadow) are the routine expressions of this dance — individual stars reaching notable positions within normal orbital variation.

The Great Aphelion (~14344) was a singular event requiring all three independent orbits to peak simultaneously. The probability is the product of three separate low-probability alignments, and the distance compounds geometrically.

Amaterasu During the Drought

Amaterasu never went dark. Its baseline sei sustained life throughout the dark ages. The world retained normal day/night cycles. What was lost was the complex magical expression that depended on the full trinary system.

Tsukuyomi — First to Fade, Last to Return

Tsukuyomi's deep red began bleeding approximately 150–170 years before the nadir (14174–14194). Its elongated orbit meant early decline would have appeared as an unusually extended Long Shadow before the deeper pattern was recognized. Transformation magic became unreliable first. Tsukuyomi was the last star to return — its deep red crossing into reliable visibility defined the Great Awakening (16693).

Susanoo — Second to Fade, First to Return

Susanoo dimmed approximately 50–80 years before nadir (14264–14294). The order watched Tsukuyomi declining for nearly a century before Susanoo followed. Susanoo's failure was the loss that reached the general population — healers losing effectiveness, maritime practices becoming unreliable. Tsukuyomi's decline was a practitioner problem; Susanoo's was a human one. Susanoo was also first to return — the first Talents (15962) correlate with its partial recovery, consistent with healing and purification being among the earliest accessible sei expressions.

core

The Shrouded Isles rise from the Raijin no Fukai sea beneath three stars. This is Kagekuni — an archipelago of mist-veiled mountains, bamboo forests that stretch beyond sight, and castle towns where paper lanterns sway above streets of packed earth. It is a land shaped by earthquakes and typhoons, by the pull of four moons on restless tides, and by the ancient hierarchies of emperor, shogun, and clan. Here, honour is not a sentiment but a currency — earned through duty, spent through sacrifice, and lost in ways that can never be recovered. The samurai who kneels before their daimyō, the merchant who bows lower still, the priest who tends a shrine at the edge of a forest where the trees have bark of burnished bronze — each knows their place in an order older than memory, and each carries the weight of what that place demands.

For three thousand years, the world forgot magic. The energy called sei — once woven through every living thing, every river, every breath of wind — fell silent, and with it the knowledge, the institutions, and the traditions that had shaped civilisation for millennia. That silence ended fifty-one years ago. Sei has returned. The stars burn bright again in unfamiliar constellations, and across Kagekuni a generation is learning to wield power that their grandparents believed was myth. But the world that magic left behind did not stand still. Old rivalries hardened into new hatreds. Sacred places fell to ruin. Things that slumbered in the dark ages have begun to stir. You arrive in this world at the edge of what comes next — when the questions of what was lost, what survived, and what is waking matter more than they have in living memory.

Type
core

The people of Kagekuni use "bakemono" as a broad term for anything that is neither person nor beast in any familiar sense — the changed things, the hungry things, the things that should not be where they are. Scholars at the Seishin Enclave insist on finer taxonomy. Peasants in the valleys know the taxonomy doesn't matter when you hear breathing outside the shōji and there's nothing there.

What follows is organized by the categories most commonly used by seimasters and monster-hunters, though the boundaries between them blur more often than academics care to admit.

Type
core

Power in Kagekuni flows through clans. Each is a political entity unto itself — a family at its core, expanded over centuries into a network of vassals, retainers, allied families, and sworn samurai. A clan controls territory, maintains armies, administers justice within its borders, and pursues its interests through diplomacy, marriage, trade, and war. The daimyō who leads each clan holds authority that is, within their province, nearly absolute.

For most of the empire's history, the clans answered to the Emperor. With the throne empty and the Shogunate frozen, that restraint is gone. What remains is ambition, geography, and the alliances that clans have forged to survive what comes next.

In the current climate, this deliberate opacity is both a shield and a provocation — every faction wonders what Kurohana will do, and Akihiko ensures they keep wondering.

Clan Gekkō (Status Uncertain)

Daimyō: Masota no Gekkō Race: Unknown | Age: Unknown | Province: Kaze | Capital: Tsukikage

Daimyō Masota no Gekkō has not been seen publicly in some time. His clan's silence has drawn attention from both alliances and from the other independents. Trade through Kaze province has slowed. The provincial administration has stopped communicating with Heian. Rumours vary — illness, a power struggle within the clan, or something worse.

DM Note — Clan Gekkō

Clan Gekkō's senior seimasters discovered fragmentary texts describing an Onyx Dragon ritual — a transformation rite tied to Kokuryū. Those who underwent it became Nagaji (serpent folk). The transformation spread through the clan. Daimyō Masota no Gekkō underwent it last, in desperation. He is alive in the highlands of Kaze, retaining fragments of his identity but losing coherence over time. The longer the situation persists, the less of him remains to reach.

The capital of Tsukikage stands functionally abandoned — eerily intact, personal belongings still in place, meals half-finished, as if everyone simply walked away.

The Order of the Black Lily (Monastery of the Black Lily, above Akatsuki village in Kaze province) knows the full truth. They have made a calculated decision: the information is too dangerous to release without a reversal plan. They will share the complete truth with parties who reach them — but only the complete truth.

The party has already encountered and killed several Nagaji without knowing they were Gekkō clan members. The moral reckoning is pending.

A reversal may be possible but requires rare materials, specific conditions, or Progenitor involvement. The details are TBD.

The Alliance Clans

Genso Alliance

The Genso Alliance governs the provinces of Kusa and Tsuchi through four member clans: Fuyugiri, Homoruyama, Ryūkaze, and Tsuchiura. Their strength lies in the agricultural heartland of Kusa — the most productive farmland on Hokori — and the mineral wealth of Tsuchi's mountains. The alliance's strategic depth means it can absorb territorial losses that would cripple a coastal faction.

Clan Tsuchiura is the most prominent of the Genso clans beyond Hokori, also governing the Mizuho region on the island of Tatara — the ancestral homeland of the Zirak.

Arashi Alliance

The Arashi Alliance controls Mizu and Nami through four member clans: Arashiyama, Hoshizora, Shirotsuru, and Yūgure. Their power is naval. The two great ports of Hokori — Minato-jō in the northwest and Namigashira in the northeast — both sit within Arashi territory. What moves by sea moves through them.

Clan Shirotsuru extends the Arashi Alliance's reach to Tatara, governing the Shugyoku region — the ancestral homeland of the Glimfyr.

DM Note — Arashi Naval Build-up

Minato-jō is building naval capacity beyond what defensive requirements would justify. An offensive operation involving the western sea is being planned. The details remain opaque to outsiders.

Minor Clans

Not every clan commands a province. Smaller clans exist as vassals, allies, or clients of the great clans — bound by oaths of loyalty, grants of land, or simple necessity.

Clan Seishin (Subject of Kaminari)

Daimyō: Ren Nakamura | Race: Human | Age: 52

Also known as Clan Minato by their lesser title. Ren Nakamura serves as Shichō of Kikyo within Kaminari territory.

DM Note — Clan Seishin

Ren Nakamura is quietly working to elevate Clan Seishin's status. He has formed a secret alliance with a powerful merchant guild — leveraging economic influence where political standing is insufficient.

Orders & Organisations

Beyond the clan structure, several organisations operate across — and sometimes against — the political landscape.

Order of the Tranquil Lotus

A nature-focused monastic order based on Unmeijima, near the town of Kazehama. The order emphasises contemplation, physical discipline, and harmony with the natural world. Their elder, Benkei — a Guhuza of 198 years — is among the oldest known living individuals in the archipelago.

The order occasionally dispatches members as delegates or advisors to the clans. Sun Wukong, a novice, currently serves as delegate to Clan Kaminari.

DM Note — Benkei

Elder Benkei is a member of the Order of the Ancient Guard — the secret organisation dedicated to protecting the sleeping founding dragons. His rank within the Ancient Guard is TBD, but his position as head of the Tranquil Lotus gives him a legitimate cover for influence across the archipelago.

Order of the Sacred Grove

A druidic tradition devoted to protecting specific sacred sites across Kagekuni. The order's guardians are few, scattered, and deeply committed to sites they may tend for decades.

Their former guardian, Solas Evergreen, is deceased. His successor, Relc, was appointed through a posthumous letter — an unusual and somewhat irregular transfer of authority that suggests Solas anticipated his own death. Hideaki Sato, an elder of the order, resides in Kōriwara village in Mizu province.

DM Note — Order of the Sacred Grove

Solas Evergreen was a member of the Order of the Ancient Guard — likely ranked Protector or higher. His murder was not random violence but a deliberate assassination intended to prevent the awakening of Kinryū (the Golden Dragon). Solas was protecting the path to Kinryū, and someone removed him.

Relc now carries the mission Solas died for. He possesses the Warden's Wisdom — a cipher that leads to methods for awakening Kinryū. Relc may not fully understand the significance of what he holds.

Hideaki Sato knew Solas directly and knows that Solas was a member of the Ancient Guard. One of three cipher poem stones connected to the Warden's Wisdom is located near Kōriwara.

Order of the Black Lily

Kagekuni's premier infiltration specialists, based at the Monastery of the Black Lily above Akatsuki village in Kaze province. The monastery is a secret training facility — austere dark stone construction, hidden from casual observation. The villagers of Akatsuki know the order exists and tell outsiders nothing.

DM Note — Order of the Black Lily

The Black Lily holds the complete truth about Clan Gekkō's transformation into Nagaji. They have decided the information is too dangerous to release without a viable reversal plan. Parties who reach the monastery will learn everything — but only if they reach it.

Shōnin-za

The merchant class occupies the lowest rung of the Zokumin caste, but their economic influence far exceeds their social standing. Merchant guilds operate across clan borders, moving goods, capital, and — inevitably — information. Kenta Yamada is an active guild member. Ren Nakamura of Clan Seishin maintains a secret alliance with a powerful guild branch in Kikyo.

The tension between merchant wealth and merchant status is one of Kagekuni's chronic fault lines. Guilds cannot openly challenge the social order, but their money flows where swords cannot reach.

Seiju Hyōgikai

A shadowy body whose full membership and purpose are not widely known. Arinori Senzai is a secret member.

DM Note — The Elven Council

Some members of the council are suspected of corruption. Senzai is quietly investigating from within. The council's full scope, membership, and influence are to be developed further.

Magical Institutions

The return of sei has spawned institutions dedicated to its study and application:

Seishin on the island of Unmeijima — the premier research institution for sei, founded around Hikari no Kenta, the first known Talent. What began as a place of study has grown into a city in its own right.

Hikari no Shizuku in Heian — a healing and light magic tradition operating within the imperial capital.

The Raimeiin (雷鳴院 — Institute of Thunder) and the tradition associated with the Forest of Spirits (Yōsei Mori) in Kusa were both revealed publicly during the Plague Campaign of 16609–16616. Their methods and internal workings are not widely known.

DM Note — The Forest of Spirits

During the Dark Ages, a faction survived within the Yōsei Mori and continued to study sei behavior during the magic-absent era. They hold records that would upend current seimaster orthodoxy — evidence that sei never truly disappeared but rather changed in ways the mainstream tradition failed to observe. This knowledge is contained within the deeper reaches of the forest, where navigation is unreliable and the creatures are unnervingly intelligent.

Hokori is the largest island in the Kagekuni archipelago — approximately 237,000 square miles, stretching 750 miles long and 600 miles wide. Seen from above, the island is X-shaped, its form carved by the collision of four tectonic plates that converge beneath it. The geology is restless. Earthquakes are frequent. Volcanic peaks trail smoke from the northern highlands. Tsunamis reshape the coastline. The people of Hokori have built their civilisation not despite this instability but in conversation with it — their architecture flexes, their settlements relocate, and their culture carries the pragmatic resilience of people who know the ground beneath them is never truly still.

Hokori is divided into eight provinces, each with its own geography, climate, political allegiance, and character. The imperial capital of Heian sits in the eastern province of Hana. The Emperor's Highway extends from Heian in three directions, forming the primary overland transportation network. River systems — particularly the Midori, Tsuchikawa, and Kinryūgawa — serve as major trade arteries, while coastal shipping connects the port cities of Minato-jō in the west and Namigashira in the east.

Province of Hana — The Imperial Heartland

Hana occupies the eastern coast of Hokori and is the seat of imperial history. It stretches along the island's eastern seaboard, bounded to the northwest by the mountainous interior of Sora province for the majority of its inland border, with Tsuchi and Hi to the west, and Kaze to the north.

The province's defining feature is the Serenia-kai (Selenia Sea) — a vast inland sea covering more than a thousand square miles, fed by twenty-five rivers and thirteen waterfalls cascading from the Tenchūsan Ren and the central highlands. Its surface shifts colour with the seasons. The tidal rhythms driven by Kagekuni's four moons make its edges unpredictable; the shoreline can retreat several hundred metres during low compound tides.

To the west, the Seidōrin Mori (Bronze Wood Forest) stretches for miles — an ancient woodland where the trees grow with bark of burnished copper-bronze that catches sunlight like armour. The wood is extraordinarily hard and is harvested under strict clan licence for weapons and structural reinforcement. Unlicensed logging is a capital offence.

To the northeast, the land rises sharply toward the Tenchūsan Ren. The pass through this range is the primary land route north — treacherous in autumn, impassable during winter storms. Shirogane Yama (Silver Mountain), the highest peak on Hokori, dominates the northern skyline, its summit crowned by the Hoshino Tō (Tower of Stars), an ancient astronomical observatory built during the Golden Age and still operational.

Hana's culture is the closest to the old imperial ideal — formal, ceremonially rich, and deeply aware of its historical weight. The Bronze Wood trade defines the province's economy, with seidōrin timber commanding extraordinary prices across the archipelago. Fishing on the Serenia-kai and the Kinryūgawa sustains the rural population, particularly the gold-tail fish (kinuo) that is prized as a delicacy in Heian.

DM Note — Hana Secrets

The Buried City of Kinkōkyo: The Golden Dragon Clan's capital survives structurally intact beneath the Tenchūsan Ren, sealed under hundreds of feet of rock. The gold doors at the temple entrance are an outer access point, exposed by a recent earthquake. The Bronze Wood Forest's metallic quality comes from groundwater flowing through golden veins in Kinkōkyo's buried infrastructure for thousands of years.

Kinryū no Hikari: A golden mirror deep within Kinkōkyo — not a weapon but a communication device allowing direct communion with the living Golden Dragon, Kinryū.

Hiroshi Nakamura: The Shugo of Heian is a traitor feeding intelligence to an outside party. His brother Hideo does not suspect.

Province of Hi — The Volcanic Frontier

Hi is the most geologically violent province on Hokori — a region of active volcanism, fumarole fields, obsidian plains, and mountains that periodically tear themselves apart. It encompasses the majority of the island's western side, surrounded by mountains and the sea. Tsuchi borders it to the southeast, Hana shares a small stretch of its eastern border, Sora encompasses its northern boundary, and Mizu sits along its western edge. Earthquakes are ambient. Residents learn to read tremors the way sailors read wind.

Enshiyama (Flame Peak Mountain), the third highest peak on Hokori, rises from the province's northern reaches and dominates the local landscape. The terrain is dramatic and hostile — black obsidian fields stretch for miles where ancient lava flows cooled and cracked, fumarole vents release sulphurous steam — yet the volcanic ash enriches the soil beyond anything in the southern provinces. Terraced farming on the slopes between active zones produces crops of startling quality. This contradiction — death and abundance in tight proximity — defines Hi's character.

The Honogawa (Flame River) originates from a thermal lake near Enshiyama's base and is warm to the touch for its entire upper reach. The Obsidian Fields of Kurosō yield volcanic glass of exceptional quality, prized for blades and lenses. Deep in the highlands stands the Crimson Shrine — predating the empire, never absorbed into the imperial religious system, its torii carved from natural red stone.

Hi's people are laconic, practical, and possess a dark humour about their circumstances. They do not flee volcanic activity — they have developed sophisticated systems for reading, mitigating, and living alongside it. The province is currently in contested administration; the previous governing clan was lost in the opening engagements of the Arashi-Genso war, and neither alliance has installed a replacement.

DM Note — Hi Secrets

The Crimson Shrine: Keeper Tsubaki (Initiate, Order of the Ancient Guard, ~60 years of service) communicates with something through the shrine's ember-bowl. She knows Akaryū (Crimson Dragon) is alive but does not know the dragon's location.

Enshiyama: The current low-level activity is a precursor to a significant eruption within 1–3 years. The political vacuum means no coordinating authority exists for evacuation.

Western Territories: Descendants of the Crimson Clan faction that refused Tenryū's unification live in loose tribal confederacies, preserving traditions the rest of the empire forgot.

Province of Kaze — Shadows and Mist

Kaze is a province of shadows and mist. It occupies the eastern side of Hokori's northeastern leg — Nami to the north, Kusa to the west, Hana to the south, and Sora sharing a brief stretch of its southwestern border. Sheltered from direct coastal weather by surrounding terrain, it has a microclimate of cool, damp air that never fully clears. The province averages fewer clear days per year than any other on Hokori. Its forests — dense stands of dark cedar and ancient black pine — grow so thickly that the canopy blocks most sunlight even in summer.

The terrain is mountainous, cut by deep river valleys and narrow gorges. The Kazeyama Ren (Wind Mountain Range) channels wind up the valleys in complex, disorienting patterns. Sounds carry strangely — seeming to come from the wrong direction. The Kagero River (Shimmer River) is the primary waterway, named for the heat shimmer visible over its surface on rare warm days.

Clan Gekkō has historically governed Kaze, maintaining careful neutrality through successive political upheavals. The clan's recent disappearance has plunged the province into deep unease. Trade has slowed. The provincial administration has stopped communicating with Heian. Small communities have reported strange encounters — serpentine figures glimpsed on mountain trails, abandoned buildings showing signs of violent disturbance, livestock found dead in unnatural ways.

Kaze's culture is inward-facing. The people are not cold — they are careful. A culture of watching and listening developed naturally in a province where visibility is limited and sound behaves unreliably. Primary exports have historically been information, black pine lumber, rare mountain herbs, and distinctive lacquerware.

DM Note — Kaze Secrets

The Nagaji Truth: Clan Gekkō's senior seimasters discovered fragmentary texts describing an Onyx Dragon ritual — a transformation rite tied to Kokuryū. Those who underwent it became Nagaji. The transformation spread. Masota no Gekkō underwent it last, in desperation. He is alive in the highlands, retaining fragments of his identity but losing coherence over time.

Order of the Black Lily: They know the full truth and have made a calculated decision — the information is too dangerous to release without a reversal plan. They will share with parties who reach them, but only the complete truth.

The Hollow Peaks: Three mountains in the Kazeyama Ren are demonstrably hollow — Onyx Dragon Clan structures. At least one interior is accessible from the Kagerō Gorge. Inside: ancient cultural artifacts, including documentation of the transformation ritual.

Reversal: Possible. The answer lies in the Temple of Kinryū — the Golden Dragon Clan's records about Kokuryū's original ritual and the countermeasure they developed.

Province of Kusa — The Verdant Interior

Kusa is Hokori's green heart — a province of dense forests, wide river floodplains, and grasslands so deep and tall that travellers on foot are hidden from view within a hundred paces. It occupies the western side of the northeastern leg, with Sora encroaching on its southeastern border, Mizu to the southwest, Nami to the north, and Kaze to the east. Drainage from surrounding mountain ranges converges here, creating a network of rivers, oxbow lakes, and seasonal wetlands that makes the land extraordinarily fertile and difficult to traverse without knowing the paths.

The forests are ancient and immense, their floors growing in luminous violet and deep blue hues — murasaki-gusa (purple grass) and aoi-koke (blue moss) endemic to the interior lowlands. The Midori River is the primary artery, and the capital Midoriko sits at its junction with the Futago-kawa (Twin River). The Kusayama Ren (Grass Mountains) forms the northern boundary, sheltering the Yōsei Mori (Forest of Spirits) — a region of ancient woodland where sei activity is consistently elevated and navigation is genuinely unreliable.

The Whispering Flats in the central lowlands are an unusual terrain feature — chest-high violet grass where wind creates complex auditory patterns that some claim carry intelligible whispers. Local tradition says the dead speak from the Flats during the Long Shadow season.

Province of Mizu — The Western Shore

Mizu is a province of water in all its forms — crashing coastal surf, wide navigable rivers, reed-choked estuaries, tidal flats that stretch for miles at low compound tide, and interior lakes fed by reliable rainfall. It wraps around the northwestern string of mountains on Hokori, with Hi to the southeast, Sora along its eastern and southern borders, and Kusa to the northeast. The Raijin no Fukai sea drives against its western and northern coastline with consistent force. The Kōri-no-Mori forest — a dense woodland where natural trees grow intermixed with crystal trees whose pale trunks chime faintly in the wind — occupies its northern shores.

The coastline is irregular and complex — headlands, sheltered coves, sea-stacks, and natural harbours. The Shirakawa Estuary (White River Estuary) is one of the largest navigable estuaries in the archipelago, with the city of Minato-jō occupying a raised headland at its mouth. Inland, rice production in Mizu's river valleys is among the highest in the archipelago.

Province of Nami — The Eastern Storm

Nami sits on the northeastern tip of Hokori, facing the unabated ocean without shelter. Kusa lies to the southwest and Kaze to the southeast. Its shores receive the full force of oceanic weather systems — storms that have built across open water for thousands of miles. Every structure is built low and heavy, walls thick, roofs angled away from prevailing winds, shutters reinforced with iron. During Tatsunami season, storm swells overwash lower coastal roads entirely, and some villages are evacuated to higher ground as standard annual precaution.

The coastline is rugged and often spectacular — dramatic sea cliffs dropping to churning water, narrow beaches of black volcanic sand between rocky headlands, sea arches and stacks in the offshore shallows. The Stormwatch Cliffs at the province's northern reach are the highest sea cliffs on Hokori; on clear days, Kawa island is visible in the distance. The Eastern Lighthouse Chain runs the length of the coast — signal towers and navigational aids, some with stone bases that predate recorded history. The interior rises quickly from the coastal cliffs into the eastern slopes of Hokori's central highlands.

Joint Naval Operation: Nami's Arashi-aligned clan is coordinating with Minato-jō for a joint eastern-western naval operation. The target is unknown, but intelligence suggests a landing rather than a sea battle.

Province of Sora — Above the Clouds

Sora encompasses the majority of the lightly populated mountainous interior at Hokori's centre — often the most dangerous region to traverse. The province occupies the central mountain ranges that form the connective barrier between most of the island's other provinces, bordering nearly every province in some capacity. Much of it sits above the cloud ceiling. A traveller ascending from lower provinces emerges through dense cloud into a world of startling clarity: thin air, intense sunlight, vast visibility, and a profound silence broken only by wind.

The Hoshimori Plateau (Star Keeper's Plateau) is the defining feature — wide, flat, and high enough that stars are visibly brighter than anywhere else in the archipelago. Silvered grasses catch light differently, giving the landscape an almost lunar quality. During the Golden Age, seven observatories were built here; three remain structurally intact with functional instruments — large bronze mechanisms oriented to alignments no current seimaster fully understands. A fourth, largely collapsed, contains sealed records. The Storm Road — a mountain route connecting Hana and Hi to the northern coast — crosses the province, though it is impassable in winter and deteriorating without central maintenance authority.

DM Note — Sora Secrets

Ryūshinki (Dragon Awakening): The sealed records in the collapsed fourth observatory document a celestial alignment the Golden Age seimasters considered dangerous — involving all three stars, two specific moons, and a particular planetary configuration. Their records suggest this alignment is associated with the founding dragons becoming active, visible, or vulnerable. The next occurrence is calculable and is not far away.

Ginryū (Silver Dragon): Connected to Sora through the province's astronomical nature. The plateau's unusual stellar appearance is partly her influence. She has not been seen in decades.

Province of Tsuchi — The Southern Frontier

Tsuchi occupies the southern portion of Hokori — a primarily mountainous province dominated by rugged terrain and the imposing bulk of Kurogane Yama (Black Iron Mountain), the second highest peak on the island. Hana borders it to the northeast and Hi to the northwest. The mountains here are old and weathered, less volcanically active than Hi but no less formidable — steep valleys, narrow passes, and ridgelines that catch storms rolling in from the southern sea. The southern mountains are resource-rich: mineral deposits, timber in the sheltered valleys, and stone quarried from exposed cliff faces. But the terrain resists large-scale settlement. Communities are small, isolated by geography, and accustomed to self-reliance.

The Tsuchikawa (Earth River) is the province's main artery — wide, slow, navigable for cargo barge travel, and historically important as a trade route connecting the interior to the coast. Tsuchimoto sits at the centre of the provincial plains, connected by roads in every compass direction. It is a city of markets, granaries, and administrative buildings — the quietly enormous power of whoever controls the food supply flowing through its mountain valleys. The Great Granaries of Tsuchimoto can hold enough grain to feed Hokori's population through two years of failed harvests. A Buried Road, ancient and pre-imperial, runs through the lowlands — farmers have ploughed around it for centuries without knowing where it leads.

DM Note — Tsuchi Secrets

Grain as Weapon: The Genso-aligned governing clan has been quietly restricting grain sales to Arashi-aligned provinces while maintaining normal trade with neutral parties. A slow-moving economic siege that hasn't become visible yet — when it does, it will escalate the war significantly.

Major Geographic Features

Mountain Ranges

  • Tenchūsan Ren (Heavenly Pillar Mountains) — A great range in northeastern Hana. Primary land route toward the northern provinces; treacherous in autumn, impassable in winter. Contains significant ruins and the entrance to the buried city of Kinkōkyo.
  • Kurogane Yama (Black Iron Mountain) — Second highest peak on Hokori; dominates southern Tsuchi province. Old and weathered, less volcanically active than Hi's peaks but formidable. The surrounding mountains are resource-rich with mineral deposits, timber, and quarried stone.
  • Kazeyama Ren (Wind Mountain Range) — Along Kaze province's borders. Complex disorienting wind patterns; the Hollow Peaks.
  • Kusayama Ren (Grass Mountains) — Northern boundary of Kusa; shelters the Yōsei Mori.

Bodies of Water

  • Serenia-kai (Selenia Sea) — Vast inland sea in eastern Hokori within Hana province; over a thousand square miles; complex compound tides.
  • Lake Midoriko — Peninsula setting for Heian; ferry connections.
  • Shirakawa Estuary — Largest navigable estuary in the archipelago; Mizu province.

Rivers

  • Kinryūgawa (Gold Dragon River) — Runs faintly gold at dawn; gold-tail fish trade; Hana province.
  • Midori River — Primary navigable artery of Kusa; flat-bottomed vessel traffic.
  • Tsuchikawa (Earth River) — Wide, slow, navigable for cargo barges; Tsuchi province's lifeline.
  • Honogawa (Flame River) — Thermal river in Hi; warm to the touch in upper reaches.
  • Kagerō River (Shimmer River) — Kaze's primary waterway; named for heat shimmer on rare warm days.

Forests

  • Seidōrin Mori (Bronze Wood Forest) — Metallic-barked trees in western Hana; harvested under strict licence for weapons.
  • Yōsei Mori (Forest of Spirits) — Sei-active ancient woodland in Kusa; navigation unreliable; unusual creatures of elevated intelligence in deeper reaches.
  • Kōri-no-Mori (Ice Forest) — Dense forest occupying the northern shores of Mizu province; natural trees grow intermixed with crystal trees whose pale trunks chime in the wind; cold, old, and largely unexplored.

Notable Terrain

  • Obsidian Fields of Kurosō — Vast plains of volcanic glass in Hi; exceptional quality for blades and lenses.
  • Whispering Flats — Chest-high violet grass in Kusa; sei resonance produces auditory phenomena.
  • Hoshimori Plateau — High grassland in Sora; stars visibly brighter; Golden Age observatories.
  • Stormwatch Cliffs — Highest sea cliffs on Hokori; Nami's northern reach; Kawa visible on clear days.

Transportation

The Emperor's Highway extends from Heian in three directions, forming the primary overland network. Provincial roads branch from it, connecting smaller settlements. Mountain passes — particularly the Tenchūsan Pass through northeastern Hana — are seasonal and dangerous. The Storm Road through Sora province connects the eastern and western halves of Hokori across the central mountains, but is impassable in winter and deteriorating without central maintenance. Forest trails in Kusa and Kaze are unmapped and require local knowledge.

River systems serve as major trade arteries: the Midori River connects Kusa's interior to the coast, the Tsuchikawa carries cargo barges through Tsuchi's valleys, and the Kinryūgawa supports the gold-tail fish trade in Hana. Coastal shipping connects Minato-jō in the northwest and Namigashira in the northeast, the two major ports.

Four moons orbit Seizan directly, each with its own character, orbit, and influence on the world below. Together they are called The Sisters' Tears — a name whose origin has been lost to time, though folk tales offer a dozen contradictory explanations. Their combined gravitational pull creates complex tidal patterns that shape coastal life, maritime navigation, and the rhythms of agriculture across Kagekuni. Beyond the physical, the moons carry a subtler influence — secondary sei signatures that interact with the stellar field in ways that seimasters study but do not fully understand.

Aokiba — The Blue Fang

Translation: Blue Fang Orbital Period: 17 days Character: Crystalline in appearance with an elliptical orbit that brings it dramatically close to Seizan at perigee. When near, its surface catches Susanoo's blue-white light and scatters it — the moon appears to have teeth, jagged edges of refracted brilliance that give it its name. The shortest cycle of the four — Aokiba waxes and wanes faster than some journeys take to complete. Notable Influence: Aokiba drives the most violent tidal surges, particularly during Tatsunami — the four-moon alignment convergence. Coastal communities track its orbit with the same urgency that mountain villages track avalanche seasons. Sailors consider its close approach a navigation hazard; harbormasters adjust schedules around it.

Kagetsu — The Shadow Moon

Translation: Shadow Moon Orbital Period: 33 days Character: The largest of the four moons. Kagetsu absorbs light rather than reflecting it — a dark presence against the night sky, visible primarily by the stars it occludes and the faint luminous halo that surrounds it at full phase. It dominates the sky not through brightness but through absence. Its cycle runs slightly longer than a calendar month, so its full face drifts across the seasons — never quite falling on the same date twice in succession. Notable Influence: Dreams experienced under Kagetsu's full face carry mystical significance. Diviners, spirit-speakers, and those who work with the dream-world time their practices to its cycle. Common folk avoid sleeping in direct moonlight when Kagetsu is full — not from superstition, but from the unsettling vividness of the dreams that follow.

Nagikumo — The Gentle Cloud

Translation: Gentle Cloud Orbital Period: 23 days Character: The smallest of the four moons, yet it appears disproportionately large in the sky — an optical quality that astronomers at Seishin have debated for centuries without resolution. Nagikumo carries a soft inner glow, a perpetual luminescence that persists even when the moon passes through Seizan's shadow. It never fully darkens. Its three-week rhythm gives it a steady, reassuring cadence — the most intuitive of the four cycles to track without instruments. Notable Influence: Tranquility. Nagikumo's presence in the sky is associated with calm weather, settled seas, and restful sleep. Healers note that patients recover more steadily during its visible phases. Whether this is sei influence or cultural expectation is a matter of ongoing scholarly argument.

Ryūgetsu — The Dragon Moon

Translation: Dragon Moon Orbital Period: 41 days Character: The most complex orbit of the four — Ryūgetsu's path is gravitationally linked to the outer planet Shizukanami, creating a resonance that makes its position difficult to predict without sophisticated calculation. Its surface shifts color depending on which stellar light dominates: golden under Amaterasu alone, tinged blue when Susanoo is ascendant, deepening to wine-red under Tsukuyomi's influence. Its long, irregular cycle means weeks pass between phase changes — the color of Ryūgetsu shifts so gradually that only attentive observers notice the transition. Notable Influence: Ryūgetsu periodically enters what observers call Dragon's Rest — auspicious pauses in its orbital motion where it appears to hover. These pauses are considered favorable for weather magic, spirit communication, and ceremonial work. During the astrological event Hikarishō, Ryūgetsu's full phase alignment produces celestial auroras — curtains of light that ripple across the sky in colours that echo the dragon's own shifting surface.

Conjunction Frequencies

The moons' differing periods produce conjunctions — moments when two or more moons share the same phase position in the sky. These are tracked by astronomers at Seishin and by coastal harbormasters for practical tidal calculation.

Pairwise Conjunctions (Two Moons)

Pair Frequency Approximate Interval
Aokiba + Nagikumo Every 391 days ~1.1 years
Aokiba + Kagetsu Every 561 days ~1.5 years
Aokiba + Ryūgetsu Every 697 days ~1.9 years
Kagetsu + Nagikumo Every 759 days ~2.1 years
Nagikumo + Ryūgetsu Every 943 days ~2.6 years
Kagetsu + Ryūgetsu Every 1,353 days ~3.7 years

Pairwise conjunctions are common enough that most people witness several in a lifetime. Each pairing carries its own astrological character — Aokiba–Nagikumo conjunctions are considered stabilizing (the Fang's violence tempered by the Cloud's calm), while Kagetsu–Ryūgetsu conjunctions are deeply ominous (shadow and dragon, stillness and complexity).

Triple Conjunctions (Three Moons)

Trio Frequency Approximate Interval
Aokiba + Kagetsu + Nagikumo Every 12,903 days ~35 years
Aokiba + Nagikumo + Ryūgetsu Every 16,031 days ~44 years
Aokiba + Kagetsu + Ryūgetsu Every 23,001 days ~63 years
Kagetsu + Nagikumo + Ryūgetsu Every 31,119 days ~85 years

Triple conjunctions are once-in-a-lifetime events. The rarest — Kagetsu, Nagikumo, and Ryūgetsu aligning without Aokiba — occurs roughly once every 85 years. Entire generations of astronomers may dedicate their careers to predicting and documenting a single triple conjunction.

Full Conjunction — Tatsunami

All four moons align every 529,023 days — approximately once every 1,448 years.

A true Tatsunami is not a storm but a convergence so rare that most civilizations experience it only once, if at all. The tidal forces compound catastrophically; the sei amplification reaches levels that no living seimaster has experienced. Historical records from Seishin describe the last full conjunction in fragmentary, reverential terms — the ocean withdrew beyond the horizon before returning as a wall of luminescent water, and sei-sensitive individuals reported hearing the world itself vibrate like a struck bell.

DM Note — Tatsunami Frequency and Campaign History

At ~1,448 years between full alignments, there have been roughly 11 true Tatsunami events since the founding year (year 0 of the Kagekuni calendar, ~16,744 years ago). The most recent would have fallen approximately 300–400 years before the current campaign year, placing it within recorded history but beyond living memory. The term "Tatsunami" is used colloquially for any severe multi-moon tidal event (particularly when three moons are in near-alignment), which is why coastal communities treat it as a recurring threat rather than a once-in-a-millennium catastrophe. The true four-moon convergence is something most scholars debate rather than fear.

Lunar Sei Influence

The moons carry secondary sei signatures — subtler than the stars but meaningful in combination. Scholars at Seishin track three distinct channels of lunar influence:

  • Tidal — Physical effects on water, weather, and geological activity
  • Omen — Divinatory significance; dream potency; spirit-world permeability
  • Sei Amplification — Mild magical resonance that compounds with stellar alignment

When stellar and lunar alignments coincide, the compounded effects are meaningfully greater than either alone. A Nagorikaze event during a Tatsunami convergence, for instance, produces tidal and magical conditions that exceed what either event generates independently.

DM Note — Moons and the Great Aphelion

The four moons orbit Seizan directly and were not affected by the Great Aphelion. Their physical tidal influence continued normally throughout the dark ages. However, with two of the three stellar sei sources absent, the moons' secondary sei signatures had nothing to compound with — their amplification channel was effectively inert for ~3,077 years. The return of stellar sei has reactivated lunar resonance, but whether the current lunar sei signatures match their pre-Aphelion intensity is unknown. Seishin's records do not extend that far back.

The world of Seizan exists within the Miyosai system — a trinary stellar system governed by three stars, orbited by seven planets, and watched over by four moons. It is a world where magic energy called sei flows through all living things, shaped and amplified by the celestial bodies that wheel overhead.

The archipelago of Kagekuni — the Shrouded Isles — sits within the Raijin no Fukai sea, shaped by competing celestial influences and the restless geology beneath its shores. Earthquakes, tsunamis, typhoons, and volcanic eruptions are regular features of life here, not catastrophes to be survived but rhythms to be understood. Architecture, agriculture, and culture have all adapted to a world that moves.

Above, the three stars of the Miyosai system trace their ancient paths. Their movements drive named astrological events that overlay the standard four seasons, influencing weather, tides, the flow of sei, and the behavior of the spirit world. The four moons compound these effects — their own cycles creating tidal patterns, omen windows, and subtle magical resonance that those attuned to sei can feel in their bones.

Seven planets share the system, each with its own character and influence. From molten Akahoshi burning close to Amaterasu to distant Yamiyo trailing in permanent shadow, the planetary family marks time on scales both human and cosmic.

The people of Kagekuni have watched these skies for millennia. Their calendar, their festivals, their understanding of magic and the natural world — all of it is rooted in the dance of light above them. What follows is what is known of that dance.

DM Note — The Great Aphelion

The Miyosai system's three stars orbit a common barycenter on independent orbital inclinations. Once in recorded history, all three reached maximum mutual distance simultaneously — the Great Aphelion (14344). This event caused the sei drought and the dark ages (12806–~15883). The connection between stellar position and sei availability is the campaign's deepest cosmological secret. No living scholar has assembled the complete picture. See the individual section entries for details on how this manifests in each celestial body's behavior.

Kawa is an island that breathes with the seasons. For most of the year, only its highest terrain rises above water — ridgelines, hilltops, and a handful of elevated settlements that persist as islands within an island. In winter, the waters recede and the lowlands emerge: vast, extraordinarily fertile floodplains that have been farmed for millennia using agricultural techniques found nowhere else in the archipelago. The annual cycle of submersion and emergence defines everything about Kawa — its architecture (built on stilts and elevated stone foundations), its economy (one explosive growing season), and its people (patient, methodical, and deeply attuned to tidal calendars).

Kawa lies to the east of Hokori, visible from the Stormwatch Cliffs in Nami province on clear days. The waters surrounding it are navigable but treacherous — shifting sandbars and unpredictable currents created by the interaction of four lunar tidal patterns make piloting around Kawa a specialist skill.

Points of Interest

The Great Library sits at Nagisawa, on the shores of Seirei Mizuumi (Spirit Lake) — a body of water said to connect to the underworld. The library was built during the reign of the First Emperor, Tenryū no Mikado, and remains one of the most significant repositories of knowledge in the archipelago. It was partially destroyed by an earthquake during the Dark Ages and restored during the Jinshō Reformation (~15642–15691).

Seirei Mizuumi itself is a place of deep spiritual significance. The Battle of Seirei Mizuumi — fought during the era of imperial unification — secured Kawa for the empire and broke the Azure Clan navy. The lake's waters remain a site of pilgrimage and scholarly study.
