The spiritual life of Kagekuni is layered, ancient, and deeply woven into daily existence. There is no separation between the sacred and the mundane — a farmer who plants rice in the spring does so with a prayer to the kami of the paddy. A samurai who draws their blade offers a silent word to their ancestors. A merchant who opens their shop at dawn bows to the small shrine beside the door, and means it. Religion in Kagekuni is not practiced in isolation; it is practiced in everything.

The Divine

At the foundation of Kagekuni's faith is a single supreme divine being — an ultimate creator whose nature is understood to transcend mortal comprehension. This entity is not named in common speech, not depicted in art, and not the subject of direct worship in the way a familiar god might be. It simply is. The divine is the origin point from which all other spiritual beings descend, the source of the natural order, and the reason the world holds together rather than falling apart.

Beneath this supreme being, a hierarchy of venerated figures serves as intermediaries between the divine and the mortal world. These figures — historical heroes, legendary seimasters, mythologised rulers, and great spiritual teachers — occupy a role analogous to saints. Shrines and temples may be dedicated to specific figures without contradiction; a shrine to a legendary healer and a shrine to a dragon ancestor both point upward toward the same ultimate source.

This structure allows for enormous local variation. A fishing village on the coast of Nami may venerate a storm-calming saint unknown in the interior of Kusa. A mountain monastery may honour a philosopher whose name has never been spoken in Heian. The faith accommodates these differences without strain — local devotion and universal truth coexist.

Kami — The Spirits of the World

Kami are the spiritual inhabitants of the natural world — beings of place, element, and phenomenon who exist alongside the mortal population. They are not gods. They are not saints. They are something else entirely: presences that dwell in rivers, mountains, ancient trees, crossroads, waterfalls, and any place where the natural world gathers unusual weight or beauty.

A kami may be benevolent, indifferent, or dangerous — and sometimes all three, depending on how it is treated. The kami of a river might bless the villages along its banks with clean water and good fishing for generations, then drown a child who wades too deep without offering respect. This is not cruelty. It is nature. Kami do not operate by human morality. They operate by their own logic, which mortals can learn to read but never fully control.

Shrines mark the resting places and territories of known kami. These range from grand structures maintained by dedicated priests to simple roadside markers — a torii gate, a stone basin, a length of sacred rope tied around an ancient tree. The distinction between a great shrine and a humble one is not a measure of the kami's power but of the community's resources. A village kami honoured with a mossy stone and a daily cup of rice may be every bit as potent as one housed in a lacquered hall.

Interaction with kami follows established protocols: purification before approach, offerings appropriate to the spirit's nature, prayers spoken with correct form, and gratitude expressed whether the request is granted or not. Disturbing a kami — through disrespect, pollution of its territory, or destruction of its shrine — invites consequences that can persist for generations.

Ancestor Veneration

The dead do not leave. Not entirely. In Kagekuni's understanding, the boundary between the living and the deceased is less a wall than a screen — translucent, permeable, and never quite solid. The ancestors watch. They listen. And they care, deeply, about the conduct of their descendants.

Every household of any standing maintains a butsudan — a family shrine where the names, images, and memorial tablets of the dead are kept. Daily offerings of rice, incense, water, and sometimes sake are made to the ancestors, accompanied by prayers that range from formal invocations to quiet conversation. A samurai may inform his grandfather's tablet of a promotion. A merchant may ask a deceased parent's forgiveness for a poor decision. A child may simply say good morning.

At the community level, temples maintain records of the dead and conduct ceremonies marking the anniversaries of passing, seasonal remembrances, and festivals where the boundary between worlds thins and the ancestors are believed to return briefly to the mortal realm. These are not sombre occasions — they are celebrations, feasts, and reunions with the dead conducted in a spirit of joy and gratitude rather than grief.

Ancestor veneration carries practical weight in Kagekuni's political life. A daimyō whose ancestors served with honour can invoke that legacy as a source of authority. A family whose ancestors committed shameful acts may carry that burden for generations. The dead vote, in a sense — their reputation shapes the living's standing in ways that no amount of present achievement can entirely overcome.

The Seven Dragons

The founding dragons occupy a unique position in Kagekuni's spiritual landscape — elevated above saints, distinct from kami, revered as something closer to demigods. They are the seven Progenitors who ruled the archipelago before the first human emperor rose to power, and whose bloodlines, according to tradition, flow through the veins of the dragonborn elite and the imperial line itself.

Clan Dragon Color Domain
Crimson Clan Akaryū Red Fire, volcanic power, strength
Azure Clan Aoryū Blue Water, storms, coastal protection
Emerald Clan Midoryū Green Nature, earth, healing, balance
Onyx Clan Kokuryū Black Shadow, darkness, cunning, mystery
Golden Clan Kinryū Gold Honour, justice, nobility, mediation
Silver Clan Ginryū Silver Grace, purity, ice, moon and stars
Amethyst Clan Murasakiryū Purple Arcane knowledge, divination, mystical arts

Each dragon clan once ruled from a specific island or region of the archipelago, and the cultural memory of those domains persists in regional identity, local festivals, and the heraldry of the clans that claim descent from them. Temples and shrines dedicated to the founding dragons are found across Kagekuni — some grand and well-maintained, others ancient and half-forgotten, their stonework crumbling under moss and rain.

The first emperor, Tenryū no Mikado, is said to have descended from both the Crimson and Golden bloodlines — fire and justice united in a single line. His unification of the warring dragon clans approximately eight thousand years ago established the imperial dynasty and the political order that persists, in increasingly fractured form, to this day.

In the current era, the founding dragons are considered historical and mythological figures. The world at large believes them long dead or ascended beyond mortal reach. Dragon eggs — occasionally unearthed from ancient sites — are treated as fossils and collectibles rather than signs of living beings.

Dragonborn within the Kugai elite claim direct descent from the founding dragons, and this claim forms the bedrock of noble authority in many clans. Whether the genealogies are genuine or constructed, the social power they convey is real.

DM Note — The Dragons Live

All seven founding dragons are still alive. They are not dead, not ascended, and not mythological. They are hidden — withdrawn into deep slumber across the archipelago, their locations known only to the Order of the Ancient Guard, the secret organisation dedicated to their protection.

The world considers the Progenitors purely historical. The Ancient Guard works to maintain this belief, understanding that the revelation of living dragons would destabilise every political, religious, and military institution in Kagekuni simultaneously.

Dragon eggs are not fossils. Their viability is unknown to the world at large, but the Ancient Guard treats them as potentially living.

The implications for religious life are profound: the saints and demigods that the faithful venerate are not distant memories but sleeping beings, physically present somewhere beneath the mountains, the forests, or the sea. The shrines built in their honour sometimes sit directly above the sites where they rest.

Ritual Purification

Purification is the most universally practiced spiritual act in Kagekuni. It crosses caste, clan, and regional boundaries. The principle is simple: contact with death, blood, illness, spiritual pollution, or moral transgression creates impurity that must be cleansed before a person can properly interact with the sacred.

In practice, purification takes many forms. Water is the most common agent — the ritual washing of hands and mouth at a shrine's temizuya (water basin) before entering. Salt is scattered at thresholds to ward off impurity. Incense smoke purifies spaces. Priests perform formal ceremonies of cleansing for individuals, buildings, and even weapons. Before a battle, entire armies may undergo purification rites — not for divine protection, but to ensure they enter combat in a state of spiritual clarity.

The most significant purifications mark life transitions: birth, coming of age, marriage, and death. A house where someone has died is purified before the living resume normal activity. A blade that has taken a life may be ritually cleansed. A warrior returning from battle washes not just the blood from their skin but the spiritual residue of killing from their soul.

This practice intersects with the caste system in uncomfortable ways. The Burakumin — whose occupations involve constant contact with death and spiritual pollution — are considered permanently impure by those who observe the strictest interpretations of purification law. Their segregation is, in part, a spiritual justification layered over social prejudice.

Kannazuki — The Month of No Gods

The tenth month of the calendar is called Kannazuki — the Month of No Gods. Tradition holds that during this month, the kami leave their shrines and territories to gather at a great convocation, leaving the mortal world temporarily unattended. Shrines see reduced attendance. Certain rituals are suspended. The month carries a faint unease — a feeling of being unwatched, which in Kagekuni is not a comfort but a vulnerability.

The name is ancient — far older than the current empire — and its origin has been debated by scholars and priests for millennia without resolution.

DM Note — The True Origin of Kannazuki

The name is a historical fossil from the earliest age when the seven Progenitor dragons did physically gather during the tenth month. The tradition outlived the practice by millennia. The Ancient Guard recognises the irony — the "Month of No Gods" was originally the month when all the gods were present in one place. Now, with the Progenitors slumbering, the name is accidentally accurate again for entirely different reasons.

Temples & Monastic Traditions

Monasteries serve as centres of learning, contemplation, and — not infrequently — political refuge. The monastic traditions of Kagekuni draw on a contemplative philosophy that emphasises mindfulness, detachment from worldly desire, and the cultivation of inner stillness. Monks and nuns withdraw from the hierarchies of secular life, though in practice monasteries are never entirely free from political entanglement.

Several monastic orders maintain influence across the archipelago:

The Order of the Tranquil Lotus on Unmeijima combines nature-focused spirituality with rigorous physical discipline. Their elder, Benkei — a Guhuza of 198 years — is among the oldest known living individuals in Kagekuni.

The Order of the Sacred Grove follows a druidic tradition devoted to protecting specific sacred sites. Their guardians tend individual locations for decades, maintaining a quiet vigil that most of the world never notices.

The Order of the Black Lily, based above Akatsuki village in Kaze province, is less a spiritual order than a professional one — Kagekuni's premier infiltration specialists, operating from a monastery that serves as both temple and training facility.

The tension between worldly duty and spiritual withdrawal runs through all of these traditions. A monk who retreats from the world still lives in it. A monastery that claims neutrality still sits on land that someone claims to own. The spiritual life of Kagekuni is never purely spiritual — it is always, in some measure, political.

The Practice of Faith

For most people in Kagekuni, religion is not a matter of doctrine but of practice. A farmer does not study theology. He maintains his family shrine, makes offerings to the kami of his fields, honours his ancestors at the butsudan, and visits the local temple on festival days. His faith is expressed through action — through the rituals that mark the rhythm of the year, the prayers that accompany daily work, and the quiet understanding that the world is populated by forces larger and older than himself.

This practical faith produces a population that is simultaneously devout and pragmatic. The people of Kagekuni believe in the spiritual world because they live in it — because the rivers glow faintly at night, because the fog sometimes carries incense from no source, because the trees in certain forests have bark of burnished bronze and no one considers this remarkable. The sacred is not separate from the ordinary. It is the ordinary, seen clearly.

Seven planets orbit Amaterasu, travelling with the primary star as it traces its own path through the Miyosai system. Their positions relative to Seizan shift in predictable patterns — the movements of siblings sharing a common parent rather than independent wanderers. Astronomers at Seishin track their orbits with precision, and the agricultural, maritime, and spiritual calendars of Kagekuni all reference planetary positions for timing and omen-reading.

The Inner Worlds

Akahoshi

Translation: — Position: Innermost planet Character: A molten world locked in perpetual proximity to Amaterasu. Akahoshi is visible in daylight as a faint crimson point — the only planet that can be observed without waiting for darkness. Astrologers consider it a marker of urgency and immediacy. Its transits across Amaterasu's face are tracked as timing indicators for short-term decisions.

Akasa — Red Sand

Translation: Red Sand Position: Second from Amaterasu Character: A crimson desert world, dry and wind-scoured. Akasa's influence on Seizan is primarily atmospheric — during Tatsunami, its orbital position correlates with shifts in weather patterns that amplify or dampen the tidal convergence. Whether this is gravitational, sei-related, or coincidental remains debated at Seishin.

Asahikawa — River of Dawn

Translation: River of Dawn Position: Third from Amaterasu (Seizan's inner neighbour) Character: Golden and highly reflective — Asahikawa is the brightest object in Seizan's morning sky, visible before sunrise as a steady golden point. It is called the herald of celestial events because its position relative to the three stars often signals upcoming astrological shifts before they become apparent in weather or sei. Navigators and astronomers prize it as a reference point.

Seizan — The Balance Point

Position: Fourth from Amaterasu

Our world. Seizan sits at the habitable heart of Amaterasu's planetary family — close enough for warmth, far enough for temperance. Its four moons, its complex tidal patterns, and its position within the trinary stellar system give it the most elaborate celestial environment of any world in the Miyosai system.

The Outer Worlds

Shizukanami — Silent Wave

Translation: Silent Wave Position: Fifth from Amaterasu (Seizan's outer neighbour) Character: A frozen ocean world — its surface is a cracked and ancient sheet of ice over a deep, still sea. Shizukanami is gravitationally linked to Seizan's moon Ryūgetsu; the two bodies influence each other's orbital behaviour in ways that make both difficult to predict independently. Under Susanoo's blue-white light, Shizukanami takes on an eerie blue glow visible to the naked eye.

Kōrigami — God of Ice

Translation: God of Ice Position: Sixth from Amaterasu Character: A world of eternal winter — vast, pale, and silent. Kōrigami's influence on Seizan is most felt during Shinmyōji, when its orbital position reaches peak proximity and winter severity across Kagekuni intensifies. The luminescent mists that settle over the islands during Shinmyōji are attributed to Kōrigami's presence, though the mechanism is not understood.

Yamiyo — Eternal Night

Translation: Eternal Night Position: Outermost planet Character: The most distant world in the Miyosai system, trailing in permanent shadow at the edge of Amaterasu's reach. Yamiyo is associated with shadow magic — practitioners of concealment, illusion, and darkness-aspected sei report increased potency when Yamiyo is well-positioned. DM Note — Planets and the Great Aphelion

Because the planets orbit Amaterasu and travel with it, the seven planets did not participate in the Great Aphelion. Their positions relative to Seizan shifted only in their normal orbital patterns throughout the entire drought period. In the Tenkū-ji orrery, this is visible and striking: the planetary armatures continue their normal motion while the two secondary stellar arms go dark. The machine keeps working, the planets keep moving — two of the three stars are simply not where they should be.

Sei is the magic energy that flows through all living things on Seizan. It is not an external force to be harnessed or a resource to be mined — it is present in the blood, the breath, the roots of trees, and the currents of rivers. Sei is woven into the fabric of the world, expressed through celestial alignment and natural forces, amplified or diminished by the positions of stars and moons overhead.

The Nature of Sei

Sei responds to the Miyosai system's celestial bodies. The three stars provide its primary signatures — Amaterasu sustains the baseline, Susanoo governs water magic, healing, and purification, and Tsukuyomi shapes transformation and energy manipulation. The four moons contribute secondary resonance: tidal, divinatory, and amplificatory. When stellar and lunar alignments coincide, the effects compound beyond what either produces alone.

Sei is not evenly distributed. Certain places — ancient groves, mountain peaks, volcanic vents, river confluences — concentrate it naturally. Others are sei-dead, drained by catastrophe or corruption. Most people live their entire lives within sei's presence without consciously feeling it, the way a fish does not feel the water. Those with the talent to sense and shape sei are rare, and rarer still are those with the discipline to master it.

Seimasters

Seimasters are arcane scholars and researchers — though not necessarily practitioners. The title connotes scholarship over raw power. A seimaster studies sei as a discipline: mapping its flows, theorizing about its celestial dependencies, documenting the correlations between stellar alignment and magical expression. A non-casting seimaster may outrank a gifted practitioner socially, in the same way a physician who researches disease may outrank the healer who treats it.

Those who do manifest sei practically map to the familiar arcane traditions — wizards, sorcerers, monks — though in Kagekuni these distinctions carry different cultural weight than in other lands. Study typically occurs in mountaintop monasteries, removed from the noise of lowland life where the celestial influences can be observed more clearly.

Magical Factions

Several institutions study, practice, or govern the use of sei across Kagekuni:

  • Seishin — The premier magical research institution, located on the island of Unmeijima. Seishin maintains the most comprehensive observational records of celestial alignments and their correlations to sei fluctuation.
  • Raimeiin (雷鳴院) — Publicly declared during the Plague Campaign. Focus and methods are not widely known outside scholarly circles.
  • Forest of Spirits — Publicly declared during the Plague Campaign. Associated with naturalistic sei traditions.
  • Hikari no Shizuku — A healing and light magic tradition operating within the capital city of Heian.

The Sei Drought

Sei began declining during the era of the War of Fractured Banners (~12605). The decline was gradual — the first secondary star was lost to naked-eye visibility around ~12806, marking the beginning of what scholars now call the dark ages. By ~13088, when the last major sei institution — the Temple of Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji — fell, sei was effectively inaccessible.

The period without accessible sei lasted approximately 3,077 years (12806–15883). During those millennia, the magical traditions of Kagekuni were extinguished. Knowledge was lost, institutions crumbled, and the cultural and intellectual life of the archipelago collapsed — though the physical world survived, sustained by Amaterasu's baseline energy.

Sei slowly returned through the emergence of Talents beginning 15962 — individuals born with an innate capacity to sense and shape sei, the first in over three thousand years. The process accelerated until the Great Awakening (16693), when sei was considered fully restored. The current campaign date of 16744 is just 51 years post-Awakening — living memory. The eldest practitioners remember a world without magic.

The drought's cause is officially unknown. Scholars debate whether it was a consequence of the War of Fractured Banners itself, a natural celestial cycle, or something else entirely. No consensus exists.

Kuroyami no Akuma and the Plague Campaign

Not all who shape sei do so in service of the living. Kuroyami no Akuma — formerly Takeda Arata — discovered a necromantic tome within Kuroshi Temple on the haunted island of Yurei. The knowledge within allowed him to wage the Plague Campaign (16609–16616), a war of undeath and corruption that scarred Kagekuni.

Kuroyami no Akuma was defeated but never captured or killed. He escaped, and his whereabouts remain unknown. His followers, the Eikyū Yami Clan, persist — a reminder that sei is a tool, and tools serve the hand that holds them.

DM Note — The True Cause of the Sei Drought

The sei drought was caused by the Great Aphelion — the simultaneous maximum separation of all three stars of the Miyosai system. The causal chain (aphelion → Progenitor slumber → drought, or aphelion → both independently) is unknown even to the Ancient Guard. The slow orbital return of the secondary stars correlates precisely with sei's gradual restoration, but the orbital correction is not yet complete. Tsukuyomi's projection, while present, carries slightly less intensity than its pre-decline readings.

No living scholar has assembled the complete picture. The data exists in fragmentary astronomical records across multiple institutions, but no one has connected stellar position to sei availability. The Golden Dragon Clan's observatory at Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji contained the most complete model of the Miyosai system ever constructed — the mechanical-arcane orrery capable of projecting celestial positions across millennia. It has not been operational since the temple fell in 13088.

DM Note — Murasakiryū's Sei Awareness

Every sei use in Kagekuni passes through the awakened Progenitor Murasakiryū's awareness. Every spell the party casts, every druidic invocation, every monk ability — all of it is potentially observed. Whether Murasakiryū actively monitors individual sei users or maintains passive background awareness is unresolved. Whether the party registers as notable is unknown.

Seizan experiences four standard seasons that mirror the familiar cycle of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These provide the foundational rhythm of agricultural life, festivals, and daily existence across Kagekuni. Overlaying these are the astrological events driven by the Miyosai trinary system — celestial phenomena that alter weather, tides, the flow of sei, and the behaviour of the natural and spirit worlds.

The Four Seasons

Season Name Months Character
Spring Haru (春) Yayoi, Uzuki, Satsuki New growth pushes through indigo grass. Rivers swell with snowmelt and glow faintly at night. The air carries the scent of blossoms — and, in sei-rich areas, of incense without a source. Planting season begins. Spirits stir.
Summer Natsu (夏) Minazuki, Fumizuki, Hazuki Heat settles over the islands. Monsoons sweep in from the Raijin no Fukai, bringing floods and storms that test coastal defences. The bronze-barked trees of Seidōrin Mori ring faintly in the humid wind. Sei flows strongly — summer is peak season for magical work, martial training, and the festivals that mark the height of the year.
Autumn Aki (秋) Nagatsuki, Kannazuki, Shimotsuki The harvest. Violet grasses darken to near-black. Crystal-barked trees chime in cooling winds. The spirit world presses closer — autumn is when the boundary thins, when ancestors visit, and when the great observances of remembrance and gratitude are held. Tatsunami tidal convergences typically begin in late Aki.
Winter Fuyu (冬) Shiwasu, Mutsuki, Kisaragi Cold descends from the northern mountains. Snow blankets the highlands while lowland rivers slow and darken. Luminescent mists gather during Shinmyōji. Winter is the season of endurance, of stories told by firelight, and of debts settled before the new year. Kawa's lowlands emerge from beneath retreating waters.

Astrological Overlays

The astrological events of the Miyosai system are not seasons in their own right — they are recurring celestial phenomena that overlay the standard four seasons, sometimes reinforcing their character and sometimes disrupting it. A Nagorikaze event during summer intensifies the monsoons; the same event during winter creates eerie blue-white frost patterns and unseasonal coastal surges.

Solar Events

Event Driven By Effects on the Seasons
Nagorikaze Susanoo's close approach Ghost rainbows and blue-white atmospheric phenomena. Water magic intensifies. Weather becomes more volatile — storms strengthen, rainfall increases, coastal waters surge. The effect compounds whatever season it overlays.
Long Shadow Tsukuyomi at maximum distance Transformation magic weakens. Shadows stretch, split, or move against the light. An unsettling quality pervades the landscape — things feel slightly wrong without being identifiably so. Shapeshifters and illusionists struggle; mundane craftspeople report tools behaving oddly.
Shinmyōji Kōrigami at peak influence Luminescent mists settle over Kagekuni. Winter severity increases. Even during autumn or early spring, Shinmyōji brings a cold that cuts deeper than temperature — a cold that feels ancient and patient.

Lunar Events

Event Driven By Effects on the Seasons
Tatsunami Four-moon alignment convergence Destructive tidal surges and coastal flooding. Navigation becomes hazardous. Typically occurs late Aki through mid-Haru — the colder half of the year, when communities are already hunkering down. Preparation begins months in advance; harbour towns board their seawalls and relocate stores to higher ground.
Hikarishō Ryūgetsu full phase alignment Celestial dragon auroras ripple across the sky. Sei amplification across all disciplines — practitioners report heightened sensitivity, increased range, and unpredictable surges. Spirit activity increases markedly. Considered the most auspicious event in the celestial calendar; ceremonies, weddings, and oaths sworn under Hikarishō carry special weight.

Additional astrological events exist but are less commonly named or studied. The interactions between solar and lunar events — a Nagorikaze coinciding with Tatsunami, for instance — produce compounded effects that exceed what either generates alone. Seimasters at Seishin maintain observational records tracking these overlaps and their consequences.

Kagekuni follows a traditional twelve-month calendar rooted in the agricultural and spiritual rhythms of the land. Each month carries a name that reflects the character of its days — what grows, what changes, what is demanded of the people who live through it. The names are ancient, predating the dark ages, and their meanings have weathered millennia of use without losing their aptness.

The current year is 16744. The current date is Nagatsuki 1 — the first day of the ninth month, the opening of Aki (autumn).

The Twelve Months

Month Name Characters Meaning Season
1 Mutsuki 睦月 Month of Affection Fuyu (Winter)
2 Kisaragi 如月 Month of Changing Clothes Fuyu (Winter)
3 Yayoi 弥生 Month of New Life Haru (Spring)
4 Uzuki 卯月 Month of Deutzia Haru (Spring)
5 Satsuki 皐月 Month of Early Rice Haru (Spring)
6 Minazuki 水無月 Month of Water Natsu (Summer)
7 Fumizuki 文月 Month of Letters Natsu (Summer)
8 Hazuki 葉月 Month of Leaves Natsu (Summer)
9 Nagatsuki 長月 Month of Long Nights Aki (Autumn)
10 Kannazuki 神無月 Month of No Gods Aki (Autumn)
11 Shimotsuki 霜月 Month of Frost Aki (Autumn)
12 Shiwasu 師走 Month of Running Priests Fuyu (Winter)

Notes on the Calendar

Mutsuki opens the year with the Month of Affection — a time for rekindling bonds, settling debts carried over from the old year, and renewing oaths of loyalty. Despite winter's grip, it is a month of warmth between people.

Kisaragi, the Month of Changing Clothes, marks the first tentative preparations for the season ahead. Heavy winter garments are aired and stored; lighter layers are brought out, though the cold has not yet released its hold.

Satsuki, the Month of Early Rice, is the agricultural pivot — the planting that determines whether the year will be one of plenty or hardship. Communities work together; even samurai households may contribute labour during Satsuki in rural provinces.

Minazuki is paradoxically named the Month of Water despite the kanji literally reading "month without water" — a reference to the rice paddies drinking the rains dry as fast as the monsoons deliver them.

Fumizuki, the Month of Letters, reflects the summer tradition of correspondence — poetry exchanges between allies and rivals, love letters carried by trusted messengers, and the formal diplomatic communiqués that shape the political landscape of the following seasons.

Kannazuki — the Month of No Gods — carries the common saying that "the gods are away" during the tenth month, though no one remembers where they supposedly go. The name is accepted without question by most, treated as folk tradition rather than literal truth.

Shiwasu, the Month of Running Priests, closes the year. Even the most contemplative monks are said to be running during the twelfth month — settling accounts, performing final rites, and preparing shrines for the new year. It is the busiest month for temples and the most frantic for merchants.

DM Note — Kannazuki's True Origin

The name Kannazuki is a historical fossil from the earliest age when the seven Progenitor dragons did physically gather during the tenth month. The tradition outlived the practice by millennia. The Ancient Guard recognizes the irony — the "Month of No Gods" was originally the month when all the gods were present in one place. Now, with the Progenitors slumbering, the name is accidentally accurate again for entirely different reasons.

Discovery path: Research in the Great Library of Kawa; conversations with Ancient Guard members; study of pre-Reckoning texts.

Kami

Kami are minor spiritual beings that inhabit natural features — a particular waterfall, an ancient tree, a stone at a crossroads worn smooth by centuries of travelers' hands. They are not ghosts. They are not yokai. They are the spiritual expression of a place or thing that has accumulated enough presence, enough meaning, to develop something like awareness.

Most kami are subtle. A shrine maiden sweeping the steps of a waterfall shrine may feel the kami's approval as a faint warmth in the spray. A woodcutter who asks permission before felling a tree in a kami-touched grove may find his axe biting cleaner and his back aching less. A traveler who leaves an offering at a roadside stone may discover the weather holding fair for exactly as long as they need it to.

Kami do not speak, as a rule. They communicate through environmental response — a shift in wind, a change in light, the behavior of local animals. Interpreting these responses is an art form, and the shrine priests and miko who maintain kami relationships undergo years of training to read the signs correctly.

When angered — through desecration, neglect, or the destruction of their physical anchor — kami can become tatari-gami, spirits of curse and misfortune. A tatari-gami doesn't attack directly; it curdles luck. Crops fail. Children sicken. Tools break at the worst possible moment. The affliction continues until the offense is addressed, and addressing it requires first identifying which kami was offended and how — a process that can take months and may require specialist intervention.

Kodama

Tree spirits. Specifically, the spirits of trees old enough and significant enough to have developed individual awareness — a process that takes centuries in ordinary forests but may happen faster in sei-rich environments like the Yōsei Mori.

Kodama manifest as faint lights among the branches, as echoes that don't quite match the original sound, or — very rarely — as small humanoid figures of bark and leaf that watch from the canopy with expressions of ancient patience. A forest rich in kodama has a particular quality: sound carries differently, paths seem to shift between visits, and the feeling of being observed is constant and not entirely uncomfortable.

They are guardians of their groves. Kodama do not prevent logging — they are patient enough to understand that trees grow back — but they respond to wanton destruction with a hostility that manifests as navigational confusion, persistent bad weather over the affected area, and a gradual encroachment of roots and undergrowth that can reclaim cleared land within a single season.

Serpentine humanoids reported in increasing numbers across the mountainous interior of Hokori. Scaled, cold-blooded, and driven by instincts that make them unpredictable, nagaji are unlike any catalogued species — their origin is a matter of active speculation among the few scholars aware of their existence.

They are not mindless. Nagaji organize into squad-like formations and coordinate through a sibilant language — rhythmic, tonal, and clearly purposeful even if its meaning is opaque to outside listeners. Whether they possess true intelligence or are operating on something closer to hive instinct remains unclear. They are territorial, aggressive when provoked, and show a marked preference for enclosed spaces — caves, ruins, and mountain tunnels.

What little is known suggests they are relatively recent arrivals. No historical text describes anything matching their physiology, and their range appears to be expanding from the high mountain regions downward into the foothills and valleys. How they came to be, and what they want, are questions no one has satisfactorily answered.

General Physiology

Nagaji are humanoid in general proportion but wrong in the details. The neck is slightly too long, the limbs bend at subtly incorrect angles, and the torso tapers in ways that suggest a skeletal structure fundamentally different from any known race. Their skin is scaled — mottled grey-green in most observed specimens, though coloration may vary — and cold to the touch. Their eyes are lidless, with vertical slit pupils that reflect light in low visibility. They appear to have no hair, no external ears, and no obvious nostrils, though they clearly sense their environment with precision.

They are cold-blooded. They seek warmth instinctively, coiling in enclosed spaces when at rest. When threatened, they become absolutely still — a predatory stillness that precedes explosive, violent action. This pattern is consistent across all observed variants.

Observed Variants

Nagaji encountered in the field organize into distinct roles that mirror military unit structures. Whether this reflects deliberate organization or instinctive social behavior is unknown, but the consistency across observed groups suggests it is not random.

Ashigaru

The most numerous variant. Nagaji ashigaru form the bulk of any encountered group, typically six to a squad. They are lighter in build than other variants — faster, more agile, and prone to flanking maneuvers rather than direct engagement.

Physiology: Slighter frame than other variants. Scales tend toward darker mottling, providing natural camouflage in shadow and stone environments.

Weaponry: Crude and improvised. Ashigaru carry repurposed metal shards lashed to wooden shafts — functional spears assembled from scavenged material rather than manufactured equipment. Some have been observed using sharpened stone or broken masonry as thrown projectiles.

Armor: Limited. Most ashigaru wear no protection of any kind, though some have been observed wearing crude leather coverings — hides lashed across the chest and shoulders — that provide marginal additional protection. Whether this is scavenged or deliberately fashioned is unclear.

Tactics: Ashigaru are aggressive. They charge into combat with little hesitation, closing distance quickly and relying on numbers and flanking angles to overwhelm targets. In enclosed spaces, they use side corridors, pillar shadows, and elevated positions to attack from multiple angles simultaneously. Their coordination through the sibilant language is most evident here; repositioning calls precede movement by only a heartbeat, suggesting the communication is instinctive rather than deliberated. However, ashigaru are quick to break. When their commanding bushi falls, morale collapses almost immediately — ashigaru scatter into side passages and flee rather than fight on without direction. This is the single most exploitable weakness in nagaji squad composition.

Hohei

Heavier infantry variants, typically two per squad. Hohei anchor the formation while ashigaru maneuver around the flanks.

Physiology: Noticeably larger and more heavily built than ashigaru. Broader across the shoulders and chest, with thicker scaling that appears to function as natural armor — denser, overlapping plates rather than the finer scales of the ashigaru. Some observed specimens show ridged scaling along the forearms and spine.

Weaponry: Similar improvised construction to ashigaru but heavier — longer hafted weapons, crude clubs fashioned from stone or salvaged metal. Hohei have been observed using their natural weapons as well: powerful jaw strikes and a constricting grip from their tails that can pin an opponent in place.

Armor: None manufactured, but the natural scaling provides meaningful protection. Bladed weapons that slide off ashigaru scales may bite into hohei plates and stick — a different problem, but still protective.

Tactics: Hohei hold ground. They position themselves between threats and the rest of the squad, absorbing attention and damage while the ashigaru work the edges. They do not retreat easily. A hohei that has committed to a position will fight from that position until it is dead or the threat has withdrawn. They are not berserkers — they fight with a cold, mechanical efficiency — but they do not appear to value self-preservation when the squad is engaged.

Bushi

Squad leaders. One per group. The bushi directs the squad's movements and appears to make tactical decisions in real time.

Physiology: Similar in size to hohei but leaner, with a bearing that suggests authority even across species lines. Bushi specimens show more varied coloration — some with faint patterning along the jaw and throat that may indicate age or status. Their movements are more deliberate and controlled than other variants, with less of the twitching, reactive quality seen in ashigaru.

Weaponry: Better equipped than the rank and file. Bushi carry weapons that show more care in construction — metal blades properly hafted, bindings that hold under stress. Some have been observed carrying what appear to be salvaged weapons of conventional manufacture, suggesting they can recognize and repurpose quality equipment when they find it.

Armor: Occasionally observed wearing fragments of salvaged armor — a shoulder plate, a partial breastplate — fitted imprecisely but functional. Whether they scavenge this deliberately or acquire it from defeated opponents is unclear.

Tactics: The bushi coordinates. It vocalizes more frequently than other variants, and the sibilant calls it produces precede squad-wide behavioral shifts — a formation change, a withdrawal, a sudden concentrated attack on a single target. The bushi does not lead from the front in the manner of a samurai; it positions itself where it can observe the full engagement and direct resources. When forced into direct combat, it fights with a precision and adaptability that exceeds the other variants — suggesting either greater retained intelligence or more sophisticated combat instincts.

Kannushi

The rarest observed variant. Kannushi appear to fill a spiritual or ritualistic role within nagaji groups, though the nature of that role is poorly understood.

Physiology: Slender, almost gaunt compared to other variants. Kannushi move differently — slower, more fluid, with a swaying quality that is unsettling to watch. Their scales sometimes carry a faint iridescence not seen in other variants, and their slit pupils are wider, as though adapted to perceive something beyond ordinary light.

Weaponry: Kannushi have not been observed carrying weapons. This does not mean they are unarmed — their behavior in the presence of sei-charged environments suggests capabilities that may not require physical implements.

Armor: None.

Tactics: Kannushi are drawn to spaces with spiritual or magical significance — shrines, meditation chambers, places where sei pools or concentrates. They return to these spaces compulsively, coiling on raised surfaces in postures that resemble meditation. Despite their ritualistic nature, kannushi are actively hostile. When a squad engages in combat near a kannushi's claimed space, the kannushi engages aggressively, leveraging whatever sei-related capabilities it possesses to defend its territory and support the squad. Their role in the squad structure is not fully understood, but they are not passive observers — they fight.

Sōhei

Warrior monks. Sōhei occupy a position below the kannushi in the nagaji hierarchy — more disciplined than ashigaru, more spiritually attuned than hohei, but serving a combat role rather than a ritualistic one. They are uncommon but not rare; where a kannushi is present, sōhei are usually nearby.

Physiology: Compact and densely muscled, with a stillness to their posture that distinguishes them from the twitching restlessness of ashigaru. Their scaling is tighter and more uniform than other variants — smooth, dark plates that fit close to the body like lacquered armor. Some specimens show faint patterning along the throat and wrists similar to kannushi iridescence, though duller and less pronounced.

Weaponry: Sōhei fight with their bodies. Strikes are precise and devastating — open-palmed blows, elbow strikes, and sweeping kicks delivered with a speed that belies their compact frames. Some have been observed wielding short staves or improvised tonfa-like implements, but unarmed combat appears to be their preferred and most effective mode.

Armor: None manufactured. Their natural scaling is denser than ashigaru but lighter than hohei — they trade raw protection for mobility.

Tactics: Sōhei fight with a focused, almost meditative discipline. Where ashigaru swarm and hohei anchor, sōhei target specific threats — isolating the most dangerous combatant and engaging with relentless, methodical pressure. They are difficult to shake once they have committed to a target. In the presence of a kannushi, sōhei appear to coordinate more tightly, as though receiving direction through means that are not purely vocal. Whether this is sei-mediated communication or simply familiarity is unknown.

Zasu

The apex of the nagaji hierarchy — a chief seimaster of terrifying capability. Only one has been observed, and that observation was enough. The zasu is what remains when a powerful seimaster undergoes the same transformation that created the nagaji, but retains — or perhaps transcends — their original intelligence and magical ability. Where other nagaji are creatures shaped by a failed ritual, the zasu may be something closer to the ritual's intended result.

Physiology: The zasu has moved further from humanoid form than any other variant. The body is elongated and serpentine, the limbs reduced to vestigial appendages or absent entirely. Multiple serpentine heads or hood-like expansions of scaling have been reported, though accounts are inconsistent — possibly because the zasu's form is difficult to perceive clearly, or possibly because it changes. The creature is large, filling a corridor or chamber with coiled mass. Its scales carry the same iridescence as the kannushi, but intensified — shifting colors that seem to pulse in rhythm with ambient sei.

Weaponry: The zasu does not carry weapons. It does not need them. It commands sei directly — channeling destructive force, manipulating the environment, and bending perception. It has been observed producing effects consistent with high-level warlock invocations: bolts of concentrated energy, zones of magical darkness, and — most dangerously — invisibility. The zasu uses invisibility not defensively but tactically, vanishing and repositioning across the battlefield to strike from unexpected angles before disappearing again.

Armor: None. The zasu's natural scaling is dense and heavily layered, and its command of sei may provide additional protection beyond the physical. Conventional weapons are unlikely to be the primary threat it presents.

Tactics: The zasu is a battlefield controller. It does not hold a position or charge a line — it moves, constantly, using invisibility to reposition and striking where the party is weakest or most exposed. It fights like a warlock with centuries of instinct: probing defenses, punishing overextension, and retreating into invisibility the moment pressure mounts. Direct engagement is on its terms or not at all. The zasu retains enough intelligence — or something that functions like intelligence — to make tactical decisions, prioritize targets, and adapt its approach mid-fight. Whether fragments of the original person persist beneath the transformation is an open question, and one the party may have opportunity to test.

Squad Tactics

A standard nagaji squad consists of one bushi, two hohei, and six ashigaru — nine total. This composition has been observed consistently enough to suggest it is not coincidental.

Engagement pattern: The squad does not attack on sight at range. It positions first. Ashigaru move to flanking positions using available cover — pillars, side corridors, elevated terrain. Hohei advance to block the most direct line of retreat. The bushi observes. The attack begins simultaneously from multiple angles, initiated by a sharp vocalization from the bushi.

Communication: The sibilant language is constant during engagement — short, rhythmic bursts that correspond to tactical shifts. The speed of coordination suggests the communication is partially instinctive; the delay between a bushi's call and the squad's response is faster than deliberate interpretation would allow.

Adaptability: Nagaji squads adjust to setbacks. If ashigaru flankers are neutralized, the remaining squad contracts rather than continuing a compromised plan. If the bushi falls, the squad fractures — the hohei assume a defensive posture and hold ground, but the ashigaru break almost immediately, scattering into side passages and fleeing the engagement. Eliminating the bushi is the fastest way to collapse a nagaji squad.

Ambush preference: Nagaji strongly prefer to fight on their terms. They know the terrain they occupy intimately and use it. Shadow corridors, narrow passages, and spaces with limited visibility are not obstacles for them — they are advantages. Their low-light vision and comfort in enclosed spaces means that fighting nagaji in their territory is fighting them at their best.

Avoidance behavior: Nagaji have been observed avoiding certain spaces entirely — areas with strong residual magical presence or specific environmental qualities. Whether this reflects fear, discomfort, or something else is unknown, but it is consistent and can be exploited by those who recognize the pattern.

Type
core

Dragons

The seven Progenitor Dragons founded the civilization of Kagekuni in the deep past. Their dragon clans — Crimson, Azure, Emerald, Onyx, Golden, Silver, and Amethyst — established the framework of society, religion, and magical practice that persists to this day. They are remembered as historical and mythological figures whose legacy shapes every aspect of life in the Shrouded Isles.

Non-Progenitor dragons are extraordinarily rare in the current era. Sightings occur perhaps once in a generation, usually in remote locations — the volcanic peaks of Fushichō, the deep waters around Kawa, the highest ridges of the Tenchūsan Ren. These encounters are poorly documented because the witnesses tend to be isolated travelers whose accounts are received with skepticism.

Dragon eggs surface occasionally in excavations, in the hoards of other creatures, or in the treasure vaults of noble houses. They are believed to be fossils of the founding era — beautiful, collectible, and prized as relics.

Ryūjin

Dragon-blooded beings. Not dragonborn — who are a distinct race claiming descent from the Progenitors — but creatures in which draconic blood manifests as something between beast and legend. A ryūjin might appear as an enormous serpent with vestigial wings, or a lizard the size of a war-horse with scales that refract light into colors that don't exist in the normal spectrum.

Ryūjin are tied to specific environments and elements. A river ryūjin commands the currents and can call floods or droughts. A mountain ryūjin causes tremors and rockslides, sometimes deliberately and sometimes as a byproduct of rolling over in its sleep. They are venerated in local tradition and placated with offerings, and the distinction between a ryūjin and a kami is a subject of ongoing theological debate.

lore.name: Sei-Touched — The Changed and the Changing

text.content:
Type
core

Sei does not merely fuel magic. It saturates the world, and where it pools or flows in concentrated currents, the things that live in those currents change. The sei drought suppressed this process for three millennia. Since the Great Awakening, it has resumed — and the world is still adjusting.

Sei Beasts

Ordinary animals exposed to elevated sei concentrations over time. The changes are cumulative and unpredictable: a deer in the Yōsei Mori might grow a third eye that perceives sei flows, or develop antlers of crystallized amber that resonate in the presence of magic. A hawk nesting near a sei wellspring might produce offspring with feathers of metallic bronze that cut like razors.

Sei beasts are not inherently aggressive, but they are often territorial in ways their mundane counterparts are not, and their altered physiology can make them dangerous even without hostile intent. A sei-touched boar that generates localized tremors when it charges is not trying to hurt anyone — it's just running. The tremors are incidental. The fact that they can collapse a hillside is a separate problem.

The Yōsei Mori in Kusa province has the highest concentration of sei beasts in Hokori. Deeper reaches of the forest harbor creatures of significantly elevated intelligence — animals that plan, coordinate, and in some cases appear to communicate in ways that defy natural explanation.

Sei Aberrations

When sei concentrations spike beyond what the local environment can integrate, the result is not gradual change but sudden, violent transformation. Sei aberrations are creatures — or were creatures — that have been overwhelmed by magical energy. Their bodies twist, merge with their surroundings, or develop properties that contradict their original nature: a fish that burns, a bird made of liquid stone, a tree that bleeds and screams when cut.

Sei aberrations are unpredictable and almost always hostile, not because they choose to be but because the transformation is agonizing and they lash out at anything nearby. They are most common near sei wellsprings, ley line intersections, and sites where magical catastrophes have occurred. The ruins of pre-Aphelion institutions — temples, laboratories, libraries — are particularly prone to aberration formation, as residual enchantments interact with returning sei in ways their builders never anticipated.

Nagaji

Serpentine humanoids of unknown origin, reported in increasing numbers across the mountainous interior of Hokori. Enough has been observed of their behavior, physiology, and organization to warrant a dedicated entry.
