text.content:
Geography & Terrain

Hana occupies the eastern coast of Hokori and is the seat of imperial history. It stretches along the island's eastern seaboard, bounded to the northwest by the mountainous interior of Sora province for the majority of its inland border, with Tsuchi and Hi to the west, and Kaze to the north.

The province's defining feature is the Serenia-kai (Selenia Sea), a vast inland sea covering more than a thousand square miles, fed by twenty-five rivers and thirteen waterfalls cascading from the Tenchusan Ren and the central highlands of Hokori. Its surface shifts color with the seasons. The tidal rhythms driven by Kagekuni's four moons make its edges unpredictable; the shoreline can retreat several hundred meters during low compound tides.

To the west, the Seidorin Mori (Bronze Wood Forest) stretches for miles -- an ancient woodland where the trees grow with bark of burnished copper-bronze that catches sunlight like armor. Their leaves shed entirely in one night when the temperature drops below a certain threshold. The wood itself is extraordinarily hard and is harvested under strict clan license for weapons and structural reinforcement.

To the northeast, the land rises sharply toward the Tenchusan Ren. The pass through this range is the primary land route north. The mountains are sacred in Hana's religious tradition; several peak-top shrines are maintained by hermit monks.

Shirogane Yama (Silver Mountain), the highest peak on Hokori, dominates the northern skyline -- a pale peak streaked with natural mineral deposits that catch moonlight. At its summit sits the Hoshino To (Tower of Stars), an ancient astronomical observatory built during the Golden Age. The city of Kumoji sits at its base.

Key Waterways: Kinryugawa (Gold Dragon River), Midorikawa (Green River), Sutariba (Star River)

Points of Interest:

  • Seidorin Mori (Bronze Wood Forest) -- Ancient woodland with metallic-barked trees. Harvested under strict Clan Kaminari license. The interior is unnervingly quiet -- sound behaves strangely under the canopy. Unlicensed logging is a capital offense.
  • Serenia-kai (Selenia Sea) -- The great inland sea. Major artery for trade and travel. The most dangerous tidal event is Ryugetsu's Embrace, when three moons align over the sea simultaneously.
  • Hoshino To (Tower of Stars) -- Ancient observatory on Shirogane Yama summit. Still operational; maintained by a small order of seimasters. Instruments calibrated to all three stars and four moons simultaneously.
  • Kodan no Jinja -- Ancient roadside shrine. Grants divine boons to supplicants for a period of days equal to three times the recipient's experience level (maximum sixty days). Only one boon at a time.
  • Shadowfen Bridge -- Stone bridge near Sakura Mura crossing into marsh forest. Legend claims a river spirit demands one honest secret spoken aloud; liars find the far bank leads somewhere unintended.
  • Tenchusan Ren (Heavenly Pillar Mountains) -- The mountain range forming Hana's northwestern boundary. The pass is treacherous in autumn and impassable during winter storms. Significant ruins exist within the range.

Settlements

Settlement Type Population Notes
Heian City Large Imperial capital; major port; seat of clan governance
Fujisato City Medium Northeastern coastal port; fishing and trade
Kikyo City Medium Eastern edge of Bronze Wood; lumber trade; Clan Seishin subject
Ayame Town 638 Military waypoint; base of Tenchusan Ren pass
Kumoji Town Medium Base of Shirogane Yama; near Hoshino To observatory
Momiji Town Small Peaceful western lakeside town on Serenia-kai
Sakurano Town Small On Lake Midoriko; Heian ferry connection
Natsumura Village 161 Fishing village at mouth of Sutariba
Nishihara Village 180 Rolling hills; weekly market; Temple of Ancestors
Sakura Mura Village 150 Grew from highway inn; Shadowfen Bridge
Kawaguchi Village Small River crossing settlement
Takamine Village 97 Poor iron mining village; shadow of Kinryuzan

Culture & Trade

Hana's culture is the closest to the old imperial ideal -- formal, ceremonially rich, and deeply aware of its historical weight. The proximity to Heian means merchants, scholars, monks, and diplomats pass through constantly, and even small villages carry themselves with a certain civic dignity uncommon in frontier provinces.

The Bronze Wood trade defines the province's economy. Seidorin timber commands extraordinary prices across the archipelago -- weapons and armor crafted from it are status symbols as much as tools. The licensing system for harvesting creates significant corruption opportunities at every level of local administration.

Fishing on the Serenia-kai and the Kinryugawa sustains much of the rural population. The Gold Dragon River runs fat with a fish called kinuo (gold-tail) that is considered a delicacy in Heian and commands premium prices at market.

History

Hana is the oldest continuously inhabited province in the archipelago. The Golden Dragon Clan held dominion over these southern highlands long before human settlement -- their capital Kinkokyo is believed to have stood somewhere in or beneath the Tenchusan Ren, buried by the avalanche triggered during the Onyx Rebellion. The province's rivers still run faintly gold at dawn -- a phenomenon locals call Kinryu no Namida (the Golden Dragon's Tears).

Heian was chosen as the imperial capital by the First Emperor Tenryu no Mikado for strategic and spiritual reasons -- it stood at the convergence of three rivers, on a defensible peninsula, and was reportedly the site of a vision in which Kinryu declared the land under divine protection.

The province suffered heavily during the Dark Ages -- Heian was sacked twice -- but its infrastructure proved resilient. The Emperor's Highway remains largely intact through Hana.

Clan Kaminari has governed Hana for the past several centuries. The clan rose to prominence when Raijin no Kazuhiko unified the province under a single authority following a period of fractious minor-clan governance.

• The Bronze Wood Forest's metallic quality has a deeper origin than simple mineral runoff -- connected to the buried city of Kinkokyo beneath the Tenchusan Ren.
  • The Shadowfen Bridge exhibits genuine sei resonance that produces mild disorientation in those who speak falsehoods while crossing.
  • A seimaster from Hoshino To has gone missing after reporting an unusual celestial alignment that matches nothing in the records.

The Buried City of Kinkokyo

The Golden Dragon Clan's capital is not simply buried rubble. Significant portions survived structurally intact, sealed beneath hundreds of feet of rock and earth. The gold doors the party currently stands before are an outer entrance to this buried complex, exposed by a recent earthquake. The temple above is connected to Kinkokyo below. Ko'jiri's research is essentially correct.

Kinryu no Hikari

The artifact exists. It is held in a sealed vault deep within the temple, in the farthest underground section of Kinkokyo. It is not a weapon or a key. It is a communication device: a golden mirror that allows direct communion with Kinryu, the living Golden Dragon, wherever she is hidden. She will answer if called by someone she deems worthy.

The Bronze Wood Secret

The Seidorin Mori grows over a second branch of the buried Kinkokyo canal system. The metallic quality of the trees is caused by trace mineral content in the groundwater -- water flowing through golden veins in the buried city's infrastructure for thousands of years. Ren Nakamura (Shicho of Kikyo) knows this. The merchant guild he is allied with wants to find the source and exploit it directly.

Hiroshi Nakamura -- Traitor in Place

As Shugo of Heian, Hiroshi controls the administrative heart of the province. His access to Clan Kaminari intelligence is nearly total. He has been feeding information to an outside party (undeveloped) for at least three years. His warm, approachable public persona is his most effective weapon -- even his brother Hideo does not suspect how deep the betrayal runs.

Plot Hooks

  • Unlicensed Bronze Wood poaching tied to a merchant guild front operation in Kikyo -- Ren Nakamura's faction or a rival?
  • Strange behavior reported in Shadowfen Bridge area -- a traveler arrived at the wrong destination and has no memory of the crossing
  • A seimaster from Hoshino To has gone missing after reporting an unusual celestial alignment that matches nothing in the records

Type
settlement

"The city that outlasted every empire built within it."

Overview

Heian is the oldest continuously inhabited city in the archipelago and the seat of imperial authority for over eight thousand years. It stands on a peninsula where the Nagisa Sea meets Lake Midoriko -- a position offering both a defensible landward approach and open water access in two directions.

The city is beautiful in the way that things shaped by deep time become beautiful -- through the accumulation of craftsmanship, care, and purpose. Ancient trees line the main avenues, their roots lifting paving stones that are reset around them generation after generation. The Imperial Palace complex dominates the skyline. Shirogane Yama is visible on clear days forty miles to the north and northwest.

The Emperor's Highway extends from Heian in three directions -- north through Tenchusan Ren toward Kaze, east along the coast, and west by ferry connection to Sakurano and the interior. With no emperor, the city is a center without a purpose -- the streets are still busy, the markets still active, but there is a quality to civic life: the posture of a city holding itself together while waiting for resolution.

Districts / Landmarks

Hikari Zon -- Knowledge District Libraries, academies, schools, and scholarly institutions. Low, wide buildings with sliding walls. The central library holds the largest collection in Hana. Seimasters and scholars from across the archipelago spend time here.

Hinode-ku -- Eastern Residential Ward Mixed residential for artisans and merchants. Workshops opening onto narrow streets. A lively night market operates along the canal.

Ichiba Chiku -- Market District The economic heart. The largest open market in Hokori operates six days out of seven. The Market District never truly closes.

Inari Kyoku -- Religious District Temples, shrines, and spiritual institutions. Torii gates multiply inward from the boundary. A shrine to each of the seven dragon clans exists here.

Kaze-sho -- Wind District Open spaces, windmills, farming plots within the city boundary. The windmills power grain milling and workshop machinery.

Kinrin Chiku -- Palace Surrounding Quarter Residential and administrative district surrounding the Imperial Palace. Noble families and senior officials. Access is controlled. Streets are wider for ceremonial processions.

Kokyo Chiku -- Imperial Palace Complex Palace grounds surrounded by walls, gates, and a water moat. Centuries of accumulated construction. With no emperor, maintained by skeleton staff under the Kokushi Kyokai. Sections have been sealed.

Kurogane-sho -- Steel Precinct The forge district. Smiths, armorers, weapons specialists. Runs hot year-round. Home to Taro's Forge.

Mizu-gai -- Riverside Ward Along the water's edge. Water gardens, seafood restaurants, fish markets, fishing family residences. The morning catch market is a Heian institution.

Ryu Jikuchiku -- Dragon Borough Nightlife, theater, teahouses, entertainment. Operates on a shifted schedule -- fully alive after dark. Hosts noh theater, storytellers, gambling establishments, and renowned teahouses.

Sakura-ku -- Cherry Blossom Ward Parks, public gardens, festival infrastructure. Famous cherry tree avenues. Hosts major seasonal festivals.

Tabibito Gai -- Traveler's Street Eastern gate neighborhood for transient visitors. Inns, stables, money changers, translation services. Character shifts constantly.

Tenku Zon -- Hilltop Ward Highest elevation residential area. Reserved for nobility and senior officials. Finest architecture in Heian.

Tensho no Mon -- Military District Barracks, command infrastructure, training grounds. Home to Taisho Hideo Nakamura's command headquarters. Where the party received their mission briefing.

Notable Establishments

Taro's Forge (Kurogane-sho) -- Master blacksmith Taro Fukomoto's workshop. Renowned for quality and integrity. Produces exceptional weapons and armor. Taro teaches those who demonstrate genuine commitment.

The Moonlit Garden (Ryu Jikuchiku) -- Teahouse in the Dragon Borough with a garden famous for nighttime aesthetics -- white stone, silver-leaved trees, reflecting pool. The party first convened here. Renowned for discretion.

Hikari no Shizuku (Hikari Zon) -- Healing and light magic enclave in the Knowledge District. Provides medical services and trains healing-aligned sei practitioners.

Key Figures

  • Hiroshi Nakamura -- Shugo (Governor) of Heian -> npcs/hiroshi-nakamura.md
  • Hideo Nakamura -- Taisho (General); military commander -> npcs/hideo-nakamura.md
  • Taro Fukomoto -- Master blacksmith -> npcs/taro-fukomoto.md

• The Imperial Palace's sealed sections contain something found after the Emperor's death that the Kokushi Kyokai does not know how to handle.
  • The Moonlit Garden teahouse serves a deeper function as a neutral meeting ground for intelligence exchanges.
  • Multiple individuals have arrived in Heian with claims to imperial succession.

DM Secrets

Hiroshi Nakamura -- Traitor in Place As Shugo, Hiroshi has near-total access to Clan Kaminari's intelligence and administrative operations. He is feeding intelligence to an outside party and has been for at least three years. He is aware that Hideo is investigating and is actively monitoring that investigation. His public persona is a performance of exceptional consistency.

The Imperial Palace -- Sealed Sections Something was found in the imperial apartments after Ryujin no Mikado died that the Kokushi Kyokai administrators do not know how to handle. It is not evidence of murder -- it is evidence of something older and stranger.

The Moonlit Garden's True Function The owner is a retired intelligence operative who maintains it as a neutral meeting ground for the Elven Council, among other groups. Information exchanges here regularly under the social protection of tea ceremony neutrality. The staff are trained to notice and remember without appearing to.

Hideo Nakamura's Investigation Hideo is hunting a traitor he does not yet know is his brother. He has narrowed the leak to a small circle of senior staff. The question is whether he reaches the conclusion before Hiroshi learns how close Hideo is and takes action.

The Succession Crisis in Heian Multiple claimants with genealogical documents of varying plausibility. The Kokushi Kyokai handles them through administrative delay. Three serious claimants are being watched. Two are probably fraudulent. One may not be.

Plot Hooks

  • Hideo Nakamura asks the party to carry out intelligence work he cannot assign to his own staff -- suggests he suspects someone close
  • An unusual request arrives from the sealed section of the Imperial Palace: someone inside has sent a note requesting outside contact; the Kokushi Kyokai doesn't know how this happened
  • A succession claimant approaches the party specifically, wanting independent witnesses to a document verification

frontmatter.name: Heian
frontmatter.climate: Temperate; cherry blossom springs; warm summers; brilliant autumns; mild winters

text.content:
Geography & Terrain

Hi is the most geologically violent province on Hokori -- a region of active volcanism, fumarole fields, obsidian plains, and mountains that periodically tear themselves apart. It encompasses the majority of the island's western side, surrounded by mountains and the sea. Tsuchi borders it to the southeast, Hana shares a small stretch of its eastern border, Sora encompasses its northern boundary, and Mizu sits along its western edge. Earthquakes are ambient. Residents learn to read tremors the way sailors read wind.

The province takes its name -- Hi, meaning fire -- from the volcanic peaks that define it. The largest, Enshiyama (Flame Peak Mountain), is the third highest peak on Hokori. It last erupted in full approximately two hundred years ago.

The terrain is dramatic and hostile. Black obsidian fields stretch for miles where ancient lava flows cooled and cracked. Fumarole vents release sulfurous steam. Soil, where it exists, is extraordinarily fertile -- volcanic ash enriches it beyond anything in the southern provinces. Terraced farming on the slopes between active zones produces crops of startling quality. This contradiction -- death and abundance in tight proximity -- defines Hi's cultural character.

Rivers here run fast and hot from thermal sources. The Honogawa (Flame River) originates from a thermal lake near Enshiyama's base and is warm to the touch for its entire upper reach.

Points of Interest:

  • Enshiyama (Flame Peak Mountain) -- Dominant volcano of Hokori's north. Currently active at low levels. Crater contains a mineral-rich lake that glows faintly orange at night.
  • Honogawa (Flame River) -- Warm thermal river. Upper reach near the source is hot enough to scald. Runs through a narrow volcanic gorge.
  • Obsidian Fields of Kuroso -- Vast plains of black volcanic glass. Obsidian of exceptional quality, ideal for blades and lenses. Seismically active and hazardous.
  • The Crimson Shrine -- Deep in the volcanic highlands, predating the empire. Torii of natural red stone. Local tradition holds Akaryu's presence can be felt during major eruptions. Never absorbed into the imperial religious system.
  • Onsen-machi Hot Springs -- The only genuinely comfortable location in Hi. Natural hot spring pools developed into a resort town maintaining political neutrality.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Enshiro Town Provisional garrison capital; military administration; base of active clan competition
Kazan Mura Village Slopes of Enshiyama; volcano watchers; evacuation specialists
Kurokawa Village Black river settlement; obsidian crafting; trade in volcanic glass
Onsen-machi Town Hot spring resort town; wealthy visitors; nominal neutrality
Takibi Village Remote highland farming community; terraced volcanic fields

Culture & Trade

Hi's culture is defined by proximity to death. The people are laconic, practical, and possess a dark humor about their circumstances. They do not flee volcanic activity -- they have developed sophisticated systems for reading, mitigating, and living alongside it. Hi's volcano-guides, engineers, and evacuation specialists are prized across the archipelago.

Primary exports are obsidian, volcanic sulfur (used in alchemy and sei-related preparations), hot spring minerals, and surprisingly excellent agricultural products from volcanic terraces. The Onsen-machi resort draws wealthy visitors from across Hokori and beyond.

History

Hi was long considered a backwater -- too dangerous and too remote. The Crimson Dragon Clan had their true stronghold here before unification, and the western reaches refused submission to Tenryu no Mikado. That refusal left a cultural legacy: Hi's people are fiercely independent and deeply skeptical of imperial authority.

During the Dark Ages, Hi was almost entirely abandoned by formal authority. Small communities developed their own governance structures, spiritual practices, and martial traditions largely divorced from the broader empire.

The province is currently in contested administration. The previous governing clan was wiped out in the opening engagements of the Arashi-Genso war, and neither alliance has installed a replacement. Several smaller clans are vying for the position.

• The Crimson Shrine's keeper, Tsubaki, has served for sixty years and communicates with something through the shrine's ember-bowl.
  • The western territories of Hi are home to descendants of the Crimson Clan faction that refused unification, organized into loose tribal confederacies preserving forgotten traditions.
  • Seimasters debate whether Enshiyama's current activity signals a major eruption building.

The Crimson Dragon Clan's Hidden Presence

Akaryu, the Crimson Dragon, is still alive and hidden. She maintains a tenuous connection to Hi through the Crimson Shrine. The shrine's keeper Tsubaki is an Initiate of the Order of the Ancient Guard. She does not know Akaryu's location, but knows the dragon is alive. Offerings burned in the shrine's ember-bowl reach something that responds.

The Western Territories

The western reaches are effectively a separate entity. Descendants of the Crimson Clan faction that refused Tenryu's unification live there in loose tribal confederacies that have preserved traditions the rest of the empire forgot. They are fiercely territorial and know things about the volcanic highlands that no imperial map captures.

Enshiyama and the Coming Eruption

The current low-level activity is the precursor to a significant eruption -- within one to three years. The seimasters who know this are divided on whether to publicize it; the political vacuum means there is no coordinating authority capable of organizing evacuation. This is an unlit fuse.

The Contested Administration

The three clans competing for Hi's governance are being quietly manipulated by a fourth party -- a merchant consortium that wants provincial administration too weak to enforce trade regulations. The current chaos is, to some degree, manufactured.

Plot Hooks

  • A volcano-guide from Kazan Mura has seen something in the upper reaches of Enshiyama -- something that moved against the wind -- and is too frightened to go back alone
  • The Crimson Shrine's ember-bowl responded to an offering in a way it never has before; Tsubaki needs discreet help interpreting what it means
  • A seimaster studying the eruption precursors has disappeared; her notes suggest she found something in the obsidian fields that was not geological

Master Timeline

Period Years Name
Pre-Imperial Before 8000 Age of Dragons
Imperial Founding ~8000–8611 Era of the First Emperors
First Golden Age 8611–13050 Kagekuni's Golden Age
Age of Strife 13050–13088 War of Fractured Banners
Dark Ages 13088–15642 The Long Dark
Recovery 15642–15691 Jinshō Reformation
Second Golden Age 15691–15757 Era of New Discovery
Subtle Awakening 15757–16620 Return of Talents
Great Awakening 16620–present Magic Restored
Current 16744 Post-Imperial Crisis

Key Historical Events

Age of Dragons (Pre-8000)

  • Seven dragon clans ruled the archipelago before human settlement
  • Early settlers integrated, paid tribute, joined clans
  • Intermingling produced near-immortal arcadian (elf) leaders — first daimyo
  • Dragons gradually withdrew from direct rule

Era of the First Emperors (~8000–8611)

  • Tenryū no Mikado ascended ~8000 at age 852; descended from Crimson and Golden Dragon bloodlines
  • United fragmented clans through diplomacy and martial campaigns
  • Key conflict: Crimson Clan (Akaryū) refused submission; withdrew into Akaho Sanmyaku; eastern faction joined empire; western lands became barbarian territory
  • Battle of Seirei Mizuumi — secured Kawa; defeated Azure Clan navy
  • Onyx Rebellion (8238–8611) — Kokuryū led 400-year guerrilla war from Tatara; ended with destruction of Kuroi Yama; Kokuryū escaped
  • Tenryū died 8694; succeeded by son Ryūhiko no Mikado (already 794 years old)

Golden Age (8611–13050)

  • Eight emperors; unprecedented peace and prosperity
  • Major constructions: Imperial Palace (Heian), Great Library (Seirei Mizuumi), Grand Canal (Mizushima), Hoshino Tō observatory (Shirogane Yama), Kokuyō Ryūkyūjō fortress (Tatara)
  • Emperor's Highway built 11248
  • Emperors: Tenryū, Ryūhiko, Seiryū, Byakuryū, Kinryū, Shoryū, Inaryū, Kōryū

War of Fractured Banners (13050–13088)

  • Tensions between Zirak and Glimfyr on Tatara spread empire-wide
  • Emperor Kōryū no Mikado slain on battlefield 13053
  • Son Ryūjin no Mikado II established the Shogunate; appointed first Shogun Kazutaka no Kazuhiko
  • Key battles: Defense of Midoriko, Pursuit to Kumoji, Campaign in Tatara, Burning of Shirotsuru, Siege of Fushichō, Ambush at Tatsumaki Gorge, Battle of the Thunder Plains
  • War ended 13062; Seiryu and Hagane clans wiped out; magic vanished completely

Dark Ages (13088–15642)

  • Rampant famine, disease, population decimation
  • Magic completely absent
  • Little documentation survives

Jinshō Reformation (15642–15691)

  • Emperor Jinshin no Mikado enacted sweeping reforms
  • Agricultural revival, infrastructure rebuilding, trade stimulation, educational revival
  • Great Library partially restored (had been destroyed by earthquake)
  • Established Kokushi Kyōkai with Seimu Daijin and Zaiumu Daijin

Era of New Discovery (15691–15757)

  • Expedition of 15691 led by Admiral Taira no Akinori and General Tokugawa no Ryuji
  • Diplomat Hōjō no Kaoru also key figure; later became first Gaikō Daijin
  • Discovered lands beyond Kagekuni; returned with slaves, precious metals, new knowledge
  • 150+ expeditions over next 60 years; clan rivalries intensified
  • Emperor appointed Minamoto no Katsuro (Tenshiko Clan) as Shogun ~16012
  • Shogun enacted: Expedition Regulation Act, Resource Distribution Act, Peace and Mediation Act, Defense Enhancement Act
  • Shogunate retired; Gaikō Daijin established under Hōjō no Kaoru

Era of Subtle Awakening (15757–16620)

  • Talents (individuals with innate magic) began emerging ~15757
  • First known Talent: Hikari no Kenta — storm magic; born 15757
  • Talents persecuted; formed underground communities
  • Notable Talents: Mizuki no Hana (Gekkō Clan; shadow magic), Fujimoto no Aiko (Ryūkaze Clan; wind manipulation)
  • Seishin Enclave founded on Unmeijima; grew into city of Seishin
  • Hikari no Shizuku — healing/light magic enclave within Heian
  • Epoch of Factional Flux (16204–16434): Clans merged, dissolved, restructured
    • Hōjō Clan civil war → merger with Minamoto → became Clan Kaminari (honoring Raijin)
    • Ryūkaze Clan absorbed smaller clans; dominant in northwest
    • Yamamoto Clan splintered; Ishikawa Clan dissolved
    • Clan Tetsujin emerged as mercenary clan from Ishikawa remnants
  • Peasant Uprising (16442–16461): Sparked by crackdown at Midoriko village
    • Shogun Takeda no Hiroshi appointed 16443
    • First Fukushi Daijin: Hayashi no Haruto appointed 16453
    • Combined military/diplomatic approach ended uprising 16461
  • Plague Campaign of Kuroyami (16609–16616):
    • Kuroyami no Akuma (formerly Takeda no Arata) found necromantic tome in Kuroshi Temple, Yurei
    • Established Eikyū Yami Clan cult; led undead legions
    • Shogun Minamoto no Katsuro appointed 16610; recruited Talents
    • Seishin Enclave, Raimeiin, Forest of Spirits publicly revealed themselves
    • Kuroyami defeated but never captured — escaped; whereabouts unknown
    • Eikyū Yami Clan persists in some form

Great Awakening (16620–present)

  • Magic officially returned ~16687 — daimyo actively recruit mages

• Reforms of Ryūjin no Mikado (16732): 18th emperor; last near-immortal elf; banned Kokushi Kyōkai from appointing Shogun without imperial approval
  • End of Imperial Line (16739): Ryūjin no Mikado died under mysterious circumstances; officially old age; foul play suspected but unproven
  • Widespread Aggression (16742): War between Genso and Arashi alliances begins
  • Current Year: 16744

frontmatter.name: History & Timeline
frontmatter.description: Master timeline from pre-imperial era to current year 16744

text.content:
Geography & Terrain

Kaze is a province of shadows and mist. It occupies the eastern side of Hokori's northeastern leg -- the X-shape's upper-right arm. Nami sits to the north, Kusa to the west, Hana to the south, and Sora shares a brief stretch of its southwestern border. Sheltered from direct coastal weather by mountain ranges, it has a microclimate of cool, damp air that never fully clears. The province averages fewer clear days per year than any other on the island. Its forests -- dense stands of dark cedar and ancient black pine -- grow so thickly that the canopy blocks most sunlight even in summer. Locals navigate by landmark and feel rather than by sun or stars.

The terrain is mountainous, cut by deep river valleys and narrow gorges. The Kazeyama Ren (Wind Mountain Range) runs along the province's southern border, channeling wind up the valleys in complex, disorienting patterns. Sounds carry strangely here, seeming to come from the wrong direction.

The Kagero River (Shimmer River) is the primary waterway -- named for the heat shimmer visible over its surface on rare warm days, caused by thermal differential between the water temperature and the cool air.

The town of Akatsuki (Dawn) occupies a peculiar position -- its name suggests emergence and new light, but it is one of the most shrouded settlements in the archipelago. The name predates the current settlement.

Points of Interest:

  • Tsukikage (Moonlit Shadow) -- Abandoned former capital of Clan Gekko. Not destroyed or obviously fled in panic -- it simply emptied gradually over several months. Personal belongings remain in homes. The daimyo's residence is locked from the outside.
  • Monastery of the Black Lily -- Above Akatsuki village, accessible by stone staircase cut into rock. Dark stone and iron construction; austere; forbidding. The Order of the Black Lily operates here -- Kagekuni's most skilled infiltrators and intelligence operatives.
  • The Kagero Gorge -- Narrow river gorge with complex, disorienting acoustics. The gorge wall contains numerous carved reliefs depicting serpentine figures that do not match any known iconographic tradition.
  • The Hollow Peaks -- Three mountains in the Kazeyama Ren that are demonstrably hollow. Cold air vents from fissures at their bases year-round. Sei-sensitive individuals report a powerful residual presence.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Tsukikage Town Traditional Gekko capital; functionally abandoned; eerie and intact
Akatsuki Village De facto administrative center; above it: Monastery of the Black Lily
Kazetani Village Deep valley settlement; largely cut off; residents haven't left in months
Kirigakure Village Literally "hidden in mist"; the most isolated settlement; some suggest it moves
Mikazuki Village Crescent Moon Village; southern border; last outpost before Hana

Culture & Trade

Kaze's culture is inward-facing. Primary exports have historically been information -- Clan Gekko's intelligence networks and the Order of the Black Lily's trained specialists. In tangible terms, Kaze produces excellent black pine lumber, rare mountain herbs for medicine and alchemy, and distinctive lacquerware using naturally sourced pigments from mineral-rich soil.

The people of Kaze are not cold -- they are careful. A culture of watching and listening developed naturally in a province where visibility is limited and sound behaves unreliably. They form deep loyalties within small groups and extend trust to outsiders only after extended familiarity.

History

Kaze was historically the domain of Clan Gekko, an independent clan that maintained careful neutrality through successive political upheavals. The Gekko were notable for producing seimasters specializing in shadow and illusion magic -- linked to the province's physical character and lingering influence from the Onyx Dragon Clan.

The province was never fully subdued -- even Tenryu no Mikado secured Gekko cooperation through negotiation rather than conquest. This arrangement eventually crystallized into the Order of the Black Lily, Kagekuni's premier infiltration school.

Clan Gekko's recent disappearance has plunged the province into deep unease. Trade has slowed. The provincial administration has stopped communicating with Heian. Small communities have reported strange encounters -- serpentine figures glimpsed on mountain trails, abandoned buildings showing signs of violent disturbance, livestock found dead in unnatural ways.

• Clan Gekko's disappearance was not caused by an outside force -- the senior seimasters attempted something that went catastrophically wrong.
  • The Order of the Black Lily knows the truth about what happened and has made a calculated decision about when to reveal it.
  • The Hollow Peaks were structures of the Onyx Dragon Clan -- hollow mountains used as nesting and storage spaces.
  • The gorge carvings depict something connected to the transformation that befell Clan Gekko.

The Nagaji Truth -- Core Campaign Revelation

Clan Gekko's disappearance was not caused by an outside force. The clan's senior seimasters, searching for a way to elevate their shadow magic capability, discovered fragmentary texts describing an Onyx Dragon ritual -- a transformation rite tied to Kokuryu. It transformed those who underwent it into Nagaji -- serpentine humanoids driven by new instincts they cannot fully suppress. The transformation spread. Masota no Gekko himself underwent the ritual last, in a desperate attempt to maintain control. He is now Nagaji as well -- somewhere in the Kaze highlands.

The Order of the Black Lily -- What They Know

The Order knows the truth about the Nagaji transformation. Several operatives witnessed the early stages. The Order has made a calculated decision: the information is too dangerous to release without a reversal plan. They will share the complete truth with parties who reach them -- but only the complete truth, no partial admissions.

Is the Transformation Reversible?

Yes -- but the answer lies in the Temple of Kinryu, specifically in the clan's records about Kokuryu's original ritual and the countermeasure that the Golden Dragon Clan developed. This creates a direct link between the party's current location (the gold doors) and the Kaze storyline.

Masota no Gekko -- Current State

He is alive, in the Kaze highlands. He retains fragments of his original identity but the transformation suppresses rational thought during stress or combat. He is not a villain. He is a leader who made a terrible decision in desperation. A potential redemption arc exists if the party can find a reversal.

The Hollow Peaks

These were Onyx Dragon Clan structures. The interior of at least one is accessible from the gorge. What remains inside is ancient and significant: Onyx Clan cultural artifacts, including documentation of the transformation ritual.

Plot Hooks

  • The Order of the Black Lily sends a message via an intermediary: "Come to Akatsuki. Come alone. Come before the moon is full."
  • Masota no Gekko leaves something behind at a ransacked site -- something a transformed being could not have done deliberately unless part of him was still trying to communicate
  • A scholar in Mikazuki has been studying the gorge carvings for years and has just realized what they depict

Type
settlement

"The city that built its fortune on something older than itself."

Overview

Kikyo sits at the eastern edge of the Seidorin Mori -- the Bronze Wood Forest -- organized entirely around harvesting and trading a resource it did not create. The Bronze Wood is to Kikyo what a great mine is to a mining town, except the resource is renewable (slowly), carefully managed, and far more politically complicated.

The city's architecture uses Bronze Wood extensively -- older buildings have developed a patina of aged copper giving streets a warm metallic glow at sunset. Newer construction uses it more sparingly due to licensing restrictions, creating visible stratification between old-money establishments and newer buildings.

Kikyo's economy runs on the licensing system. Every piece of Bronze Wood leaving the forest passes through a licensing transaction administered by Ren Nakamura's office. The paperwork is meticulous; the opportunities for licensed abuse are significant.

Districts / Landmarks

Commercial Quarter -- Trading heart. Merchant warehouses, guild offices, the commodity exchange for Bronze Wood contracts. Ko'jiri was caught performing here.

Administrative Quarter -- Ren Nakamura's offices and civic administration. The licensing offices are among the most visited buildings in Kikyo.

Residential Quarters -- Mixed; older areas near the forest edge contain original families; newer development pushed outward.

Kikyo Guard Compound -- Haruto Masashige's base of operations. Small but highly capable force focused on licensing enforcement and forest protection.

Notable Establishments

Notable establishments are primarily the licensing offices, merchant guild headquarters, and the Guard Compound -- all integral to the Bronze Wood trade that defines the city.

Key Figures

  • Ren Nakamura -- Shicho (Mayor) and Daimyo of Clan Minato -> npcs/ren-nakamura.md
  • Haruto Masashige -- Captain of the Guard; Gold Dragonborn -> npcs/haruto-masashige.md

• Ren Nakamura has discovered the true source of the Bronze Wood's metallic quality and is working with a merchant guild to exploit it.
  • Haruto Masashige is building an informant network and has noticed irregularities in the licensing records.
  • Ko'jiri carries both a legitimate letter from Ren Nakamura and a forged version -- a ticking clock.

DM Secrets

The Bronze Wood Secret The Seidorin Mori grows over an underground branch of Kinkokyo's ancient canal system. The metallic quality is caused by trace gold and copper in groundwater flowing through the buried city's infrastructure for thousands of years. Ren Nakamura has discovered this. His allied merchant guild wants to locate and exploit the source directly, bypassing tree-harvesting -- requiring excavation that would destroy the forest.

Haruto Masashige's True Purpose Masashige suspects something significant about the licensing system. He has noticed irregularities -- specific harvesting zones consistently licensed to a single merchant entity with documentation that obscures the pattern. He is three to four months from a coherent accusation.

Ren Nakamura's Alliance The merchant guild is based in Heian with operations across Hana and beyond. The alliance provides financial support for Clan Minato's elevation ambitions and exclusive export contracts. Nakamura is not villainous by nature but has made compromises requiring further compromises to sustain.

Ko'jiri's Forged Letter -- Ticking Clock Ko'jiri carries a legitimate letter and a forged version requesting additional materials. The real letter has already been sent to Heian through official channels. When the discrepancy is discovered, Ko'jiri's Conditional Pardon will be immediately at risk. Estimate: 2-4 sessions.

Ancient Dragonborn Ritual Knowledge Haruto Masashige's knowledge of ancient Dragonborn rituals includes a purification and restoration rite preserved in his family's oral tradition -- directly applicable to the Nagaji situation if someone connected the dots.

Plot Hooks

  • Haruto sends word to the party in Heian: he has found something in the licensing records connecting to their mission
  • A merchant guild representative in Kikyo attempts to discourage the party from returning there with unusual vehemence
  • Ren Nakamura contacts Ko'jiri separately with an additional, unwritten request

text.content:
Type
settlement

"Not every important place announces itself."

Overview

Koriwara sits in the foothills where Mizu province's maritime lowlands begin to rise toward Hokori's interior ranges. It is unremarkable by any visible standard -- small-scale farming and herding, modest architecture, a self-contained community with little need for outside contact. A traveler passing through would find nothing to distinguish it from dozens of similar villages.

What distinguishes it cannot be seen from the road: the presence of Elder Sato Hideaki, whose decades of accumulated knowledge, his connection to the Order of the Sacred Grove, and his quiet role as a node in networks extending far beyond a mountain foothills village give Koriwara significance disproportionate to its size.

The sacred grove that Sato tends is a small stand of ancient trees on the hillside above the village, reached by a foot path behind the northernmost homes. The grove is not marked, not fenced, not formally maintained -- it simply exists, and the village has always known to leave it alone.

This is Relc's home village.

Key Figures

  • Sato Hideaki -- Choro (Village Elder); 78 years old -> npcs/sato-hideaki.md

• Elder Sato knows far more than he has shared with Relc about the Order of the Sacred Grove, the Order of the Ancient Guard, and Solas Evergreen.
  • One of the three stones referenced in Solas's cipher poem is in the sacred grove above the village.
  • A stranger recently arrived in Koriwara asking questions about Relc.

DM Secrets

Sato's Full Knowledge Sato is a mid-rank member of the Order of the Sacred Grove. He has interacted with Order of the Ancient Guard agents, including Solas Evergreen directly. He knows Solas was Ancient Guard (not just Sacred Grove). He knows what the Ancient Guard is and broadly what it protects. He has not told Relc because he was following Solas's instruction and because he judged Relc was not yet ready.

The Cipher Poem One of the three stones is in Koriwara -- in the sacred grove above the village. A naturally occurring stone with unusual surface striations that, viewed from a specific angle at dawn, produce a visual pattern. Sato knows this stone. He knows what the Warden's Wisdom is: protected knowledge about the living dragons held by the Order of the Sacred Grove.

Solas's Murder -- What Sato Knows Sato does not know who killed Solas, but knows the category of entity capable of it. The killing required significantly superior capability or intimate familiarity -- someone Solas trusted. This points to either a very powerful practitioner or someone inside the Orders themselves.

Plot Hooks

  • Sato sends word through a traveling merchant heading toward Heian: he needs to speak with Relc; something has happened near the sacred grove
  • A stranger arrived asking questions about Relc and where they had gone; Sato gave nothing away but is concerned about whether Relc is being watched

Geography & Terrain

Kusa is Hokori's verdant interior -- a province of dense forests, wide river floodplains, and grasslands so deep and tall that travelers on foot are hidden from view within a hundred paces. It occupies the western side of Hokori's northeastern leg, with Sora encroaching on its southeastern border, Mizu to the southwest, Nami to the north, and Kaze to the east. Drainage from surrounding mountain ranges converges here, creating a network of rivers, oxbow lakes, and seasonal wetlands that makes the land extraordinarily fertile and difficult to traverse without knowing the paths.

The forests are ancient and immense, dark-trunked hardwoods with canopies that diffuse light into a permanent green twilight. The forest floor grows in luminous violet and deep blue hues -- murasaki-gusa (purple grass) and aoi-koke (blue moss) -- endemic to the interior lowlands and giving the province a distinctive visual character unique in Hokori.

The Midori River is the primary artery -- wide, slow-moving, navigable for flat-bottomed vessels. The capital Midoriko sits at the junction of the Midori and its largest tributary, the Futago-kawa (Twin River).

The Kusayama Ren (Grass Mountains) forms the province's northern boundary. Notable for the Yosei Mori (Forest of Spirits), a region of ancient woodland where sei activity is consistently elevated and unusual phenomena are reported year-round.

Points of Interest:

  • Yosei Mori (Forest of Spirits) -- Sei-active ancient woodland. Navigation is genuinely unreliable. The Forest of Spirits faction maintains sanctuaries within. Unusual creatures in deeper reaches exhibit significantly elevated intelligence.
  • Heiwa-mizo (Peace Ditch) -- Old defensive trench in Midoriko, now a long public garden with cherry trees. Hosts the Sakura no Nagori (Lingering Cherry Festival) -- a political event as much as a cultural one.
  • The Whispering Flats -- Unusual terrain in Kusa's central lowlands where violet grass grows to chest height and wind creates complex auditory patterns that some claim carry intelligible whispers. Local tradition says the dead speak from the Flats during the Long Shadow season.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Midoriko City Provincial capital; river junction; rebuilt from siege; significant military infrastructure
Kusamoto Town Northern gateway to Kusayama Ren; staging point for forest expeditions
Kawatsuki Town River trading town; barge terminus; merchant hub
Mori no Sato Village Near the Yosei Mori border; Forest of Spirits' public-facing community
Hiranohara Village Grassland farming community; large flat-field agriculture

Culture & Trade

Kusa's economy is built on agriculture, river trade, and the unique resources of its forests. The Midori River supports extensive barge commerce connecting the interior to coastal trade routes. The Forest of Spirits faction, which publicly revealed itself during the Plague Campaign, operates from sanctuaries within the Yosei Mori and represents a significant if unusual economic and cultural presence.

History

Kusa was a battleground during the War of Fractured Banners. The Defense of Midoriko was one of the war's early major engagements -- the provincial capital was besieged and nearly fell before a relief force broke through. The scars of that siege are still visible in Midoriko's architecture.

During the Dark Ages, the Forest of Spirits became a refuge -- its elevated sei activity, present even when magic was absent everywhere else, drew survivors. The communities formed there eventually became the Forest of Spirits magical faction that publicly revealed itself during the Plague Campaign.

• The Forest of Spirits faction holds research and findings from the Dark Ages that they have not shared publicly -- discoveries about sei behavior during the magic-absent era that would upend current seimaster orthodoxy.
  • The Whispering Flats produce sounds that are not random and not the dead -- they are sei resonance from a buried structure beneath.

The Forest of Spirits

The faction's sanctuary in Yosei Mori is more significant than their public profile suggests. During centuries in the forest, they didn't just survive -- they studied. They have records, experiments, and findings from the Dark Ages that would upend current seimaster orthodoxy.

Midoriko's Garrison

The city's military infrastructure is controlled by a Genso Alliance-aligned clan. Its strategic location in the center of Hokori makes it a key pressure point -- control of Midoriko means control of Hokori's interior road network.

The Whispering Flats

The sounds are sei resonance from a buried structure beneath the flats -- a pre-imperial site, possibly connected to the Emerald Dragon Clan (Midoryu). The structure has not been rediscovered. The violet grass grows most densely directly over it.

Plot Hooks

  • The Forest of Spirits has a problem they cannot handle internally -- related to something their research during the Dark Ages disturbed that has recently become active again
  • Someone in Midoriko is passing military intelligence to the Arashi Alliance; the Genso governing clan needs quiet investigation

Sei Fundamentals

  • Sei = magic energy flowing through all living things
  • Present throughout Seizan; expressed through celestial alignment and natural forces
  • Began declining during the War of Fractured Banners era (~12605); first secondary star lost to visibility ~12806; effectively inaccessible by ~13088 (when the last major sei institution — Oryuzan Tenku-ji — fell)
  • Period without accessible sei lasted approximately 3,077 years (12806–15883)
  • Slowly returned through Talents from ~15962
  • Fully restored ~16693 (Great Awakening)
  • The drought's cause is officially unknown; scholars debate whether it was consequence of the war itself or a natural cycle

Seimasters

  • Arcane scholars and researchers — not necessarily practitioners
  • Study sei as discipline; map, theorize, document celestial alignments
  • Title connotes scholarship over power
  • A non-casting seimaster may outrank a gifted practitioner socially
  • Some manifest as wizards, sorcerers, monks in D&D terms
  • Study in mountaintop monasteries

Magical Factions (Publicly Known)

  • Seishin (City, Unmeijima) — premier magical research institution
  • Raimeiin (雷鳴院 — Institute of Thunder) — publicly declared during Plague Campaign
  • Forest of Spirits — publicly declared during Plague Campaign
  • Hikari no Shizuku — healing/light magic; operates within Heian

Kuroyami no Akuma

  • Formerly Takeda no Arata
  • Found necromantic tome in Kuroshi Temple, Yurei
  • Led Plague Campaign 16609–16616
  • Defeated but never captured or killed — escaped; whereabouts unknown
  • Eikyū Yami Clan persists

The Sei Drought and the Great Aphelion

The sei drought was not caused by the War of Fractured Banners — it coincided with the Great Aphelion, a once-in-millennia event in which all three stars of the Miyosai trinary system reached maximum mutual distance from their common barycenter simultaneously. The planets, which orbit Amaterasu and travel with it, did not participate — nor did the moons, which orbit Seizan directly. The event was exclusively a three-star separation across three independent orbital inclinations, compounding geometrically.

The true timeline: stellar decline began 12605; dark ages started ~12806 (first star lost to visibility); the temple fell in 13088; the Great Aphelion nadir occurred ~14344; dawn (first star returned) ~15883; First Talents ~15962; Great Awakening ~16693. The drought spanned approximately 3,077 years (12806–~15883).

The causal chain (aphelion → slumber → drought, or aphelion → both) is unknown even to the Ancient Guard. The slow orbital return of the secondary stars correlates with sei's gradual restoration — but the orbital correction is not yet complete.

See also: core/world.md [SEALED] — The Great Aphelion and the Sei Drought; core/great-aphelion.md — full canonical timeline and orbital mechanics.

Murasakiryū's Sei Awareness

Every sei use in Kagekuni passes through the awakened Progenitor Murasakiryū's awareness. This means every spell the party casts, every druidic invocation, every monk ability — all of it is potentially observed. The implications for Ko'jiri's sorcery, Relc's druidic power, and Sun Wukong's ki are significant but unexplored.

Key question (unresolved): Does Murasakiryū actively monitor individual sei users, or is it passive background awareness? Does the party register as notable?

frontmatter.name: Magic & Sei
frontmatter.description: Sei fundamentals, seimasters, magical factions, and the history of magic's disappearance and return

text.content:
Type
system-reference

In Kagekuni, nothing is taken lightly from the land. A hunter who kills a deer owes the forest an accounting. A smith who pulls iron from the mountain asks the stone's permission before the first strike of the pick. A cook who gathers mountain sage bows to the plant before cutting. The materials of the world are not commodities — they are borrowed, and the borrower is expected to honor the source.

This document covers the worldbuilding context for Kagekuni's material categories and the mechanics that govern gathering and craft. Individual material entries — names, rarities, values, descriptions, grades, and DM notes — live in items/materials.json, which is the canonical source of truth for all material definitions and the input for Foundry item generation. When a recipe in core/recipes.md references an ingredient, it references an entry in items/materials.json. When a player asks "what can I forage in the cedar forest," the answer comes from Part II of this document.

How This Document Works

The file is organized in two parts.

Part I — Category Context & Schema. Each of the twelve material categories has a worldbuilding introduction describing its cultural, economic, and narrative role in Kagekuni. Individual material entries (names, rarities, values, descriptions, grades, DM notes) live in items/materials.json. Part I never describes where a material comes from — that belongs in Part II.

Part II — Gathering & Yield Tables. The mechanic for harvesting materials, the five activities used to gather them, the grade system at the point of harvest, failure modes for both gathering and crafting, the seasons and seasonal events of Kagekuni, the biomes of the archipelago and what each one yields, and the named beast harvests that produce one-time legendary rewards.

Cross-references between the two halves use markdown anchors: [Ōkami-niku](#ōkami-niku). Part II tables link back to Part I entries so the DM can jump from "what did they find" to "what does that mean" in one click.

Knowledge Tiers

All Part I entries respect the campaign's three-tier knowledge system:

  • [KNOWN] — Information the players have learned through play. Safe to reference anywhere.
  • [DISCOVERABLE] — Exists in-world and could be learned. Lives in the DM Notes section of each entry. Quest seeds marked
QUEST SEED . - [SEALED] — Campaign-level secrets. Never surface in player-facing descriptions. Mark undecided elements as TBD.

The player-facing description field of each entry is always safe to export to Foundry or share with players. The DM Notes field is never exported.

On Grades and Foundry

Every material that supports grading exists as four distinct Foundry items — one per grade (並 Nami, 上 Jō, 特上 Tokujō, 極上 Gokujō). In items/materials.json, each material has a single entry with grade defaults defined at the top level (gradeDefaults) and per-material overrides where needed. The 4× proliferation exists only in Foundry. The full grade system is documented in Part II.

Part I — Category Context & Schema

Part I provides the worldbuilding context for each of the twelve material categories and the entry schema that governs items/materials.json. Individual material entries live in the JSON file; this section describes each category's cultural, economic, and narrative significance.

Part I Entry Schema (Reference)

Every Part I entry must use this schema. Fields in square brackets are optional and may be omitted if irrelevant.

### [Material Name] ([日本語名]) ([English Gloss])

**Category:** Niku | Yakusō | Kinoko | Chōmiryō | Shushoku | Kegawa | Hone | Sen'i | Kōseki | Hōseki | Mokuzai | Ekitai
**Rarity:** Common (並) | Uncommon (上) | Rare (特上) | Very Rare (極上) | Legendary (伝説) | Artifact (神器)
**Source Type:** Foraged | Hunted | Mined | Harvested | Scavenged | One-Time | Purchased
**Biomes:** [list of biomes where found, referencing Part II biome names]
**Seasons:** Haru | Natsu | Aki | Fuyu | All | [or seasonal event tag like Hikarishō]
**Yield per Success:** [e.g., "1d4 per resource point" or "fixed: 1 sample"]
**Weight:** [per portion/unit]
**Base Value:** [gold pieces per unit, before grade multiplier]
**Preservation:** [fresh shelf life / preserved shelf life]
**Tool Proficiency:** [tool needed to harvest or process, if any]
[**Restrictions:** any legal, cultural, or ritual constraints on harvest]

#### Grade Variants

| Grade | Value Multiplier | Craft Modifier | Foundry Item ID |
|---|---|---|---|
| 並 Nami (Run-of-the-mill) | ×0.75 | −2 | tbd |
| 上 Jō (Clean / Standard) | ×1.0 | +0 | tbd |
| 特上 Tokujō (High-Purity) | ×1.5 | +2 | tbd |
| 極上 Gokujō (Legendary Bloom) | ×2.5 | +5 or advantage on craft check | tbd |

*Legendary and Artifact materials may specify a fixed grade; see individual entries.*

#### Description (Player-Facing)

Sensory, evocative, spoiler-free prose. This is what a player with full knowledge sees in Foundry when they inspect the item. Never contains [DISCOVERABLE] or [SEALED] content.

#### Unidentified Description

What the item looks like to a player who has *not* identified it — found in a crate, pulled from a beast with no naming knowledge, sitting on a shrine altar. Visual and tactile description only. Foundry shows this to players who have not yet identified the material.

#### Image Prompt

Prompt for watercolor-style token generation. Should evoke the material without depicting a specific shape or branded pose. Muted natural palette. Soft edges. The image is a suggestion of the thing, not a catalog photograph.

#### Used In

*(This section is auto-populated by the reindex skill by crawling recipes.md. Do not edit manually.)*

#### DM Notes

Lore, ecology, cultural significance, harvesting taboos, plot hooks, alternate uses. May contain **[KNOWN]**, **[DISCOVERABLE]**, or **[SEALED]** content with tier markers. This field is never exported to Foundry player-facing descriptions.

Niku 肉 — Meat & Edible Animal Products

The meat of Kagekuni runs the full span from humble river fish to the heart of a mountain god. Hunting traditions are deeply tied to the warrior caste — the samurai on a hunt is not pursuing food but practicing the discipline of the kill — while fishing and small-game trapping belong to the peasantry and to the half-feral communities of the deep forest. Edible organs carry their own significance; the liver of a bear is a gift to an elder, the heart of a killed enemy is a ritual offering, and certain rare beasts yield parts that are considered medicine more than food.

Entries: items/materials.json → category "niku"

Yakusō 薬草 — Herbs & Medicinal Plants

Yakusō covers culinary herbs, medicinal plants, teas, and any green gathered for its flavor, scent, or healing property. The boundary with Kinoko is soft — many traditional formulas combine the two — and the boundary with Chōmiryō is cultural rather than botanical. A mountain sage is Yakusō; a sage dried, ground, and mixed into a spice blend is Chōmiryō. The distinction is use, not species. Herbal knowledge in Kagekuni is concentrated in the shrine maiden tradition and in the scattered communities of forest-dwelling druids, with village healers working from whatever lineage their teacher left them.

Entries: items/materials.json → category "yakuso"

Kinoko 茸 — Mushrooms & Fungi

The fungi of Kagekuni’s forests are prized beyond their weight in silver. Some are food, some are medicine, some are sei-resonant and used in the preparations of seimasters, and a few are lethally poisonous in ways that imitate the safe ones precisely enough to kill the careless. Mushroom gathering is a trained art; a forager who cannot distinguish the ryūkinoko from its deadly mimic does not forage for long. The best flushes follow the tsuyu-no-toki rains of early summer, and the deep cedar forests of Kaze produce varieties that grow nowhere else.

Entries: items/materials.json → category "kinoko"

Chōmiryō 調味料 — Seasonings & Fermented Goods

Salt, miso, soy sauce, vinegar, rice wine for cooking, dried spice blends, fermented pastes, pickled vegetables. The backbone of every Kagekuni kitchen and the element that most distinguishes regional cooking. A Mizu fisherman’s stew and a Tsuchi farmer’s stew may share every other ingredient and still taste nothing alike because of the Chōmiryō applied. Fermentation is considered a sacred art — the kōji mold that underpins miso, soy sauce, sake, and a dozen other staples is sometimes described as a gift of the kami, and an old fermentation house is tended like a shrine.

Entries: items/materials.json → category "chomiryo"

Shushoku 主食 — Staples, Grains & Cooking Fats

Rice in all its varieties, wheat and barley in the north and south, millet in the poor mountain soil, and the rendered fats that every kitchen relies on. Oils from pressed seeds, lard from butchered pigs, rendered beast-fats from large game, and clarified butter from the few herds that exist on Hokori’s high pastures. Shushoku is the foundation of every meal — everything else is applied to the staple, not the other way around. Rice especially carries weight far beyond its nutrition: a bowl of rice is a political act, the grain is an object of veneration in shrine offerings, and the control of rice paddies is the single most important lever of power in rural Kagekuni.

Entries: items/materials.json → category "shushoku"

Kegawa 毛皮 — Hides, Pelts & Leather

The worked and unworked hides of Kagekuni’s beasts. Deer leather for common armor, bear hide for the winter coats of mountain provinces, wolf pelts for the cloaks of warriors who can earn the right to wear them, and the rare spirit-touched hides that carry their own faint charge of sei. Kegawa work is a caste profession — tanners occupy a complicated social position, necessary but ritually impure — and the best leatherworkers are concentrated in communities that outsiders rarely visit. The distinction between raw pelt and finished leather matters both mechanically and economically: a raw hide is worth a tenth of a finished one, but finishing requires weeks of downtime and specialist tools.

Kegawa is primarily a secondary-harvest category: almost every Niku entry with a mammalian source yields hide material as part of the butchering process. Routine hides (deer, boar, bear, fox) will be catalogued as the campaign surfaces specific needs; for now, Kegawa entries are reserved for named-beast harvests and sei-touched pelts where the material’s identity matters enough to track individually.

Entries: items/materials.json → category "kegawa"

Hone 骨 — Bone, Horn, Shell & Sinew

The hard parts of beasts. Bone for carving, horn for ornament and functional tool-making, shell for lacquerwork inlay and protective scaling, sinew for bowstrings and for the binding of composite materials. Tooth, claw, antler, and keratin-adjacent materials all live here. In Kagekuni’s spiritual framework, these parts are considered the most sacred portion of a slain beast because they are what remains when everything else has rotted or been eaten — they are the memory of the animal. Carved bone and horn objects are frequently offered to shrines as memorial pieces, and a weapon or tool made from the bone of a named creature carries a fragment of that creature’s legend with it.

Like Kegawa, Hone is primarily a secondary-harvest category — nearly every hunted animal yields bone material, and routine bones (deer antler, boar tusk, fish bone) will be catalogued as the campaign surfaces specific needs. For now, Hone entries are reserved for named-beast harvests and resonant bones where the material’s identity matters enough to track individually.

Entries: items/materials.json → category "hone"

Sen’i 繊維 — Fibers & Cordage Materials

Silk, hemp, ramie, cotton where it grows, plant fibers for rope and net-making, and the rare materials used in ceremonial weaving. Silk production is concentrated in the temperate lowlands of Hana and Kusa and is controlled by merchant guilds with clan backing. Hemp is grown everywhere and is the material of peasant clothing, rope, and paper. Specialist fibers — sei-conductive threads, spirit-silk from certain rare cocoons, fireproof woven minerals from volcanic regions — exist at the high end.

Entries: items/materials.json → category "seni" — Framework category; entries added as the campaign introduces them.

Kōseki 鉱石 — Ores, Metals & Stone

Iron, copper, tin, silver, gold, and the rarer metals that flow through Kagekuni’s legendary metallurgy — mithral where it can be found, the sei-conductive alloys of the Golden Age, the obsidian of the Kuroso fields that is technically not a metal but is worked like one for blade-making. Mining in Kagekuni carries its own ritual weight: the mountain is asked, the first strike is blessed, and the miners who practice their trade full-time are often regarded with a mixture of respect and unease by the communities around them. Kurogane Yama in Tsuchi and the scattered mineral deposits of Hi province are the principal canonical sources.

Entries: items/materials.json → category "koseki" — Framework category; entries added as the campaign introduces them.

Hōseki 宝石 — Gemstones & Crystals

Quartz, jade, amethyst, and the rarer sei-resonant crystals that form in specific conditions — Dragon Crystal, the artifact-tier material that forms only where a Progenitor’s breath has touched stone; moon-pearls from the deep tidal caves; star-touched quartz from Hoshimori. Gemstones in Kagekuni are prized more for their metaphysical properties than for their beauty — a raw, unfinished crystal with strong sei resonance is worth more to a seimaster than a perfectly cut stone with none.

Entries: items/materials.json → category "hoseki" — Framework category; entries added as the campaign introduces them.

Mokuzai 木材 — Wood, Bark, Sap & Resin

The wood of Kagekuni’s forests, from common pine and cedar for construction to the legendary bronze-bark of Seidorin Mori for weapons and structural reinforcement. Bark for dyes and medicines, sap for resins and lacquer, specialty woods for instrument-making and temple construction. Logging is heavily regulated in the canonical forests — Seidorin Mori is license-only on pain of capital punishment — and the best timber passes through clan-controlled supply chains that keep the highest-grade material out of common hands.

Ekitai 液体 — Oils, Inks, Dyes & Distillations

The liquid materials that don’t fit elsewhere. Lamp oils pressed from seeds, calligraphy inks ground from soot and bound with resin, natural dyes for textiles, poisons extracted from frogs and snakes and certain plants, alchemical distillations, and the rare sei-infused liquids that seimasters harvest from specific sites — the luminescent water of certain rivers, the incense-scented fog of the high marsh, the tears wept by certain statues on certain nights. Ekitai is the most esoteric category and will fill slowly.
