Part II — Gathering & Yield Tables

Part II defines how materials are found and where. It is the mechanical heart of the gathering system and the reference the DM consults during play when a player declares they want to forage, hunt, mine, cut timber, or scavenge.

The Gathering Mechanic

Gathering in Kagekuni resolves in three stages. A full attempt takes one in-world hour and resolves with a single opportunity roll plus one to five yield rolls.

Stage 1 — Declare the Activity

Before any dice are rolled, the gathering character declares which of the five activities they are attempting. Each activity uses different skills, tools, and yield tables. A character pursues only one activity per attempt — an hour spent foraging herbs does not incidentally yield game, ore, or timber. A character who wants to gather across categories must spend multiple attempts.

The five activities are:

  • Saishū 採集 — Foraging. Hunting for plants, fungi, fruits, nuts, and small surface materials. Skill: Wisdom (Survival) or Intelligence (Nature). Tool: Herbalism kit recommended; a failure without proficiency imposes disadvantage on the opportunity roll. Yields from: Yakusō, Kinoko, some Shushoku, some Ekitai, occasional Sen'i.
  • Shuryō 狩猟 — Hunting. Pursuing game of any size, on land or in water. Both land hunting and fishing fall under Shuryō — a rabbit snare and a river line are mechanically the same activity for the purposes of the gathering system. Skill: Wisdom (Survival). Tool: weapons or fishing tackle. Yields from: Niku, Kegawa, Hone, occasional Ekitai.
  • Saikutsu 採掘 — Mining. Extracting ore, stone, and gems from surface deposits, cave walls, riverbed gravel, or spoil heaps. Skill: Strength (Athletics) or Intelligence (Investigation). Tool: miner's tools (mattock, pick, chisel). Yields from: Kōseki, Hōseki, sometimes Ekitai (thermal waters).
  • Batsuboku 伐木 — Timber Harvest. Cutting wood, stripping bark, collecting sap and resin. Skill: Wisdom (Survival) or Strength (Athletics). Tool: woodcarver's or carpenter's tools. Yields from: Mokuzai, some Sen'i (plant fibers), some Ekitai (saps, resins).
  • Kaishū 回収 — Scavenging. Searching ruins, battlefields, abandoned sites, crashed carts, refuse heaps, and the fringes of civilization for useful materials of any category. Skill: Intelligence (Investigation). Tool: none required. Yields from: any category, depending on the site — a ruined temple yields different things from a battlefield, a burned farmhouse, or a shipwreck.

Stage 2 — The Opportunity Roll

Once the activity is declared, the character makes a single d20 check against the biome's Opportunity DC. This roll determines how productive the attempt was — not what was found.

Biome Tier Opportunity DC Example Biomes
Accessible 10 Satoyama, Tambo, lowland Kawa to Numa
Wild 13 Kaigan, Sugi no Mori, Fumoto, lower Murasaki-hara
Hostile 16 Takane, Kazan lower slopes, deep Murasaki-hara, Kōri-no-Mori
Otherworldly 20 Hoshimori Kōgen, Yōrin, Kazan summit, Seidorin, Haikyo (for sei-touched ruins)

The margin of success determines resource points — a pool of yield rolls the character gets to make.

Roll Result Resource Points Additional Effects
Fail (any margin) 0 Time lost. Roll on the failure-mode table for the biome tier.
Meet DC (0–4) 1 A productive session.
DC + 5 to 9 2 A good find.
DC + 10 to 14 3 An excellent find.
DC + 15 or more 4 An exceptional find.
Natural 20 (with bonus d10 per house rule) +1 bonus point Unlocks the Very Rare column of the yield table.
Total of 40+ — Unlocks Legendary yields where the table supports them. Most biome tables do not carry Legendary tiers; Legendary materials are usually tied to named-beast harvests in the dedicated section below.

Attempts per rest cycle. A character may make one gathering attempt per short rest and a maximum of two per long rest. If the party is traveling the same day, the maximum drops to one per long rest. Each attempt takes one in-world hour of focused effort.

Multiple activities per day. A character may pursue a different activity on a second attempt — morning hunt, afternoon forage — and each is rolled separately. An exceptional morning does not carry over into the afternoon. A character may not pursue the same activity twice in the same day in the same biome (the area is already worked); a second attempt must either be a different activity or a different biome.

Party gathering. Multiple characters may gather simultaneously, each rolling their own opportunity roll. Characters may use the Help action to grant advantage to a companion's opportunity roll in place of their own attempt, which is often the right play when one character is significantly more skilled than the others.

Stage 3 — The Yield Roll

For each resource point, the character rolls a d20 on the relevant biome-activity-season table in the Biomes of Kagekuni section below. Results are organized by rarity column:

  • 1–10 → Common
  • 11–17 → Uncommon
  • 18–19 → Rare
  • 20 → Very Rare (only if the Very Rare column is unlocked by the opportunity roll; otherwise re-roll as Rare)

If the biome, activity, or season combination is not supported, the attempt returns nothing — Saikutsu in an open wetland, Batsuboku on a volcanic glass field. Each biome entry lists which activities are supported and in which seasons.

Yield entries are written as links to Part I material entries, with the per-roll quantity specified. For example, an entry might read: "Mountain Sage — 1d4 bundles", meaning the character rolls 1d4 to determine how many bundles this single resource point produced, and receives that many instances of Mountain Sage with the grade determined by the opportunity roll margin.

Grade at the Point of Harvest

Every material produced by a gathering attempt receives a grade, determined by the margin of the opportunity roll that produced it:

Opportunity Roll Margin Grade
Meet DC to DC + 4 並 Nami — Run-of-the-mill. Standard sample, no bonus, −2 craft modifier.
DC + 5 to DC + 9 上 Jō — Clean and standard. Baseline craft material, +0 modifier.
DC + 10 to DC + 14 特上 Tokujō — High-purity. Notable sample, +2 craft modifier, value ×1.5.
DC + 15 or more 極上 Gokujō — Legendary bloom. The kind of sample master craftsmen remember, +5 or advantage on craft check, value ×2.5.

Natural 20 rule. A natural 20 on the opportunity roll always produces at least one 特上 sample from that attempt, regardless of total margin. The luck goes into finding an exceptional specimen rather than just extra quantity.

Per-Foundry-item implementation. Each grade corresponds to a separate item definition in Foundry (Path D). When a character produces a 特上 Iron Ore on their roll, they receive the "Iron Ore (特上)" item in their inventory — not a generic Iron Ore with a grade tag. Part I entries list all four grade variants in their Grade Variants sub-block with reserved Foundry item IDs.

Legendary and Artifact materials. Most Legendary and Artifact materials do not use the four-grade variant system. They exist as a single canonical grade (usually 極上 or a fixed Legendary designation) because they are tied to specific sources — a Progenitor dragon's scale, the heart of a slain named beast, a sample from a unique location — and rolling quality on them makes no narrative sense. Individual entries specify.

Failure Modes — Gathering

When an opportunity roll fails, the character spent an hour of field time for nothing — and possibly worse. The consequence scales with biome tier.

Biome Tier On Failure On Critical Failure (natural 1)
Accessible 1 hour lost, no yield. 1 hour lost + minor setback — insect bites, torn clothing, a sprained wrist (disadvantage on next physical check).
Wild 1 hour lost + minor complication — bad weather, route unclear, small tool damaged, scavengers in the area. 1 hour lost + tool loss — herbalism kit contaminated, miner's pick snapped, fishing line cut, carpenter's blade chipped.
Hostile 1 hour lost + weather, terrain, or wildlife complication. 1 hour lost + hostile encounter — a CR-appropriate creature drawn by the noise, the smell of blood, or the disturbance to its territory.
Otherworldly 1 hour lost + sei backlash — disadvantage on the next saving throw, eerie attention from unseen watchers, a minor dissociative effect that passes after a short rest. 1 hour lost + major complication — spirit attention from a territorial entity, a cursed or tainted yield that looks valuable but carries a hidden cost, or a CR+2 encounter with something that considers the character's presence an offense.

The DM is encouraged to narrate failures as story beats, not dead ends. The hour is already spent — use it to advance something.

Failure Modes — Crafting

When a craft check fails, the consequence depends on the rarity of the item being made. Lower-tier items are forgiving; higher-tier items are not.

  • Common result — Materials recoverable on failure. The character can try again without cost beyond the time spent.
  • Uncommon result — Half the materials consumed on failure; the other half salvageable for another attempt.
  • Rare result — Most materials consumed on failure. One key component may survive at the DM's discretion, usually tied to a good roleplay moment or a clever use of tools.
  • Very Rare result — Materials fully consumed on failure. The character must re-gather before trying again.
  • Legendary result — Failure destroys all materials and may damage or destroy the tools used. A failed legendary craft is a genuine disaster, narratively and mechanically. The character may suffer reputation or honor consequences.
  • Artifact result — Materials destroyed, tools destroyed or permanently damaged, and the character may suffer a significant narrative consequence: honor loss, spirit backlash, or a lingering curse tied to the wasted material.

Critical failures (natural 1) on craft checks at Rare or above may trigger additional effects at the DM's discretion — a tainted item that looks successful until used, a cursed result, or a partial success with a hidden flaw that only reveals itself in play.

Seasons of Kagekuni

The gathering system uses four seasons plus a set of named seasonal events that transform specific biomes temporarily.

  • Haru 春 — Spring. Budding, young growth, the first fish runs, mountain snowmelt, the opening of foraging season after winter dormancy. Many herbs and wild vegetables are at their most potent in spring. Saishū is productive everywhere; Shuryō is lean until mid-spring when game emerges.
  • Natsu 夏 — Summer. Peak growth, abundance, long days, the heavy rains of tsuyu-no-toki (the rainy window of early summer). Mushroom flushes follow the rains; game is fat and plentiful; the mountain herbs set seed. The best season for most gathering activities in most biomes.
  • Aki 秋 — Autumn. Harvest, rutting season, the falling of bronze and copper leaves in the Seidorin. Kegawa is at its best in autumn when pelts are thick for the coming winter; the final mushroom flushes of the year; the last herbs before dormancy. Hunting is exceptional.
  • Fuyu 冬 — Winter. Dormancy and scarcity. Preserved stores matter most. Saikutsu and Batsuboku are actually easier in winter because vegetation is reduced and access is clearer; Shuryō is harder because animals are wary, hibernating, or gone; Saishū is nearly impossible in most biomes. Some alpine and sei-touched biomes have winter-only yields.

Seasonal Events

Certain biomes transform during named in-world events. These are catalogued here and referenced in the individual biome entries below.

  • Hikarishō 光祥 — The Dragon Aurora. Celestial alignment that produces unique sei conditions across the entire archipelago. During Hikarishō, certain Very Rare materials become temporarily gatherable that are otherwise impossible to find. Hoshimori Kōgen is the most affected biome; secondary effects touch Yōrin and Kazan. Predictable — seimasters at Hoshino Tō can calculate the window.
  • Tatsunami 龍波 — Dragon Wave Season. Nami province phenomenon during which storm swells overwash coastal roads and villages. Standard Kaigan gathering is impossible on Nami's outer coast during this window, but the Stormwatch Cliffs produce unique weather-sei materials for those willing to brave the storms. Dangerous — Hostile biome tier during Tatsunami regardless of the normal rating.
  • Nagaikage 長影 — The Long Shadow. A late-autumn Kusa phenomenon during which the Whispering Flats grow silent in a way locals say allows the dead to speak. Murasaki-hara yields shift — certain grasses and night-blooming plants become gatherable that are otherwise dormant, and some carry spirit-touched properties. Requires local knowledge to exploit; strangers rarely time it right.
  • Compound Low Tide. A recurring coastal event driven by Kagekuni's four-moon tidal system. At compound low tide, the Shirakawa Estuary flats extend for miles, the Tidal Caves of Umigakure become accessible, and the Serenia-kai's shoreline retreats several hundred meters. Kaigan and Uchi-umi yields are exceptional during these windows — materials visible that are normally underwater. The timing is predictable and published in almanacs.

Additional seasonal events will be added to this section as the campaign surfaces them.

The Five Activities — Tool Details

A brief reference on tool proficiencies and what each activity expects.

Saishū 採集 — Herbalism kit grants full opportunity roll with normal advantage rules. Without the kit, a character may still forage but rolls with disadvantage on the opportunity roll. Without any tool, the character can still gather the most obvious surface materials (nuts, berries, obvious mushrooms) at Accessible-tier biomes only, and cannot grade higher than 並 Nami.

Shuryō 狩猟 — Any weapon the character is proficient with. Hunting uses different weapons than fishing — a hunter needs bow or spear; a fisher needs line or net. Specialist equipment (falconry glove, hunting dog, trap kit) may grant advantage at DM discretion when used in the right biome.

Saikutsu 採掘 — Miner's tools (mattock, pick, chisel, wedge) grant full roll. Improvised tools impose disadvantage and cannot produce higher than 上 Jō. Specialist equipment (sei-conductive pick, dwarven stoneworking kit) may grant advantage in specific biomes.

Batsuboku 伐木 — Woodcarver's or carpenter's tools. An axe alone is sufficient for basic timber but cannot produce higher than 上 Jō; full tool kits are required for 特上 and above. A woodcarver's tools are preferred for specialty materials (sei-bark stripping, sap collection); carpenter's tools for structural lumber.

Kaishū 回収 — No tool required, but specialized tools (a torch, a crowbar, a bone saw for scavenging battlefields) may grant advantage in context. The Investigation skill is the core requirement; without proficiency in Investigation, the character may still scavenge but rolls with disadvantage.

Source Types

Beyond the five gathering activities, Part I entries may list a sixth source type: Purchased. This is used for materials that exist in the economy but are not practical to gather in the field — imports from other islands, materials that require industrial-scale processing, or goods controlled by merchant guilds. A Purchased material has no biome or season entries and instead lists the settlements, markets, or trade routes where it is available. Purchased materials never receive grades from gathering rolls; if they are graded at all, the grade is set by the source vendor and reflected in the price.

Biomes of Kagekuni

This section catalogues the gatherable biomes of the Kagekuni archipelago, drawn from the canonical geography. Each entry describes the biome, lists the activities supported, notes which seasons are productive or unproductive, identifies any restrictions or hazards, and houses the yield tables used during play.

Biomes are grouped into three tiers: Core (common biomes every party will hit), Distinctive (unique biomes with specialized yields), and Periphery (stubbed for future build-out).

Phase 3 status. Yield tables have been built for the three priority biomes the current campaign is most likely to hit: Sugi no Mori, Fumoto, and Haikyo (including the Oryuzan Tenku-ji site-specific sub-table). Other biomes carry *Tables: TBD* placeholders and will be built as the party approaches them.

Core Biomes

Kaigan 海岸 — Coastal Edge

Headlands, beaches, tidal flats, estuaries, sea caves, and the rugged shorelines of Mizu, Nami, and Hana. The boundary between Kagekuni and the Raijin no Fukai sea. Compound low tides expose materials normally submerged.

Biome Tier: Wild (DC 13) Activities Supported: Saishū, Shuryō, Kaishū Seasonal Notes: All seasons productive; exceptional yields during Compound Low Tide events. Tatsunami makes Nami coast temporarily Hostile. Typical Yields: Shellfish, seaweed, sea salt, driftwood, coastal herbs, shore game, wrecked cargo.

Tables: TBD (Phase 3 or later)

Satoyama 里山 — Village Forest

The managed coppice-edge between settlement and wilderness. The ambient biome around nearly every Kagekuni village. Regular foot traffic keeps the biome thin but accessible; traditional village knowledge keeps productive areas productive.

Biome Tier: Accessible (DC 10) Activities Supported: Saishū, Shuryō (small game only), Batsuboku (coppiced wood) Seasonal Notes: Productive in Haru, Natsu, Aki; poor in Fuyu. Typical Yields: Bamboo, small game (rabbit, fowl), common herbs, mushrooms after rain, firewood.

Tables: TBD

Sugi no Mori 杉の森 — Deep Cedar Forest

Ancient dense cedar and black pine forest, canopy so thick that sunlight reaches the floor only in scattered shafts. The signature biome of Kaze province, with smaller stretches in Kusa and the Tenchūsan Ren foothills. Mist is constant; navigation relies on landmark and feel more than sight.

Biome Tier: Wild (DC 13) Activities Supported: Saishū, Shuryō, Batsuboku Seasonal Notes: All seasons productive; Kinoko flush best in Natsu after rain (advantage on the yield roll within 24 hours of a rainfall); Kegawa best in Aki (hunters automatically trade up one yield column when the Aki rut is active); Fuyu passable but game scattered. Typical Yields: Large game (deer, boar, occasional bear), rare shade-loving mushrooms, cedar timber, black pine resin, shaded herbs.

Haikyo 廃墟 — Ruins

Promoted to core biome in the Phase 2 materials rework — the party is currently working in the Oryuzan Tenku-ji ruin, and this biome has received its full table build as part of Phase 3.

Haikyo is the scavenging biome — abandoned temples, collapsed observatories, ruined fortresses, pre-imperial sites, burned villages, the Buried Road of Tsuchi, the forgotten outposts of the Dark Ages. Each ruin has its own character, and the Kaishū activity here is far more than picking through rubble — it is historical recovery, sometimes archaeology, sometimes grave-robbing depending on perspective.

Biome Tier: Variable by site — most ruins Wild (DC 13); sei-touched or actively haunted ruins Hostile (DC 16) or Otherworldly (DC 20). Tenku-ji itself is Otherworldly (DC 20) on account of its Golden Dragon Clan preservation magic and sei-active inner chambers. Activities Supported: Kaishū primarily; Saikutsu in worked-stone ruins; occasional Saishū for plants that have overgrown the site. Seasonal Notes: Winter often makes ruins more accessible (vegetation cleared); summer conceals hazards under growth. Restrictions: Varies by site. Temple ruins may be considered sacred by local communities and disturbed at spiritual cost. Clan lands require permission. Imperial-era sites are nominally Kokushi Kyokai jurisdiction. Oryuzan Tenku-ji specifically carries its own set of conditions catalogued in locations/tenkuji-temple/. Typical Yields: Pre-imperial artifacts and tools, forgotten tools and weapons, worked stone, salvaged metal, old documents and scrolls, ceremonial materials, rare finds with attached history. Some ruins yield sei-touched items; some yield cursed ones; a few yield both and the difference is only clear later.

Cross-Biome Tags

A cross-biome tag is not a physical biome — it cannot be pointed to on a map and does not replace a biome entry on a material. It is a descriptor that modifies an existing biome to mark a distinct mode of presence. A material tagged with a cross-biome tag must also carry a physical biome (Sugi no Mori, Kaigan, Haikyo, etc.); the tag identifies which subset of that biome's sites produce the yield.

The gathering mechanic treats a tag as a tier escalator and a frequency gate: a cross-biome-tagged site is typically at least Hostile (DC 16) and often Otherworldly (DC 20), and such sites are rare enough that a party should feel finding one is an event, not a routine travel stop.

Spirit-Touched (精霊触れ)

Sei flows visibly through a Spirit-Touched site. The tag covers any location where raw sei has pooled, lingered, or bled into the material world strongly enough to alter what grows, lives, and settles there. Examples of qualifying sites include: Progenitor caverns, active shrine pools, the Yōsei Mori's oldest hardwoods, the Seidōrin Mori interior, the Hoshimori Plateau during Hikarishō, and Ginryū-associated mineral sites. The tag does not apply to routine shrine grounds — sei must be actively perceptible, not merely venerated.

Tier default: Otherworldly (DC 20) at the tagged site, regardless of the underlying biome's base tier. A Spirit-Touched Kaigan grotto is treated at DC 20 even though generic Kaigan is Wild. Activity effects: Yield tables for the underlying biome apply normally, but the Very Rare column (row 20) is considered thematically unlocked at Spirit-Touched sites — a margin-15 opportunity roll at such a site is almost certain to produce a sei-resonant result. Restrictions: Most Spirit-Touched sites sit within another faction's claim (Forest of Spirits, Hoshimori seimasters, Dragon Clan shrine remnants) or under spirit-world attention. Unauthorized harvest frequently triggers consequences that land outside the gathering system — quests, curses, or direct response. DM guidance: Spirit-Touched is the mechanism by which a handful of materials (Ryūsō, Yūrei-kusa variants, Hoshimori silver-grass, Progenitor-cavern crystals) can appear across otherwise unrelated physical biomes without breaking the biome taxonomy. Use it sparingly — the tag loses meaning if every sei-active rock qualifies.

The nat-20 harvest check locked every component at top grade at the moment of butchering; no lesser grade exists for any of this beast's material. Entries for these components do not carry the standard Nami/Jō/Tokujō/Gokujō Grade Variants table — the 極上 row stands alone.

Components by category. The full harvest is catalogued across five Part I categories. Cross-references:

Category Component Yield Tracked
Niku Ōkami-niku (Mountain God's Flesh) 8 portions ✓
Niku Shirokiba no Zui (White-Fang Marrow) 3 portions ✓
Niku Yama no Kimo (Mountain Liver) 2 portions ✓
Niku Arashi-suji (Storm-Sinew) 3 portions ✓
Niku Reikokoro (Spirit Heart) — Legendary 1 portion (feeds six) ✓
Shushoku Ōkami no Abura (Rendered Fat) 6 portions ✓
Kegawa Ōkami no Kegawa (Pelt) 1 primary + 2 secondary sections ✓
Hone Ōkami no Hone (Bones) ~350 lb carving stock ✓
Hone Ōkami no Zugai (Skull) 1 intact skull ✓
Hone Ōkami no Kiba (Fangs) 4 fangs ✓
Hone Ōkami no Tenohira (Paws) 4 paws (20 claws total) ✓

Tracking. The party currently holds all of the above. Consumption, sale, gift, and enshrinement should be recorded against dm/campaign-state.md, not against this file. When a component is exhausted, strike it through here but leave the Part I entry intact for historical reference.

Skill-check knowledge. The non-food components (Kegawa and Hone categories) each carry DM-only Religion / Nature / Arcana reveal thresholds. See the DM Notes block of each individual component entry for the specific DCs and what each check reveals. A natural 20 on any one check reveals the information across all three skills for that component.

The Reikokoro. The Spirit Heart is unique even among the Yama-no-Ōkami components — it is the only entry in the entire harvest catalogued at the Legendary tier rather than 極上 Gokujō. It feeds up to six generously from a single preparation and is suitable for a Masterwork dish. Religion, Nature, and Arcana reveals on the Reikokoro are documented with the Niku entry and should be read before the party considers consuming it.

Appendix — Document Maintenance

Source of truth. items/materials.json is canonical for individual material definitions (names, rarities, values, descriptions, grades, DM notes). This file (core/materials.md) is canonical for gathering mechanics (Part II) and category worldbuilding context. When conflicts arise, the JSON wins for material data; this file wins for mechanics.

Foundry export. The Foundry pipeline reads items/materials.json and generates four item definitions per graded material via build-material.mjs. Player-facing fields (description, unidentifiedDescription, imagePrompt) become the item's visible properties. DM notes are excluded from export.

Schema evolution. If the materials.json schema changes, all existing entries must be updated in the same pass to maintain consistency. A schema change without a full sweep is a source-of-truth corruption.

Knowledge tier enforcement. Never surface [DISCOVERABLE] or [SEALED] content in player-facing fields. The description and unidentifiedDescription JSON fields are exports; dmNotes is the only safe home for tiered content.

text.content:
Geography & Terrain

Mizu is a province of water in all its forms -- crashing coastal surf, wide navigable rivers, reed-choked estuaries, tidal flats that stretch for miles at low compound tide, and interior lakes fed by reliable rainfall. It wraps around the northwestern string of mountains on Hokori, with Hi to the southeast, Sora along its eastern and southern borders, and Kusa to the northeast. The Raijin no Fukai sea drives against its western and northern coastline with consistent force. The Kōri-no-Mori forest occupies its northern shores.

The coastline is irregular and complex -- carved into headlands, sheltered coves, sea-stacks, and natural harbors. The Shirakawa Estuary (White River Estuary) at the province's center is one of the largest navigable estuaries in the archipelago. The city of Minato-jo occupies a raised headland at the estuary's mouth.

Inland, the terrain transitions through agricultural floodplains and into the foothills of the central Hokori ranges. Rice production in Mizu's river valleys is among the highest in the archipelago -- the combination of reliable rainfall, mineral-rich alluvial soil, and excellent river irrigation infrastructure makes the province's farming output disproportionately important to regional food security.

Relc's home village of Koriwara is located in Mizu province's interior, in a foothills region where the climate shifts from maritime to montane.

Points of Interest:

  • Shirakawa Estuary -- The great river mouth. At compound low tide, the tidal flats extend so far the estuary looks almost dry. Channel navigation is complex; experienced local pilots are required for larger vessels.
  • Koriwara and the Sacred Grove Elder -- The village is unremarkable on its surface. What makes it significant is Elder Sato Hideaki, whose connection to the Order of the Sacred Grove gives Koriwara significance disproportionate to its size.
  • The Tidal Caves of Umigakure -- Sea caves accessible only during compound low tides. The caves extend far back into the coastal cliffs. Internal airflow suggests a significant interior cavity somewhere behind the accessible chambers.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Minato-jo City Provincial capital; major western port; Arashi-aligned; significant naval presence
Shirakawa Town Estuary trading town; river barge terminus; fishing fleet base
Koriwara Village Relc's home village; Elder Sato Hideaki; Order of the Sacred Grove connection
Umigakure Village "Sea-hidden"; small cove settlement; smuggling history
Inasato Village Interior rice farming; cooperative agricultural commune

Culture & Trade

Mizu's economy is built on maritime trade, fishing, and rice agriculture. Minato-jo serves as the primary western port of Hokori, handling trade routes across the Raijin no Fukai sea. The province's rice production is a strategic asset, and its river systems support extensive barge commerce connecting the coast to the interior.

History

Mizu has long been one of Hokori's most strategically important provinces due to its western coastline and natural harbors. The province's current alignment with the Arashi Alliance reflects its maritime orientation and the naval capabilities centered at Minato-jo.

• Elder Sato Hideaki in Koriwara is more than a village elder with nature connections -- he has deep ties to the Order of the Sacred Grove.
  • One of the three stones referenced in Solas's cipher poem is near Koriwara.
  • The Tidal Caves of Umigakure have started showing light from deep within during night compound tides -- a new phenomenon.

The Order of the Sacred Grove -- Koriwara Connection

Elder Sato Hideaki is a mid-rank member of the Order of the Sacred Grove. He has interacted with Order of the Ancient Guard agents, including Solas Evergreen directly. He knows Solas was Ancient Guard (not just Sacred Grove). He has not told Relc because he was following Solas's instruction to let Relc develop organically.

The Cipher Poem's Connection to Koriwara

One of the three stones referenced in Solas's cipher poem is near Koriwara -- in the foothills. Elder Sato knows this stone and knows, vaguely, what the Warden's Wisdom is: protected knowledge about the locations of the living dragons.

Arashi Naval Presence

Minato-jo's Arashi Alliance-aligned clan has been quietly building naval capacity beyond defensive requirements. Someone is planning an offensive operation involving the western sea. The scope of construction suggests something significant.

Plot Hooks

  • Sato Hideaki has sent word through a traveling merchant -- he needs to speak with Relc urgently; something happened near the sacred grove he tends
  • The Tidal Caves of Umigakure have started showing light from deep within during night compound tides -- a phenomenon not present three months ago

Geography & Terrain

Nami sits on the northeastern tip of Hokori and faces the unabated ocean without shelter. Kusa lies to the southwest and Kaze to the southeast. Its shores receive the full force of oceanic weather systems -- storms that have built across open water for thousands of miles. The province's coastal architecture reflects this: every structure is built low and heavy, walls thick, roofs angled away from prevailing winds, shutters reinforced with iron.

The coastline is rugged and often spectacular -- dramatic sea cliffs dropping directly to churning water, narrow beaches of black volcanic sand between rocky headlands, sea arches and stacks in the offshore shallows. During Tatsunami season, storm swells overwash lower coastal roads entirely, and some villages are evacuated to higher ground as standard annual precaution.

The interior rises quickly from coastal cliffs into the eastern slopes of Hokori's central highlands. The terrain is less hospitable than the island's interior -- thinner soil, more exposure, colder -- but fishing and maritime trade make the province economically significant.

Fujisato, one of Hana province's northeastern ports, sits at the provincial boundary -- a natural gateway between the two provinces' maritime economies.

Points of Interest:

  • The Eastern Lighthouse Chain -- Signal towers and lighthouses along Nami's coast, serving as navigational aids and early warning systems. Some stone bases predate recorded history. During wartime, the chain serves as a communication relay.
  • The Stormwatch Cliffs -- The highest sea cliffs in Hokori, at Nami's northern reach. On clear days, Kawa island is visible in the distance. Seimasters come here to study weather sei during Tatsunami.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Namigashira City Provincial capital; major eastern port; fortified against storm and invasion
Takaiso Town Clifftop town; lighthouse; navigation services
Kurojima Village Black sand beach settlement; fishing cooperative; storm-weathered
Arashizaki Village Headland village; name means "storm cape"; considered lucky to survive the name

Culture & Trade

Nami's culture is shaped by its exposure to the open ocean. The people are resilient, practical, and accustomed to living with the constant threat of powerful storms. Maritime trade and fishing form the economic backbone, with Namigashira serving as Hokori's primary eastern port.

History

Nami has historically served as Hokori's eastern gateway, its ports connecting the island to maritime trade routes across the open ocean. The province's current alignment with the Arashi Alliance reflects its strategic naval importance.

• The oldest lighthouse foundation at Takaiso was not originally a lighthouse -- it was built atop something much older.
  • Nami's Arashi-aligned governing clan is coordinating with Mizu's Minato-jo for a joint naval operation.

Arashi Alliance Naval Operations

Nami's Arashi-aligned governing clan is coordinating with Mizu's Minato-jo -- together, the eastern and western ports are being positioned for a joint naval operation. The target is unknown, but intelligence suggests it involves a landing rather than a sea battle.

The Ancient Lighthouse Foundation

The oldest lighthouse foundation in the chain -- at Takaiso -- is built atop something much older. The original structure was not a lighthouse. Excavation work decades ago stopped abruptly when workers reported the foundation stones were warm to the touch and something moved in the space beneath. The site was sealed and built over. The sealed space is still there.

Plot Hooks

  • A vessel arrived at Namigashira from the open ocean with no crew -- cargo intact, navigation logs ending mid-sentence, cook fire still warm
  • The lighthouse at Takaiso went dark for three consecutive nights; the keeper is missing; locals won't go near it

Type
settlement

"The sea gives and the sea takes. We have learned not to keep count."

Overview

Natsumura is a small fishing village at the point where the Star River empties into the Serenia-kai. The village has existed in essentially the same form for centuries -- a cluster of wooden thatched houses on the riverbank, a small port with drying racks and mooring posts. The Serenia-kai's tidal complexities make the approach navigable only during specific tidal windows; the village's fishermen know these windows intimately.

The kinuo (gold-tail fish) that commands premium prices in Heian runs heaviest at the Sutariba's mouth in late spring and early autumn. During these runs, Natsumura's population effectively doubles with seasonal workers and traders.

Notable Establishments

The Seaside Teahouse & Inn -- The village's sole accommodation and primary social gathering point. The proprietor is the de facto news exchange.

Fisherman's Market -- Daily fish market at the dock. Operates at dawn.

Boatwright's Shed -- Repairs and maintains the village's fishing fleet.

Net Weaver's Workshop -- Produces and repairs fishing nets adapted to Serenia-kai conditions.

Natsumura Shrine -- Small riverside shrine dedicated to a water spirit associated with the Sutariba. Receives offerings before gold-tail runs.

Key Figures

  • Takeda Haruto -- Village leader -> npcs/takeda-haruto.md

• The Star River has recently shown anomalies -- unusual turbidity, temperature changes, and dead fish with injuries inconsistent with normal predation.
  • A figure has been observed watching the village from the far riverbank at night.

DM Secrets

The Sutariba's Upper Reach The Star River has recently shown anomalies -- unusual turbidity, changes in water temperature, and dead fish floating downstream bearing injuries inconsistent with normal predation. This is a consequence of Nagaji activity in the upper pass.

Takeda Haruto's Observation The village leader has seen, twice, a figure watching the village from the far riverbank at night -- a figure that moved in a way that was not quite right. He has not reported it because he has no confidence that authority is currently functioning.

Plot Hooks

  • Investigation of the river anomalies could lead to discovery of Nagaji presence in the mountains above
  • The figure watching from across the river -- Nagaji scout, or something else?

Type
settlement

"A good market draws people together. Everything else follows."

Overview

Nishihara sits in the rolling hills west of the Kinryugawa, in the gentle agricultural country between Heian and the Tenchusan Ren foothills. It is a village that exists primarily to serve the farmers and herders of the surrounding area -- a focal point for exchange, news, and social connection in a landscape of dispersed homesteads.

The weekly market is Nishihara's defining feature. It draws traders from a surprising radius -- merchants from Heian, specialty vendors from neighboring villages, and itinerant traders whose routes include Nishihara. The market has a genuine village-fair quality; it is not purely transactional.

Notable Establishments

Market Hall -- Permanent covered structure hosting the weekly market. On non-market days it functions as a community gathering space and occasional shelter for travelers.

Temple of the Ancestors -- The largest structure in the village; a well-maintained ancestor-veneration temple serving the surrounding rural community. Seasonal festivals draw families from several hours' travel distance.

Key Figures

  • Yukari -- Village leader -> npcs/yukari.md

• Yukari has an unusually clear picture of broader regional events because she makes it her business to listen to the traveling traders.
  • The Temple of the Ancestors maintains records going back several centuries with documentation of unusual historical events.

DM Secrets

Market Intelligence Nishihara's market functions as an informal information exchange point for the rural interior. Yukari has an unusually clear picture of broader events because she listens attentively to traders. She is not an intelligence operative -- she is simply attentive. If the party passes through and asks good questions, she can provide regional context unavailable from official sources.

The Temple's Old Records The Temple maintains records going back several centuries. Among them is documentation of a regional event approximately 80 years ago -- a strange sickness affecting livestock and then people in a specific pattern before stopping suddenly. The documented symptoms, if examined by a seimaster, would match early stages of a sei-manipulation effect rather than natural illness. No one has looked at these records recently.

Plot Hooks

  • Yukari can provide regional context and rumors if approached with good questions
  • The temple records could be relevant to understanding historical sei phenomena in the region

Order of the Tranquil Lotus

  • Nature-based with monk focus
  • Monastery on Unmeijima near Kazehama
  • Elder: Benkei (Guhuza; 198 years old)
  • Sun Wukong is a novice; assigned as delegate to Clan Kaminari

Order of the Sacred Grove

  • Nature/druidic tradition
  • Protective of specific sacred sites
  • Guardian: Solas Evergreen (deceased)
  • Initiate/new Guardian: Relc (appointed by Solas's posthumous letter)
  • Elder connection: Hideaki Sato (Kōriwara village)

Seiju Hyōgikai (星樹評議会 — The Starwood Council)

  • Arinori Senzai is a secret member
  • DM Note: Some members suspected corrupt; Senzai quietly investigating
  • To be developed further

Shōnin-za (商人座 — Merchant Guild)

  • Kenta Yamada is an active member
  • Ren Nakamura has secret alliance with a powerful Shōnin-za branch in Kikyo
• This is where the truth about Clan Gekkō/Nagaji will be revealed

text.content:
Type
core

Hokori

Hokori is the largest island in the Kagekuni archipelago, covering approximately 237,000 square miles. X-shaped in form, it stretches 750 miles long and 600 miles wide. Four tectonic plates converge beneath it, producing frequent earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and tsunamis that shape both the landscape and the culture of its inhabitants.

Eight Provinces

Hokori is divided into eight provinces, each with distinct geography, climate, and political character:

Province Region Capital Alliance Character
Hana Eastern coast Heian Independent Imperial heartland; oldest continuously inhabited province
Hi Western interior and coast Enshiro Contested Volcanic frontier; fiercely independent; contested governance
Kaze Eastern side of NE leg Akatsuki Independent Shadowed forests and mist; Clan Gekko (disappeared)
Kusa Western side of NE leg Midoriko Genso Verdant lowlands; Forest of Spirits; agricultural
Mizu Northwestern coast Minato-jo Arashi Maritime province; major western port; Kōri-no-Mori forest
Nami Northeastern tip Namigashira Arashi Storm-battered coast; faces unabated ocean; lighthouse chain
Sora Central mountains Kumo-no-Ue Independent Lightly populated; mountainous; most dangerous region
Tsuchi Southern highlands Tsuchimoto Genso Mountainous; Kurogane Yama; southern frontier

Political Landscape

Hokori is currently in a state of political crisis following the death of the Emperor. The island's provinces are divided between the Arashi Alliance (Mizu, Nami), the Genso Alliance (Kusa, Tsuchi), independent provinces (Hana, Kaze, Sora), and the contested province of Hi. The Kokushi Kyokai administers in the absence of imperial authority, but its reach is limited.

Key Geographic Features

  • Sora (Central Mountains) -- The mountainous interior of Hokori; lightly populated, dangerous, and the connective barrier between most provinces
  • Kurogane Yama -- Major mountain in southern Tsuchi
  • Serenia-kai (Selenia Sea) -- Vast inland sea in Hokori
  • Seidorin Mori (Bronze Wood Forest) -- Ancient metallic-barked woodland in western Hana
  • Kōri-no-Mori -- Forest on the northern shores of Mizu province
  • Enshiyama (Flame Peak Mountain) -- Third highest peak on Hokori; active volcano in Hi
  • Shirogane Yama (Silver Mountain) -- Highest peak on Hokori; Hoshino Tō observatory at summit; Hana province
  • Hoshimori Plateau (Star Keeper's Plateau) -- High altitude observation site in Sora
  • Emperor's Highway -- Ancient road network connecting major settlements

Transportation

The Emperor's Highway extends from Heian in three directions, forming the primary overland transportation network. River systems -- particularly the Midori River, Tsuchikawa, and Kinryugawa -- serve as major trade arteries. Coastal shipping connects the port cities of Minato-jo (west) and Namigashira (east).

text.content:
Type
core

A well-prepared meal before rest does more than fill the stomach. In Kagekuni, the art of trail cooking is respected — a traveler who can turn foraged ingredients into something worth eating earns standing at any campfire.

Cooking Rules

Who Can Cook

Any character with proficiency in cook's utensils can attempt to prepare a recipe they know. A character without proficiency can prepare Common recipes only, and does so at disadvantage.

When to Cook

Cooking occurs during a long rest. A meal takes 1 hour to prepare and must be consumed during that same rest to gain its benefits. A cook can prepare one recipe per long rest — enough to serve the entire party (up to 6 servings per preparation).

How It Works

The cook makes a Wisdom (Survival) check using cook's utensils. The DC depends on the recipe's tier.

Recipe Tier Cooking DC Ingredient Rarity Required
Simple 10 Common only
Hearty 13 At least one Uncommon
Refined 16 At least one Rare
Masterwork 20 At least one Very Rare

Success: The meal is prepared. All characters who eat it gain the listed buff after completing the long rest. The buff lasts 8 hours or until the next long rest, whichever comes first.

Failure: The ingredients are consumed but the meal is unremarkable — no buff is granted. The characters still eat (no penalty), but the special properties are lost.

Failure by 5+: The meal is actively unpleasant. Ingredients are wasted. Each character who eats it must succeed on a DC 10 Constitution saving throw or suffer disadvantage on their first ability check after the rest (the aftertaste lingers).

Buff Stacking

A character can benefit from only one meal buff at a time. A new meal replaces the previous buff. Meal buffs do not stack with the Kinryū no Megumi temple blessings — the more powerful effect takes precedence.

Ingredient Grade and Cooking

All gathered ingredients now carry a grade from the materials system: 並 Nami (rough/damaged), 上 Jō (standard market grade), 特上 Tokujō (exceptional), and 極上 Gokujō (peerless). Ingredient grade modifies the cooking check and, on high-grade inputs, can lift a recipe's outcome beyond its base tier.

Ingredient Grade Cooking Check Modifier Effect on Buff
並 Nami −2 to the check Buff duration halved (4 hours) on success
上 Jō +0 (baseline) Standard buff as written
特上 Tokujō +2 to the check Buff applies with advantage on any roll it modifies, or +1 to any flat numeric bonus it grants
極上 Gokujō +5 OR advantage on the check Recipe may be prepared as if one tier higher (Simple→Hearty, Hearty→Refined, etc.) for effect purposes; the cook still rolls against the original DC, and if they would clear the higher-tier DC the meal delivers the upgraded buff described in the recipe's "Gokujō Variant" note (or, absent that note, DM discretion applies an appropriately scaled effect)

When a recipe lists multiple ingredients at different grades, use the lowest grade present as the cooking modifier, but the highest-grade ingredient determines whether the meal is eligible for tier-up. A Gokujō centrepiece can still anchor a recipe built on Jō vegetables; the result is exceptional only if the cook clears the upgraded DC.

Ingredient Cross-Reference

Every recipe ingredient below corresponds to a Part I entry in core/materials.md. When a DM or player wants the full stat block — rarity, yield, weight, base value, grade variants, biomes, cultural notes — that file is the source of truth. Recipes cite ingredients by name only; materials.md carries the mechanical detail.

Recipe List

Simple Recipes (DC 10)

Yama-usagi no Nabemono — Mountain Hare Stew

A straightforward one-pot stew simmered with whatever is at hand. Every traveler in Kagekuni has eaten some version of this on a cold mountain road.

Ingredients: Yama-usagi (1 portion) + Seri or Nobiru (1 portion) + Kome (rice, carried) Buff: Warming Rest — Resistance to cold weather exhaustion checks for 8 hours. Characters ignore the effects of temperatures down to -10°F for the duration. Where Found: Common knowledge — any character proficient with cook's utensils knows this recipe.

Kawa-gani no Suimono — River Crab Clear Soup

Delicate broth made from freshwater crab, wild garlic, and a touch of rice vinegar. Light enough for a warm evening, restorative enough for a weary body.

Ingredients: Kawa-gani (1 portion) + Nobiru (1 portion) + Rice Vinegar (carried) Buff: Clear Head — +1 bonus to Wisdom (Perception) checks for 8 hours. Where Found: Common knowledge — any character proficient with cook's utensils knows this recipe.

Uzura no Yakitori — Grilled Quail Skewers

Quail speared on green sticks and turned over coals, basted with soy paste and sake. Simple, satisfying, and impossible to ruin completely.

Ingredients: Uzura (1 portion) + Shōyu (carried) + Sake (carried) Buff: Road Endurance — +5 feet to walking speed for 8 hours. Where Found: Common knowledge — any character proficient with cook's utensils knows this recipe.

Kinoko Miso-shiru — Mushroom Miso Soup

A traveler's best friend. Dried mushrooms reconstituted in miso broth with whatever greens are available. Warm, umami-rich, and deeply comforting after a day on the road.

Ingredients: Shiitake or Nameko (1 portion) + Miso (carried) + Seri (1 portion, optional) Buff: Settled Stomach — Advantage on Constitution saving throws against poison and disease for 8 hours. Where Found: Common knowledge — any character proficient with cook's utensils knows this recipe.

☆ Tabibito no Zōsui — Traveller's Rice Porridge (Wildcard)

The most forgiving recipe on the road. Whatever meat is at hand goes into the pot with rice and water, simmered until it thickens into something warm and filling. Every version tastes different. None of them taste bad.

Ingredients: Any 1 common meat/fish (1 portion) + Kome (carried) + Shio (carried) or any 1 common herb (1 portion, optional) Buff: Trail Stamina — Recover 1 additional Hit Die at the end of the long rest. Where Found: Common knowledge — any character proficient with cook's utensils knows this recipe.

☆ Nobi no Itamemono — Roadside Stir-Fry (Wildcard)

Hot oil, whatever greens are at hand, a splash of soy paste, and the sizzle that draws everyone around the fire. Speed is the art here — cook fast, eat hot.

Ingredients: Any 2 different common herbs/greens (1 portion each) + Shōyu (carried) + Goma (1 portion, optional) Buff: Light Step — Difficult terrain costs no extra movement for 8 hours. Where Found: Common knowledge — any character proficient with cook's utensils knows this recipe.

Ayu no Shioyaki — Salt-Grilled Sweetfish

Whole sweetfish skewered and grilled upright beside the fire, salted and nothing more. The simplest preparation, and one of the best — the clean, melon-sweet flesh needs no embellishment. Festival food, trail food, good food.

Ingredients: Ayu (1 portion) + Shio (carried) Buff: Refreshed — Advantage on the first ability check made after the long rest. Where Found: Common knowledge — any settlement near a river.

☆ Kinoko no Takikomi-gohan — Mixed Mushroom Rice (Wildcard)

Rice cooked with whatever fungi are available, the mushrooms cut small and stirred through so every bite carries their earthiness. The type of mushroom changes the character of the dish entirely — a different meal at every campsite.

Ingredients: Any 2 different common fungi (1 portion each) + Kome (carried) + Shōyu (carried) Buff: Rooted Rest — +1 bonus to Constitution checks (not saving throws) for 8 hours, including checks to maintain a forced march. Where Found: Common knowledge — any character proficient with cook's utensils knows this recipe.

Hearty Recipes (DC 13)

Kinuo no Sashimi — Gold-Tail Sashimi

Thinly sliced raw kinuo, arranged with care and served with wasabi and soy. The Heian elite pay handsomely for this in restaurants — preparing it fresh from a river catch is a rare pleasure.

Ingredients: Kinuo (1 portion) + Wasabi (1 portion) + Shōyu (carried) Buff: Golden Vigor — Gain temporary hit points equal to your proficiency bonus + your Constitution modifier (minimum 1) after the long rest. These last until depleted or 8 hours, whichever comes first. Where Found: Natsumura (any fisherman will share it for a good story); Heian's Mizu-gai (purchased from a seafood stall for 5 gp).

Inoshishi no Kakuni — Slow-Braised Boar Belly

Wild boar braised for hours in sake, soy, and mountain garlic until the fat renders and the meat falls apart. Rich, dense, and fortifying. A meal for the night before a hard day.

Ingredients: Inoshishi (2 portions) + Nobiru (1 portion) + Sake (carried) + Shōyu (carried) Buff: Boar's Fortitude — +1 bonus to Constitution saving throws for 8 hours. Where Found: Ayame — the inn there serves a version of this to soldiers before the mountain crossing. The innkeeper shares the recipe with anyone who buys a round for the garrison.

Kurokaze Cha-gayu — Black Wind Tea Porridge

Rice porridge steeped with the bitter kurokaze herb of Kaze province. Not delicious, precisely — but the alertness it brings is unmistakable. Gekkō sentries drank this before night watch.

Ingredients: Kurokaze-sō (1 portion) + Kome (carried) + Shio (carried) Buff: Watchful Mind — Cannot be surprised for 8 hours. Additionally, +2 bonus to passive Perception during the duration. Where Found: Kaze province — Akatsuki village elder, or discovered in the abandoned Tsukikage settlement (scroll in a guardhouse).

Enokidake no Takikomi-gohan — Bronze Wood Mushroom Rice

Rice steamed with the copper-noted enokidake mushrooms unique to the Seidōrin Mori, seasoned with Bronze Wood Salt. A dish with a faintly metallic sweetness that lingers.

Ingredients: Enokidake (1 portion) + Seidōrin no Shio (1 portion) + Kome (carried) Buff: Ironbark Resolve — +1 bonus to AC against the first attack that hits you each combat (the bonus is consumed on the first hit, reducing damage by your proficiency bonus; minimum 1). Where Found: Kikyo — lumber merchants share this recipe freely, considering it common regional knowledge.

Hi no Ha Rāmen — Fire Leaf Noodle Broth

A searing broth built on dried dashi, laced with the volcanic hi no ha, and served over thick wheat noodles. Sweat-inducing, breath-clearing, and beloved in Hi province where the locals consider anything less spicy to be "children's food."

Ingredients: Hi no Ha (1 portion) + Dried Dashi (carried) + Kome or noodles (carried) + Shōyu (carried) Buff: Inner Fire — Resistance to fire damage from environmental sources (not attacks) for 8 hours. Additionally, immune to the effects of extreme cold weather for the duration. Where Found: Hi province — any settlement. Enshiro's garrison cooks prepare it daily. Onsen-machi serves an upscale version.

Tsukimisō no Ochazuke — Moonflower Tea Rice

A calming dish of rice bathed in moonflower tea, served with pickled vegetables and a scatter of sesame. Traditionally eaten before diplomatic meetings, but equally useful before any encounter where a steady hand matters.

Ingredients: Tsukimisō (1 portion) + Kome (carried) + Tsukemono (carried) Buff: Serene Focus — +1 bonus to Charisma (Persuasion) and Wisdom (Insight) checks for 8 hours. Where Found: Heian — a tea house in the Ryū Jikuchiku sells this recipe for 10 gp. Alternatively, shrine monks at Kodan no Jinja share it with respectful visitors.

Unagi no Kabayaki — Grilled Eel with Sweet Glaze

Freshwater eel split, boned, and grilled repeatedly with a glaze of soy, sake, and a touch of sweetness. The fat renders between each pass over the coals until the skin crisps and the flesh melts. Regarded as a stamina food across all provinces — no coincidence that eel vendors do brisk business before military campaigns.

Ingredients: Unagi (1 portion) + Shōyu (carried) + Sake (carried) + Sanshō (1 portion) Buff: Eel's Endurance — Advantage on Constitution checks to maintain concentration and to avoid exhaustion from forced marches for 8 hours. Where Found: Natsumura — the eel-griller on the wharf teaches the technique to anyone patient enough to watch. Nishihara's river market also knows it.

☆ Yama no Nabe — Mountain Hot Pot (Wildcard)

The quintessential trail meal for a cold evening in high country. A communal pot over the fire, filled with whatever the day's foraging turned up — any game, any greens, any mushroom. The broth does the work.

Ingredients: Any 1 uncommon meat/fish (1 portion) + any 1 common or uncommon herb/green (1 portion) + any 1 common or uncommon fungi (1 portion) + Dried Dashi or Miso (carried) Buff: Shared Warmth — All characters who share the meal gain +2 to saving throws against cold weather effects and exhaustion from exposure for 8 hours. If at least 3 characters share the meal, each also gains 1d4 temporary hit points. Where Found: Ayame — soldiers share their version around the garrison fire. Takamine — the mountain guides know a dozen variations.

Kamo no Tsukune — Wild Duck Meatball Skewers

Wild duck minced with ginger and scallion, shaped into small balls and grilled over charcoal. The outside chars while the inside stays tender. Simple construction, but the richness of the duck meat carries a depth that domestic poultry cannot match.

Ingredients: Kamo (1 portion) + Myōga (1 portion) + Shōyu (carried) Buff: Sharpened Senses — +2 to passive Perception and +1 to initiative rolls for 8 hours. Where Found: Koriwara — a retired samurai who runs a yakitori stall in the market ward teaches the recipe to anyone who compliments his cooking with apparent sincerity.

Umikaze Chazuke — Sea Wind Rice

A coastal traveller's meal — hot dashi poured over rice, topped with the thick, salty umikaze greens and flaked fish. The briny greens cut the richness of the broth. Nami fishermen eat this before dawn watches when the storms are coming.

Ingredients: Umikaze-na (1 portion) + any 1 common fish (1 portion) + Kome (carried) + Dried Dashi (carried) Buff: Storm Ready — Advantage on Strength (Athletics) checks made to resist being knocked prone or pushed, and advantage on saving throws against effects caused by wind or lightning for 8 hours. Where Found: Nami coastline — any fishing village. The recipe travels with the tides.

Iwatake no Nimono — Simmered Rock Mushroom

Rock mushroom rehydrated in dashi, simmered slowly until the leathery texture softens into something rich and gelatinous. The mineral depth of the fungus fills the broth. Monk's food — austere, deliberate, and quietly satisfying.

Ingredients: Iwatake (1 portion) + Dried Dashi (carried) + Shōyu (carried) + Miso (carried) Buff: Mountaineer's Grip — +2 to Strength (Athletics) checks for climbing and advantage on saving throws against falling for 8 hours. Where Found: Takamine — a monastery cook shares this with pilgrims who help with kitchen duties. Also known at high-altitude shrines throughout Sora.

Refined Recipes (DC 16)

Seireiuo no Sunomono — Spirit Fish Vinegar Salad

Translucent spirit fish, briefly cured in rice vinegar, served over shredded daikon with a whisper of wasabi. The flesh still carries a faint luminescence on the plate. The taste is unlike anything from ordinary waters.

Ingredients: Seireiuo (1 portion) + Wasabi (1 portion) + Rice Vinegar (carried) Buff: Sei Attunement — +1 bonus to spell attack rolls and spell save DCs for 8 hours. Non-casters instead gain advantage on saving throws against magical effects. Where Found: Yōsei Mori — the Forest of Spirits faction shares this with allies who prove trustworthy. Alternatively, a scroll may be found in ruins with sei-active water sources.

Ryūjika no Sumibi-yaki — Charcoal-Grilled Dragon Deer

Dragon deer venison, seared over hardwood charcoal and finished with a glaze of sake and dragon salt. The meat's natural warmth intensifies over the flame. Those who eat it report a sensation of quiet strength settling into the bones.

Ingredients: Ryūjika (1 portion) + Ryūjio (1 portion) + Sake (carried) Buff: Draconic Fortitude — Gain advantage on death saving throws for 8 hours. Additionally, when you spend Hit Dice during a short rest within the duration, you may reroll any Hit Die that shows a 1 or 2 (keeping the new result). Where Found: Ancient Guard knowledge — Benkei knows this recipe and will share it with a party that has earned his trust. May also be inscribed on stone near Progenitor shrine sites.

Kageboushi no Ankake — Shadow Cap Mushroom in Thickened Broth

Shadow mushrooms simmered in a rich thickened dashi, their smoky depth intensified by slow reduction. The broth is dark as ink and just as staining. Eaten in near-darkness in Kaze, where they say the dish teaches you to see without light.

Ingredients: Kageboushi (1 portion) + Kuro-koshō (1 portion) + Dried Dashi (carried) + Shōyu (carried) Buff: Shadow Sight — Gain darkvision 30 feet for 8 hours. Characters who already have darkvision extend its range by 30 feet. Additionally, +2 to Dexterity (Stealth) checks in dim light or darkness. Where Found: Kaze province — the Black Lily monastery. The recipe is not secret, but the monastery shares it only with those who have done the Order a service.

Seikinoko no Chawanmushi — Sei Mushroom Custard

A savory egg custard steamed with luminescent sei mushrooms, their violet-blue glow dimming slowly as the custard sets. Served in ceramic cups and eaten with a small wooden spoon. The flavor is elusive — forest, rain, and something older.

Ingredients: Seikinoko (1 portion) + Seri (1 portion) + Dried Dashi (carried) Buff: Sei Reservoir — Recover one expended spell slot of 1st or 2nd level at the end of the long rest (in addition to normal recovery). Non-casters instead recover an additional Hit Die. Where Found: Mori no Sato village on the Yōsei Mori border — the village herbalist teaches it to those who bring her a fresh seikinoko specimen as proof of their foraging ability.

Hinotake no Dengaku — Fire Stalk Grilled with Miso Glaze

Fire stalk mushrooms, carefully peeled to avoid the caustic outer membrane, then glazed with sweetened miso and grilled until the edges char. The heat builds slowly — not unpleasant, but insistent. Hi province miners eat this before descending into volcanic shafts.

Ingredients: Hinotake (1 portion) + Miso (carried) + Sake (carried) Buff: Volcanic Resilience — Resistance to fire damage (all sources, including attacks) for 8 hours. Where Found: Hi province — Kurokawa village. The obsidian crafters share it with outsiders who help with a day's labor in the fields. Also found carved into a wall near the Crimson Shrine's outer approach.

Oniuo no Nitsuke — Demon Fish Braised in Soy

The demon fish's bony plates are pried apart to reveal dense white flesh, braised in a dark reduction of soy, sake, and ginger until the meat turns glossy and falls from the bone. The fishermen who hunt oniuo say the fight to land one is half the preparation — the braising is the easy part.

Ingredients: Oniuo (1 portion) + Tsuchi-shōga (1 portion) + Shōyu (carried) + Sake (carried) Buff: Predator's Tenacity — When you are reduced below half your hit point maximum, gain +1 to attack rolls until the end of your next turn. This triggers once per combat. Where Found: Kaze province — a ferryman on the Kagerō River who has fished its deep pools for forty years. He teaches the recipe as payment for help clearing debris from his crossing.

Kumokiji no Mushiyaki — Cloud Pheasant Steamed in Leaves

Cloud pheasant breast wrapped in murasaki-ha leaves and steamed over a low fire. The purple leaf imparts a faint sweetness and tints the meat a pale violet. A dish of high altitude and rare beauty — the kind of thing you eat once and remember for the rest of your life.

Ingredients: Kumokiji (1 portion) + Murasaki-ha (1 portion) + Yuzu (1 portion) Buff: Clarity of the Heights — Advantage on Wisdom saving throws for 8 hours. Where Found: Takamine — an elderly guide who leads parties above the cloud line. She cooks this at the summit camp and shares the recipe only with those who complete the ascent without complaint.

☆ Sansai no Sunomono — Wild Harvest Vinegar Salad (Wildcard)

A dish of raw preparation — whatever rare greens and herbs are at hand, sliced thin and dressed in vinegar with a scatter of sesame. No cooking, no broth, no fire. The ingredients must be exceptional, because nothing hides behind heat.

Ingredients: Any 2 different rare herbs/greens (1 portion each) + Rice Vinegar (carried) + Goma (1 portion) Buff: Sei Sensitivity — Gain the ability to detect sei-active objects and creatures within 10 feet for 8 hours (functions as detect magic, but limited to sei energy only). Where Found: Yōsei Mori border communities — shared among herbalists who trade in rare plants. A version of the recipe circulates among the Seishin Enclave's outer circle.

Kaseki-gani no Kani-miso — Stone Crab Tomalley Gratin

The dense claw meat of the stone crab, mixed with its own tomalley and broiled in the upturned shell until it sets into a rich, savoury custard. The mineral crust of the shell chars and seasons the dish from without. A cave-diver's reward — earned by anyone brave enough to wade into a tidal cavern.

Ingredients: Kaseki-gani (1 portion) + Umi-shio (1 portion) + Sake (carried) Buff: Ironhide — Gain +1 to AC for 8 hours (does not stack with shield or magical armor bonuses above +2). Where Found: Mizu coastline — the pearl-divers of Umigakure know it. Also traded among the sailors who shelter in Nami's cove villages during storm season.

Yūrei-kusa no Chakai — Ghost Grass Ceremony Tea

Not a meal in the traditional sense — a tea ceremony built around the pale, cold-to-the-touch ghost grass of Kaze's ruined settlements. The preparation is slow and deliberate: the grass is steeped three times, each steeping drawing out a different quality. The first is bitter. The second is smooth. The third carries something that makes the drinker acutely aware of nearby presences.

Ingredients: Yūrei-kusa (1 portion) + Kome (carried, for accompanying rice cakes) + Shio (carried) Buff: Spirit Sight — Gain the ability to see invisible creatures and objects within 15 feet for 8 hours. Additionally, you cannot be surprised by undead or spirit creatures. Where Found: Akatsuki — an elderly herbalist living on the edge of the settlement. The recipe is also referenced in fragmentary notes found in Tsukikage's abandoned guardhouse.

Masterwork Recipes (DC 20)

Ryūketsu Kaiseki — Dragon's Blood Banquet

A multi-course meal built around the impossibly rare dragon's blood flower. The petals are incorporated into every element — infused into the broth, pressed into the rice, scattered over seared venison. The meal takes two hours to prepare and demands the cook's complete attention. Those who eat it feel, for a time, as though something ancient is watching over them.

Ingredients: Ryūketsu-bana (1 portion) + Ryūjika (1 portion) + Kinuo (1 portion) + Ryūjio (1 portion) + Kome (carried) Buff: Progenitor's Blessing — +1 bonus to all saving throws for 8 hours. Once during the duration, when you are reduced to 0 hit points, you may immediately regain hit points equal to 1d10 + your character level. This consumes the blessing entirely. Where Found: Cannot be purchased or casually discovered. Possible sources: deep within Progenitor-associated ruins; a gift from a being of great age and wisdom; reward for completing a quest tied to dragon legacy.

Seiryoku Nabe — Sei-Vigor Hot Pot

A communal hot pot built around the luminous seiryoku grass, simmered with spirit fish, sei mushrooms, and whatever the wilderness provides. The pot glows faintly as it cooks. The ingredients must all be fresh — no dried or preserved components. Eating it is a communal act; the buff only functions if shared among at least two people.

Ingredients: Seiryoku-gusa (1 portion) + Seireiuo (1 portion) + Seikinoko (1 portion) + any 2 common herbs/greens Buff: Sei Communion — All characters who share the meal gain the following for 8 hours: advantage on concentration checks, +1 to all ability checks, and the ability to communicate telepathically with other characters who shared the meal (30 ft range). Requires at least 2 participants. Where Found: The Seishin Enclave on Unmeijima. Alternatively, fragments of this recipe appear across multiple locations — a hermit's cave in Sora, a shrine wall in the Yōsei Mori, a damaged scroll in the Temple of Kinryū. Assembling the complete recipe from fragments is itself a quest.

☆ Hoshizora Kaiseki — Starlight Banquet (Wildcard)

A multi-course meal that can only be prepared under open sky when Ryūgetsu is visible. The centrepiece is a dish built around any very rare ingredient — meat, herb, or fungus — supported by complementary rare and uncommon components. The specific courses change depending on what the cook has gathered. No two Starlight Banquets are alike. The meal takes two hours to prepare and demands the cook's full attention and a flawless performance.

Ingredients: Any 1 very rare ingredient (1 portion) + any 1 rare ingredient from a different category (1 portion) + any 1 uncommon seasoning (1 portion) + Kome (carried) Buff: Starlit Resolve — +1 to all ability scores (not modifiers) for 8 hours. Additionally, the first time during the duration that you would fail a saving throw, you may choose to succeed instead (consumes this portion of the blessing). Where Found: Cannot be purchased. The recipe exists as a philosophical framework rather than a fixed formula — learned from a master cook of extraordinary skill. Possible sources: a retired imperial chef living in seclusion, the kitchens of the Hoshimori observatory, or a spirit of the road who tests travellers with riddles before teaching the art.

Ryūkinoko Ryōri — Dragon Fungus Feast

A meal built around the impossible warmth of the dragon fungus, its golden glow casting slow amber light across the cook's hands as the flesh is sliced thin and layered with seasonal accompaniments. Those who eat it describe a feeling of being held — not restrained, but supported, as though the earth itself had placed a hand beneath them.

Ingredients: Ryūkinoko (1 portion) + Ryūjio (1 portion) + any 1 rare herb (1 portion) + Dried Dashi (carried) Buff: Progenitor's Calm — For 8 hours, you are immune to the frightened condition. Additionally, you gain advantage on death saving throws and may add your Wisdom modifier to death saving throws. Where Found: A Progenitor-associated cave system deep beneath the mountains. The recipe is understood instinctively by anyone who has been in the presence of a living Progenitor. It may also be discovered carved into stone near a dragon's resting chamber.

Named Beast Recipes — Yama-no-Ōkami

These recipes exist only because the party slew the Mountain God of the Tenchūsan Ren and harvested the beast with uncanny skill. Every component is single-grade-locked at 極上 Gokujō (see core/materials.md → Named Beast Harvests → Yama-no-Ōkami (Slain)), which means each dish below automatically clears the grade modifier for tier-up eligibility. A competent cook who can clear the upgraded DC delivers a peerless meal; a less skilled cook still produces an exceptional one. There is no "ordinary" preparation of these components — the beast will not permit it.

These recipes are not on the random loot table. They can only be learned by DM placement — a retired hunter's journal, a shrine-keeper who remembers the old rites, or a moment of insight at the campfire after a long day of travel. They are one-time rewards for a one-time harvest.

Ōkami no Kakuni — Mountain God's Braised Fang-Meat (Masterwork)

Ōkami-niku slow-braised for hours in sake, shōyu, and mountain garlic until the fat renders and the meat falls apart in sheets. The flesh is impossibly tender and carries a faint metallic brightness on the tongue — the taste of a beast that lived at the edge of the spirit world. Those who eat it describe dreams of high passes they have never walked.

Ingredients: Ōkami-niku (2 portions, Gokujō) + Nobiru (1 portion) + Sake (carried) + Shōyu (carried) Cooking DC: 20 (Masterwork) Buff: Mountain God's Fortitude — For 8 hours, gain +2 to Constitution saving throws and resistance to cold damage. The first time during the duration you would drop to 0 HP, you instead drop to 1 HP; this benefit is consumed on use. Gokujō Variant (tier-up): As above, plus the eater gains advantage on Strength checks and saving throws for the duration, and may add +1d4 to any single attack roll, ability check, or saving throw during the duration (consumed on use). Where Found: Not on the scroll tables. Learned only from direct instruction — a hunter who witnessed the harvest, or intuited by a character with proficiency in cook's utensils who spends downtime experimenting with the ingredients.

Reikokoro no Kaiseki — Spirit Heart Banquet (Masterwork, Legendary)

A single-sitting banquet built around the Reikokoro — the Spirit Heart — cooked in a sealed clay vessel with the marrow, liver, and storm-sinew of the same beast. The heart is cooked whole, and the vessel must not be opened until the moment of serving. The meal feeds six and cannot be preserved, split, or carried. It is eaten in silence, by the same fire that prepared it, within the same rest period. Those who share it describe sensing the wolf's final thoughts — the smell of snow, the weight of the mountain, the brief and perfect stillness before death.

Ingredients: Reikokoro (1 portion, Gokujō, feeds six) + Shirokiba no Zui (1 portion, Gokujō) + Yama no Kimo (1 portion, Gokujō) + Arashi-suji (1 portion, Gokujō) + Kome (carried) + Sake (carried) Cooking DC: 22 (Masterwork — single hardest check in the recipe list) Buff: Bond of the Mountain God — All characters who share the meal gain the following for 24 hours (not 8): +2 to all saving throws, advantage on Wisdom (Survival) checks made in mountain terrain, and the ability to sense the direction and approximate distance of any one willing participant at will. Additionally, the first time each character would drop to 0 HP during the duration, they instead drop to 1 HP. This benefit is consumed individually per character. Gokujō Variant (tier-up): As above, plus each participant gains 2d10 temporary hit points for the duration, and once during the 24 hours may choose to succeed on a single failed saving throw (each character, once, consumed on use). Where Found: Cannot be purchased, found, or stumbled upon. The recipe is knowledge carried by those who remember the old compacts between hunters and mountain kami. Possible sources: a retired hunter who served a daimyo of the Tenchūsan Ren; a shrine-keeper at a high-altitude shrine who senses the components the party carries; a dream-vision received by a character during a long rest in the mountains while carrying the Reikokoro. One-time meal: The ingredients for this recipe cannot be reassembled. Once the Reikokoro is consumed, this dish cannot be made again.

Arashi-suji no Dashi — Storm-Sinew Broth (Refined)

A broth rendered from the beast's sinew — stringy, slow to cook, and startlingly clear when it finishes. The first sip is unremarkable. The second carries the taste of wind over a high ridge. The drinker finds their step lighter and their lungs deeper.

Ingredients: Arashi-suji (1 portion, Gokujō) + Shio (carried) + any 1 uncommon herb (1 portion) Cooking DC: 16 (Refined) Buff: Storm-Lung — For 8 hours, walking speed increases by 10 ft, you can hold your breath for three times the usual duration, and you have advantage on Constitution saving throws made to resist exhaustion from forced march or harsh weather. Gokujō Variant (tier-up): As above, plus you gain the ability to take the Dash action as a bonus action (once per round) for the duration. Where Found: The simplest of the Yama-no-Ōkami recipes. A character with proficiency in cook's utensils can derive this from the sinew itself after spending an hour studying it at a campfire — the preparation is obvious to anyone who has worked with beast sinew before.

Loot Table — Recipe Scrolls

Recipes found during exploration are written on scrolls, carved into surfaces, or passed down verbally. The DM can place specific recipes as loot, or roll on the following table when a recipe discovery is called for.

Random Recipe Discovery (d100)

The expanded recipe list uses a d100 for finer control. Wildcard recipes (marked ☆) are particularly valuable early — they accept flexible ingredients and reward creative foraging.

Roll Recipe Tier Notes
01–06 Yama-usagi no Nabemono Simple
07–12 Kawa-gani no Suimono Simple

25–28 ☆ Tabibito no Zōsui Simple Wildcard — any common meat
29–32 ☆ Nobi no Itamemono Simple Wildcard — any common herbs

Masterwork Sub-Table (d6)

Roll Recipe Notes
1 Ryūketsu Kaiseki Dragon's Blood Banquet
2 Seiryoku Nabe Sei-Vigor Hot Pot

5–6 DM's choice

Recipe Acquisition by Location

For targeted placement, the following summarizes where each recipe is most naturally found.

Location Recipes Available
Any settlement All Simple recipes (including wildcards)
Natsumura Kinuo no Sashimi, Unagi no Kabayaki
Nishihara Unagi no Kabayaki
Ayame Inoshishi no Kakuni, ☆ Yama no Nabe
Akatsuki / Tsukikage Kurokaze Cha-gayu, Yūrei-kusa no Chakai
Kikyo Enokidake no Takikomi-gohan
Koriwara Kamo no Tsukune
Hi province (any) Hi no Ha Rāmen, Hinotake no Dengaku
Heian Tsukimisō no Ochazuke, Kinuo no Sashimi
Kaze province (Kagerō River) Oniuo no Nitsuke
Kaze province (Black Lily) Kageboushi no Ankake
Nami coastline Umikaze Chazuke
Mizu coastline / Umigakure Kaseki-gani no Kani-miso
Takamine ☆ Yama no Nabe, Iwatake no Nimono, Kumokiji no Mushiyaki
Sora (Hoshimori) ☆ Hoshizora Kaiseki
Yōsei Mori / Mori no Sato Seireiuo no Sunomono, Seikinoko no Chawanmushi, ☆ Sansai no Sunomono
Progenitor ruins Ryūjika no Sumibi-yaki, Ryūketsu Kaiseki, Ryūkinoko Ryōri
Benkei Ryūjika no Sumibi-yaki
Seishin Enclave Seiryoku Nabe, ☆ Sansai no Sunomono
Fragmented (multi-location) Seiryoku Nabe (alternative path)

Design Notes (DM Only)

Wildcard Recipes (☆): Recipes marked with ☆ accept flexible ingredient substitutions — "any common meat," "any 2 rare herbs," etc. These are deliberately front-loaded in the system so players who engage with gathering early feel rewarded regardless of which specific ingredients they find. Wildcards also encourage experimentation and make the system feel less like a shopping list. The DM should let players describe what they're making with the specific ingredients they chose — this creates organic flavour and roleplay moments without requiring a unique recipe for every combination.

Power Calibration: Meal buffs are intentionally minor — comparable to a cantrip or a minor boon, not a spell effect. They reward engagement with the gathering and cooking system without creating a mandatory pre-combat checklist. The Masterwork recipes are deliberately harder to achieve and more impactful, serving as adventure rewards in their own right.

Encouraging the System: The best way to introduce this is organically — an NPC cooking at a campfire, a recipe scroll found as incidental loot, a grateful innkeeper sharing a family recipe. Let the players discover that the system exists rather than presenting it as a mechanic to optimize.

Sei Ingredients and Mystery: The sei-active ingredients (seireiuo, seikinoko, seiryoku-gusa, ryūketsu-bana) are deliberately tied to the world's deeper lore. Finding them should feel meaningful — these are ingredients that connect to the living magic of the world, not commodity goods. Their inability to be preserved reinforces this: they are gifts from the moment, not resources to stockpile.

Interaction with Kinryū no Megumi: The temple pool blessings are significantly more powerful than meal buffs and represent divine-tier effects. Meal buffs are mortal-tier — the difference should be felt. If both are active, the more powerful effect (always the temple blessing) takes precedence; the meal buff is suppressed but not consumed, resuming if the blessing expires first.
