text.content:
The Divine Structure

  • Single supreme divine entity — analogous to Christianity's monotheism
  • Historical deities venerated as saint-equivalents — subordinate to supreme being
  • Shrines and temples may be dedicated to specific divine figures without contradicting monotheistic faith
  • Different clans/regions have patron divine figures
  • Dragons occupy a unique revered position — between saints-equivalent and kami
  • Kami (nature spirits) exist as a separate category of minor spiritual beings

The Seven Dragon Clans — Founding Era

Clan Dragon Color Island Domain
Crimson Clan Akaryū Red Fushichō Fire, volcanic power, strength
Azure Clan Aoryū Blue Kawa Water, storms, coastal protection
Emerald Clan Midoryū Green Hokori Nature, earth, healing, balance
Onyx Clan Kokuryū Black Tatara Shadow, darkness, cunning, mystery
Golden Clan Kinryū Gold Hokori (central highlands) Honor, justice, nobility, mediation
Silver Clan Ginryū Silver Fuukajima Grace, purity, ice, cold, moon/stars
Amethyst Clan Murasakiryū Purple Shizukajima Arcane knowledge, divination, mystical arts

First Emperor

Tenryū no Mikado — descended from both Crimson and Golden bloodlines; united clans ~8000; established first imperial dynasty

Dragon Legacy in Society

  • Dragonborn within Kugai claim descent from dragon founders — legitimizes noble authority
  • Many daimyo trace lineage to founding dragons
  • Temples, shrines, festivals honor dragon ancestors annually
  • The arcadian (elf) imperial line descended from dragon-settler intermingling

Dragons Today — CRITICAL SECRET (DM Only)

  • All seven founding dragons are still alive — hidden, withdrawn
  • World considers them purely historical and mythological
  • Dragons are extremely rare in current era — occasional individuals exist
  • Dragon eggs believed to be fossils — viability unknown to world at large
  • Dragon eggs are highly collectible
  • The Order of the Ancient Guard exists specifically to protect the living dragons

text.content:
Type
settlement

"It grew because travelers needed a reason to stop. Now they stop because it grew."

Overview

Sakura Mura did not begin as a planned settlement -- it accumulated around a single inn on the Emperor's Highway that proved well-positioned for a rest stop. Over generations, the inn attracted other services, the services attracted residents, and the residents built a community. The village retains its highway-dependent character.

A river runs east-west through the village, spanned at the north end by Shadowfen Bridge -- a stone bridge leading into a stretch of marsh forest. A secondary road path continues north from the bridge's far bank.

The village is surrounded by forest on three sides, with a lake visible to the southeast. The cherry trees that give the village its name line the Highway approach for a quarter-mile -- planted two centuries ago by a traveling monk as a gift.

Notable Establishments

Oka-tei Inn -- The original settlement's reason for existing. Large, well-run, designed for highway travelers. Stabling for horses and oxen; common room with a good fire; private rooms at premium rates.

Takahashi's Hunting Lodge -- Equipment, local guides, and hunting licenses for the surrounding forest. Serves both dedicated hunters and travelers wanting fresh game.

Key Figures

None specifically documented.

• The Shadowfen Bridge exhibits a genuine sei phenomenon -- a low-level resonance that produces mild disorientation in those who speak falsehoods while crossing.
  • The marsh forest north of the bridge contains remnants of an ancient, consumed structure.

DM Secrets

Shadowfen Bridge The local legend has a basis in actual sei phenomenon. A low-level sei resonance exists at the bridge, likely from the marsh forest on the far bank. It is not strong enough to genuinely redirect travelers, but sei-sensitive individuals feel a strong pull toward honesty when crossing. Someone who speaks a significant lie experiences mild but unmistakable disorientation.

The Forest North of the Bridge The marsh forest past Shadowfen Bridge contains remnants of a structure predating Sakura Mura by many centuries. Not accessible without knowing what to look for -- the marsh has largely consumed it. Local hunters know to avoid a specific area they describe as "wrong-feeling." The structure's origin and purpose are unknown.

Plot Hooks

  • Investigation of the Shadowfen Bridge sei phenomenon could reveal the ancient structure beneath the marsh
  • Local hunters' avoidance of the "wrong-feeling" area could lead to discovery of pre-imperial ruins

text.content:
Type
core

The road between cities is long in Kagekuni, and the land provides for those who know how to ask. A traveller with sharp eyes and a steady hand can supplement dried rations with wild game, foraged herbs, cave-grown fungi, and seasonings drawn from the earth itself. A traveller who can also cook — truly cook, not merely char meat over a fire — can turn those ingredients into meals that settle the nerves, warm the bones, and sharpen the senses for what lies ahead.

The practice is called sanzai — the wild harvest — and it is as old as travel itself. Every province of Hokori offers something different. The volcanic slopes of Hi grow things that would wither in Kusa's wet lowlands. The mist-shrouded forests of Kaze harbour herbs that have never seen full sunlight. And in places where sei flows close to the surface, the land produces ingredients that carry something more than flavour.

Gathering

Foraging takes time and attention. An hour spent searching — during a rest, while the party travels at a slow pace, or in dedicated downtime — is enough to turn up what the terrain has to offer. What you find depends on where you look, what you know, and how carefully you search.

Those trained in wilderness survival will recognise edible plants, track game, and distinguish safe fungi from their poisonous cousins. An herbalism kit helps with the finer work of identifying medicinal and aromatic plants. Cook's utensils grant an instinct for what is worth eating and what is not.

Rarer ingredients are harder to find — they grow in specific terrain, appear only in certain seasons, or require knowledge of where to look that most travellers simply do not have. The rarest of all are tied to places where sei is active, and a skilled cook who can bring such an ingredient home intact has something worth boasting about.

Hunting

Wild game is plentiful across Hokori, from mountain hares in the Tenchūsan Ren to boar in the forests of Hana and Kaze. Hunting requires tracking and either combat or trapping, followed by the practical work of butchering. Larger animals yield more meat but demand more effort to bring down. Bakemono and yokai are not safe to eat unless someone with specific knowledge says otherwise.

Fishing

Rivers, lakes, and coastlines offer their own harvest. Line and hook is the most common method, though nets, spears, and overnight traps each have their place. Tidal windows, seasonal runs, and water conditions affect what can be caught and where. A fisherman who knows the local waters will always outperform a stranger.

Cooking

A well-prepared meal before rest does more than fill the stomach. Certain combinations of ingredients — prepared with skill and the right knowledge — produce effects that linger into the following day. A warming stew that keeps the mountain cold at bay. A broth that sharpens the senses. A dish so fortifying that the body recovers faster than it should.

Cooking happens during a long rest. One meal per rest, enough to share with companions. The complexity of the recipe determines how much skill it demands — simple trail food is forgiving, while refined dishes require precision and rare ingredients. A failed attempt wastes the ingredients but causes no harm beyond disappointment. A truly botched effort is best not spoken of.

Recipes

Recipes are not innate. You learn them by finding them — purchased from a cook in a market town, taught by a grateful innkeeper, discovered on a scroll tucked inside an abandoned pack, or carved into the wall of a mountain shrine by someone who thought the knowledge worth preserving. Some recipes are common enough that any competent cook knows them. Others are regional secrets, passed between specific communities. A few are so rare that assembling the complete instructions is an undertaking in itself.

Spoilage

Fresh ingredients do not last forever. Meat and fish spoil within a day unless the weather is cold. Herbs keep for two days, fungi for three. Smoking, salting, drying, or pickling extends the life of most ingredients considerably — and with skill, even the rarest of harvests can be brought home from the wilderness intact.

The land provides. Learn where to look.

Geography & Terrain

Sora -- Sky -- is the highest-altitude province in Hokori and encompasses the majority of the lightly populated mountainous interior at the island's center. It is often the most dangerous region to traverse. Much of it sits above the cloud ceiling. A traveler ascending from lower provinces will emerge through dense cloud into a world of startling clarity: thin air, intense sunlight, vast visibility, and a profound silence broken only by wind.

The province occupies the central mountain ranges that form the connective barrier between most of Hokori's other provinces. It borders nearly every other province in some capacity -- a sprawling, thinly governed wilderness between centres of population. The plateau itself is high grassland -- silvered grasses that catch light differently, giving the landscape an almost lunar quality. Standing water freezes for months; the ground is rocky and thin-soiled.

The Hoshimori Plateau (Star Keeper's Plateau) is the defining feature -- wide, flat, and high enough that stars are visibly brighter than anywhere else in the archipelago. This made it the site of observatories and sei-research installations during the Golden Age, several of which still stand.

The province has few settlements relative to its area, but the routes through it connect northern Hokori to the central, and controlling them carries strategic importance disproportionate to population.

Points of Interest:

  • Hoshimori Plateau (Star Keeper's Plateau) -- Exceptional astronomical observation site. The sky here behaves slightly differently -- star density appears higher and moons seem slightly larger. Whether this is optical illusion or something else has not been resolved.
  • The Golden Age Observatories -- Three of seven observatories built during Emperor Kinryu no Mikado's reign remain structurally intact. Their instruments -- large bronze mechanisms -- are still functional and oriented to alignments no current seimaster fully understands. A fourth, largely collapsed, contains sealed records.
  • The Storm Road -- Mountain route through Sora connecting Hana/Hi to the northern coast. Impassable in winter; deteriorating without central maintenance authority.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Kumo-no-Ue Town "Above the Clouds"; provincial capital; cold year-round
Hoshimori Village On the plateau; observatory town; seimaster community
Kanransha Village Mountain pass waypoint; transit community; temporary lodging industry

Culture & Trade

Sora's small population is centered around the observatory communities and the transit routes that cross the province. The seimaster community at Hoshimori represents a concentration of astronomical and magical expertise. The province's isolation and altitude make it a natural retreat for those seeking contemplation or research.

History

During the Golden Age, Sora was a center of astronomical research and sei study, with seven observatories constructed on the Hoshimori Plateau. The Dark Ages saw these installations abandoned. The province's strategic importance lies in controlling the mountain routes connecting northern and central Hokori.

• The functional observatories are producing readings that match a pattern the ancient seimasters considered significant -- the Ryushinki (Dragon Awakening).
  • A seimaster from Hoshimori has been trying to reach Heian with urgent information for three months and has not arrived.

The Abandoned Observatory Records

The sealed records in the collapsed fourth observatory contain documentation of a celestial alignment the Kinryu-era seimasters considered dangerous. The alignment -- involving all three stars, two specific moons, and a specific planetary configuration -- they called Ryushinki (Dragon Awakening). Their records suggest this alignment is associated with the founding dragons becoming active, visible, or vulnerable. The next occurrence is calculable and is not far away.

The Silver Dragon Connection

Ginryu, the Silver Dragon, is connected to Sora through the province's astronomical nature. She has been known to spend time on the Hoshimori Plateau. The plateau's unusual stellar appearance is partly her influence. She has not been seen in decades, but her presence would explain the plateau's anomalous sei readings.

Plot Hooks

  • One of the functional observatories has started producing readings matching the Ryushinki pattern ahead of schedule -- something is wrong with the calculation, or something is accelerating
  • A seimaster from Hoshimori sent a letter ahead that references "something moving in the clouds that is not a cloud"

Type
settlement

"The mountain owes us nothing. We dig anyway."

Overview

Takamine is a village of honest poverty. It sits in the shadow of Kinryuzan (Gold Dragon Mountain) at the head of the Star River, in a valley receiving less direct sunlight due to the mountain's angle. The small iron mine that sustains the village produces modest yields -- enough to keep the operation viable, not enough to generate real prosperity. Thin, rocky soil supplements mining income through limited farming.

The community is close-knit in the way that difficult circumstances produce -- people who depend on each other genuinely. Visitors are noticed. Help is offered and received as a matter of course. The village has a pride rooted in endurance.

Notable Establishments

Ryu no Tetsu Ryokan (Dragon's Iron Inn) -- The village's single inn. Comfortable by local standards. The innkeeper's family has run it for four generations.

Ryu no Iki Kajiba (Dragon's Breath Forge) -- The village forge, working primarily in local iron. The smith produces tools and hardware; technically capable of weapons work.

General Shop -- Combined general goods; also serves as the mine company store.

Village Temple -- Small and well-maintained despite the village's poverty. The community invests disproportionately in its upkeep as collective identity.

Key Figures

  • Yamamoto Kenji -- Village leader -> npcs/yamamoto-kenji.md

• The mine has recently started encountering an unusual material in the deeper work face -- not iron, not gold, but something with remarkable properties.
  • Yamamoto Kenji has quietly sent a sample to Heian for identification.

DM Secrets

What the Mine Actually Contains The deeper work face has started encountering a dark, lustrous metal with unusual properties: it doesn't rust, is harder than anything the village smith has worked, and holds an edge that standard iron cannot match. Yamamoto Kenji has quietly sent a sample to Heian, but the political vacuum has slowed response.

The material is a trace deposit of an alloy associated with Onyx Dragon Clan presence. Kokuryu's domain was never here, but volcanic geology has carried the material far from its origin. The vein is small but uniquely suited for sei-conductive tools and weapons.

Yamamoto Kenji's Dilemma If the mine material becomes known, Takamine loses control. The village is too poor and too politically isolated to defend a valuable find. Kenji is trying to get information before events overtake him. He would respond warmly to trustworthy outsiders who could help.

Plot Hooks

  • The mysterious metal could draw unwanted attention from merchant guilds or military factions
  • Kenji needs help identifying the material and deciding how to protect his village's interests

text.content:
Geography & Terrain

Tsuchi occupies the southern portion of Hokori -- a primarily mountainous province dominated by rugged terrain and the imposing bulk of Kurogane Yama, the second highest peak on the island. Hana borders it to the northeast and Hi to the northwest. The mountains here are old and weathered, less volcanically active than Hi but no less formidable -- steep valleys, narrow passes, and ridgelines that catch storms rolling in from the southern sea.

The southern mountains are resource-rich -- mineral deposits, timber in the sheltered valleys, and stone quarried from exposed cliff faces. But the terrain resists large-scale settlement. Communities are small, isolated by geography, and accustomed to self-reliance.

The Tsuchikawa (Earth River) is the main artery -- wide, slow, navigable for cargo barge travel, and historically important as a trade route connecting the interior to the coast.

Tsuchimoto sits at the center of the provincial plains, connected by roads in every compass direction. It is not a dramatic city -- no spectacular geography, no great harbor. It is a city of markets, granaries, administrative buildings, and the quietly enormous power of whoever controls the food supply.

Points of Interest:

  • The Great Granaries of Tsuchimoto -- Immense storage structures capable of holding enough grain to feed Hokori's population through two years of failed harvests. One of the most strategically important sites in the archipelago.
  • The Buried Road -- An ancient paved road that farmers have plowed around for centuries. Predates the Emperor's Highway by thousands of years -- pre-imperial, possibly pre-human. Where it goes and why it exists is unknown.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Tsuchimoto City Agricultural capital; granary city; market center; Genso-aligned
Tashiro Town River town; barge trade; grain export hub
Komugi Village "Wheat"; small farming commune; exemplary agricultural management
Inaka Village Meaning literally "countryside"; deliberately generic; culturally proud of it

Culture & Trade

Tsuchi's culture reflects its agricultural identity -- practical, organized, and deeply connected to the land and seasons. The province's grain production is a strategic asset that gives its governing authority disproportionate political leverage. River trade along the Tsuchikawa connects the interior to coastal markets.

History

Tsuchi has long been Hokori's breadbasket. Its strategic importance has made it a prize in every major conflict. The province's current Genso Alliance alignment gives the alliance control over a significant portion of Hokori's food supply -- a fact with profound implications for the current political crisis.

• The Buried Road leads somewhere significant -- it is far older than any known human construction in the region.
  • The Great Granaries' contents are being used as an economic weapon in the current conflict.

The Granaries as Political Weapon

The Genso Alliance-aligned governing clan has been quietly restricting grain sales to Arashi-aligned provinces while maintaining normal trade with neutral parties. This is a slow-moving economic siege strategy. It hasn't become visible yet. When it does, it will escalate the current conflict significantly.

The Buried Road

The ancient road leads eventually to a pre-imperial site associated with the Emerald Dragon Clan (Midoryu) -- a "green court" predating any recorded human settlement. Traceable sections exist at intervals. The site it leads to is in the Kusa province border region, beneath what is now part of the Whispering Flats. Midoryu is alive and maintains a particular connection to this buried court.

Plot Hooks

  • A farmer plowing a new field in eastern Tsuchi has found an intact structure beneath the buried road -- a sealed room -- and reported it to local authorities; those authorities are now not responding to outside inquiries
  • The granary administrator in Tsuchimoto is receiving death threats; she has information about grain supply restrictions that she wants to share with someone she trusts -- which is no one, currently

Type
core

Image prompts for the Kagekuni Campaign Guide bestiary. Style ranges from photographic (common creatures players will encounter regularly) through painterly (uncommon) to fine-art and ink wash (rare, mythical, or divine).

Global setting notes for all prompts:

  • World is feudal Japanese-inspired but not Earth — trees with bronze bark, indigo-hued grasses, faintly luminescent rivers at night, unfamiliar constellations
  • Architecture is Sengoku/Edo period: timber and paper construction, torii gates, mountain temples, castle towns
  • Magic (sei) manifests as subtle ambient light — soft gold, cool blue, faint violet — never garish
  • Lighting should feel natural and atmospheric: mist, dusk, lantern-light, forest-filtered sun

Yokai

Oni

Style: Semi-realistic, painterly. Dark palette with selective warm accents.

A massive horned humanoid crouched at the edge of a mountain pass, one hand resting on a stone outcrop, the other holding a crude iron tetsubō. Red-skinned with deep shadows in the creases of its face, wearing a tattered tiger-pelt loincloth. Its expression is not rage but patient evaluation — watching a distant traveler on the road below. Behind it, a narrow cliff trail winds upward into mist. Stone cairns along the road mark the boundary of its territory. The setting is late afternoon, low autumn sun casting long shadows across indigo-tinged grasses. Mountain peaks behind, faintly violet in atmospheric haze.

Tengu

Style: Traditional ink wash (sumi-e) with selective color. Elegant, austere, mysterious.

A tall, thin figure standing on a high pine branch, silhouetted against a pale sky. Corvid features — a sharp beak, dark feathered wings folded behind like a cloak. It holds a long, slightly curved sword with casual mastery. Wind moves through the canopy but the tengu is perfectly still. The composition is vertical, emphasizing height. Below, a mountain forest canopy stretches into mist. Trees with pale crystalline bark catch faint light. The tengu's eyes are sharp and bright against the ink-dark face. A single red-orange autumn leaf drifts past. Minimal detail in the background — suggestion of depth through gradations of ink wash.

Kitsune

Style: Painterly, warm and cool contrast. Ethereal but grounded.

A large white fox sitting at the base of a weathered stone shrine marker at a forest crossroads, three tails fanned behind it. The fox's fur is luminous white with silver tips, and its eyes are amber with unmistakable intelligence. Around its paws, small blue-white foxfire flames hover just above the ground, casting no heat but illuminating the kanji carved into the shrine stone. The setting is deep twilight — the sky is indigo fading to dark, with unfamiliar stars emerging. The crossroads is lined with ancient trees whose bark has a bronze sheen. A worn dirt path leads in three directions into darkness. The fox is watching something approach from the viewer's perspective with an expression that could be curiosity or amusement.

Tanuki

Style: Photographic with warm, slightly humorous tone. Rich autumnal color.

A pot-bellied raccoon-dog sitting upright on a sake barrel outside a lantern-lit roadside inn at dusk. It wears a wide straw hat tilted at a rakish angle and holds a sake cup in one paw. Its round belly is prominent, its expression somewhere between mischievous and deeply satisfied. Autumn leaves — copper and amber — are scattered on the ground. A half-eaten rice ball sits beside it. The inn's paper lanterns cast warm pools of orange light. In the background, other tanuki shapes are barely visible — one appears to be haggling with a merchant, another is examining a leaf with great concentration. The tone is warm, lived-in, slightly comedic.

Jorogumo

Style: Fine art, dark and beautiful. Renaissance chiaroscuro meets ukiyo-e.

An enormous spider the size of a small horse suspended at the center of a web that fills the main hall of a ruined estate. Its body is jet-black and glossy, segmented legs spanning the full width of the room, each ending in a point as fine as a calligraphy brush. The abdomen is patterned — pale markings that, in the right light, resolve into the suggestion of a woman's face. Silk threads radiate from its spinnerets in every direction, anchored to cracked ceiling beams, shattered shoji frames, and a collapsed tokonoma alcove. The web itself is a thing of terrible beauty — geometrically perfect, each strand catching the afternoon light that enters through the ruined wall like strings of liquid glass. Wrapped shapes hang at intervals along the outer threads, human-sized, silk-shrouded, still. Near one forelimb, a porcelain tea set sits on a lacquered tray, unbroken and recently used — two cups, one empty, one full. The spider's cluster of eyes reflects the light with cold intelligence. Wisteria has overtaken the wooden beams above, its purple blossoms drifting into the web and sticking there.

Nure-Onna

Style: Fine art, atmospheric horror. Cool blue-green palette, high contrast.

A figure half-submerged in a river at a stone bridge crossing, visible from the chest up. A woman with ink-black hair plastered wet against pale skin, holding a cloth-wrapped bundle to her chest. The water around her is dark and still despite the current flowing past the bridge pilings. Her expression is anguished, convincing — one hand extends toward the viewer as though begging for help. Below the waterline, barely visible through the murky surface, an enormous serpentine body coils around the bridge's foundation, many times longer than the human torso suggests. The setting is a misty river crossing at dawn. Shimenawa warning ropes are tied to posts on the near bank. A single lantern on the bridge casts a sickly yellow glow. The far bank is lost in fog.

Tsukumogami

Style: Photographic, warm interior lighting. Domestic, intimate, slightly uncanny.

A traditional Japanese household interior at night, lit by a single oil lamp. On a wooden shelf, a tea kettle has shifted slightly off its hook — one spout tilted as though peering at the room. Beside it, a writing brush has rolled to the edge of the desk and appears to have left a small, elegant ink character on a blank sheet of paper. An old paper umbrella in the corner leans against the wall at an angle that doesn't quite match gravity. A folding fan on the tatami has opened itself halfway. Nothing is dramatically wrong — every object is just slightly more present, more attentive, than objects should be. The room is otherwise normal: tatami mats, shoji screens, a low writing desk. Warm amber light, deep shadows in the corners.

Yurei

Yurei

Style: Fine art, ink wash with selective pale color. Cold, sorrowful, atmospheric.

A translucent figure in a white burial kimono standing at the far end of a dark wooden corridor in a traditional Japanese estate. Long black hair hangs unbound, obscuring the face. The feet do not touch the floor — a gap of a few inches between the hem of the kimono and the polished wood. The figure's hands hang at its sides, palms forward, fingers slightly curled. The corridor is lit by a single guttering candle on a stand, and the temperature differential is visible — the viewer's breath would fog near the figure. Frost crystals have formed on the nearest wooden beam. The composition uses the corridor's linear perspective to draw the eye to the figure, which is slightly out of focus, as though the air between viewer and spirit resists clear sight.

Bōrei

Style: Oil painting quality, Rembrandt lighting. Solemn, dignified, uncanny.

The translucent figure of an elderly priest seated in formal posture at a low writing desk in a temple chamber. He wears layered ceremonial robes, now faintly luminous and colorless. His brush hand is poised over a scroll, mid-character, as though interrupted by the viewer's arrival. His face is visible — aged, composed, with an expression of calm authority and deep weariness. The chamber around him is real and deteriorating — dust, cracked wood, cobwebs on the ceiling beams — but the desk area is immaculately maintained by the spirit's presence. A real torch on the wall has dimmed but not extinguished. The light in the room comes partly from the torch, partly from the figure itself — a cold, pale luminescence that casts no shadows.

Gashadokuro

Style: Dramatic fine art, ukiyo-e woodblock print aesthetic. High contrast, bold composition.

An enormous skeletal figure — fifteen feet tall — standing in an empty battlefield at night, assembled from hundreds of mismatched bones. It is framed against a blood-red moon and an unfamiliar star field. Its skull tilts downward, jaw open, teeth the size of daggers. The bones are not clean — fragments of armor, scraps of cloth, and the residue of earth still cling to them. The ribcage is a hollow cathedral of interlocking bones from different bodies. It stands in a field of trampled indigo grass, broken weapon hafts, and scattered war banners half-buried in mud. No living thing is visible. The composition is from below, looking up at the skeleton against the sky, emphasizing its impossible scale. Wind moves the tattered banners. The silence is the point.

Gaki

Style: Photographic with desaturated color. Uncomfortable, pathetic, documentary.

A cluster of emaciated translucent figures gathered outside a shuttered food market stall at night. Their bodies are wasted — visible ribs, stick-thin limbs — but their bellies are grotesquely distended. Their mouths are tiny, barely able to open. One reaches a skeletal hand toward a covered basket of rice, fingers passing through the lid without making contact. Another crouches near a sake barrel, mouth working soundlessly. Their forms overlap slightly — they crowd together without acknowledging each other. The market stall is real and solid; the gaki are faded, washed-out, like a double exposure. Lantern light from a nearby shop illuminates the scene with mundane warmth that makes the figures more disturbing by contrast. Food in the stall has begun to discolor at the edges.

Sei-Touched

Sei Beasts

Style: Photographic, National Geographic quality. Natural, awe-inspiring.

A large stag standing in a forest clearing in the Yōsei Mori. Its pelt shifts between copper and deep slate in the dappled light. Its antlers are crystallized amber — translucent, warm gold, catching light like faceted gemstones. A third eye, smaller than the primary pair, sits centered on its forehead, its iris a faint violet that suggests it perceives something beyond the visible spectrum. The stag is alert but not alarmed, head raised, one foreleg slightly advanced. The forest around it is otherworldly — trees with bark of pale crystal that catches light, undergrowth in deep indigo, and a faint golden mist at ground level where sei pools visibly. A stream behind the stag glows faintly where it catches the light. The lighting is morning sun through canopy, warm with cool shadows.

Sei Aberrations

Style: Surreal fine art, Francis Bacon meets Yoshitaka Amano. Disturbing, beautiful, wrong.

A creature that was once a river fish, now something else entirely — its body elongated and twisted, scales fused with river stones and aquatic plants that have become part of its flesh. Flames lick along its dorsal fin where water should be. It hovers above the surface of a shallow stream, suspended in a knot of visible sei energy — threads of gold and violet light that coil through its body like veins. Its mouth is open in what might be a scream. The stream around it has gone wrong — the water flows backward near the creature, and the riverbed stones have partially liquefied. The surrounding forest is normal, which makes the localized wrongness more striking. Warm afternoon light, but the light bends near the creature, creating a heat-shimmer effect.

Nagaji (General)

Style: Semi-realistic, dark and tactical. Cool palette, military tension.

A serpentine humanoid standing in the mouth of a mountain cave, partially obscured by shadow. Scaled skin in mottled grey-green, cold and reptilian. The body is humanoid in general proportion but wrong in the details — the neck is slightly too long, the joints bend at subtly incorrect angles, and the eyes are lidless with vertical slit pupils that catch the light. It wears no clothing but carries what appears to be a crude weapon — a repurposed metal shard lashed to a wooden shaft. Behind it, in the deeper shadow of the cave, the reflected light of multiple pairs of eyes suggests others waiting in formation. The cave entrance is in a mountain cliff face, surrounded by hardy alpine vegetation and loose scree. Overcast sky, flat grey light. The creature is perfectly still, watching.

Nagaji Ashigaru

Style: Semi-realistic, photographic tension. Action composition, low-light environment.

Three nagaji ashigaru mid-ambush in a ruined stone corridor. They are lighter and faster than the other variants — lean, angular builds with darker mottled scaling that renders them nearly invisible against the shadowed walls. One clings to a pillar at head height, body pressed flat against the stone in an impossible posture, crude spear angled downward. Another emerges from a side passage at a low crouch, weapon already extended. A third is mid-lunge from the opposite side, caught in the instant before impact — mouth open, showing rows of small, sharp teeth. Their weapons are improvised: metal shards lashed to wooden shafts with cord, functional but rough. No armor, no clothing. The corridor is ancient stonework, partly collapsed, lit by a single distant light source that catches the reflection of six slit-pupil eyes. The composition conveys coordinated violence — three angles of attack arriving simultaneously.

Nagaji Hohei

Style: Semi-realistic, heavy and imposing. Frontal composition, confrontational.

A nagaji hohei filling a narrow stone doorway, blocking passage. It is significantly larger than the ashigaru — broad across the shoulders and chest, with thick overlapping scale plates along the forearms, chest, and spine that function as natural armor. The ridged scaling catches dim light along its edges. It stands square, low center of gravity, one hand gripping a heavy improvised weapon — a chunk of shaped stone lashed to a thick wooden haft, somewhere between a club and a mace. Its tail is braced against the doorframe behind it for leverage. The posture is unmistakably defensive: this ground is held. Its eyes are fixed forward with the flat, cold patience of something that will not move. Behind it, partially visible, the movement of ashigaru repositioning in the room beyond. The doorway is carved stone, ancient, cracked. The hohei's bulk and the architecture conspire to say the same thing: you do not pass.

Nagaji Bushi

Style: Painterly, dark palette with cold highlights. Authority and intelligence.

A nagaji bushi standing on a raised stone platform at the junction of two corridors, observing a combat engagement below. It is lean like the ashigaru but carries itself differently — upright, controlled, deliberate. Faint patterning along its jaw and throat distinguishes it from the rank and file. It holds a properly hafted metal blade — not the crude lashed-together weapons of the ashigaru but a salvaged sword, re-gripped with cord wrapping, held with evident familiarity. A fragment of scavenged shoulder armor is strapped to its left side, imprecisely fitted but functional. Its mouth is slightly open, mid-vocalization — a sibilant call directing the squad below. The composition places the bushi above the action, observing, directing. Below and out of focus, the shapes of hohei and ashigaru moving in response to its call. The lighting is from below — torchlight from the lower corridor casting the bushi's face in sharp upward shadow, emphasizing the vertical slit pupils and the cold intelligence behind them.

Nagaji Kannushi

Style: Fine art, eerie and spiritual. Cool iridescent palette, stillness.

A nagaji kannushi coiled on a raised stone dais in what was once a shrine chamber. It is slender, almost gaunt — thinner than any other variant, with a fluid, boneless quality to its posture. Its scales carry a faint iridescence that the other variants lack, shifting between grey-green and a pale violet depending on the angle of light. It is utterly still, coiled in a posture that resembles meditation — head bowed, body wound in a tight spiral, the tip of its tail resting precisely at the center of the dais. Its slit pupils are wider than those of other nagaji, dark and unfocused, as though perceiving something beyond the room. The shrine chamber around it is ancient stone — carved walls with worn iconography, a cracked incense holder, dust on every surface except the dais where the kannushi rests. Faint traces of residual sei energy are visible in the air — barely there, gossamer threads of pale gold drifting toward the creature. The mood is not threatening but deeply unsettling: something is happening here that cannot be explained by what is visible.

Kami

Kami

Style: Impressionist fine art, luminous and ethereal. Minimal subject, maximum atmosphere.

A roadside stone shrine at a forest crossroads, weathered smooth by centuries of travelers' hands. No figure is visible — the kami is suggested, not shown. The evidence of its presence: a shaft of warm golden light falls on the shrine stone despite the canopy overhead being unbroken. Wildflowers at the base of the stone are blooming out of season. A small offering of rice and a folded paper sits on the stone's flat surface, and the paper is stirring in a breeze that moves nothing else. The air around the shrine has a faint luminous quality — not glowing, but brighter than it should be given the forest shade. A bird perches on a nearby branch, facing the stone, head tilted. The forest is quiet and deep, trees with bronze-sheened bark receding into green shadow.

Tatari-gami

Style: Dark impressionist, oppressive atmosphere. Muted palette with sickly undertones.

The same shrine crossroads, but wrong. The stone is cracked. The offerings have rotted. The wildflowers are withered to black. The light is flat and grey despite what should be midday. A rice paddy visible through the trees has yellowed weeks too early. The path is scattered with tools — a broken hoe, a cracked water jug — abandoned rather than placed. No entity is visible, but the composition creates a sense of malevolent attention radiating from the damaged stone. Crows perch in the trees, too many of them, all facing the same direction. The air has a faint greenish-brown cast, like bruised fruit. Everything is slightly too still.

Kodama

Style: Fine art, bioluminescent. Quiet, ancient, watchful.

The interior of an ancient forest at night. Among the high branches of a massive tree — its trunk wider than a house, bark pale and faintly crystalline — small points of warm white-green light float and drift. They are not fireflies; they hold position relative to the branches, moving only when the tree moves. In the deepest shadow of a hollow where two branches meet, the faintest suggestion of a small figure — bark-textured, leaf-crowned, no larger than a child's hand — watches from the darkness. Its features are barely distinguishable from the tree itself. Below, the forest floor is carpeted in deep indigo moss. Sound is implied by the composition — the feeling of echo, of the forest listening. The lights in the canopy are reflected faintly in standing water at the tree's roots.

Ryū

Dragon (Progenitor Legacy)

Style: Grand fine art, mythological. Gold leaf and ink wash fusion — shrine painting aesthetic.

A colossal golden dragon rendered as it might appear in a temple ceiling mural that has been brought to half-life. The dragon coils through clouds above a mountain landscape, its body serpentine and vast — each scale the size of a shield, rendered in burnished gold. Its face is regal and ancient, with long whiskers trailing like banners and eyes that hold the weight of eight millennia. The style should evoke the ceiling paintings of Japanese Buddhist temples — flat gold backgrounds, flowing cloud patterns, powerful brushwork — but with a quality of depth and presence that suggests the image might move. The landscape below is Kagekuni: mountain peaks, a distant inland sea, forests of bronze and crystal. The dragon is partially obscured by clouds, conveying scale by what is hidden rather than what is shown.

Ryūjin

Style: Fine art, dramatic naturalism. Power and elemental force.

An enormous serpentine creature coiled around a river boulder in a mountain gorge, its body the size of a mature oak trunk. Scales in deep iridescent blue-green refract the light into spectral colors that don't appear in nature — ultraviolet suggestions, impossible greens. Vestigial wings, folded tight against its body, are translucent membranes stretched over delicate bone structures. Its head rests on the boulder, one vast amber eye half-open, watching the river flow. The water bends around the creature — not parting for it, but responding to it, the current shifting in deference. Moss and river plants have grown over portions of its body, suggesting it has been here for a very long time. The gorge walls rise steeply on either side. Late afternoon light catches the spray where the river tumbles over rocks downstream.

Yajū (Wildlife)

Deer of Hokori

Style: Photographic, wildlife documentary. Natural beauty with otherworldly details.

A pair of deer at a forest stream at dawn. Their pelts are in seasonal transition — patches of deep copper alongside cool slate grey, the shift visible across their flanks like the turning of a leaf. The buck's antlers are normal bone but carry a faint metallic sheen at the tips. They drink from a stream that glows faintly where the early light hits it. The forest around them is recognizably temperate — oak and maple analogues — but the undergrowth is deep indigo rather than green, and the bark of the nearest tree has a bronze patina. Morning mist. A single shaft of warm light through the canopy. Natural, peaceful, subtly alien.

Mountain Cat of Tenchūsan Ren

Style: Photographic, rare wildlife sighting. Telephoto compression, atmospheric.

A large grey-furred mountain cat crouched on a rocky ledge above a steep mountain trail, barely visible against the stone. Its fur is dense and slate-grey, blending with the crystalline mountain rock. Its eyes — pale gold — are the most visible feature, fixed on something below with the absolute stillness of a predator that has decided not to attack yet. The setting is high altitude: thin air suggested by the clarity of distant peaks, sparse alpine vegetation clinging to cracks in the rock, a dusting of snow on higher elevations. The composition uses a long focal length, suggesting the observer is far away and the cat knows it. Cold blue-grey light, overcast sky.

Cranes of Kagekuni

Style: Photographic, elegant. Japanese aesthetic sensibility.

Three cranes wading in the shallows of Serenia-kai at sunrise. Their plumage is brilliant white with black flight feathers and crimson crowns. They move through water that reflects the warm sky — peach, gold, and pale violet. One is in mid-step, one has wings partially extended for balance, one stands perfectly still with its head raised. The great inland sea stretches behind them, calm and vast. In the far distance, the silhouette of a fishing village with curved rooftops is visible through morning haze. The water's surface catches the sunrise in bands of color. Reeds at the shore edge are the deep indigo-green of Kagekuni's vegetation.

Goldtail Fish

Style: Photographic, underwater/surface split-shot. Vivid, commercial quality.

A school of goldtail fish running upstream during the Aki season, captured at the moment several break the surface. The signature feature — an iridescent gold flash on the tail fin — catches the light in a burst of warm metallic color against the cool blue-green of the river. Below the surface, the school is dense and purposeful, silver bodies with that distinctive gold tail marking visible on each fish. Above the surface, the river is lined with autumn foliage in copper and amber. Fishermen's nets are visible in the middle distance, and a riverside settlement with thatched roofs sits on the far bank. The water is clear enough to see rounded river stones on the bottom. Bright midday light, the energy of seasonal abundance.

Nightjars of Yōsei Mori

Style: Photographic with subtle enhancement. Nocturnal, mysterious.

A nightjar perched on a low branch in the Yōsei Mori at dusk, its plumage a complex pattern of brown, grey, and deep indigo that renders it nearly invisible against the bark. Its mouth is open mid-call, and from its throat, a visible harmonic ripple extends into the air — a subtle distortion, like heat shimmer, but in concentric rings that suggest the call interacts with something beyond sound. The forest around it is transitioning from day to night: the last warm light in the upper canopy, deep blue shadow below. In the background, faint points of sei energy — barely visible gold motes — respond to the call, drifting slightly toward the bird. The forest floor is indigo moss and crystalline root structures.

Fireflies

Style: Photographic, long-exposure aesthetic. Romantic, magical.

A rice paddy at the edge of a village at night, filled with fireflies. Their light is not the uniform yellow-green of Earth fireflies — it shifts across the swarm in gentle waves of color: warm gold near the water, cool blue-white higher up, and a faint violet at the edges nearest the tree line. The colors shift slowly, breathing in and out. A crescent moon — an unfamiliar blue-tinged moon — hangs low on the horizon, and the fireflies nearest it trend toward matching its color. The paddy water reflects both the fireflies and the stars, creating a mirror of light. A single farmhouse in the background has a warm lantern in one window. The village is dark and quiet otherwise. The sky is deep and full of unfamiliar constellations.

Silk Moths

Style: Photographic macro, scientific beauty. Extreme detail.

A silk moth resting on a mulberry leaf, shot in close macro. Its wings are broad and pale — cream-white with a faint pearlescent sheen that shifts to warm gold at certain angles. Its body is plush and dense-furred. The detail is in the silk: a fine thread extends from the moth's spinneret, catching the light with an intensity that seems impossible for organic material — the thread doesn't just reflect light, it seems to conduct it, carrying a faint warm glow along its length. The mulberry leaf beneath is deep emerald with veins that carry a suggestion of indigo. Soft natural light, shallow depth of field, the background a blur of green and bronze.

Taikobutsu (Deep Past)

Guardian Constructs

Style: Grand fine art, archaeological mystery. Dark, ancient, monumental.

A stone figure standing in a partially excavated chamber deep within a pre-imperial ruin. The construct is humanoid but not human — eight feet tall, proportioned like a temple guardian statue, carved from a dark stone that absorbs light. Its surface is covered in fine geometric patterns that might be decorative or might be functional — channels for sei, worn smooth by millennia but still faintly visible. Its head has no eyes, only smooth stone where a face would be, yet it is oriented directly toward the viewer with unmistakable attention. One hand is raised, palm outward — a gesture that could be greeting or warning. Dust motes drift in the beam of light entering from a crack in the ceiling above. The chamber walls are carved with script in a language that predates any known writing system. The construct's feet are still partially embedded in the stone floor, as though it grew from the foundation rather than being placed upon it. Ancient, patient, still on duty.

Astrological Events

Seizan's complex stellar and lunar system produces named astrological phenomena that overlay the standard seasons. These are not seasons themselves but recurring celestial events with observable effects on weather, tides, sei, and the natural world.

Solar Events (driven by the three-star system):

Name Celestial Cause Effects
Nagorikaze Susanoo draws close to Seizan Blue-white atmospheric phenomena; ghost rainbows; water magic intensifies
Shinmyōji Kōrigami at peak influence Luminescent mists over Kagekuni; winter severity increases
Long Shadow Tsukuyomi at furthest point (aphelion) Transformation magic weakens; shadows behave strangely

Lunar Events (driven by the four-moon system):

Name Celestial Cause Effects
Tatsunami Four-moon alignment convergence Destructive tidal surges; coastal flooding; navigation hazards. Typically late Aki through mid-Haru.
Hikarishō Ryūgetsu full phase alignment Celestial dragon auroras; sei amplification; spirit activity increases

Additional solar and lunar events exist but are less commonly named or studied. Seimasters at Seishin maintain observational records of celestial alignments and their correlations to sei fluctuation.

Kannazuki — The Month of No Gods

The name Kannazuki predates recorded history. Common folk use it without thought — "the gods are away" is a saying during the tenth month, though no one remembers where the gods supposedly go. Ancient texts in the Great Library of Kawa reference a gathering of "the great ones" during this month, but the passages are fragmentary and often dismissed as allegory.

Discovery path: Research in the Great Library; conversations with Ancient Guard members; study of pre-Reckoning texts.

Kannazuki — The True Origin

The name is a historical fossil from the earliest age when the seven Progenitor dragons did physically gather during the tenth month. The tradition outlived the practice by millennia. The Ancient Guard recognizes the irony — the "Month of No Gods" was originally the month when all the gods were present in one place. Now, with the Progenitors slumbering, the name is accidentally accurate again for entirely different reasons.

The Great Aphelion and the Sei Drought

The sei drought began with the stellar decline of the War of Fractured Banners era (~12605). As Susanoo and Tsukuyomi entered their long retreat from the barycenter of the Miyosai trinary system, sei accessibility diminished gradually. The first secondary star crossed below naked-eye visibility around ~12806, marking the beginning of the dark ages. The Temple of Oryuzan Tenku-ji fell in 13088 — a consequence of the drought, not its cause.

The three stars of the Miyosai system orbit a common gravitational center (barycenter) on different orbital inclinations. Planets orbit Amaterasu and travel with it; moons orbit Seizan directly. Neither participated in the Great Aphelion — only the three stars reached maximum mutual distance. The Great Aphelion itself (~14344) was the absolute nadir: Amaterasu at one extreme of its barycentric arc carrying Seizan with it, while Susanoo and Tsukuyomi sat at opposing extremes on their own inclined planes. The geometry was not a uniform recession but a three-dimensional separation — the distances compounded geometrically.

Amaterasu never went dark. Its baseline sei sustained life, agriculture, and the physical world throughout the dark ages. The world retained normal day/night cycles. What was lost was the complex magical expression that depended on the full trinary system — Susanoo's contribution to water magic and healing, Tsukuyomi's contribution to transformation and energy manipulation. The dark ages were cultural and intellectual collapse rather than extinction.

The Progenitors entered their slumber during this same period. Whether the aphelion caused the slumber, the slumber caused the sei drought, or the aphelion caused both remains unknown — even to the Ancient Guard. The slow return of sei beginning 15962 (First Talents) correlates with Susanoo's partial orbital return after dawn (15883). The Great Awakening (~16693) marks the moment all three stars became clearly visible simultaneously — effectively the moment Tsukuyomi's return crossed the threshold of reliability. The orbital correction is still ongoing — the current celestial configuration has not yet fully returned to its pre-Aphelion state.

This connection is not understood by any living scholar. The data exists in fragmentary astronomical records across multiple institutions, but no one has assembled the complete picture. The Golden Dragon Clan's observatory at Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji contained the most complete model of the Miyosai system ever constructed — mechanical and arcane, capable of projecting celestial positions across millennia. It has not been operational since the temple fell.

See also: core/great-aphelion.md — full canonical timeline, orbital mechanics, and orrery projection sequence.

The Archipelago of Kagekuni

Five Major Islands

Island Character Key Feature
Hokori Largest; four tectonic plates; X-shaped Primary campaign island; capital Heian
Kawa Eastern; mostly submerged except winter Agricultural heartland; Great Library; Seirei Mizuumi
Fushichō Northern; volcanic Hi no Toride mountains; ancient secrets; Akaho Sanmyaku erupting
Yurei Haunted; barren; avoided Ancient curse; specters and monsters; Kuroshi Temple
Tatara Southern; mountainous Dwarven/gnomish heartland; Zirak vs Glimfyr conflict

Minor Islands

Fuukajima, Gyoshima, Kakujima, Shukajima, Unmeijima, Ryūhajima, Shizukajima, Takarajima, and others.

Unmeijima — Home of the city of Seishin (magical research); Order of the Tranquil Lotus monastery at Kazehama.

Tone, Aesthetic & Design Principles

Core Tone

  • Medieval Japan as cultural and historical backbone — not generic fantasy
  • High fantasy layered over authentic historical touchstones
  • Shifts fluidly: quiet beauty ↔ political intrigue ↔ brutal conflict
  • Honor, shame, duty, tension between order and chaos are recurring themes

The World Feels Otherworldly

Consistent cosmetic departures from reality — woven naturally, never called out as anomalies:

  • Trees with bark of burnished bronze or pale crystal
  • Grass in deep violet or indigo hues
  • Rivers faintly luminescent at night
  • Fog carrying incense scent without source
  • Constellations that don't match our sky
  • The bronze-leafed Seidōrin Mori — metallic trees harvested for weapons
  • Sei flowing visibly through natural phenomena

Historical Grounding (Second Priority After Continuity)

  • Feudal structure: Emperor, Shogun, Daimyo, Samurai, Peasantry — titles and land rights carry real weight
  • Bushido and social codes: honor, duty, sacrifice, and shame govern behavior
  • Religion and spirituality: Shinto animism, Buddhist philosophy, ancestor veneration
  • Arts and architecture: tatami, shoji, castle towns, torii gates, tea ceremony, noh theatre
  • Conflict and politics: clan rivalries, succession disputes, ronin, peasant uprisings

D&D 5e Compatibility

  • All mechanical content grounded in 5e rules
  • Homebrew clearly labeled
  • Seimasters map to wizards, sorcerers, monks
  • Honor mechanic: -2 on Honor ability checks for marginalized races in social situations

Foundry VTT Notes

  • Secret blocks used within journal entries for DM-only content
  • Player handouts prefixed with character name for easy sorting
  • Location journals pinned to maps
  • Active Objectives journal maintained as living document
  • One entry per subject; use journal links for wiki-style navigation

Preserve Mystery

  • Not everything needs to be explained
  • Leave room for improvisation and surprise
  • The living dragons secret is the campaign's deepest thread — never surface prematurely

description.value: An @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.equipment24.Item.phbagArcaneFocus]{Arcane Focus} is bejeweled or carved to channel arcane magic. A Sorcerer, Warlock, or Wizard can use such an item as a Spellcasting Focus.

items.name: Divine Burst

description.value: [[/attack extended]]. [[/damage average extended]].

items.name: Spellcasting

description.value:
The [[lookup @name lowercase]]{monster} casts one of the following spells, using Intelligence as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC [[lookup @attributes.spell.dc]]):

At Will: @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplDetectMagi]{Detect Magic}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplLight00000]{Light}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplMageArmor0]{Mage Armor} (included in AC), @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplMageHand00]{Mage Hand}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplPrestidigi]{Prestidigitation}

2/Day Each: @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplFireball00]{Fireball} (level 4 version), @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplInvisibili]{Invisibility}

1/Day Each: @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplConeofCold]{Cone of Cold}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplFly0000000]{Fly}

items.name: Misty Step

description.value: The [[lookup @name lowercase]]{monster} casts @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplMistyStep0]{Misty Step}, using the same spellcasting ability as Spellcasting.

items.name: Misty Step

description.value: Briefly surrounded by silvery mist, you teleport up to 30 feet to an unoccupied space you can see.

items.name: Protective Magic

description.value: The [[lookup @name lowercase]]{monster} casts @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplCounterspe]{Counterspell} or @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplShield0000]{Shield} in response to the spell's trigger, using the same spellcasting ability as Spellcasting.

items.name: Counterspell

description.value: You attempt to interrupt a creature in the process of casting a spell. The creature makes a Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, the spell dissipates with no effect, and the action, Bonus Action, or Reaction used to cast it is wasted. If that spell was cast with a spell slot, the slot isn't expended.

activation.condition: when you see a creature within range casting a spell with Verbal, Somatic, or Material components

items.name: Shield

description.value: An imperceptible barrier of magical force protects you. Until the start of your next turn, you have a +5 bonus to AC, including against the triggering attack, and you take no damage from @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplMagicMissi]{Magic Missile}.

activation.condition: when you are hit by an attack roll or targeted by the Magic Missile spell

effects.name: Imperceptible Barrier
effects.description: Until the start of your next turn, you have a +5 bonus to AC, including against the triggering attack, and you take no damage from Magic Missile.

items.name: Detect Magic

description.value:
For the duration, you sense the presence of magical effects within 30 feet of yourself. If you sense such effects, you can take the Magic action to see a faint aura around any visible creature or object in the area that bears the magic, and if an effect was created by a spell, you learn the spell's school of magic.

The spell is blocked by 1 foot of stone, dirt, or wood; 1 inch of metal; or a thin sheet of lead.

items.name: Light

description.value:
You touch one Large or smaller object that isn't being worn or carried by someone else. Until the spell ends, the object sheds Bright Light in a 20-foot radius and Dim Light for an additional 20 feet. The light can be colored as you like.

Covering the object with something opaque blocks the light. The spell ends if you cast it again.

items.name: Mage Armor

description.value: You touch a willing creature who isn't wearing armor. Until the spell ends, the target's base AC becomes 13 plus its Dexterity modifier. The spell ends early if the target dons armor.

effects.name: Mage Armor
effects.description: The target's base AC becomes 13 + its Dexterity modifier.

items.name: Mage Hand

description.value:
A spectral, floating hand appears at a point you choose within range. The hand lasts for the duration. The hand vanishes if it is ever more than 30 feet away from you or if you cast this spell again.

When you cast the spell, you can use the hand to manipulate an object, open an unlocked door or container, stow or retrieve an item from an open container, or pour the contents out of a vial.

As a Magic action on your later turns, you can control the hand thus again. As part of that action, you can move the hand up to 30 feet.

The hand can't attack, activate magic items, or carry more than 10 pounds.

items.name: Prestidigitation

description.value:
You create a magical effect within range. Choose the effect from the options below. If you cast this spell multiple times, you can have up to three of its non-instantaneous effects active at a time.

Sensory Effect. You create an instantaneous, harmless sensory effect, such as a shower of sparks, a puff of wind, faint musical notes, or an odd odor.

Fire Play. You instantaneously light or snuff out a candle, a torch, or a small campfire.

Clean or Soil. You instantaneously clean or soil an object no larger than 1 cubic foot.

Minor Sensation. You chill, warm, or flavor up to 1 cubic foot of nonliving material for 1 hour.

Magic Mark. You make a color, a small mark, or a symbol appear on an object or a surface for 1 hour.

Minor Creation. You create a nonmagical trinket or an illusory image that can fit in your hand. It lasts until the end of your next turn. A trinket can deal no damage and has no monetary worth.

items.name: Fireball

description.value:
A bright streak flashes from you to a point you choose within range and then blossoms with a low roar into a fiery explosion. Each creature in a 20-foot-radius Sphere centered on that point makes a Dexterity saving throw, taking 8d6 Fire damage on a failed save or half as much damage on a successful one.

Flammable objects in the area that aren't being worn or carried start burning.

Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot. The damage increases by 1d6 for each spell slot level above 3.

materials.value: a ball of bat guano and sulfur

items.name: Invisibility

description.value:
A creature you touch has the &Reference[invisible apply=false] condition until the spell ends. The spell ends early immediately after the target makes an attack roll, deals damage, or casts a spell.

biography.value:
Deprived of much of its magic as a special punishment, a deathlock wight lingers between the warlock it was and the wretched existence of a wight.

Deathlocks

The forging of a pact between a warlock and a patron is no minor occasion—at least not for the warlock. The consequences of breaking that pact can be dire and, in some cases, lethal. A warlock who fails to live up to a bargain with an evil patron runs the risk of rising from the dead as a deathlock, a foul Undead driven to serve its otherworldly patron.

An powerful necromancer might also discover the wicked methods of creating a deathlock and then subjugate it, acting as the deathlock’s patron.

description.value:
For the duration, you sense the presence of magic within 30 feet of you. If you sense magic in this way, you can use your action to see a faint aura around any visible creature or object in the area that bears magic, and you learn its school of magic, if any.

The spell can penetrate most barriers, but it is blocked by 1 foot of stone, 1 inch of common metal, a thin sheet of lead, or 3 feet of wood or dirt.

items.name: Detect Magic

description.value:
You make yourself--including your clothing, armor, weapons, and other belongings on your person--look different until the spell ends or until you use your action to dismiss it. You can seem 1 foot shorter or taller and can appear thin, fat, or in between. You can't change your body type, so you must adopt a form that has the same basic arrangement of limbs. Otherwise, the extent of the &Reference[ill]{illusion} is up to you.

The changes wrought by this spell fail to hold up to physical inspection. For example, if you use this spell to add a hat to your outfit, objects pass through the hat, and anyone who touches it would feel nothing or would feel your head and hair. If you use this spell to appear thinner than you are, the hand of someone who reaches out to touch you would bump into you while it was seemingly still in midair.

To discern that you are disguised, a creature can use its action to inspect your appearance and must succeed on an &Reference[int]{Intelligence} (&Reference[inv]{Investigation}) check against your spell save DC.

items.name: Disguise Self

description.value: You touch a willing creature who isn't wearing armor, and a protective magical &Reference[force]{force} surrounds it until the spell ends. While &Reference[frightened]{frightened} by this spell, a creature must take the Dash action and move away from you by the safest available route on each of its turns, unless there is nowhere to move. If the creature ends its turn in a location where it doesn’t have &Reference[line]{line} of sight to you, the creature can make a &Reference[wis]{Wisdom} saving throw. On a successful save, the spell ends for that creature.

description.value:

The spell has no effect if the target is &Reference[undead]{undead}, if it doesn't understand your language, or if your command is directly harmful to it.

Some typical commands and their effects follow. You might issue a command other than one described here. If you do so, the DM determines how the target behaves. If the target can't follow your command, the spell ends.

Approach. The target moves toward you by the shortest and most direct route, ending its turn if it moves within 5 feet of you.

Drop. The target drops whatever it is holding and then ends its turn.

Flee. The target spends its turn moving away from you by the fastest available means.

Grovel. The target falls &Reference[prone]{prone} and then ends its turn.

biography.value:
With snakes for arms, pit masters are yuan-ti malison priests who have made a pact with the god Merrshaulk and seek to rouse him from his slumber by sacrificing Humanoids to him. They are the most traditionalist yuan-ti and believe that they are best equipped to achieve the goals of their people.

Pit masters are deeply involved in yuan-ti’s long-term plan to take over Humanoid governments, as well as in the ongoing effort to protect their cities from discovery or attacks by hostiles. They oppose reckless behavior and argue for a slow, cautious approach in all matters.

You can use your action to control the hand. You can use the hand to manipulate an object, open an unlocked door or container, stow or retrieve an item from an open container, or pour the contents out of a vial. You can move the hand up to 30 feet each time you use it.

The hand can't attack, activate magic items, or carry more than 10 pounds.

You point your finger toward a creature within range and whisper a message. The target (and only the target) hears the message and can reply in a whisper that only you can hear.

You can cast this spell through solid objects if you are familiar with the target and know it is beyond the barrier. Magical silence, 1 foot of stone, 1 inch of common metal, a thin sheet of lead, or 3 feet of wood blocks the spell. The spell doesn't have to follow a straight &Reference[line]{line} and can travel freely around corners or through openings.

items.name: Message

description.value:
You suggest a course of activity (limited to a sentence or two) and magically influence a creature you can see within range that can hear and understand you. Creatures that can't be &Reference[charmed]{charmed} are immune to this effect. The suggestion must be worded in such a manner as to make the course of action sound reasonable. Asking the creature to stab itself, throw itself onto a spear, immolate itself, or do some other obviously harmful act ends the spell.

The target must make a &Reference[wis]{Wisdom} saving throw. On a failed save, it pursues the course of action you described to the best of its ability. The suggested course of action can continue for the entire duration. If the suggested activity can be completed in a shorter time, the spell ends when the subject finishes what it was asked to do.

You can also specify conditions that will trigger a special activity during the duration. For example, you might suggest that a knight give her warhorse to the first beggar she meets. If the condition isn't met before the spell expires, the activity isn't performed.

If you or any of your companions damage the target, the spell ends.

items.name: Suggestion

description.value:
Choose a &Reference[humanoid]{humanoid} that you can see within range. The target must succeed on a &Reference[wis]{Wisdom} saving throw or be &Reference[paralyzed]{paralyzed} for the duration. At the end of each of its turns, the target can make another &Reference[wis]{Wisdom} saving throw. On a success, the spell ends on the target.

At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, you can target one additional &Reference[humanoid]{humanoid} for each slot level above 2nd. The humanoids must be within 30 feet of each other when you target them.

items.name: Hold Person

description.value:
A creature you touch becomes &Reference[invisible]{invisible} until the spell ends. Anything the target is wearing or carrying is &Reference[invisible]{invisible} as long as it is on the target's person. The spell ends for a target that attacks or casts a spell.

At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, you can target one additional creature for each slot level above 2nd.

items.name: Swarm

description.value: The swarm can occupy another creature's space and vice versa, and the swarm can move through any opening large enough for a Tiny rat. The swarm can't regain Hit Points or gain Temporary Hit Points.

The target must succeed on a [[/save con 10 format=long]] or its hit point maximum is reduced by an amount equal to the damage taken. This reduction lasts until the creature finishes a long rest. The target dies if this effect reduces its hit point maximum to 0.

The [[lookup @name]] uses [[lookup @item.name]].

A young mother fleeing with her infant child. Encountered on the Emperor's Highway on the first day of travel north from Heian toward Ayame. She was out of breath, visibly distressed, claimed to be carrying a precious package, and asked the party to hold it — the package was her infant child. She spotted figures running toward her, tossed the child to the party, and bolted. The figures turned out to be boys out for a run, not a threat. Relc caught and returned her.

Personality

Capable of managing independently under normal conditions but was operating in a state of fear-driven poor decision making when the party found her. Behavior under stress and useful skills are undeveloped — flagged for development in the DM Notebook.

Relationship To Party

Traveling with the party. The party offered to take her north through the Tenchūsan Ren to Sunsato on the far side, where she might find safety and a new beginning near Relc's home region. She is currently inside the Temple of Kinryū with the party — a civilian in a dungeon. She cannot fight. She needs protection or a defensible position during encounters. Her presence affects the party's tactical decisions and roleplay.

Black scales with a glossy sheen; glowing red eyes; intricate dragon tattoos on his back.

Captain of the Guard — Kikyo

Appearance

Gold scales; bright blue eyes.

Public Role

Captain of the Guard in Kikyo, operating from the Kikyo Guard Compound. Maintains a small but highly capable force; primary duties are licensing enforcement and forest protection for the Seidōrin Mori (Bronze Wood Forest). Building an informant network in Kikyo.

Personality

Stoic, disciplined; fierce loyalty; strong sense of justice.

Relationship To Party

Arrested Ko'jiri in Kikyo before the situation was resolved by Ren Nakamura's offer of the Summons and Conditional Pardon. Their initial interaction was adversarial but professional. Can become a staunch ally to those who prove their integrity.

True Nature

Building his informant network not simply for Kikyo's local security but because he suspects something significant is happening with the Bronze Wood licensing system. He has noticed irregularities in the licensing records — specific harvesting zones consistently licensed to a single merchant entity, with documentation that is technically correct but structured to obscure the pattern. He is three to four months away from having enough evidence to bring forward as a coherent accusation.

Connections

Knows ancient Dragonborn rituals potentially crucial to certain quests. His family's oral tradition preserves knowledge from the Golden Dragon Clan's Dragonborn lineages.

Quest Seeds

QUEST SEED Haruto sends word to the party in Heian: he has found something in the licensing records that connects to their mission and needs outside help to pursue it.

Campaign Secrets

Haruto Masashige's knowledge of ancient Dragonborn rituals is not merely historical curiosity. It includes a purification and restoration rite that the Golden Dragon Clan's Dragonborn lineages preserved — a rite that is part of the process for reversing certain magical transformations. He doesn't know its current relevance, but the ritual exists in his family's oral tradition and would be directly applicable to the Nagaji situation if someone connected the dots.

His licensing investigation is on a collision course with Ren Nakamura's secret alliance with the merchant guild. When these threads converge, Haruto will be in danger.

Plot Threads

  • Bronze Wood licensing investigation — will eventually expose Ren Nakamura's merchant guild alliance
  • Ancient Dragonborn restoration rite — directly applicable to reversing the Nagaji transformation
  • Ko'jiri connection — their adversarial first meeting could become a significant alliance
  • Potential danger when his investigation threatens the merchant guild's interests

Chōrō (Village Elder) of Kōriwara — Order of the Sacred Grove

Appearance

Gray hair tied back; weathered skin; sharp contemplative brown eyes; long flowing beard.

Public Role

Village elder (chōrō) of Kōriwara, a small foothills village in Mizu province. Relc's home village. Keeper of the sacred grove on the hillside above the village — a small stand of ancient trees reached by a foot path, unmarked and unfenced but respected by the community.

Personality

Deep wisdom; duty-driven; slightly skeptical of outsiders until familiarity is established; profound knowledge of ancient traditions.

Relationship To Party

Advised Relc to leave Kōriwara and journey outward. Blessed Relc's departure. Relc visited Elder Sato before departing. He has not told Relc everything he knows.

True Nature

More than a simple village elder. His decades of accumulated knowledge, his connection to the Order of the Sacred Grove, and his quiet role as a node in networks that extend far beyond a mountain foothills village give Kōriwara significance entirely disproportionate to its size.

Connections

Mid-rank member of the Order of the Sacred Grove. Has interacted with Order of the Ancient Guard agents on multiple occasions, including with Solas Evergreen directly. His community network in the Mizu foothills region could help establish Yasutake Mai in Sunsato if the party makes the connection.

Quest Seeds

QUEST SEED Sato sends word through a traveling merchant heading toward Heian: he needs to speak with Relc; something has happened near the sacred grove that he cannot explain and cannot address alone. [QUEST SEED] A stranger arrived in Kōriwara asking questions about Relc and where they had gone; Sato gave nothing away but is concerned about whether Relc is being watched. [QUEST SEED] If the party introduces Yasutake Mai to Sato's community network, they earn a favor with Sato and plant a contact in the north Mizu foothills.

Campaign Secrets

Sato knows Solas was Ancient Guard (not just Sacred Grove). He knows what the Ancient Guard is and, broadly, what it protects. He has not told Relc because he was following Solas's instruction to let Relc develop organically — and because he judged Relc was not yet ready for the weight of the full picture.

One of the three stones referenced in Solas's cipher poem is in Kōriwara — specifically, in the sacred grove above the village. It is a naturally occurring stone with unusual surface striations that, when viewed from a specific angle at dawn, produce a visual pattern. Sato knows this stone. He knows what the Warden's Wisdom is — not its specific content, but its general nature: protected knowledge about the living dragons held by the Order of the Sacred Grove for safekeeping.

Sato does not know who killed Solas, but he knows the category of entity capable of it. Solas was skilled, cautious, and not easily surprised. The killing required either significantly superior capability or intimate familiarity — someone Solas trusted and did not guard against. This points to either a very powerful practitioner or someone inside the Order of the Sacred Grove or the Ancient Guard itself.

Plot Threads

  • Relc's personal quest — the cipher poem's first stone is in Kōriwara's sacred grove
  • Solas's murder — knows the category of killer but not the identity
  • Order of the Ancient Guard knowledge — has not yet shared with Relc
  • Sacred grove disturbance — something has happened he cannot explain
  • Stranger asking about Relc — someone is tracking the party's druid
  • Yasutake Mai connection — can help establish her in the Sunsato/Kōriwara community
